5. The Fifth [Section]: The Great Disparity in Attaining Names.
This section contains two parts.
First, the ancient teachings are discussed;
subsequently, the present interpretations are analyzed.
Regarding the discussion of the ancient teachings:
The ancient masters explained the names and meanings of various dharmas merely according to their own inclinations, each offering a single interpretation;
since these lack any authoritative basis, they are difficult to rely upon as standards.
If the meaning diverges from the substance, it results in error and confusion.
Some say that names are established by manifesting the substance itself;
others say that names are designated based on the meaning.
Some say it is named according to that which depends [upon it];
some say it is established by name according to its basis;
others say it is named according to number and in accordance with its meaning.
Alternatively, it may be designated according to its associated intensification;
or the two entities may be contradictory.
Thus, there are various such differing interpretations.
All of these merely follow their own personal sentiments and do not constitute authoritative standards;
consequently, various masters fall into confusion and give rise to divergent doctrines,
leaving later students with no one from whom they may receive instruction.
This is entirely due to the translators' lack of proficiency in local dialects;
though their words may appear harmonious, the profound essence remains obstructed. Since the teachers have already fallen into error, [the fault lies with them].

"Accompanied" (saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa) means to carry along or to be accompanied by. When the essence of a dharma carries along several dharmas as its name, it is called a "name accompanied by a number" (saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa-nāman).
This is as stated in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
That which is called "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) refers to the dharmas elucidated therein.
These twenty items are the numerical names of the verses;
they are named by taking the numbers as their designations.
This is called a *saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa* (compound with a numeral).
One should understand that works such as the *Śata-śāstra* follow this same principle.
Herein, these six types of compounds have been briefly presented according to common tradition to illustrate their essential meanings.
The detailed analysis of their characteristics is as explained elsewhere.
That is to say, among these six, the first is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
in which of the eight case-inflections (*vibhakti*) is it analyzed?
The same applies even when questions are posed using numerical designations;
all such cases are as explained elsewhere. Furthermore, there is another explanation regarding the etymology [of these terms].
As stated in the *Commentary on the Wheel of Tenets* (*Siddhāntavyavasthāpana-śāstra*), fearing that it would become overly prolix, I shall here briefly indicate the essential points.
The preceding general summary has concisely elucidated the meanings common to all the teachings.
The remaining trainees (śaikṣas) should appropriately apply this;
if one expounds a different school, one should employ the meaning of these words within each respective section.
One should conclude by returning to one's own position;
otherwise, it would be far too cursory.
This concludes the examination and explanation of all the principles contained herein.
All [of these] were personally resolved by the Great Master himself;
it is merely that the transmitted versions contain errors and omissions, yet they are not without a lineage of transmission.
May all those who possess wisdom take heed of this.
Chapter Five: The Five Minds. The five minds, beginning with the "sudden" (saṃkṣepa) mind, are briefly analyzed through twelve sections.
First, the enumeration of names.
Second, the analysis of characteristics;
third, the existence or non-existence of the eight consciousnesses;
fourth, the number of moments.
5. The arising of the distracted and the undistracted;
6. The comparative analysis of various states of mind;
7. The detailed and abbreviated treatments of the beginning and the end.
8. The deficiency of the various stages;
9. Subsumption under the three natures;
10. The general and specific aspects of dependent origination.
11. What measure does it encompass?
12. A brief clarification through questions and answers.
1. The First Section: Enumeration of Names. Regarding the enumeration of names:

First, the impulsive mind; second, the seeking mind; third, the determinative mind; fourth, the defiled or pure mind; fifth, the resultant mind. As stated in the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the section on the "Fivefold Body of Consciousness" (*Pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi*): [The five minds are: 1. the impulsive mind, 2. the seeking mind, 3. the determinative mind, 4. the defiled or pure mind, and 5. the resultant mind.
From the arising of visual consciousness, three types of mind can be obtained,
in their respective order: namely,
the sudden mind (*ābhoga-citta*), the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), and the determining mind (*niścaya-citta*).
The first is visual consciousness and the second is mental consciousness;
it is only after the determinative mind (*niścaya-citta*) that defilement or purity occurs.
Following this, there arises the visual consciousness of uniform outflow (*nisyanda*).
The transformation of the wholesome and unwholesome is the same for the arising of visual consciousness up to tactile consciousness,
because the nature and category of the first three types of consciousness are identical.
Although only three terms are mentioned, they actually encompass the latter two as well. 2.
Discerning Characteristics, Part Two. Regarding the discernment of characteristics:
take, for example, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The initial descent upon an object is called the "sudden descent of the mind" (*ābhoga-citta*); at that same time,
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has not yet previously taken this object as its cognitive domain.
Now, the initial simultaneous arising is also termed "sudden" (sūr-er).
Thus, the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is spontaneously distracted."
When encountering an object with which one is not habituated,
desire and so forth do not arise;
at that time, the mental consciousness is termed the "sudden-occurring mind" (*ābhoga-citta*).
This is because desire and so forth give rise to seeking and the like;
furthermore, it is stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and in the seventy-sixth section of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*:
"At the same time as the five consciousnesses, there must necessarily be a conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with them."
Therefore, the mind associated with the eye is called the "sudden" (*saṃtīraṇa*) mind,
because it first suddenly falls upon the object;
since this is the initial apprehension.
Not yet knowing whether a particular object is wholesome or unwholesome,
one subsequently gives rise to investigation in order to ascertain it;
for this [investigation] functions together with desire, as it hopes for that object.
Having already sought and identified the previous object,
one subsequently gives rise to certainty,
thereby sealing and understanding the object.
Having definitively recognized the distinctions among objects,
one grasps the characteristics of the primary causes and so forth,
and dwells in malice toward enemies.
One dwells in friendliness toward those who are dear,
in equanimity toward those who are neutral,
and thus a mind that is either defiled or purified arises.
Consequently, with this defiled or pure mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as a precursor,
it induces the arising of visual consciousness that is of the same nature— whether wholesome or defiled—
and occurs in accordance with what preceded it.
It is called the mind of outflow (*niṣyanda-citta*).
Just as the visual consciousness arises, so too do the auditory and other consciousnesses.
Third, regarding the existence or non-existence of the eight consciousnesses: as for the third point, the existence or non-existence of the eight consciousnesses—
The first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states only that these five mental states exist within the six consciousnesses,
and does not mention the seventh or eighth.
Furthermore, it is only the interrupted consciousness (*vicchinna-vijñāna*) that possesses these five.
It is not a consciousness that is constantly continuous;
however, while the seventh consciousness has not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
its objects are constant, and it functions spontaneously and subtly.
Only the final three [factors] can be said to be complete within a single moment;
the eighth is not so.
At the stage of initial birth within the realms, there is the *sa-ter* (sudden/arbitrary) mind;
this is because the objects of the form and formless realms differ in their breadth and narrowness.
Regarding the three types of mental objects—determinate, defiled/pure, and outflowing—their mental states may be either new or old.
Alternatively, because they may be complete when viewed in relation to what precedes and follows,
there is simply no seeking,
as it does not coexist with desire.
Because the seventh consciousness-element, although arising for the first time,
has an object that is always of a single category,
it lacks the two mental states of sudden encounter and seeking.
The stage of the initial transformation of the basis may be termed "sudden" (*ābhoga*);
this is precisely the mind that is definitively either defiled or pure.
After the second moment, however—
This is the outflow (*niṣyanda*).
When the two moments of consciousness are combined in meaning, it is said that there are four minds.
Alternatively, at the second moment, a pure consciousness may arise again.
The initial moment of thought consists of these four types of mind.
This is because they are the outflow (*nisyanda*) of the minds previously arisen;
however, as they now first encounter an object, there is a sudden, impulsive engagement (*ābhoga*).
In this context, for the time being, we shall rely on the treatise’s exposition of the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the various minds possessed by the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] according to principle,
it is stated that, in terms of logical reasoning, the sixth consciousness possesses five [mental factors].
Regarding the preceding five consciousnesses,
when cause and effect are explained together, there may be five mental states; however,
as for the causes alone, there are only four.
Seeking is that which occurs during the interval before one has fully understood what has been seen or heard;
it is also a form of mental engagement (*manasikāra*) because there is an expectation.
Otherwise, this mind would not be included within the five [consciousnesses],
for at the very first moment of sudden occurrence,
determination has not yet arisen.
If one does not seek [this], it is a great loss.
Since the determinative consciousness has already persisted for a long time,
neither defilement nor purity has yet arisen.
The five [mental factors] function according to circumstances.
If they are not determinate, what kind of mind are they?
Among the five in the causal stage, there is no fourth category of defiled or pure.
Because the cause lacks the power to produce itself,
whereas the fruit possesses that power and is thus superior;
this is one interpretation.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) attain mastery;
they also induce one another, resulting in both defilement and purity.
It is accepted that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses can induce subsequent moments, functioning as minds of defilement or purity.
Why is it not so for the five [consciousnesses]?
Therefore, we know that the causes of the five consciousnesses also possess these five [factors]. To summarize them:
The first six [consciousnesses] possess five types of mind;
the seventh and eighth each possess four.
Regarding this, there is an interpretation that the five sensory consciousnesses possess only two.
There are only the impulsive (*ābhoga*) and the outflowing (*niṣyanda*) minds;
among the five types of seeking and so forth,
those that arise subsequently are admitted to be outflowing minds because they are allowed to arise distractedly.
For now, this is explained based on the most prominent dharmas;
all other cases should be understood accordingly.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that among the first three moments of mind, the first consists of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
The second is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, it is said that defilement and purity belong to the mental consciousness;
they arise as its outflow (*niṣyanda*), whereas the five sensory consciousnesses do not.
Furthermore, this is explained based on an object that is singular, capable of being apprehended without confusion, and easy to discern.
For what reason is it not admitted that repeated seeking occurs when the initial seeking fails to comprehend the object?
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Having attained the state of mastery, [the mind] functions spontaneously and with certainty, without requiring further seeking.
At that time, the five bodies of consciousness must necessarily continue in succession.
Therefore, it is known that the five consciousnesses possess five types of mind.
It does not contradict yoga and is superior in principle as well. 4.
Regarding the fourth point, the quantity of moments: as for the quantity of moments—
The five consciousnesses arise abruptly for only a single moment.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third [chapter], states:
"Furthermore, the five bodies of consciousness do not arise in succession with two moments following one another."
Furthermore, once the five consciousnesses have arisen for a single moment,
a mental consciousness (manovijñāna) necessarily arises immediately thereafter;
therefore, the five consciousnesses last for only a single moment at most.
When seeking has not yet been completed, the five consciousnesses arise again;
since these five consciousnesses consist solely of seeking,
the group of five consciousnesses does not frequently involve sudden [perceptions].
It is said that the five groups of consciousness possess vitarka and vicāra because they involve extensive seeking;
those without vitarka and vicāra are associated with desire.
There is also seeking.
Regarding what is stated in various places that the five consciousnesses lack definitive seeking,
they are said to be "without" it because they lack deep and extensive modes of activity (*ākāra*).
It is not that there is no subtle [consciousness].
Whether it be the mind arising alone or the mind associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses], [it exists].
The stage of the casual mind (*saterī-citta*) also lasts for a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains the first three types of mind;
the first is the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
The second is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the third, it is also stated that the mind (*manas*) possesses sudden engagement (*sa-er*).
Although these [definitions] appear contradictory, this is because the two subsequent types of mind must necessarily be the mind.
In the very first moment of thought, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is briefly not mentioned;
furthermore, since there is no word "only" (*kevala*/*mātra*), logically this does not exclude its presence.
Some say that because the mental consciousness is admitted to be continuous, [it must be present].
There is no fault in saying that the *saṃtīraṇa-citta* (investigative mind) arises through many moments;
the former interpretation is superior because it first falls upon the object.
The subsequent [state] is not merely impulsive;
it is determined over many moments.
This is because, although one has sought and may have known [the object], the defiled or pure mind has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, because one emerges from meditative concentration in order to seek and know sounds heard within it,
many moments [of consciousness] are involved; yet,
having attained mastery, [the process] occurs spontaneously and with certainty.
Therefore, the mind of determination also arises through many moments;
the minds of defilement and purity are likewise so,
continuing in a succession of many moments.
Because it is difficult for [such a mind] to arise,
this [mind] takes the five consciousnesses as its outflowing cause (*niṣyanda-hetu*). If it were an outflow of the mental consciousness (*manas*), [it would not be so].
Defilement and purity consist in a single moment of thought;
for the subsequent second moment is its outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Regarding this outflowing mind, there are briefly two explanations.
There is no contradiction in the mental consciousness continuing as a stream of similar outflow (*niṣyanda*).
One view holds that the five sensory consciousnesses arise for only a single moment,
and thus even a mind of similar outflow is said not to continue in succession.
As previously cited:
secondly, it is said that the five consciousnesses are admitted to arise in a continuous stream;
as for the "single moment," this refers to the *sater-er* (sudden/arbitrary) perception.
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* also states that the six consciousnesses are established as equivalent immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in relation to one another;
therefore, it is admitted that minds of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-citta*) arise in succession.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also says:
Just as it is necessarily a continuous stream in cases such as the Hot Hells or the Heaven of Delighting in Forgetfulness,
the correct principle here is that,
for the most part, such sudden occurrences consist of only a single moment of thought.
The other four [types of arising] are mostly continuous, or alternatively, they may all pertain to multiple moments.
Fifth is "arising that is both distracted and non-distracted. Regarding "arising that is both distracted and non-distracted":
First, non-confusion is clarified;
subsequently, the arising of confusion is clarified.
Within the clarification of non-confusion and its arising, there are further three gates.
First, neither oneself nor others are distracted; second, others are distracted while one is not;
third, one is distracted while the mind [of others] is not.
Regarding "neither oneself nor others are distracted":
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third [section],
states: "Furthermore, once the five consciousnesses have arisen in a single moment,
immediately thereafter, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) necessarily arises."
Immediately following this, if there is no distraction,
a second determinate mind necessarily arises within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This is because these two types of consciousness— seeking and determining— serve as the causes for the conceptualization of objects.
Defiled and pure phenomena arise;
because they are induced by this [storehouse consciousness],
defiled and pure phenomena arise immediately thereafter within the visual and other consciousnesses.
However, this does not occur through the power of one's own conceptualization;
because it is non-conceptual, it attains defilement and purity solely by being induced.

"Another is disordered while one is not disordered" means that while another consciousness arises intermittently in the interim, five moments of one's own consciousness still arise sequentially before and after;
for example, when the eye perceives a form, the *sūtrera* (sudden) mind arises.
There must necessarily be a seeking that continues from the arising of the initial mind.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, once the five consciousnesses have arisen in a single moment..."
Because from this there must immediately arise mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"In meditative concentration, one hears sounds."
If there is an expectation that [the mind] will emerge at a later time,
this expectation is itself the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*). Therefore,
after the five [sensory consciousnesses] have arisen in a state of sudden surprise (*ābhoga*), the seeking mind subsequently arises.
Some say that there are cases where a sudden, impulsive [cognition] arises but is not followed by a subsequent search;
this is not so, for it contradicts both scripture and reasoning.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states:
"Seeking [the object] without interruption,
yet at times distracted."
Alternatively, one of the other five consciousnesses may arise.
Thus, following the stage of seeking, one either enters another state of mind or gives rise to a definitive judgment.
Although other minds may arise in the interim, they are distracted by other objects and are not superior;
because they cannot induce the cessation of another's consciousness for a long duration,
one necessarily returns again to the visual consciousness.
At the time of the arising of a definitive [cognition],
it either arises again as a seeking-investigation or arises as a definitive [cognition] itself.
With determination as the cause,
if there are no other conditions,
defilement and purity arise spontaneously.
There is the usurpation by another consciousness,
whereby one's own defiled or pure states do not arise.
Once that other consciousness has ceased, [one's own states arise].
Only through one's own mind can one enter the states of defilement and purity.
When these states of defilement and purity arise,
they may either revert to entering a state of certainty or immediately give rise to further defilement and purity.
The following cases should all be understood accordingly;
they will not be explained separately,
as they involve many moments of thought.
If, after a defiled or pure mind, there is no other condition, it arises as its own natural outflow; however,
when consciousness arises through another condition,
its own subsequent defiled or pure outflow is not produced.
Once that consciousness has ceased, its own natural outflow arises;
from the time the visual and mental consciousnesses arise until they proceed toward other objects,
they continue to evolve in a constant succession for that duration.
This is called "being distracted by others while one is not distracted oneself.
Third, regarding "being distracted oneself while the mind is not distracted":
it is like when the eye first perceives the forms of a large assembly.
Having impulsively sought out a determinate continuity that has not yet arisen,
there appears before one a certain superior semblance of form;
the visual consciousness then shifts toward other forms.
Furthermore, one gives rise to a sudden, impulsive mind, a mind of investigation, or perhaps a mind of certainty, or minds that are either defiled or pure;
having seen the reflected image, one then contemplates the various surrounding forms.
Because it has already been seen previously, it does not arise as a mere sudden occurrence (*ābhoga*);

or, having first arisen as a seeking (*paryeṣaka*), it induces a definitive [cognition] (*niścaya*), since it is admitted that seeking lasts for many moments; or it arises directly as a definitive cognition.
The subsequent cases should all be understood by analogy.
Alternatively, from the initial stage until the point of certainty, one again perceives the color of fire;
above this color of fire, there arise the *sater* (sudden) and other mental states.
Having seen the fire according to the extent of one's mental focus,
one then contemplates various forms, whereupon defilement and purity first arise;
following this mind of defilement and purity, one may then contemplate the color of clouds.
Once the spontaneous [cognition] and the others have arisen according to their respective degrees,
one subsequently observes various forms and gives rise to the subsequent [cognition],
all of which follow the previous explanation.
This is called "disturbing oneself while the mind is not disturbed.
Above, the state of being undisturbed was clarified;
hereafter, the state of being disturbed will be clarified.
Within this, there are two types:
first, when another is distracted and one is also distracted; second, when one is distracted and the mind is also distracted.
Regarding "when another is distracted and one is also distracted":
For example, when visual consciousness arises, having first given rise to a sudden and searching cognition toward a single form-color,
and after that, another sound arrives and again gives rise to a sudden and searching cognition;
subsequently, the form emits light.
Once the light of the image has newly appeared,
the *pūrvaka* (preliminary) *mārgaṇā* (seeking) arises;
subsequently, the *ābhoga* (spontaneous), *mārgaṇā*, and *niścaya* (ascertainment) arise again.
Furthermore, there are other distinct odors that manifest before one and are smelled, which again give rise to sudden perceptions and so forth;
these cause the reflected image and its light to change color after the mind of determination.
Again, having arisen in a state of sudden impulse, it reaches the mind that is either defiled or pure;
then, encountering a superior flavor manifest before it,
one tastes it and subsequently gives rise to the tongue-consciousness and various mental states.
Looking back at the light of the image,
the light may be large or small;
this follows from the defiled or pure mind.
Again, there arise the *ābhoga* (initial application), *paryeṣaṇā* (investigation), and *niścaya* (ascertainment).
In this manner, it continues until there is again contact with a sublime object (*praṇīta-sparśa*).
Once these, beginning with *ābhoga*, have arisen—
Upon observing the light of the image again,
the light immediately departs from its substance and manifests in various colors;
furthermore, thoughts such as sudden surprise arise.
If two, three, or up to four moments of mind arise [in succession],
it is termed "distraction" (vikṣepa); however,
if they arise in continuous succession up to the state of an outflowing mind (niṣyandacitta), it is not.
This is precisely what is called "non-distraction.
Other states of mind are analogous.
As for the case where both the self and the distracted mind are distracted:
This is merely following others' confused talk.
For example, when the visual consciousness arises, it takes a single form-color as its object;
by the time the process of seeking has concluded, that form-color appears before one.
Yet, one may suddenly give rise to impulsiveness;
or, when an image emits light,
one may again give rise to impulsiveness, seeking instead for a mind of equanimity.
In this way, it continues until it does not even reach the outflow;
it differs from the preceding distraction solely by means of the distinction between one's own and another's objective spheres.
The remaining procedures are the same. 6.
The Comparative Analysis of the Various Minds. Regarding the comparative analysis of the various minds:
for example, the sudden-arising mind (*saṃhatābhinirhṛta-citta*) of visual consciousness.
It can also arise simultaneously with other consciousnesses, such as the *sater* (sudden) mind;
this applies equally to the *nisyanda* (outflowing) mind as well. Thus it is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts.
Because the eight consciousnesses can arise simultaneously,
there are also cases where the *sater* (sudden) visual consciousness arises together with the four [mental activities] such as the *xiunqiu* (seeking) auditory consciousness; that is,
the visual consciousness is in a state of seeking.
It arises together with the ear-consciousness and its three determinate [mental factors],
the two [factors] of defilement and purity, and so forth,
up to arising simultaneously with a single mind of outflowing result (*niṣyanda*).
Furthermore, there is the case where visual consciousness is sudden,
auditory consciousness is seeking,
and olfactory consciousness is determinative.
The gustatory consciousness is defiled or pure;
it arises simultaneously with the bodily consciousness as its outflow,
for there is no principle that would preclude this.
Just as it is with the arising of visual consciousness,
so too should the other types, up to tactile consciousness, be understood accordingly.
Some say that [the object] is not apprehended.
Since it is not consistent with the correct principle, it is not explained here. 7.
The Seventh [Section]: Extensive at the Beginning and Brief at the End. Regarding "extensive at the beginning and brief at the end":
Alternatively, there may be cases where the mind of spontaneous seeking is predominant and the mind of natural outflow is scarce;
this is because initially many objects appear,
whereas subsequently few objects appear.
In some cases, there may be few *ābhāsagata* (sudden encounter) minds and many *nisyanda* (outflow) minds;
this is because they are induced by the successive forces of prior defiled or pure states,
and because one encounters various distinct objects such as sudden encounters and so forth.
Regarding the three intermediate moments of mind, it is generally said that they are the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), though their specific number is not distinguished.
If one is in the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), all existing minds may arise simultaneously; there is no fault in this according to the circumstances.
Since it is already granted that the five consciousnesses at the stage of the cause possess five types of mind,
these five minds may all exist simultaneously according to their respective conditions,
with their number being indefinite.
8. Regarding the "possessors of the eighth stage":
this refers to the five moments of mind that arise sequentially and distinctly, based solely on a newly encountered object during the causal stage.
Because there is that which is not yet known;
if one encounters a former object,
there is only determination, defilement, purity, or outflow.
Alternatively, there may be only two types of mind—defiled and pure—which are both outflowing; or only outflowing;
or only defiled and pure.
Alternatively, it is because [the mind] is determined to be a single moment that does not continue;
thus, there is no mere seeking (*paryeṣaka*) that does not arise as a sudden encounter (*ābhoga*).
If something were subject to seeking, it would necessarily have been previously uncomprehended (*anirūpita*).
There must certainly be the *saṃtīraṇa* (investigating) mind;
for among the five consciousnesses, there is no case where there is only the *ābhoga* (initial encounter) mind without the seeking mind,
according to what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Because it is not any other consciousness, the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established;
this continues from the eighth stage until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Because they are spontaneously determined and do not require seeking,
there are only four; however, according to the general discussion of the three vehicles, the untainted [path] possesses all five.
Because there is seeking,
the various moments (kṣaṇa) are said to exist as distinct entities;
they do not arise sequentially.
The initial transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and so forth have already been explained as before.
Ninth, regarding what is subsumed under the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The first three minds are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The fourth and fifth superknowledges (*abhijñā*) possess all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
This is based on the fact that, during the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*), there may be objects that are not subject to confusion.
Regarding the teaching that one among the five consciousnesses arises in succession with the sixth consciousness:
if this occurs during the causal stage,
the objective sphere is powerful and predominant.
The various consciousnesses arise in combination, arising simultaneously with five types of mind;
they are all encompassed by the three natures. However, in the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*) or when mastery has been attained, they are for the most part virtuous (*kuśala*).
10. The Tenth Topic: The General and Particular Aspects of Dependent Origination. Regarding the general and particular aspects of dependent origination:

since it is admitted that a single consciousness can induce six consciousnesses to arise in immediate succession, it is likewise possible for many consciousnesses to induce a single consciousness to arise in immediate succession.
Therefore, for the most part, a single consciousness is impulsively produced, followed by the arising of a mind of investigation,
and so forth, as explained at length.
A single defiled or pure mind produces many subsequent consciousnesses of its own kind.
This meaning is definitive,
for it is admitted that a single consciousness and a single mind can give rise to multiple consciousnesses and minds within a single moment.
By this principle, it is established.
The various consciousnesses can possess five mental states within a single moment;
as for objects, there are new and old ones, and the consciousnesses that project them differ.
This principle is subtle and profound.
The wise should reflect upon this.

11. Regarding what measure it is subsumed under: as for what measure it is subsumed under, within the causal stage there are either five consciousnesses, or four, or two, or perhaps five moments of mind.
All of these are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehending objects of the present.
Furthermore, the four types of consciousness associated with the five sensory consciousnesses within the category of fruition are also exclusively direct perception.
It takes the objects of the three time periods as its conditions.
According to one interpretation, it also takes non-temporal objects as its conditions.
It is accepted that during the seventh causal stage, there are three types of cognition, all of which are subsumed under non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).
The essential object and its reflected image exist only in the present.
The mental aspect does not operate upon objects of the [other] time periods.
At the stage of fruition, there are four types of consciousness, all of which are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It universally takes as its objects the three periods of time as well as that which is non-temporal.
Regarding the eighth [consciousness], both cause and effect are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
when it is in the state of a causal condition, it exists in the present.
The fruit takes as its objects the three time periods as well as that which is non-temporal.
When the sixth mental consciousness is established in its specific state,
all five types of mind are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
They take as their objects the three periods of time as well as the non-temporal realm.
If they occur in a state of distraction as five independent mental states, they are both inferential and non-perceptual cognitions,
taking as their objects the three periods of time as well as the non-temporal realm.
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) also functions as a worldly or non-worldly understanding.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that when the mental consciousness is distracted and falls suddenly into a state of mind directed toward the past:
Because the mental consciousness associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses] mostly takes those five as its objects;
and according to one interpretation, because the five minds concomitant with the mental consciousness are realized through direct perception alone (*pratyakṣa*).
In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the Bodhisattva Dignāga states that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore,
even if it simultaneously takes all eighteen dhātus as its objects, it is still subsumed under direct perception.
Because it clearly apprehends the five present objects as they appear,
some maintain that its nature is not even indeterminate,
let alone being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* does not state that the meaning of the five [sensory consciousnesses] arising together is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
How can you definitively judge this?
Since you firmly insist on it, you must admit that inferential cognition (*anumāna*) also arises together with the five.
It is not logically tenable that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

therefore, the meaning of "concomitant with the five [sensory consciousnesses]" encompasses both direct perception and inference (*anumāna*), as well as non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). It also universally takes as its objects those belonging to the three times as well as the non-temporal realm.

If [the mind] takes a single object and arises simultaneously with the five [sensory consciousnesses], whether as a sudden (ābhoga) or a natural flow (nisyanda), it is necessarily direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The three intermediate minds do not arise simultaneously with the five; they are either inferential (anumāna) or invalid cognition (apramāṇa).
Regarding the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*) that takes past objects as its cognitive condition,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The mental consciousness that arises immediately after the five sensory consciousnesses— whether in its stage of seeking or its stage of determination—
should be said to take only the present object as its condition;
this is because it is designated as "present" based on the completion of the sequence of events within a particular state.
The Yogācāras themselves state that if this [consciousness] arises by taking that object as its condition,
then the same applies to both the defiled and the pure;
thus, the nature of the three types of mind is identical.
Therefore, the treatise speaks of them selectively.
12. Question and Answer: A Brief Simplification, Number Twelve. Regarding this "Question and Answer:
A Brief Simplification," why are five mental states established, neither more nor less?
Answer: Based on the most prevalent cases, there are five determinate [minds];
based on the minimum, there is one, as it is not complete.
Question: Do these five minds also include the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
Answer: All five are common [to both].
This is because the concentration of mind through hearing sounds is common to both the outflow-free (anāsrava) and the mundane;
and because there is aspiration based on the outflow-free mind.
Some say that vitarka and vicāra are pervasive of the untainted (anāsrava); even if they were not pervasive of the untainted, they would still be associated with desire.
This mind of seeking also pervades the untainted.
Question: Does it pervade all three realms?
Answer: It is comprehensive.
Since there is no principle that excludes it, each individual moment of mind also takes the three realms as its object.
Regarding the various types of consciousness within the minds of the three realms, they may coexist as appropriate.
Question: For what reason must these five types of mind be distinguished?

Answer: It is for the purpose of causing one to understand the states of the mind and to enter into the characteristic of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) and the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
Question: When this discourse on the five minds is heard while taking the teaching as an object, how many syllables does it comprise?
Answer: For the time being, based on this region, even a single syllable constitutes a name and is capable of expressing meaning.
Upon hearing a single syllable, one immediately possesses five mental states.
For example, upon hearing the word "Buddha":
An example of possessing two characters is "Bodhisattva" (菩薩).
An example of possessing three characters is "Maitreya Buddha" (慈氏佛).
An example of possessing four characters is "Tathāgata Śāntamati" (能寂如來).
Regarding the possession of the five factors, it is as when one hears such precepts as "Do not commit any evil deeds," and so forth,
up to an immeasurable number of instances. Upon hearing, reflecting upon,
and understanding them, one immediately possesses the five mental states.
It is not necessary to limit the number of syllables heard such that the five minds are only fully present at a specific point.
If the explanation of the principles and phenomena has not yet reached its conclusion, the five minds are not fully present;
only when the hearing is complete are the five minds fully present.
That is to say, as soon as the number of syllables, names, or phrases spoken has concluded,
if the mental understanding is complete, it is said that the five minds are possessed;
for as long as that duration lasts, the five consciousnesses induced by the mental consciousness arise accordingly.
It is also not contrary to reason that the mental consciousness and its associated mental factors are subsumed under those [six]; therefore,
each of the six possesses all five [aggregates].
"Seventy-eight [consciousnesses] are only four;
this is profoundly appropriate.
This concludes the third chapter on the meaning of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) from the *Vijñaptimātrārthakārikā-vyākhyā*.
This shall be explained briefly by means of ten sections:
first, the determination of its essence;
second, the analysis of its name.
Third, the analysis of combinations and separations;
fourth, which consciousness constitutes the contemplation;
fifth, the manifestation of the distinctions among categories.
Sixth, the stages of cultivation and realization;
seventh, the nature of the dharmas of contemplation;
eighth, the basis for the arising of the various stages.
Ninth, it severs all obstacles and defilements;
tenth, it returns to and encompasses the two kinds of emptiness.
First, regarding the determination of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). First, the determination of its essential nature: [The text continues: "First, the determination of its essential nature."
This consists of two types:
first, the object of observation;
second, the subject that observes.
That which is observed as consciousness-only has all phenomena as its own essence,
because it universally observes both existence and non-existence as consciousness-only.
Briefly, there are five stages.
First is the consciousness that dispels the unreal and preserves the real:
one contemplates that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) arises solely as false and utterly lacks essence or function.
One should correctly dispel [the notion of] emptiness,
for while it exists conventionally, it is non-existent ultimately; thus, one contemplates the reality of the essence of all phenomena as dependent and perfected,
which is the objective domain of the two wisdoms.
It should be correctly understood that [sentient beings] exist [conventionally], because it is logically impossible for them to be non-existent.
As the verse by Asaṅga states:
Name and thing are mutually guests;
their nature should be investigated.
Regarding these two, one should also infer that they are merely measure and merely designation.
Through the contemplation of ultimate wisdom, one realizes that objects do not exist and that there is only conceptual construction.
Because those [objects] are absent, this [construction] is also absent;
this is precisely the entry into the three natures.

The statement "Establishing Consciousness-Only" (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) uses the term "consciousness" to collectively indicate that every sentient being possesses eight consciousnesses, six classes of mental factors, the objective and subjective aspects (nimitta-dṛśya-bhāga) they transform, their various states and distinctions, and the suchness (tathatā) revealed by the principle of emptiness.
Because it is the self-characteristic of consciousness, because it is associated with consciousness,
and because it is the transformation of both.
Because of the three stages and because of the four real natures,
all such phenomena do not exist apart from consciousness.
The general designation "consciousness" is established solely to exclude the real existence of form and so forth as distinct from consciousness, as asserted by the ignorant.
There are many such passages that serve as clear evidence for this.
Because from beginningless time one has clung to the self and phenomena as being existent,
and has repudiated facts and principles as being empty,
within this contemplation:
"Sending away" refers to the contemplation of emptiness,
which counters and destroys the attachment to existence;
"preserving" refers to the contemplation of existence.
To eliminate the attachment to emptiness:
now, by observing both emptiness and existence, one eliminates the existence of emptiness; if the existence of emptiness is absent, [then emptiness itself is gone].
Nor do emptiness and existence exist [independently],
for they are established through mutual dependence.
If there were only existence or only emptiness, whose would emptiness and existence be?
Therefore, those who wish to realize and enter the ineffable nature of phenomena must all rely on these skillful means to do so;
it is not that emptiness and existence are both definitively established as such.
The stage of realizing true contemplation is neither existent nor empty;
because the non-conceptual nature of phenomena transcends verbal expression,
it is said that one must contemplate emptiness in order to realize the truth.
This means that one enters into true reality by taking the observation of the emptiness of that which is conceptually constructed as the gateway;
yet the true essence itself is not empty.
This term "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) already negates the grasped object.
If one clings to the idea that the various consciousnesses truly exist as mere objects of representation,
then since they are likewise objects of clinging, they too should be eliminated.
This is the first gate of the *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) that is to be contemplated.
In all stages, one contemplates, cultivates, and realizes [the truth].
Second, one abandons the confusions and retains pure consciousness;
although one contemplates both phenomena and principle, neither is ever separate from consciousness.
However, this internal consciousness possesses both objects and mind,
because the arising of mind necessarily depends upon the production of internal objects; thus,
while the term "consciousness" (vijñapti) implies "only" (mātra), it does not mean "only objects."
The statement "establishing Vijñapti-mātra" means that consciousness exists only internally,
whereas objects also extend externally.
Fearing that this might be misconstrued as applying to external objects, it is said that there is "consciousness-only.
Furthermore, all foolish commoners, being deluded and attached to objective realms,
give rise to afflictions and karma, thereby sinking into the cycle of birth and death.
Because they do not understand the contemplation of the mind and instead strive only for liberation [from external objects], the Buddha,
out of compassion for them, spoke the teaching of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra),
so that they might contemplate their own minds and attain liberation from birth and death.
This does not mean that internal objects are entirely non-existent like external ones.
Because external objects involve ambiguity, the term "not corresponding" (*asadbhūta*) is discarded;
since the essence of the mind is pure, it is retained and termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states:
"The objects of the mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all not apart from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, I teach that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) with nothing else. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras state that the triple world is mind-only (*citta-mātra*).
The *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching) states: "Therefore, you all should properly restrain the mind.
When it is restrained in a single place, there is no task that cannot be accomplished," and so forth.
All are subsumed within this gate.
Third, the derivative consciousnesses are subsumed back into the fundamental consciousness;
thus, the objective realms apprehended within the mind become manifest.
The mental activity of the internal apprehending subject is likewise so;
this seeing and its objective aspect both depend upon consciousness for their existence,
being devoid of any intrinsic nature apart from consciousness itself.
Because [the self and phenomena] will certainly not exist in the age of the final dharma (mofa). The Thirty Verses states:
"By means of conventional designations, there are the self and phenomena."
There are various modes of transformation;
these depend on what is transformed by consciousness.
This transforming [consciousness] is of only three kinds.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Transformation" means that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as two parts;
both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) arise based upon its own substance.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"The objects of all consciousnesses are merely manifestations of consciousness.
This is because it subsumes the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*)—the derivative ends—back into the fundamental consciousness.
The explanations of principle and phenomena, the truths of ultimate and conventional reality, the contemplations, and so forth,
are all subsumed within this gate.
Fourth is the consciousness that conceals the inferior and reveals the superior.
Both the mind and its mental factors are capable of manifesting [transformations];
however, it is said to be "mind-only" (cittamātra) rather than "mental factors only," because the essence of the mind-king (citta-rāja) is preeminent.
The mental factors depend on the inferior, while the primary mind arises from the superior;
thus, the inferior is concealed and not manifested, and only the superior dharma is revealed.
Therefore, the World-Honored One Maitreya said:
It is admitted that the mind appears as if it were two;
likewise, it appears as if it were greed and so forth,
or as if it were faith and so forth.
There are no separate defiled or wholesome dharmas.
Although the substance of the mind itself can transform to manifest as the appearance of those two— the seeing and the object—
greed, faith, and so forth each likewise have the capacity to transform their own substance into the manifestation of their respective seeing and objects.
Because the mind is predominant, it is said that the mind appears as two;
because mental factors are subordinate, they are hidden and not mentioned.
It is not that they cannot appear as such.
Vimalakīrti said: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled;
because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure," and so forth.
All are subsumed within this gate.
Fifth is the consciousness that realizes the nature by dispelling signs;
the term "consciousness" indicates that both principle and phenomena are fully present.
Phenomena, as characteristics and functions, are to be discarded and not grasped;
principle, as the essential nature, should be sought and realized.
Thus, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* speaks of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* verse states:
"One gives rise to the perception of a snake regarding a rope;
upon seeing the rope, one realizes it is non-existent."
When one perceives that portion [of the rope],
one knows that the cognition of a snake was a delusion.
What is stated here is that when the cognition of a rope arises, the cognition of a snake is dispelled.
The analogy of observing the dependent nature dispels the cognition of the grasped;
seeing the various parts of a rope dispels the cognition of the rope.
This is analogous to seeing the perfected nature dispelling the cognition of the dependent nature.
This meaning is clearly indicated:
both types of cognition that are to be eliminated are of the nature of the dependent (*paratantra*).
This is because one abandons these defilements.
The apprehended real snake, real rope, self,
and dharmas no longer accord with the mind;
because they are not [perceived] as being based on or distinct from one another, they are all mutually eliminated.
The snake arises from delusion; both its substance and function are non-existent.
The rope is produced based on hemp and thus possesses provisional function that is not non-existent.
Hemp is a metaphor for ultimate truth.
The rope serves as a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). By knowing the substance and function of the rope and the hemp,
the delusion of the snake naturally ceases.
Because the nature of the snake has ceased, the snake does not correspond to that nature;
this is called the elimination of what is grasped.
It is not like the dependent nature, which must be severed by the Noble Path.
Therefore, one gradually enters the truth, realizing that the snake is empty while awakening to the division of the rope;

upon attaining the stage of true contemplation, one illuminates the ultimate truth and conventional phenomena become manifest. Once both principle and phenomenon are manifest, the grasping at self and dharmas naturally ceases.
This is precisely the single layer of the object of observation (*ālambana*).
The observing consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) takes the wisdom of the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
This is stated in the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
For what purpose does one enter the nature of representation-only?
It is by means of supramundane wisdom consisting of calm abiding and insight that takes all dharmas as its object.
Regarding this, Wu-xing’s commentary states:
Because of non-erroneous wisdom arising from samāhita (meditative equipoise),
some explain that it is able to contemplate *vijñapti-mātra* (representation-only), having both śamatha and vipaśyanā as its essential nature.
This is also not the case.
If it takes the four aggregates associated with grasping as its essence,
or if it includes their attendants, it then comprises all five aggregates.
For now, based on the name, we observe that its essence is solely wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, Wu-xing stated: "Because it is the wisdom of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)."
Furthermore, it is said that through non-erroneous wisdom (*aviparyāsa-jñāna*) arising from *samāhita* [meditative equipoise],
one takes only the wisdom produced within concentration as the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
This is because the superior contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), such as thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*), must necessarily reside within meditative concentration.
It does not state that cessation itself constitutes the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, the *Saṃgrahaṇī* says:
"By means of the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four cognitions of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*)."
Since all such things are likewise equally unapprehendable,
the bodhisattvas, in accordance with reality,
practice the preparatory application (prayoga) for entering into representation-only (vijñaptimātra).
That is to say, regarding the mental verbalization that resembles words and resembles meanings,
one investigates that the words and names are merely mental verbalization,
and so forth, as explained at length.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*,

it is stated that both investigative reflection (*vitarka*) and knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature. Investigative reflection is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
whereas knowledge of reality pertains to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Entering the characteristics of the knowable" refers to that which is based upon the cultivation of extensive learning and is not subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna*.
This passage merely indicates that the untainted seeds increase in that state;
thus, they are termed "hearing-perfuming" (śrutavāsanā) and are said not to be the ālayavijñāna.
However, it is not the case that all observing consciousnesses are exclusively untainted.
If it were not so, the four thorough investigations would not be preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Although this has been stated in general terms,
if one were to explain it specifically:
Briefly, there are two categories:
first, cause;
second, fruit.
Because it penetrates the three types of wisdom and is exclusively with-outflow (sāsrava),
it takes the wisdoms accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation as its essential nature of contemplation.
This is solely the nature of clear, sharp discernment;
it is not a virtue acquired at birth.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Mental verbalization that resembles phenomena and resembles meanings,
which arises from the signs and characteristics of the Mahāyāna teachings,
[pertains to] the stage of practice through resolute belief, the path of seeing, the path of meditation, and so forth.
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"Regarding 'consciousness-only' herein,
it refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*)."
Through hearing and reflection, one is able to develop deep faith and understanding;
in the stage of application (*prayoga*),
one gives rise to investigation and so forth to induce true vision (*darśana*).
The fruit is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) constitutes its essential nature as the object of contemplation,
because it takes both correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as its own essence.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts state:
"Because it penetrates reality as it is,
and because it remedies all obstacles."
Because one is free from all obscurations, one perceives the paths of seeing, cultivation,
and no-more-learning in their respective order;
thus, one realizes the true reality, which is consciousness as pure essential wisdom (*svabhāvajñāna*).
The consciousness that realizes conventional phenomena is exclusively subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The text is extensive and its meaning is clear;
thus, I shall not cite scriptural authority to establish this.
Although the preceding discussion has distinguished between the subject and object of contemplation, to state the general meaning:
if one speaks generally, "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) encompasses both the subject and object of contemplation;
however, "the contemplation of consciousness-only" refers exclusively to the subject and not the object.
It encompasses both the outflow-free and the outflow-possessing;
it encompasses both the distracted and the concentrated;
and it consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Its essential nature consists of the three types of wisdom: the preparatory, the fundamental, and the subsequently attained.
If one speaks of the samādhi of *vijñaptimātra*, it encompasses both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
It is exclusively in a state of meditative concentration and not in a distracted state; it is exclusively the wisdom of cultivation and not the wisdoms of hearing or reflection;
it pervades all three types of wisdom.

If it is said that direct realization of consciousness-only is exclusively untainted (anāsrava) and not tainted (sāsrava), and exclusively in a state of meditative concentration (samāhita) and not in a state of distraction (asamāhita).
It consists solely of wisdom derived from meditation, not that derived from hearing or reflection;
it is solely correct gnosis of the subsequent attainment,
not the preparatory stage.
This is not a statement of the true meaning.
For it is not the case that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the others do not also pertain to hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*),
as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
This will be understood in detail below.
However, in general, when examining all that is taught throughout the various scriptures regarding "all is consciousness-only," it does not exceed five types.
A single object is consciousness-only.
As the Abhidharma Sūtra says:
"Ghosts, animals, humans, and devas..."
Because the mind varies according to each individual's respective engagement with equivalent objects,
it is admitted that the referent is not ultimately real.
Passages such as these that speak only of the objects perceived by consciousness all indicate that the object is consciousness-only;
these are the two scriptural teachings on consciousness-only.
The verses beginning with "Due to the attachment of one's own mind" and so forth,
as well as the teachings on Consciousness-Only found in the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*,
and other texts, all teach Consciousness-Only.
Third is the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The *Triṃśikākārikā* states: "These various consciousnesses undergo transformation;
there is the subject of discrimination (*vikalpa*) and the object discriminated (*vikalpya*)."
Because those [objects] are all non-existent due to this,
everything is consciousness-only.
Thus, the principle of establishing consciousness-only is entirely the principle of consciousness-only.
The four modes of practice regarding consciousness-only:

the verse beginning with "The bodhisattva, in the state of meditative equipoise," and the four kinds of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).
All phenomena are consciousness-only;
the five fruits are consciousness-only.
As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom:
all sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses manifest within it.
Furthermore, the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* states:
The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness is the pure, untainted realm,
liberated from all obstructions.
It is associated with the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"This is the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu)."
Inconceivable, virtuous, and eternal;
the body of blissful liberation.
This is called the Dharma of the Great Muni.
Thus, all these explanations regarding the attainment of the fruit of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) maintain that the fruit is indeed consciousness-only.
Among these, five kinds of consciousness-only are here explained.
This comprehensively encompasses all aspects of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) without exception.

Nevertheless, within the various teachings, different explanations regarding the consciousness-only nature of objects have been presented according to the specific meanings and capacities of sentient beings.
Alternatively, one may distinguish "consciousness-only" based on what is grasped;
the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states that it arises from attachment to one's own mind.
The mind appears as if it were external objects;
since those objects do not exist,
it is therefore said that there is "mind-only."
It is simply because [objects] appear falsely based on the grasping mind;
or, one clarifies *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) by relying on the fact that [phenomena] are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The triple world is mind-only."
This is because it speaks of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) in relation to the world;
or rather, it establishes consciousness-only by way of what is grasped and in accordance with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
As the *Triṃśikākārikā* states:
Based on the conventional designation of self and phenomena,
various appearances arise;
these depend upon the transformations of consciousness.
The self-substance of consciousness gives rise to the perceived aspect (nimittabhāga) and the perceiving aspect (darśanabhāga),
because the two types of grasping arise;
alternatively, one may distinguish "consciousness-only" by relying on sentient beings.
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra states:
"Because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure;
because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled."
Alternatively, one may distinguish *vijñapti-mātra* by relying on all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent,
as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that "the objects of all consciousnesses are merely manifestations of consciousness. Or,
one may distinguish *vijñapti-mātra* by referring to specific instances.
The verses of the Abhidharma Sūtra state:
"Hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas each [experience their results] according to what is appropriate for them."
Because each individual point is explained according to the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only),
there are immeasurable scriptural gateways of this kind.
These six gateways are cited here as a classification to encompass all such teachings.
The fifth teaching alone exhausts the principles and meanings,
because it generally explains everything as being solely consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Alternatively, they may be condensed into three.
This refers to the object, the practice, and the fruit, as is extensively analyzed in the *Praise of the Heart Sūtra*.
Second, the discernment of names. Regarding the discernment of names:
In Sanskrit it is called *vijñapti*;
here it is translated as "consciousness" (*śī*).
Consciousness means the sense of discerning and distinguishing.

The self-characteristic of consciousness, the association with consciousness, the transformations of consciousness, the stages of consciousness, and the true nature of consciousness— because these five factors,
both in terms of phenomena and principles, do not depart from consciousness, they are called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
If it were not so, true suchness would not be "consciousness-only," nor would it be "the single mind alone" without any other entities. Rather,

10. The Tenth Chapter: Subsuming the Two Emptinesses. Regarding the subsumption of the two emptinesses, various treatises speak of two types of emptiness:

the wisdom arising from thorough investigation penetrates both the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena.
As the basis for the arising [of awakening],
one merely contemplates phenomena,
with the mind seeking the knowledge of all modes.
Because one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one gives rise to correct understanding regarding the two kinds of emptiness;

This is because the treatise speaks of "clarity" (awakening). Why, then, does it describe "delusion" in contrast to awakening?
The grasping at a self-nature (pudgala-grāha) necessarily entails the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha).
Returning from delusion is explained as awakening;
