The indeterminate lineage (aniyata-gotra) consists of the first, second, and a portion of the eighth among the ten;
the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) is the ninth.
As for the remaining six types, they are partially explained as having the distinct meaning of the One Vehicle;
it is not the case that all of them are indeterminate or merely transformation bodies.
Nor is it that those without nature become Buddhas; this constitutes the first point.
The twenty-six meanings elucidated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* are included within the ten meanings and need not be explained separately.
However, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* opens the gate of skillful means (*upāya*) to reveal the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Taking the two vehicles as skillful means and the one vehicle as the ultimate truth;
this is based on the Śrīmālā-sūtra.
If the Tathāgata, in accordance with their inclinations,
employs skillful means to teach that there is only the One Vehicle and no Two Vehicles,
this intention reveals that the two vehicles are subsumed within the Great Vehicle.
The teaching of the One Vehicle is speech adapted to the inclinations of others;
because they are suitable to hear it, it is also a skillful means taught as the existence of a single vehicle.
It is not the ultimate reality;
one of indeterminate lineage is not granted a prediction of enlightenment,
because such a person is not singular [in their potential].
Because sentient beings without lineage do not attain Buddhahood,
the first assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra* addresses those with indeterminate capacities,
employing two [aspects] as skillful means.
The One Vehicle is the ultimate truth.
In the Śrīmālā-sūtra,
this is established through comprehensive reasoning, as the capacities of sentient beings are not fixed.
Since the four vehicles are the reality,
it is not contradictory to say that the teaching of the one vehicle is a skillful means (*upāya*) spoken in accordance with the inclinations of others.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaparyāya of the One Vehicle* (Fa-hua yicheng) relies solely on inclusion and entry;
because its essence and function are narrow, it is taught as a provisional means.
[In contrast is] the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra’s* One Vehicle.
Birth and inclusion are both fully complete;
therefore, it is the reality.
Furthermore, the Flower Garland One Vehicle speaks only of having the nature [of Buddhahood] as its basis;
therefore, it is a provisional means.
The Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra One Vehicle also speaks of lacking the nature [of Buddhahood] as its basis.
Therefore, this [teaching] is the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, because the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks exclusively of those with indeterminate natures, it is a provisional means (*upāya*);
whereas the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also speaks of the determinate lineage (*gotra*), it is the ultimate truth.
Because it was appropriate for them to hear it within a single assembly,
the *Lotus Sūtra* clearly identifies wisdom as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*),
while speaking cryptically of *tathatā*.
Although it is said that the conjured city is not a true cessation,
and both are described as the place of jewels,
the true *nirvāṇa* has not yet been clearly explained.
The nirvāṇa attained by those of the two vehicles is both termed "transformation," because they do not attain bodhi at all;
this demonstrates that wisdom constitutes the single vehicle (ekayāna).
This causes them to aspire with joy.
Śrīmālā, moreover, takes ultimate truth as the One Vehicle;
she does not speak of wisdom.
The two aspects of inclusion and birth are both exhausted;
although the fruit of Buddhahood, nirvāṇa, and bodhi are all one vehicle,
this is stated in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The Lotus Sūtra speaks cryptically of the One Vehicle;
while it generally discusses four types of śrāvakas,
at the beginning of the Lotus Sūtra there are only three types of śrāvakas, excluding those who have set their minds on quiescence.
The two predictions are made only after those with overweening pride have subsequently departed.
According to this principle, although the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is taught, it does not contradict other teachings;
furthermore, within the teaching of the Two Vehicles, the Pratyekabuddha is not mentioned separately.
It speaks only of the superior and inferior [faculties], as in the "power of the superiority and inferiority of faculties" among the ten powers.
This is because there are only two [vehicles]. This is due to the fact that both the spiritual capacities and the teachings consist of two categories.
Furthermore, among both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there are those who are fixed and those who are unfixed.
This initial generation of the mind of awakening all relies upon sound to ultimately achieve fruition;
it also relies partially upon sound.
For those of indeterminate lineage, one causes them to hear the sound of the Buddha-way.
They may both be designated as "śrāvaka" (disciples).
Furthermore, because those pratyekabuddhas do not have many distinct categories of teaching and are subsumed under the terms "Hīnayāna" and "Śrāvakayāna," they are not mentioned separately.
Moreover, they are also termed the two vehicles of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Since these are combined because they share the same category as the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha),
for what reason are the three types— those of fixed lineage and those of unfixed lineage— combined into three?
Within the category of the unfixed lineage, both two and three [vehicles] are present.
Because the distinctions of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) ultimately result in no more than three fruits;

and because humans and devas represent a shallow and proximate state that is not an ultimate destiny, they are not mentioned among the four [lineages] in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, nor is the indeterminate lineage mentioned therein.
The ultimate [vehicles] are also not mentioned in detail because they are fully subsumed within the three vehicles alone.
As for the inclusion of humans and devas, it is because they both lack the nature [of the higher vehicles], share the same category, and are alike in being shallow and mundane.
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras do not speak of those without lineage (agotra),
because they are not the ultimate vehicle; rather,
they open the way for those of indeterminate lineage.
Because the superior virtues of hearing the sutras and the cultivation of skillful means differ,
it is shown that one ultimately attains nirvana.
For what reason does the *Laṅkāvatāra* praise and separately explain the five vehicles?
Because there are four distinctions based on whether one's lineage is fixed or unfixed;
because humans and devas belong to the same shallow and proximate category;
and because other sources further state that humans and devas constitute five [categories].
The fruits received differ because of the distinctions between the various destinies;
furthermore, those of indefinite lineage are subsumed within the three [definite lineages] and do not exceed them.
Therefore, those with a definite lineage are not further divided to constitute a fourth category.
Regarding the statement that "the absence of lineage (agotra) makes two, thereby making six":
the various teachings speak only of five distinct lineages,
as their types are limited to five.
There is no logical contradiction in establishing six [categories];
however, there is no textual evidence for it,
as seven and so forth are not mentioned.
Because there are no further categories.
Question and Answer Section Five: Regarding the analysis through questions and answers, herein lies the principle of the One Vehicle.
It should be only one, without remainder, rather than two or three.
As the Lotus Sūtra says:
"Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas..."
"Having heard the Dharma I have preached,
even as little as a single verse,
all shall undoubtedly attain Buddhahood."
The Nirvāṇa Sūtra also states:
"All sentient beings who possess a mind shall all attain unsurpassed bodhi."
For what reason, then, is it said that this is intended to lead those of indeterminate nature,
and so forth, until all sentient beings of the five vehicles possess Buddha-nature and ultimately all attain the supreme fruit of the Mahāyāna?
Why is it that those who ultimately belong to the vehicles of humans and devas do not take refuge in the Buddha?

In response: the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the Buddha taught the One Vehicle for ten reasons, while the twentieth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) states that the Buddha taught the One Vehicle for six reasons.
As has already been analyzed above,
the intended meaning of the present explanation is that,
according to ultimate reality, the five vehicles are each distinct.
As established by the scriptural citations and logical reasoning presented above,
the teaching of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*) was spoken for the sake of certain types of beings;
it does not mean that there is only one vehicle and no second or third.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
"There are four types of śrāvakas;
the first is those who seek tranquility."
Second, the regression from the bodhicitta;
this is also called the redirection of the bodhicitta.
Third, the transformational manifestation.
Regarding the four types of overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
the Sūtra records the prophecy for those who have regressed from the bodhicitta and those who are subject to transformation (*nirmāṇa*) alone;
the World-Honored One does not bestow prophecies upon the other two types.
Regarding those who are śrāvakas through transformation:
they are as described in the sūtras as being intoxicated by the wine of samādhi,
remaining unaware for kalpas.
Only after arising from that state do they subsequently give rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).
Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others manifest such transformational forms,
acting as members of the class of Śrāvakas.
The former sages entered parinirvāṇa many kalpas ago;
yet even now they still resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. How much more so for us!
Therefore, for the sake of those who are to be transformed through response, he taught the One Vehicle and the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood.
This is because the ninth of the ten reasons in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* concerns "transformation."
This is precisely that.
Śāriputra and others had previously resolved upon the Great Mind,
but because of the giving of their eyes, they regressed and sought the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Now, for their sake, he teaches the single vehicle (ekayāna) and bestows the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
Therefore, it is said that he also teaches the single vehicle and so forth for those who have regressed from the bodhicitta.
Otherwise, it would contradict the fivefold spiritual lineages (gotra) taught in the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra and the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra.
Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"At one time, I taught a single vehicle,
a single path, a single practice, and a single object of focus."
I have taught that those from the stage of srotāpanna up to the arhat all attain the Buddha-way;
yet my disciples, failing to understand my intention,
proclaim such words before the great assembly.
The Tathāgata has said that those from the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the arhat all attain the Buddha-way.
If they all become Buddhas, they would then understand the Buddha’s intention.
Why, then, is it said that they do not understand the Buddha’s intention?
Therefore, one should know that it must be understood exactly as stated here.
Question: The Sūtra itself says: "In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma."
There is neither two nor three,
except for the Buddha’s skillful means;
this refers to the refutation of duality and the refutation of triad in order to clarify the One Vehicle.
Why, then, is it said that there is a distinction between three or five vehicles?
Answer: According to the explanation in the Sanskrit original, the verses of the sūtra should state that there is neither a second nor a third;
yet, when counting the three vehicles, the Pratyekabuddha is designated as the second.
The śrāvaka is the third.
This is for the purpose of attracting those of indeterminate lineage and supporting the rest;
thus, it is said that there is no second or third [vehicle] as a skillful means.
This is not a true refutation.
The Lotus Sūtra itself declares:
"Only this one fact is real."
The other two are not the truth;
one never uses the Lesser Vehicle to deliver sentient beings.
If these three are refuted,
why then do you say that the other two are not true and are not used as "small" means of salvation?
One should likewise say that they do not use the Mahāyāna for the purpose of delivering beings.
Since the sutra merely states that the other two [vehicles] are not true and does not mention the "Small" [vehicle] as being refuted,
it is clear that the Mahāyāna is not what is being subverted.
That same sutra further states:
Since there are not even two vehicles, how much less could there be three?
"Two" refers to the second;
"three" refers to the third.
It does not mean that the two vehicles and the three vehicles are called "two" and "three.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra states:
"The vehicle of the śrāvaka and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha..."
This is precisely the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is itself the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Therefore, this merely reconciles the two vehicles of those with indeterminate lineage.
Nor does it mean that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures are brought together;
how much less so for those of the Mahāyāna?
Furthermore, there is no manifestation of the three vehicles as being identical to one.
It is not that the Mahāyāna is refuted by asserting that there is only one vehicle;
how could this principle be in error?
If one were to reconcile this with the refutation of the three vehicles:
It is the greatest among the three;
that is, the ox-carts promised within the burning house,
which were equally provided upon exiting the gate— all being ox-vehicles.
If one were to break up the former ox and give it separately to another ox,
what difference would there be between the two oxen?
Furthermore, the "great" among the three [vehicles] is precisely sudden enlightenment.
How can one cause them to enter into oneness?
Would this not mean that sudden enlightenment becomes gradual enlightenment?
Furthermore, what is the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in terms of understanding and practice?
To say that one abandons three and proceeds toward one,
thereby removing the web of doubt for bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds,
refers to the "sustaining of the remainder" among the ten meanings.
The One Vehicle has not yet been taught;
fearing that their diligence might be destroyed and they would fall back by giving rise to doubt,
[the Buddha] now hears of the One Vehicle to eliminate their state of uncertainty.
This refers to abandoning a lower stage to proceed to a higher level;
it does not mean abandoning the Mahāyāna to enter into a single [vehicle].
Otherwise, the ten stages would merely involve abandoning the lower to proceed to the upper.
One should also say that [the other two] break the three and unify into one;
furthermore, one should state that the other three are not true—
why speak only of two?
Śrīmālā spoke again:
"If the Tathāgata, in accordance with their inclinations, teaches through skillful means, this is itself the Mahāyāna; there are no two vehicles."
Therefore, the teaching that the two vehicles converge into one is an expedient explanation,
not the ultimate truth.
Although the sūtras state that they open the gate of expedient means (upāya-mukha) to reveal the mark of reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa),
and thus speak of those of the two vehicles who possess indeterminate lineage (aniyata-gotra),
this is merely the gate of expedient means.
Because it causes those who are far removed to enter into reality,
the teaching of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) now leads them toward the ultimate fruit, which is called "reality" (tattva).
This does not mean that the two [vehicles] do not exist at all, and that only the name "One" constitutes reality.
Therefore, the Lotus Sutra speaks of "secretly dispatching two men who were one-eyed and of short stature," and does not mention three.
It further says:
Because there are two stages of rest, it speaks of two and not three.
If one says that taking a circuitous route to enter the Great Stage is called the Mahāyāna,
whereas entering the Great Stage directly is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), then according to the sūtras and śāstras, the One Vehicle is in fact not fixed.
This current interpretation lacks authoritative evidence;
no authentic textual passage has been seen.
How could the One Vehicle of the Lotus Sūtra be attained by proceeding directly?
Now, what is the distinction between these two stages of practice? Therefore,
we know that as a skillful means (*upāya*), [the Buddha] concealed the existence of the two vehicles and taught the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*),
because it was what was appropriate for those in this single assembly to hear.

Some say that even after completing three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Buddha is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and that he attains the stage of *bodhi* in thirty-four moments of thought (*cittakṣaṇa*).
Now, in order to refute this attachment, it is said that there is but a Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*); furthermore, this also serves to refute the [notion of] three vehicles.
Not so. This is merely a biased view of the Hinayana following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
how could it have been made by the Buddha while he was still present, such that he would hold this attachment to a Buddha as true?
Now, because this is taught as a refutation, it refutes only the two [vehicles].
Question: Why are one vehicle and five vehicles established, rather than one collection (piṭaka) and five collections?
It is taught that there are six *piṭakas*, but not six vehicles (*yāna*).
The two *piṭakas* and three *piṭakas* taught in such works as the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* correspond to the two vehicles and three vehicles, respectively.
Answer: "Vehicle" (yāna) has the meaning of conveying;
it clarifies the vehicle in terms of the practice according to the capacities [of sentient beings].
"Treasury" (piṭaka) has the meaning of containing.
The teachings are categorized as "Pitakas" (baskets) in relation to their principles;
thus, the reasons why the one, five, and sixfold classifications differ,
as well as the two, three Pitakas and the two, three vehicles mentioned in the sūtras, [are explained].
They manifest their activity through the functioning of capacities and distinguish their teachings by confronting the principles of those capacities;
it is for this reason that they may be considered identical.
It is not yet appropriate to declare them all identical or all distinct; rather,
for the time being, they are provisionally divided into Vehicles and Pitakas according to what is suitable,
such that these distinctions and similarities correspond to one another.
In general, there is a commonality of characteristics that does not contradict reason;
however, I have not yet seen the textual source for this.
Furthermore, according to the first fascicle of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka:
The ten perfections and the ten adverse qualities are equal in number as they mutually counteract one another; however,
the four wheels and the eight unfavorable conditions differ in their respective numbers and modes of counteraction,
so they should not be held to be identical.
Question: A vehicle has the meaning of conveying [one across].
While a Bodhisattva may possess a vehicle, the Tathāgata has already crossed over. How can he have a vehicle?
One might argue that the Buddha Vehicle should not be established;
the answer is that it can be mounted by both oneself and others,
for the Bodhisattva possesses two types of capacity.
If saving others does not constitute saving oneself, what prevents the establishment of the Buddha Vehicle?
Question: For what reason is it said in some places that there is the Buddha Vehicle?
It is also called the Bodhisattva Vehicle,
but it is only called the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
it is not called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
The answer is: with respect to the fruit alone, it is called the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna).
When both vehicles can be cultivated, it is called the Bodhisattva Vehicle (Bodhisattvayāna).
Because its practices and so forth are extensive, it is named the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Because it excludes the other two, it is also called the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna).
Pratyekabuddhas have no separate teaching system;
even their initial practice arises from sound.
Therefore, it is called the Śrāvaka-yāna and not the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
When the two vehicles are discussed collectively, they are generally termed the Hīnayāna,
because their faculties, practices, and so forth are equally narrow and inferior.
There is no contradiction.
Question: Since you have already paired the fruit with the name "Buddha Vehicle" (buddhayāna), you should likewise pair the fruit with the name "Buddha Treasury" (buddhagarbha).
Why is it called only the *bodhisattvapiṭaka* and not the *buddhapiṭaka*,
even though both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas receive the name "piṭaka"?
This shall be explained in detail within the chapter on the "Piṭaka" itself.
Question: Are the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit all of one vehicle (ekayāna) in essence, identical or different?
Answer: The rain falls everywhere, so the teaching is the same while the capacities of the recipients differ;
the three animals cross the river, so the principle is the same while their realizations differ.

The six sense bases are the same in their great causal activity, yet differ in their cultivation; the three vehicles are the same in their provisional inducement as a fruit, yet differ in their manifestation.
Whether differing or identical, there is no need for laborious fixed criteria; the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* brings together both cause and fruit.
The Lotus Sūtra brings together the three aspects of teaching, practice, and fruit.
The "one rain" refers to the teaching;
the "nine divisions" refer to the practice.
The three vehicles refer to the fruit;
this reveals that, according to the provisional teaching, there are only the stages of practice and fruit.
Esoterically, however, there are actually four.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, [the relationship between] the same and the different.
By the Dharma-in-Seal (Hōin), Provisional Great Sōjō (Gondaisōjō) Seikan, sixty-seven years of age, at Fukuen-in.
The Treatise on the Forest of Meanings in the Mahāyāna Dharma Garden, Volume Two, Composed by Ji:
Chapter on the Various Collections (Pitakas). Chapter on the Various Collections.
The various Piṭakas are briefly analyzed by way of ten sections.
First, the origins of the councils.
Second, the increase and decrease of names and numbers;
third, the analysis of what is discarded and established;
fourth, the determination of essential nature.
Fifth, the explanation of names and meanings;
sixth, the manifestation of distinctions;
seventh, the revelation of the Buddha’s own exposition of the general and specific categories.
Eight, the establishment of teacher and disciple;
nine, the sequential analysis;
ten, the explanation that resolves doubts and difficulties.
1. The First Account of the Council: Regarding the origin of the first council, there is a separate single fascicle among all the sūtras titled *The Tradition of the Compilation of the Tripiṭaka*.

Along with the *Dharmatrāta-dharmagupta-śāstra*, the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the second fascicle of Paramārtha’s *Samayabhedoparacanacakra-vyākhyā*, the ninth fascicle of the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, etc.
Now, I have carefully examined and compiled these accounts for exposition.
I wished to record them individually in full detail,
but fearing that the text would become too voluminous and difficult for students to comprehend, I have instead presented them here in this concise form.
The *Xiyuji* states: "It is located at the very center of the kingdom of Magadha,
the site where the ancient and former kings resided."
The superior and auspicious *kuśa* grass emerged there,
hence it was called the City of Superior Grass (*Kuśāgrapura*), which is the city of Kauśāmbī.
Surrounded on all four sides by lofty mountains, it forms an outer rampart;
a narrow path leads westward,
and a mountain gate opens to the north.
It is long from east to west and narrow from south to north,
with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty *li*.
The remaining foundations of the inner city measure more than thirty *li* in circumference.
Traveling about one li from the north gate of the city of Śrāvastī,
one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove, on the northern side of the southern mountain, [is the Jetavana].
In the Great Bamboo Grove, there is a large stone chamber,
the place where Mahākāśyapa held the council.
King Ajātaśatru...
For the sake of the compilers [of the canon],
various halls were constructed at the foot of the western mountain to the southwest outside the north gate of the city of Śrāvastī;
Paramārtha states this was the Seven-Leaf Rock (Saptaparṇa-guhā) in Rājagṛha.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* tradition states that it was north of the city of Śrāvastī;
this is consistent across the three accounts.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* claims it was at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, but this is incorrect.
This mountain lies fourteen or fifteen *li* due north of the royal palace city,
bordering the southern slope of the northern mountains.
The council was convened outside the northern gate of the great city.
The records and traces still exist;
therefore, we know that [the claim] is incorrect.
The three texts have distinct titles.
The location is not different.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eleven,
states that when the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa...
The earth shook in six ways;
all the rivers flowed backward;
violent winds arose with black clouds, thunder, lightning, hail, and rain.
Stars fell everywhere;
lions and other fierce beasts roared and howled;
gods and humans wailed in lamentation.
All the devas and humans uttered these words:
"How swift is the Buddha's entry into nirvana!
At this time, calamities and transformations are immeasurable and boundless."
All the great sages have entered into parinirvāṇa.
The *Xiyu ji* states:
"At that time, Mahākāśyapa..."
While sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he was suddenly illuminated by a brilliant light.
Furthermore, observing an earthquake, he asked, "What omen is this?
Witnessing such extraordinary phenomena, he used his divine eye to see that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"From the gods of the six heavens of desire up to the devaputras of the Śubhakṛtsna heaven,
they all saw that the arhats had entered parinirvāṇa."
He thought to himself:
"The Sun of the Buddha has already set;
his disciples, too, have followed him into disappearance."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Once the elephant king has passed away, the elephant calf follows him;
now that the merchant of the Dharma has departed, from whom shall one seek the treasure of the Dharma?
At that time, the devas prostrated at Kāśyapa’s feet and spoke these verses:
"O Elder, desire, anger, and pride have been eliminated;
Your form is like a pillar of purple-gold."
From head to toe, he was majestic and peerlessly sublime;
his eyes were pure like lotus flowers.
He spoke to Kāśyapa:
O Benevolent One, do you know?
The ship of Dharma is shattered;
the city of Dharma has collapsed.
The ocean of the Dharma has dried up;
the banner of the Dharma has fallen;
the lamp of the Dharma is about to be extinguished.
The lay community wished to depart;
those who practiced the Way were few,
while evil people grew increasingly numerous.
One should establish the Buddha-dharma through great compassion.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa’s mind was as tranquil and unmoving as the great ocean.
After a long while, he replied,
"It is indeed as you have said," and silently accepted his request.
Having prostrated at his feet, the devas suddenly vanished.
The second fascicle of Paramārtha Tripiṭaka’s *Commentary on the Treatise on the Tenets of the Schools* states:
"Seven days after the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa,
Kāśyapa summoned his followers."
He wished to go to the city of Kuśinagara.
On the way, he encountered a non-Buddhist practitioner named Upaka,
which in this language means "One of Near-Nature."
Kāśyapa asked, "From where have you come?
The non-Buddhist replied:
"I have come from the place where the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa.
Seven days have already passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Immeasurable devas and humans have offered incense, scattered flowers, and presented various offerings."
I picked up these mandārava flowers from the presence of the Buddha and showed them to Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa then went to the place where Ajātaśatru was.
He said to the king,
"I require eight troughs;
I pray that Your Majesty will have them brought."
The king followed the instructions and again summoned the royal physician;
the king likewise complied with the command.
He questioned the physician about various medicines:
"Which medicine treats wind disorders?
Which medicine cures sores?"
He requested it from the king again,
and the king granted it all accordingly;
he then ground the medicine into a powder.
He boiled it to make an ointment,

neither the Buddha nor his disciples ever taught a separate sub-sect for the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
However, within the various sūtras, that which elucidates the locus of wisdom is termed Abhidharma;
the treatises of the disciples merely explain these sūtras and commentaries.
It is not subsumed [within those two];
as stated in the first fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra*.
However, within the Mahāyāna as well, the two collections (*piṭaka*) are distinguished according to the teachings (*deśanāmukha*) based on the capacities and practices of sentient beings.
First, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
second, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

This is extensively established by Vasubandhu himself in the twenty-fifth, thirty-eighth, eighty-first, and eighty-fifth fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the eleventh fascicle of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, and the sixth and twentieth fascicles of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, as well as in the first fascicle of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*).
Because the Pratyekabuddha teachings— regarding doctrine, reasoning, practice, and fruition— are fewer than those of the Śrāvaka teachings,
they are designated as the "Śrāvaka Piṭaka" based on their relative abundance. Thus,
the two piṭakas are distinguished according to whether they are partial or complete.
Therefore, because Pratyekabuddhas realize only the emptiness of sentient beings and sever only the grasping at a personal self, they are subsumed within the Śrāvakas. Furthermore,
because their initial generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) also relies upon the voice [of the Buddha],
and because they enter [the path] from that [source], they are also called Śrāvakas.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*,
and other texts, the Mahāyāna as well as various schools such as the Sarvāstivāda all agree that there are three piṭakas:
first, the Sūtra-piṭaka.
Second, the Vinaya;
third, the Abhidharma.
The meaning of Sarvāstivāda is as explained in the Vibhāṣā.
Regarding the Mahāyāna teachings, as previously cited,
the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* and the *Ajātaśatru-kaukṛtya-vinodana Sūtra* also state that there are three piṭakas:
first, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Second, the Pratyekabuddhas;
third, the Śrāvakas.
Because their capacities differ, their teachings also differ.
Previously, because their practices and so forth were for the most part not different, they were subsumed within the Śrāvakas;
now, based on the fact that there are slight differences in their faculties, fruits, and practices, they are separately established.
Alternatively, it is said that there are four piṭakas, as in the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya and the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-sūtra*.
The Mahāsāṃghika school established a separate *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Piṭaka) in addition to the Tripiṭaka consisting of the Sūtras and so forth;
that is to say, they held that what explains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) alone is called the *Sūtra*,
while what explains ethical discipline (*śīla*) alone is called the *Vinaya*.
If it explains only wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called Abhidharma;
if it combines two explanations or three explanations, it is called the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka*.
The *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-sūtra* provides a detailed explanation of these four distinctions.
According to the tradition of the *Saṃyuktapiṭaka*, there are two categories: first, the Sūtras;
second, the Vinaya.
The third is the Mahādharmaparyāya;
the fourth is the Kṣudrakapiṭaka.
After Kātyāyana had completed its composition, he presented it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Because it is the supreme dharma, it is called the Great Dharma.
Within it, one destroys delusion and benefits the world;
because these various sutras clarify this, it is called the Great Dharma."
There are two further interpretations of this kind,
which I shall not cite here for fear of being too prolix.
The Buddha spoke of these past causes and conditions.
Arhats also spoke therein,
as did celestial Māras and non-Buddhist practitioners;
therefore, it is called the "Mixed Piṭaka."
Within it, there are many verses that inquire about the twelve links of dependent origination;
because these enter [the path] in various ways, it is called the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
Now, observing this tradition:
The meaning of the first interpretation is that only the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, spoke of his own past causes and conditions, which are called *sūtra*.
The meaning of the second interpretation is that even Arhats speak [of such matters], and these are termed the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection).
If it were only the exposition of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that was termed *sūtra*,
while that which also expounds wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth was called the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection),
then [one might ask]: regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), since each enters differently and expounds wisdom, [how would they be categorized]?
This first interpretation here corresponds to the second tradition of that [text].
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīya school also speaks of four collections (*piṭaka*):
first, the Sūtra;...
Second, Vinaya;
third, Abhidharma;
fourth, Vidyā-mantras.
Because this treasury collects all mantras, it consists of five types of dharma-treasuries:
those of the three times, the unconditioned, the inexpressible, and so forth.
That which is explained as their referent is not [identical to] this which expresses them.
Within the Dharmaguptaka school, it is taught that there are five piṭakas;
that is, these four [piṭakas] with the addition of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka,
which elucidates the original practices performed by all bodhisattvas.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that there are five collections (*piṭaka*):
having mentioned the three collections, it further mentions the Miscellaneous Collection (*kṣudraka-piṭaka*) and the Bodhisattva Collection (*bodhisattva-piṭaka*).
However, within the Mahāyāna as well, six collections are taught.
The commentaries on the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, the *Abhidharma*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Vasubandhu state that both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas each have their own Tripiṭaka.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
One must not associate with the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna;
thus, it is known that the Mahāyāna also possesses a Tripiṭaka,
which together constitute six divisions.
The teaching of the Pratyekabuddhas is brief;
furthermore, there are no separate codes of discipline (*vinaya*) and so forth.
Therefore, there are no Tripiṭakas that can be divided into nine.
There may be seven meanings:
the Hīnayāna explains four,
while the Mahāyāna explains three.
Thus, according to this interpretation, there are seven [piṭakas]. However, there is no separate textual authority for this.
Furthermore, the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* and the Mahāsāṃghika school also speak of eight piṭakas.
Because there are four each for both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas,
they may also be said to be nine;
for the *Samantaprabhā* and other sūtras state that there are three.
Since each of these constitutes three, nine categories are established by way of meaning;
alternatively, they constitute eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma.
Thus, through such increases and decreases, they are briefly summarized into seven variations.
That is to say, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight;
if stated individually, there are eighty-four thousand,
and according to this extensive explanation, there are eighty koṭis and forty lakṣas.
This is fully analyzed in detail in the *Prabhāvatī-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*).
This concludes the second section: the increase and decrease of numerical categories.
3. Discerning Abolition and Establishment. Regarding the third section, discerning abolition and establishment:
The divergent teachings of the Hīnayāna are not elucidated in our school.
Within the Mahāyāna, we establish only two collections (piṭaka), two types of three collections, as well as six collections, eighty-four thousand [teachings], and so forth.
The *Vyākhyā* on Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states:
"Because there is a distinction between the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna within these three piṭakas, they are divided into two piṭakas.
The meaning of this statement is as follows:
However, because the teaching, reasoning, practice, and fruit of the Pratyekabuddhas are inferior to those of the Śrāvakas,
they are subsumed within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and collectively designated as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
Furthermore, regarding the powers (*bala*),
although there are intermediate powers within the hierarchy of superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*),
when the superior and inferior are compared with one another, there are only two categories.
Whether above or below,
the intermediate force is not mentioned;
now, the upper and lower are contrasted with one another in their respective movements.
The teaching of the Pratyekabuddhas is included within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka;
their faculties are dull and their karma is shallow.
Thus, that which is abandoned, that which is cultivated, that which is realized, and the benefit therein [are limited].
In all cases, these do not encompass everything, because they are not comprehensive. Therefore,
only the two Piṭakas are taught.
In the *Lalitavistara* and other sūtras, the Tripitaka is established as consisting of the Bodhisattva, Pratyekabuddha, and Śrāvaka collections.
These three collections are established according to the differences in the capacities of beings and the distinctions in their vehicles and practices; they are neither more nor less than this.
Furthermore, regarding the establishment that the Tripiṭaka, consisting of the Sūtras and so forth,
is neither increased nor diminished, Master Vasubandhu has four commentaries;
the first two of these [cycles of] exposition are identical to those in the Abhidharma.
The *Paramārtha* states:
"All faults, in brief, are of three kinds.
The first is doubt."
Second, practicing the two extremes;
third, clinging to one's own views.
Regarding these, at first one is unwilling to practice them.
Next, one cultivates the inverted views and subsequently understands that they are not real.
To counteract those [inverted views], the three Piṭakas are taught in their respective order; therein, the definitive meaning is explained for them so as to cause them to enter [the path].
Because the Vinaya permits one hundred and one items, it causes one to abide in the middle way;
because the Śāstra illuminates the characteristics of all phenomena, it causes true wisdom to arise.
This, then, is the basis for those who have not yet entered, those who have already entered, and those who realize [the fruit].
Secondly, this is also explained in terms of the initial abandonment of all afflictions and karma,
because these three are all abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore,
the cause for proceeding toward the two extremes is precisely the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Thirdly, because it is taught in reference to the afflictions and karmas that obstruct entry into the Path,
all afflictions consist of only two categories:
first, hesitation (*vimati*).
First is doubt as the precursor;
second is determination,
with the grasping at views as its chief.
These two types encompass all afflictions; thus,
although one seeks to enter the Path and practices sublime conduct,
because one clings to the extremes of suffering and pleasure, one cannot realize the truth correctly.
That is to say, for the sake of removing the delusions and karma of the present,
the Tripitaka was taught solely for those of the householders who indulge in the extreme of sensual pleasure, and for the various non-Buddhists who practice the extreme of self-mortification.
Fourth, furthermore, among all categories of training (*śikṣā*), none surpasses the three types:
namely, ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Each of these is explained differently according to the specific emphasis of various schools regarding the three trainings.
Therefore, the Three Piṭakas alone are neither more nor less [than necessary].
Furthermore, the fifth [set] was established in three successive stages for those with improper discipline, those with excessive distraction, and those with excessive afflictions.
The Vinaya, Sūtra, and Abhidharma; and sixthly, the three [collections] were established in sequence for those with an abundance of misconduct, an abundance of craving, and an abundance of views.
The seventh [set] is established as three for those who have an excess of hatred, an excess of greed, and an excess of delusion, respectively.
The eighth is established as three for those who fear the miserable destinies, fear the desire realm, and fear the three realms, respectively.
The ninth is for the sake of attaining the three matters of Great Parinirvāṇa:
through the Abhidharma one attains prajñā; through the Vinaya one attains eloquence;
and through the Sūtras one attains the Dharmakāya.
The tenth [reason] is that the Three Piṭakas are established for the sake of attaining the two bodies:
because through the Vinaya one attains the liberation of the nature of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya),
and through the Śāstras one attains the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya).
Because wisdom constitutes its very essence,
one attains the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) through the sūtras;
for it is by relying on meditative concentration that supernormal powers are manifested.
Such are the distinctions.
Because these three piṭakas neither increase nor decrease,
they are further divided into the upper and lower vehicles according to this same principle to constitute the six piṭakas.
There is no other meaning;
the eighty-four thousand [teachings] correspond exactly to the afflictions to be remedied, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Based on this, they further constitute eight million billion treasuries of dharmas.
As stated in the eleventh fascicle of the Abhidharma-śāstra,
however, the Buddha’s teachings were not fixed, as he spoke according to what was appropriate for his listeners;
sometimes, based on the gate of abandoning the heterodox and returning to the orthodox, he taught that there is only one Piṭaka.
This refers to the treasury of the teaching of the True Dharma (saddharmadeśanā-piṭaka). In contrast to the treasury of the meanings to be expressed, it speaks of only one treasury,
namely, the treasury of syllables (vyañjana-piṭaka).
Some say there are two, up to eighty-four thousand,
as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Buddha, however, speaks of only one cause and condition.
That is to say, it refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*),
or even as far as what is taught through the twelvefold division because they ought to be heard;
this Piṭaka is likewise so.
What has been established according to the circumstances cannot be challenged;
this concludes the third section, the analysis of what is to be rejected and what is to be established.
Fourth, regarding the determination of the essential nature: as for the determination of the essence—
The essential nature and categories of the three baskets (*piṭaka*) are not different;
in the preceding brief summary, the four bases have already been revealed.
For instance, within the four kinds of bases according to Dharmapāla, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*kāritra*) are discussed separately.
This refers, in general, to that which is manifested upon the mind of the speaker;
its essential nature consists of sound, names, phrases, and syllables—distinguished as being either conventional or real.

As appropriate, these are subsumed under the three natures, the five dharmas, and the aggregates, bases, and elements, as has been explained extensively above regarding the doctrines and principles they convey.
5. Explanation of Names and Meanings, Part Five. Regarding the explanation of names and meanings, it is divided into two sections.
First is the explanation of the general title.
Next, the specific names are explained.
To explain the general name,
Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
For what reason is it called a "piṭaka" (basket)?
Because it is capable of containing;
that is to say, it contains all meanings that ought to be known.
The meaning of this statement is as follows:
because the expressive teaching can encompass all objects of knowledge that ought to be known so that they are not lost, it is established with the name "Piṭaka" (Basket).
Furthermore, another explanation states:
The meaning of "containing" (piṭaka) is the meaning of "receptacle" (kośa).
All dharmas that are to be known are contained herein;
it maintains the dharmas thus contained so that they are not lost.
It is called a "pitaka" (basket).
These distinct types vary, numbering two, three, and so forth;
two, three, and six are their numerical categories.
Among the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), this is an analytical compound with a numeral prefix (*dvigu*).
According to ancient explanations of the term, "pitaka" (basket) carries the meaning of "recording"; the teachings of the Noble Ones are able to record and define all phenomena.
It is called a "piṭaka" (basket).
To explain these specific names:
first, within the two piṭakas...
First, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
second, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Regarding the term "bodhisattva":
In the Sanskrit language, it should be called *bodhisattva*.
Because this term is abbreviated, it is simply named "Bodhisattva.
As Vasubandhu explains in his commentary:
Because the Bodhisattva takes awakening as his object of focus, he is called a "Bodhisattva.
The term "Bodhisattva" is established based on his words of great vow;
this is what is meant by that statement.
There are practitioners who have made great vows,
seeking great enlightenment to deliver all classes of sentient beings.
The name "bodhisattva" is established based on these two kinds as the objects of focus;
this is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound,
because one is called a "bodhisattva" by virtue of having those two kinds as the objects of focus.
Alternatively, it is an analysis by way of opposition:
[the term] "bodhi" and "sattva" are distinct because of the difference between wisdom and compassion.
Furthermore, it is said that one who takes that very mind as the basis for seeking bodhi,
possessing both the aspiration and the capability, is therefore called a bodhisattva.
This meaning is stated as follows:
*Bodhi* is the fruit sought;
*sattva* has the meaning of "valiant.
This refers to the mind of the practitioner, which seeks unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
One who possesses great resolve and is capable of enduring [all hardships],
endowed with these superior virtues, is called a bodhisattva;
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
Because he is a *sattva* who seeks great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Alternatively, *sattva* here means "sentient being" (*sattva*);
thus, it refers to a sentient being who seeks great enlightenment.
The *puruṣakāra* (human effort) is as explained previously;
although the phrasing in the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* differs slightly, its meaning is the same as this.
The *Ekādaśamukha-sūtra* states:
"Bodhi is prajñā; sattva refers to upāya."
These two dharmas likewise benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
"Bodhisattva" (bodhi-sattva) is also analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Regarding the term "śrāvaka": "śabda" (sound) refers to vocal sound, specifically the sounds of the Buddha’s preaching;
"śravaṇa" (hearing) refers to the act of listening. Thus, a śrāvaka is one who hears [the Dharma].
If a practitioner hears the Buddha preach the Dharma,
and through faith and diligence transcends the three realms,
they are called a śrāvaka.
Therefore, at the beginning of the second fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said:
"If there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within,
they hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and receive it with faith."
With earnest diligence,
they desire to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvana for themselves;
this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
This is based on the initial entry into the stage of the Śrāvaka vehicle,
as one enters the path primarily by relying on the teachings; however,
at the time of later realization of the fruit, it is not necessarily the case that everything must rely on sound.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The sound of the holy teachings of all Buddhas is the foremost;
one hears this sound of the teachings from teachers and spiritual friends."
Through successive cultivation and realization, they transcend the world forever;
thus they are called *śrāvakas*, which is interpreted as "hearing by means of sound" (*śabdena śravaṇam*), employing a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Furthermore, this refers specifically to those who abide in the understanding of their own vehicle.
Its name is established solely on the basis of practice for one’s own benefit.
This principle would not hold true if one were of indeterminate nature.
Therefore, at the end of the second fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says:
They are called *śrāvaka* (hearers) because they cause all beings to hear the sound of the Buddha-way;
this refers to those who, having turned their minds [toward enlightenment], abide in the Buddha-vehicle and engage in altruistic practice.
They are called *śrāvaka* because they cause others to hear by means of sound.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
Alternatively, because they hear the sound [of the Dharma], they are called "Hearers" (*śrāvaka*);
this is a *bahuvrīhi* (dependent) compound.
When Pratyekabuddhas first enter the stage of their own vehicle, they also for the most part rely upon the voice of the Buddha;
furthermore, because it teaches the Lesser Vehicle, it is designated as a Piṭaka from the perspective of its majority content;
moreover, this refers to what is practiced and realized.
Together with the attainment of what has been abandoned,
those who do not possess the vast [attainments] are collectively termed Śrāvakas;
according to their respective capacities, these two types of practitioners are thus accommodated.
All the meanings of the phenomena within these two objects of knowledge are subsumed herein;
these are precisely what are called the "Pitakas of the Bodhisattvas" and the "Pitaka of the Śrāvakas.
Both Pitakas are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
Among the alternative names for the Tripiṭaka,
the first two names for the Tripiṭaka as explained in the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra) are as previously stated.
As for the "Pratyekabuddha Piṭaka":
The Lotus Sūtra states:
"If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
believe and accept it, and practice with earnest diligence."
Seeking spontaneous wisdom and delighting in solitary tranquility,
one deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena;
this is called the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Always delighting in tranquility and not wishing to dwell among the mundane,
one fulfills the cultivation of preparatory application."
Having attained spontaneous and solitary awakening without the instruction of teachers or friends,
and because they have forever transcended the world, they are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers). Because they awaken alone through their own realization, they are named Pratyekabuddhas.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).
Alternatively, because they realize the fruit of sainthood by depending upon conditions (*pratyaya*),
they are also called *Pratyekabuddhas*.
"Awareness through waiting for conditions" is also an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (dependent determinative compound).

"Solitary Buddha" (*pratyekabuddha*) is an *upapadasamāsa* (dependent compound), as previously explained in the *Sūtra* and other parts of the Tripiṭaka. As for the "Three Piṭakas," they are [to be understood] according to the *upapadasamāsa*.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Sūtra refers to direct verbal discourse.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states:
The term *sūtra* has five meanings:
namely, "birth," "fountain," "manifestation," "plumb line," and "garland.
This is the explanation according to the Mahāyāna.
The Sanskrit term *sūtra* is here called "Discourse" (*kṣetra*).
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 25,
and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 6, state:
What is the *sūtra*? All discourses (*sūtras*) are briefly subsumed under twenty-four categories.
"Discourse" (*sūtra*) carries the meaning of being in accordance with, reaching toward, and harmonizing with [the truth].
Regarding what is called "sūtra," Vasubandhu’s commentary explains:
it is so named because it is able to string together [the teachings] according to their basis and their characteristics.
Because it is the Dharma and because it is the meaning, it is called Sūtra.
That which is spoken of in a particular context, by means of something, for the sake of something,
is called a "basis" (*āśraya*). This refers to the characteristics of the ultimate and conventional truths.
That which is called "characteristic" refers to the ten skillful dharmas and so forth;
that which is called "dharma" refers to the phenomena themselves.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to the explanation of all phenomena according to their underlying intention (*samdhāya*) and so forth;
this is designated as "meaning. It is [established] by means of four kinds of meaning.
Regarding the explanation of the Sūtras,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 25) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (fascicle 20) state that the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, [taught as follows]:
In that place, for the sake of those sentient beings,
in accordance with the various distinctions of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be transformed,
he proclaims immeasurable discourses associated with the aggregates (*skandha*).
...and so forth, as explained at length.
As for those who compiled the Dharma:
they gathered together the noble words so that the Dharma might endure for a long time, arranging them in sequence with elegant and sublime language.
That which penetrates and stitches together, which can lead to benefit and profit,
and through which one is able to practice the holy life—
this is the true, virtuous, and sublime meaning.
It is called a *sūtra*.
Although previously the term *sūtra* was explained through the sense of "stringing together," in this case it means that the teaching strings together the meaning.
To gather and sustain living beings through teaching is called a sūtra;
it is like a thread that strings flowers together, as a warp holds the woof.
In the Western Regions, terms such as *hu-jí-sō*, "sewing thread," "matting," and "sacred teachings" are all called *sūtra*.
Through the guidance of these teachings, sentient beings are gathered and prevented from scattering into the evil destinies.
Because its meaning and principles are permeated by the teaching and are neither lost nor obscured,
the noble teaching is called "Sūtra" (Kṣepaṇa).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"It is like various flowers scattered upon a table;
when the wind blows, they fall and scatter because there is no string to thread them."
Twelve years ago, their faculties were such that they were capable of receiving the concise teaching;
yet there arose various divergent views among those who had gone forth and those who remained at home.
It causes the True Dharma to perish as swiftly as the wind.
The meaning of all sutras is called "flowers";
if there is any scriptural teaching that penetrates correct principle, [it is a flower].
Since there is no divergent view regarding the Dharma, it does not perish.
Thus, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because it can penetrate and encompass, it is called a Sūtra."

The Buddha’s holy teaching is termed "sūtra" (discourse) because it strings together, encompasses, and maintains the meanings that are to be explained as well as the sentient beings who are to be converted.
A sūtra that accords with the truth is called a "Sūtra of Accordance" (sūtra-vinaya).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
If it were merely called "Sūtra," it would not be this [type of] explanation;
however, the essence of the *sūtra* is itself the Piṭaka.

The Ninth: Sequential Analysis. Regarding the sequential analysis, one should examine and verify it across various locations.
This sequence of exposition is briefly of two kinds:
first, the sequence of shallow and deep.
In Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, it is stated that the Śrāvaka-piṭaka comes first and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka follows later;
in other sources as well, the sequence of superiority and inferiority is explained in this same manner.
Taking the Bodhisattva-piṭaka as the first and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka as the last,
the sequence for the three piṭakas of the Pratyekabuddhas and so forth, explained according to this principle, is likewise.
Furthermore, there are three types of sequential order.
Regarding the first type of sequence:
first is the Sūtra, next is the Vinaya, and last is the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
There are five reasons for this sequence.
First, it follows the order of exposition;
as stated in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*:
Sixty-three days after the Buddha had attained enlightenment,
he was at the Deer Park of the Sages in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
where he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
That is the Sūtra. Next, at Śrāvastī,
because of Kalandakanivāsin, the rule against unchaste conduct was established, and subsequently the Vinaya was taught.
Later, at the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, at the Hall of Universal Assembly, the Buddha,
having observed the origins and circumstances concerning the elder bhikṣus such as Bāṣpa,
taught the abandonment of the five fears, and subsequently taught the Abhidharma.
Second, the sequence of the councils:
first, Ānanda was commanded to compile the Sūtras;
next, Upāli was commanded to compile the Vinaya.
Later, Mahākāśyapa himself compiled the Abhidharma;
however, the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states that Ānanda later compiled that Abhidharma.
Paramārtha says:
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra compiled the Abhidharma;
for those to be trained, he taught the Sūtras as a sequential introduction to the Dharma.
For those who have already entered the Dharma, the Vinaya is taught;
for those who possess what is to be abandoned and realized, the Abhidharma-piṭaka is taught.
These are the fourfold sequence of root and branches.
The sūtras are the foundation;
from them precepts arise,
and only then can wisdom be established.
Fifth, the sequence of breadth and narrowness:
the *sūtras* elucidate the arising of the three trainings (*śikṣā*),
while the *vinaya* elucidates the arising of two trainings.
Since the Abhidharma exclusively explains wisdom (*prajñā*),
the Sūtra comes first and the Abhidharma follows;
this is the sequence of the second [section].
This is explained according to the sequence of practice:
ethical discipline is coarse and easy to cultivate;
next comes meditative concentration.
Subsequently, wisdom is the most difficult to accomplish.
This is because the nature of the Dharma is such that one practices from the shallow toward the profound.
First the Vinaya, next the Sūtras,
and finally the Abhidharma.
Regarding the third sequence,
it is explained according to superiority and inferiority.
The Abhidharma is the basis for generating the seeds of wisdom and the root of all-encompassing knowledge (*jñāna*).
Concentration can clarify and purify the mind, giving rise to wisdom and enabling the realization of the Dharma;
morality abandons all evils and subdues body, speech, and mind.
Therefore, the Abhidharma comes first.
Next is the Sūtra, followed by the Vinaya; furthermore,
there is no fixed sequence, as they are taught according to necessity.
However, most sūtras explain the Three Piṭakas based on the first of these ten sequences.
The sequence of the Six Piṭakas should be understood according to their respective meanings.

the *Garbhakośa-sūtra* in eight fascicles is likewise included in the Mahāsāṃghika school.
This is not the meaning of the Mahāyāna.

In the third section, which distinguishes between what is established and what is discarded, it is asked: "Is a 'vehicle' (yāna) defined by its capacity to deliver beings according to their spiritual faculties?"
Thus, one establishes the One Vehicle and the Five Vehicles;

furthermore, it is permitted that these may be designated as "Pitakas" (collections) based on their capacity to encompass and sustain specific spiritual faculties. Accordingly, one permits the establishment of a single Pitaka or five Pitakas.
Answer: Although there is no explicit textual statement, the meaning may indeed be so.
Both the *yānas* (vehicles) and the *piṭakas* (baskets) are admitted to be established according to the capacities of sentient beings;
logically, there is one *piṭaka*, as well as five *piṭakas*.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra states:
"Vinaya is precisely the Mahāyāna study;
since it encompasses the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, it is called the 'Great Study'."
Therefore, since they are identical in terms of the vehicle (yāna), only one Piṭaka is established.
One should also say: "In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only one Piṭaka of the Dharma."
There is no second or third;
this should be understood by analogy with the Buddha’s skillful means in his teaching.
In terms of their meaning, they should be established as one or five.

Since the various teachings discussed in terms of the capacities of sentient beings are minor, they do not briefly establish a single collection (*piṭaka*) or five collections; however, such principles ought to exist.
Furthermore, vehicles proceed in reliance upon capacities.
Regarding the *Zangyue jiaomen* (The Treasury’s Summary of the Teachings), its underlying intentions differ;
thus, one cannot apply a single standard, such as the equal number of ten perfections and ten obscurations that mutually counteract one another.
The four wheels and eight difficulties vary in their number;
thus, while there may be one or five vehicles, no fixed teaching is established.
In the fourth section, the essential nature and all obstacles thereof are set forth.
This has already been fully explained in the preceding portion of this brief discussion.
Regarding the fifth section, the explanation of the general and specific names, the question is asked:
"For what reason, among the two collections (piṭakas)..."
The Hīnayāna establishes the name of its Piṭaka based on the person, calling it the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
but not the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka;
the Mahāyāna establishes the name of its Piṭaka based on the person, calling it the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It is not called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Answer: The teaching of the pratyekabuddhas is inferior to that of the śrāvakas;
furthermore, those who first enter the Dharma likewise rely upon the teachings of the śrāvakas.
The Śrāvaka-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna is named after its adherents and is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
but it is not called the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka;
if it were called the Tathāgata-piṭaka, the names for its vows and practices would not be grand enough.
To manifest that the names of his vows and practices are profound, vast, and far-reaching,
it is called simply the "Bodhisattva-piṭaka" and not the "Tathāgata-piṭaka.
Furthermore, the virtuous conduct of a bodhisattva is easily accomplished in this world.
The virtuous conduct of a Tathāgata is difficult for the world to accomplish.
Desiring to encourage sentient beings so that they may easily establish themselves according to this teaching,
it is called merely the "Bodhisattva Piṭaka" and not the "Tathāgata Piṭaka."
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, the śrāvaka is the cause and the pratyekabuddha is the fruit;
it is named after its starting point and is not called the "Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka.
Within the Mahāyāna, the bodhisattva is the cause and the Tathāgata is the fruit.
From childhood, it has been designated by the name "Tathāgatagarbha.

Question: For what reason is the Bodhisattvapiṭaka named after that which is sought through vows, rather than being titled after its objective conditions, as is the case with the "Teacherless Piṭaka"?
The Śrāvaka-piṭaka is designated by way of its objective conditions;
it is not named after what is sought through vows, but rather is called the *nirvāṇa-sattva-kośa*.
Answer: As for establishing names, they are provisionally based upon a single virtue.
Since the bodhisattva’s aspiration and practice both bring about vast benefit on a grand scale,
and because one wishes to manifest the depth of their compassion and the breadth of their wisdom,
it is simply named the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
It is not called the "Teacherless Treasury.
For the Śrāvakas, the accomplishment of virtue through reliance on conditions is superior;
this is because both their aspirations and their seeking are shallow.
The name is derived from its objective conditions;
it is not called the "Nirvāṇa-sattva-garbha.
For this reason, the Pratyekabuddha is also named based on his reliance upon conditions.
It is not designated by the name "vow.
If it is asked whether, within the Tripiṭaka, that which penetrates the principles of reality is called *sūtra*,
then the other two Piṭakas should also be called *sūtras*.
The same applies to the Abhidharma as a question regarding discipline (*vinaya*).
To answer according to the actual facts:
all three piṭakas may be called *sūtra*.
Because it is said that a *sūtra* has the meaning of "stringing together," it receives its name from this fundamental sense;
other [types of texts] do not.
Just as the term "dharma-sphere" cannot be applied to anything other than form,
the same applies to the meanings of "discipline" (*vinaya*) and "phenomenology" (*abhidharma*).
Furthermore, they penetrate the principles and give rise to excellence.
Having attained this name, it is not any other;
it is superior in its mastery over the three karmas.
Having attained this name, it is not any other.
It is superior because it is directed toward non-abiding nirvana;
it alone receives this name and no other.
[These are] the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
Each receives its name according to its respective category.

Question: Among the six piṭakas, since there are slight differences in terms of practice, fruit, capacity, and principle, why do texts such as the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* establish the Pratyekabuddhas and others as a third piṭaka?
One might also establish nine collections based on the minor distinctions among those practices and so forth;
why then are there only six?
The answer is: because there are distinct categories that can only be divided into six.
Because the teaching of the Pratyekabuddhas has no distinct divisions,
it is not divided into nine;
furthermore, their spiritual capacities and natures are entirely different.
They may be established as the Three Piṭakas;
there is a slight difference in their teachings,
but they are not divided into nine.
In the sixth section, "Discriminating the Distinctions," it is asked:

based on pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one gives rise to freedom from regret and so forth, gradually attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since both the discipline that brings about concentration and the concentration itself are termed *vinaya*, [how are they distinguished?]
Since wisdom arises based on meditative concentration and gives rise to the designation "concentration" and "wisdom," both should be called Abhidharma.
Answer: Both morality and concentration belong to the category of merit;
they give rise to designations and are both termed "taming."
Concentration, wisdom, merit, and knowledge are distinct; their modes of expression differ, and they are subsumed within the various Piṭakas.
Question: Since concentration and wisdom are distinct categories, which Piṭaka do they belong to?
Question: Is there a distinction between concentration and distraction such that one is not subduing while the other is?
Answer: Although concentration and distraction differ, both are merit;
neither can sever afflictions, and thus neither constitutes true subduing.
The two categories of merit and wisdom are distinguished by their specific discernment;
there are differences in the abandonment of afflictions and their inclusion within the Pitakas.
The seventh [chapter] clarifies the general and specific divisions as spoken by the Buddha himself.
This brief summary is as explained in our own school’s tradition.
Regarding the eighth point, the establishment of the teacher-disciple relationship:
Question—Even granting the existence of the Three Baskets and the twelve divisions of the teachings...
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples were all able to analyze and expound [the teachings].
What fault would there be in this?

The answer is: if that were so, then no distinction would exist between teacher and disciple; there would be no difference whatsoever between shallow and profound dharmas, dharmas of inference and dharmas of realization, noble dharmas and ordinary dharmas, nor the dharma of omniscience and the dharma of the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, if one were to grant that there is a creator,
the teachings of the Tripiṭaka would become inconsistent;
therefore, the Buddha did not permit his disciples [to assert such] after his parinirvāṇa.
He compiled the twelvefold teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*), and so forth.
Question: Among the three realms and five destinies, in which places are these various collections fully present, and for what kind of sentient beings are they intended?
Answer: In the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*), the assembly of emanations (*nirmāṇa-saṃgha*) and the assembly of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-saṃgha*) are listed.
Furthermore, the devas of the formless realm stood by the Buddha’s side listening to the Āgama sūtras;
the dhāraṇī sūtras caused the multitudes in the hells to be extinguished.
Thus we know that the sūtras describe the true transformation bodies [of Buddhas] who reach the three realms and five destinies.
The *Lushenafo jing* (Vairocana Sūtra) speaks of the eighteen Brahma heavens, various heavenly kings, and so forth.
Since all are able to understand and fully receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts,
we know that the discipline (*vinaya*) also encompasses the bodies of those in the two realms and five destinies;
this refers to the actual body.
Since there is no ear-consciousness in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and thus no hearing of the teaching,
it is known that [the Buddha's voice] reaches only sentient beings with physical bodies in the two realms and five destinies;
for by the power of the Sūtra, even sentient beings in the hells are able to hear the Dharma.
Because various great bodhisattvas teach and cause others to receive the precepts within the hells for various reasons,
those who obtain the precepts differ in meaning accordingly.
Furthermore, those who possess this teaching exist only within the two realms.
On the fifth stage, there is no restriction;
because vitarka and vicāra can arise from higher stages toward lower ones,
there is likewise no logical fault in initiating [these states] for the purpose of teaching and transforming others.
The Abhidharma may be understood to apply to both realms (dhātu).
Although no textual passage is seen that explicitly permits its application to the five destinies (gati) or the four modes of birth (yoni), there is no prohibition against it.

However, the statement in the *Antarābhava-sūtra* that the Buddha taught sentient beings of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) during the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not a tenet of the Mahāyāna school.
According to the Mahāyāna school,
this is a transformation body for the purpose of converting sentient beings and is certainly not the true body,
because it lacks karmic fruit.
Otherwise, it would contradict the explanations in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts.
