2. Chapter Two: Distinguishing Characteristics. Regarding the characteristics within this section on distinguishing characteristics, the characteristics of the sūtras are explained in the eleventh chapter of the Abhidharma.
This refers to the prose passages that string together and briefly explain the meanings that ought to be explained;
that is, the prose sections within various sūtras that provide a brief exposition of the teachings that ought to be taught.
It is called a *sūtra*.
The eighty-first [category] is said to be the same as the *Abhidharma*;
that is to say, it is a prose discourse that strings together meanings and extensively explains the intended purport (*abhiprāya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Yogācārabhūmi, Chapter Twenty-five; *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, Chapter Six. No prose commentary is provided;
it merely states in general terms:
"The Buddha, in various locations..."
For the sake of various sentient beings,
based on their respective modes of conduct,
he proclaims immeasurable discourses associated with the aggregates, up to and including discourses associated with verified clarity.
The compilers of the Dharma gathered together the noble words so that the True Dharma might endure for a long time;
they arranged them in sequence through excellent names and so forth, as explained at length.
That which possesses true, good, and sublime meaning is called a *sūtra*.
This is the same as what is taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In the fifteenth [chapter] of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said:
From "Thus have I heard" up to "rejoiced and practiced accordingly"—
all such as these are called sūtras.
Furthermore, sūtras are both general and specific.
The "comprehensive" [classification] encompasses all twelve divisions of the teachings as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts;
the "specific" [classification], however, encompasses only the prose portions that briefly state the meanings that ought to be explained.
Because it differs from the characteristics of the remaining portions,
it is termed "distinct. Each term,
according to its own specific meaning, is likewise not contradictory.
Regarding the characteristics of *geya* (verses),
the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* and other treatises explain it in common terms:
it refers to those passages within various sūtras that are restated in verse, either in the middle or at the end [of the prose exposition].
Thereupon, he further versified the meaning of the preceding prose.
It is also said: "Sūtras of provisional meaning (neyārtha) should be further versified and explained."
Although the meaning has been explained in the prose (*gadya*), it is not yet exhaustive;
it is subsequently versified (*geya*).
For these two reasons, it is called "Verses" (*geya*).
First, it is for the benefit of those with sharp faculties who arrive later;
second, it is to clarify and purify the understanding of those listening to the Dharma by revealing that what preceded was of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is only this first sense.
The second volume of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Either the Buddha himself spoke it,
or his disciples spoke it."
It is intended to make the principles firm and prevent them from dispersing,
like flowers strung on a thread in a fixed and stable order;
furthermore, it is for the sake of adorning the words so that they may be pleasing.
Furthermore, the meaning [of this] is incorporated into the verse so that it may be concise and easily understood.
Regarding the characteristics of the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and other texts state:
This refers to those instances where the noble disciples and others are informed regarding their past lives and the distinctions between their gains and losses concerning the places of rebirth;
this is based on the Blessed One’s prophetic declarations concerning the future births of his disciples.
This records the causes and effects.
Furthermore, various treatises state:
"Moreover, the definitive sūtras (nītārtha-sūtra) are called vyākaraṇa (explanations)."
It is called "vyākaraṇa" (prediction/elucidation) because it reveals the profound, hidden intention (*saṃdhi*). "Vyā" means clarity;
"karaṇa" means differentiation (*vibhāga*).
The explicit explanation (*vyākaraṇa*) of the profound and secret meaning is called *vyākaraṇa*.
As for what is stated elsewhere— that sūtras of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) are called *vyākaraṇa*—
it means that they are termed "interpretable" because they provide a brief, summary explanation using few words.
This does not rely on explicit statements regarding the profound meaning.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgata bestows predictions upon all great beings."
"Ānanda, in the future there will be a king named Kakutsunda;
in that world he shall attain buddhahood and be named Maitreya.
This is a *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy) sutra.
According to the statements of various teachings, the term "vyākaraṇa" (prediction/prophecy) is generally defined by three meanings:
first, recording the causes and effects regarding the death and rebirth of disciples;
second, clearly and definitively recording profound and esoteric meanings.
Regarding the third record, the matter of the bodhisattvas who shall attain buddhahood:
as for the characteristics of their recitation and chanting, the *Xiányáng* (Manifestation) and other texts state:
This refers to those passages within the various sūtras that are not prose repetitions,
but are instead composed in verse;
they are spoken in units of two lines, three lines, four lines, five lines, six lines, and so forth, and are collectively termed *geya* (verses).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Excluding the *sūtras* and the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*),
all other sayings consisting of four-line verses [are included]."
Commit no evil; practice all that is good;
purify your own mind.
These are the teachings of all Buddhas;
this is called a gāthā-sūtra.
This is what is intended by the statement:
It is not spoken in prose directly,
nor is it based on causes and conditions;
rather, for the sake of others, it takes four-line verses as its primary form.
That which explains various dharmas is called a gāthā.
Since this nirvāṇa also has its own distinct characteristics as a sūtra, why would it not be included here?
Otherwise, how could it be excluded from this [category]?
Because there are only sūtras that possess general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
from those consisting of two short phrases up to those with immeasurable many phrases,
all of them are included.
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, let us cite a single verse as an illustration for instruction;
various treatises raise difficult points regarding those verses that do not complete a full stanza.
Therefore, there are only six [verses].
If there were only a single line, it would not constitute a verse,
as this would be difficult to distinguish from the prose (gadya).
To cite one and a half verses, they are said to consist of six lines;
five or seven may also be obtained,
but these are not mentioned here because they are minor.
Regarding the characteristics of "self-proclamation" (svayam-vāda), the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state:
it refers to those instances in which the requester is not explicitly mentioned.
To cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time and the True Teaching to abide for a long time in the future, he spoke this without being requested;
this is called "Spontaneous Utterance" (Udāna).
As the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
As a verse says:
"If one exerts courageous diligence toward such a Dharma as this..."
One who meditates in tranquility and reflects with discernment is then called a brahmin;
this Buddha [taught this] so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
The long endurance of the True Dharma is its practice and abiding.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"For example, when the Buddha enters meditative concentration in the afternoon..."
When morning dawned and he arose from meditative concentration,
as no one had asked him anything,
he spontaneously preached the Dharma by means of his knowledge of others' minds.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Such sūtras spoken spontaneously without being questioned are called udāna.
Although the specific instances differ, the underlying principle is the same.
Question: Why is it that if the requester remains silent, it does not constitute a formal request for an exposition?
The Tathāgata’s silence was his consent, serving as his answer.
He replied: "There are two kinds of requests: first, that which is made through mental recollection."
Second, the oral proclamation.
Because the activity of oral proclamation is performed with earnestness,
it constitutes a formal request.
However, because the mental intention is slight,
it is not termed a "request" in the sūtras.
There are two answers to this.
First is silence;
second is speech.
However, as long as it causes understanding to arise, it is called an answer.
It is not asked in the same way because it does not take into account the gravity of the offense.
Furthermore, in various sūtras, the Buddha, knowing their thoughts,
immediately preached the Dharma for them.
Therefore, although there are no words, it is still called "requesting.
It is essential to manifest the gravity of the speech to grant it the name of a request;
silence alone does not constitute a request.
He asked again:
"Since there already exists the *Aṅguttara-nikāya* (the Sūtra of Questions and Self-Explanations),
why is there not a *Saṃyukta-nikāya* (the Sūtra of Questions without Answers)?"
The answer is: Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, only those that expound the Dharma constitute sūtras.
Those that contain questions and answers constitute sūtras;
those that lack such exposition do not constitute sūtras.
If there were questions but no answers, it would not constitute a sūtra.
However, from the perspective of principle,
those [teachings] that employ the "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) response are also called sūtras.
Furthermore, in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, both of these are absent;
fragrance serves as the Buddha-work,
and there is no need for verbal preaching to establish the sūtras.
In this land, the Tathāgata’s voice constitutes the Buddha-work;
therefore, the absence of a response does not prevent it from being established as a sūtra.
Furthermore, the twelve divisions of the sūtras are not designated as "sūtras" solely because they involve questions.
Therefore, there is the *Aparapṛcchā-svayaṃbhāṣita-sūtra*.
As for the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are explained in eighty-one [discourses].
This refers to teaching the various dharmas based on a specific request,
as stated in a sutra:
"At one time, the World-Honored One [taught] based on Kṛṣṇamṛgāputra."
He proclaimed the essential points of the Dharma for the bhikṣus,
and further, according to the path arising from the cause of the Prātimokṣa,
he delivered all the discourses comprised within the Vinaya.
Furthermore, in this context, it is stated as follows:
"The Blessed One, based on such and such causes and conditions,
and based on such and such matters..."
To speak such and such words— this,
possessing three meanings, is called "causal condition" (*nidāna*).
First, it is spoken at the request [of others].
Second, the formulation of precepts due to transgressions;
third, the teaching of the Dharma according to specific circumstances.
These should be understood in their respective order.
The *Abhidharma* treatises contain only the first two [of these three],
while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* contains only the last one.
The *Abhidharma* treatises state:

Furthermore, there are causes and conditions for the establishment of the training rules (śikṣāpada).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Just as in various sūtras and verses, there is a fundamental basis.
For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a man who caught birds in a net and then released them.
The World-Honored One, knowing the beginning, end, and causal conditions of this matter, spoke these verses:
"Do not disregard small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity.

Regarding the characteristics of similes,

there are twenty-five words;
that is to say, within this there is an exposition by way of analogy.

the eighty-first [fascicle] states:

This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound).
If the fundamental essence (*mūlatattva*) is identical to the phenomenon, and the fundamental essence is identical to arising,

Fourth, regarding the general and the specific: in this context, for the sake of a preliminary discussion based on various teachings, there are both general and specific [distinctions].

Within the distinct [characteristics], nine [categories] are included, excluding only two verses.
This single line of the gateway [of practice] pairs one [element] with the rest.
That which has already been explained in detail need not be stated again below;
all this should be understood.
Furthermore, within the *geya* (verses), there are also *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies).
Although there is no explicit textual permission, there is scriptural evidence;
as the *Lotus Sūtra* states:

Passages such as these appear in various places more than once.
Therefore, there are also *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies) within the *geya* (verses).
Because these verses repeat the meaning of the preceding prose (*gadya*),
there are three types of *vyākaraṇa*.
First, recording the causes and effects of the birth and death of his disciples;
second, recording profound meanings;
third, recording the attainment of Buddhahood.
This is precisely the *geya* (verses);

As for the remaining two types of *vyākaraṇa*, they may or may not be present depending on the specific case.
Within the *geya* (verses), there is certainly no *geya* in the sense of chanting;

Therefore, within the *geya* (verses), there are also "self-expositions," such as those concerning prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth,
because there is no one who requests them.
Within the *geya* (verses), there is the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
There are three types of dependent origination:
first, that which is taught in response to a request.
Second, because of transgressions, he established the precepts;
third, because of specific circumstances,
he preached the Dharma, such as in the section on the One Vehicle in the first fascicle of the Lotus Sūtra.
Because Śāriputra had earnestly requested three times,
the World-Honored One had already finished explaining it in prose;
he now speaks it once more for the sake of further repetition.
The remaining two types of dependent origination may or may not be present according to the circumstances.
Within the *geya* (verses), there are logical arguments and parables,
such as the burning house and the impoverished son.
Since the parable of the conjured city and others are all restatements,
there must be an underlying original event within the *geya* (verses).
It is stated in the Introduction Chapter: Mañjuśrī said,
"After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you are the one who was indolent."
The Dharma Master Wonderful Light was none other than my own self in this present life.

"At that time, those who heard the Dharma were each in the presence of various Buddhas;

I gradually taught them the Buddha-way;

Therefore, there must certainly be original narratives (nidāna) within the *geya* [section],

For this reason, he encountered countless Buddhas.
Since the account of the Buddha Akṣobhya’s past lives has already been told,

Within the *geya* (verses), there is the principle of the *vaipulya* (extensive teachings).

Within the *Geya* (Verses), there is a principle of rare and marvelous phenomena.

5. The Fifth Section on Abolition and Establishment:
Why are only twelve divisions of the teaching established?
Neither increasing nor decreasing.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because it is what those capable of hearing the Dharma ought to hear."
This is explained generally according to the three vehicles.
Since the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs in three cycles, there are twelve aspects in total;
because the categories of the teachings that express these aspects are divided into twelve, [the wheel is said to have twelve aspects].
Furthermore, because one enters the twelve bases by means of breaking down the twelve links [of dependent origination],
the teaching of the Dharma is likewise divided into twelve parts.
This is the general refutation and establishment.
As for the specific refutation and establishment,
such is the sacred teaching.
The prose and verse are paired as a gateway,

the Path is the function of abandonment;
and the hindrances are that which is to be abandoned.
Therefore, the ninth chapter of the Abhidharma explains the threefold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*) as follows:

"That which is to be abandoned, that which abandons, and the nature of abandonment— these three aspects of the transformation of the basis are called 'cessation' (*prahāṇa*) in the context of ultimate truth."
The severance of hindrances is called "severing hindrances" (*āvaraṇa-prahāṇa*);
this is also an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound, as it fulfills all three [criteria for such a compound].
Only then can it be established as the designation "obstruction-severing.
2. Determining the Essential Nature: Second, regarding the determination of the essential nature:

the obstructions to be severed take as their essential nature the active manifestations and seeds of the two obstructions, along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the karmic fruits thereof.
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"What is abandoned by insight?
It refers to all defiled views and doubt that arise from conceptual construction."
And the bases of views and the bases of doubt,
and so forth, as well as the bodily and vocal actions originated by views and the rest.
Furthermore, all aggregates, elements, and bases of the evil destinities and so forth are abandoned by vision; that is,
the three evil destinies are abandoned by the path of vision.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, fascicle three, states:
"Ignorance regarding the afflictions of the miserable realms is abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*)."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:
"This refers to the karmic fruits and so forth of the evil destinies;
[it is] nirvāṇa without remainder."
Since it is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
all karmic fruits belonging to the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are to be abandoned.
Furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
The second stage abandons two kinds of delusion.
These two refer to the delusion regarding various karmic destinies.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains:
This refers precisely to the three types of karma arising from erroneous transgressions;
therefore, the karmic fruits produced by the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are likewise all to be abandoned.
This is stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
All phenomena, such as the karma and its results produced by the two obstacles,
are subsumed within those two obstacles;
thus, one should know that the two obstacles constitute grasping.
Furthermore, both the afflictions and karma, along with their fruits—all that is tainted (*sāsrava*)—are to be abandoned.
However, the essence of what is to be abandoned is that which is defiled by nature; it is this that should be abandoned.
Non-defiled karmic fruits are all free from bondage and severed;
because of this, it is said that the seeds of the two obstacles are what are termed "severed" and "abandoned.
Non-defiled outflows are termed "discarded" and "renounced."
The substance that is capable of severing hindrances has the three types of wisdom as its essence.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:
"There are two kinds of paths capable of transformation."
First is the path of subduing.
This encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths, as well as the three types of wisdom:
preparatory (*prayoga*), fundamental (*maula*), and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
According to what is appropriate, one subdues them either gradually or suddenly;
this indicates that the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) can subdue them gradually,
while the other two types of wisdom can subdue them suddenly.
By the power of this, causing [the afflictions] not to arise is termed "subduing" (*vibhava*).
It does not necessarily require the six modes of practice.
If one proceeds toward the ultimate fruit, one can subdue the various afflictions through the wisdom cultivated by means of the six modes of practice.
Because the wisdom of application (prayoga-jñāna) subsumes the progression toward the ultimate fruit;

if one does not progress toward the ultimate fruit, the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanā-jñāna) that can suppress the various afflictions through the six modes of practice is not the wisdom of application.
This consists solely of the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), not the wisdoms born of hearing or reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*).
It is the path capable of abandonment,
meaning it can eternally sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obscurations.
This path is certainly neither contaminated (*sāsrava*) nor preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*).
This is because contaminated knowledge has already been practiced previously,
and its characteristics have not yet been extinguished.
Because the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) has not yet accomplished the realization it seeks,
there are briefly two explanations regarding uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). According to one interpretation,
it is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Because the realization of the principle of emptiness is devoid of objective characteristics, it can sever the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); this is not the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
According to another interpretation, it is the subsequently attained wisdom.
Although they have not realized the principle of emptiness and thus lack the power to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that obscure that principle,
they nevertheless clearly perceive and unerringly realize the characteristics of both the established (*vyavasthāna*) and the non-established (*avyavasthāna*).
It is also able to permanently sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding delusion concerning phenomena.
This is established at length in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, as cited therein. By this reasoning:
All afflictions of wrong views and the latent tendencies (anuśaya) deluded regarding the principle that are abandoned through the path of cultivation are severed solely by fundamental wisdom,
because it directly realizes the principle.
The remaining latent tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation that are deluded regarding phenomena are severed by both types of knowledge;
these pertain to the two vehicles and not to the stage of a bodhisattva.
Because Bodhisattvas do not sever the delusions regarding phenomena (vastu-moha) while on the path of causes;
because they sever the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) simultaneously with the vajra-like mind;
and furthermore, because within the cognitive obstructions there are also those that are delusions regarding phenomena but are not characterized by grasping.
The post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva also abandons [these obstacles].
Although there are two interpretations, the latter interpretation is superior;
thus, it is able to abandon the obstacles to the path through all three types of knowledge (*tri-jñāna*).
It consists solely of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), not hearing (*śruta*) or reflection (*cintā*). It encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This refers to the four paths within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that suppress the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is not so; hearing and reflection can also suppress [the afflictions], while wisdom alone has the nature of severing them.
Its essence is the suchness (tathatā) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
Alternatively, if one follows the conventional view, its essence is cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Because the three vehicles equally attain this cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
were it otherwise, there would be no liberation.
3. Analysis Based on Consciousness: The third [section], the analysis based on consciousness.
Among these, there are three [points].
First, as for which consciousnesses the objects of abandonment reside in:
according to the Sarvāstivādins and others, those to be abandoned are common to all six consciousnesses.
According to the Vātsīputrīya school, that which is abandoned exists only in the sixth [consciousness],
because the five consciousnesses are not defiled.
According to the Mahāyāna, that which is abandoned...
According to Sthiramati, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are excluded from the seventh consciousness and reside in the remaining seven;
the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are excluded from the eighth consciousness and reside in the other consciousnesses.
This constitutes their distinction.
According to the Dharma-protector masters,
both obstacles pertain to the preceding seven consciousnesses; however,
their modes of grasping differ.
The karma produced by the hindrances arises only from the first six consciousnesses;
the seventh consciousness, not being of the nature of karma itself,
cannot produce karma.
The fruit resides in the other seven consciousnesses, not in the seventh consciousness,
because it is not produced by another.
This refers to that which arises through the force of maturation (*vipāka*), sovereign (*adhipati*), and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) karma.
It is not a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Regarding the path capable of abandoning [defilements],
according to the Sarvāstivāda, it is exclusively the sixth consciousness.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:

"One should know that [the attainment] occurs in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) at the time of detachment from desire and at the time of falling away. This is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises.
The Mahāsāṃghika and other four schools, as well as the Mahīśāsaka school,
maintain that all six consciousnesses are capable of severing the obstacles to the Path;
for they teach that the five bodies of consciousness can be free from defilement.
The Vātsīputrīyas say that it is only the sixth consciousness;
they maintain that the five groups of sensory consciousness are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because they are neither defiled nor free from defilement.
The masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* maintain that it is not the six consciousnesses;
rather, consciousness is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is only by relying on the wisdom of the final momentary mental state of the fourth dhyāna that one correctly abandons [the afflictions].
The Mahāyāna exists solely within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
because neither its suppression nor its abandonment occurs elsewhere;
this applies to both regression and the departure from desire.
The first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that because it is the sixth unique karma (*āveṇika-karman*),
other consciousnesses are incapable of performing it.
It is said that it is not so, because the arising of the knowledge of equality is induced by others.
Third, if it were of a nature capable of severing [afflictions].
Only the ninth consciousness is [the true nature], because it is the true nature of consciousness;
it is not a dependent consciousness.
4. Analysis by Way of the Path (Mārga-vibhāga).
This refers to the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), and the path of advancement (viśeṣa-mārga).
The "application" (prayoga) refers to the application of effort and practice with a longing for the path of abandonment.
The "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) refers to that which can directly abandon the afflictions without any interval.
The "liberation" (vimukti) refers to the realization of unconditioned liberation.
Those who progress further cultivate other superior paths;
these four are all common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Which path is able to abandon the afflictions?
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:
"When those of the two vehicles, whose faculties are dull,
gradually sever the obstructions, they must each separately give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)."
Whether applied separately or collectively, these refer to the preparatory (prayoga) and the superior (viśeṣa) stages;
the meaning of this passage is that through the preparatory stage, one proceeds toward abandonment (prahāṇa).
In the higher progress of cultivation, one does not sever the afflictions;
because the faculties are dull, the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation arise such that this cannot immediately constitute the distinct characteristics of the three paths.
Therefore, they arise individually.
The ninth fascicle states:
"Because the mental orientations regarding the period for severing afflictions and realizing extinction differ."
The two paths are established as distinct:
within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one abandons the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that category;
therefore, both the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation are capable of being paths of abandonment.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) are uninterrupted;
liberation consists in the relinquishing of the heavy residues (dausthulya).
Thus, at these two moments, two kinds of paths arise.
When the six impure factors function as the four paths,
any one of the three— suffering, coarseness, or hindrance— serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and any one of the three— tranquility, excellence, or detachment— serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The preparatory (*prayoga*) and progressive (*viśeṣa*) stages are the same as previously described in their general and specific aspects.
Even within the untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) of the two vehicles, the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberated (*vimukti*) moments are distinct;
how much more so for the tainted sixfold practice (*ṣaḍākāra-saṃskāra*), where the uninterrupted and liberated moments are not distinct.
However, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter nine, states:
"The preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths belonging to a subsequent stage are all the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) of the preceding stage."
Why is it that in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* it is called "superior progress" (*viśeṣagamana*) or "distinct"?
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speaks in terms of the characteristics of distinct practice,
whereas the *Abhidharma* speaks in terms of progressing forward according to principle.
This is not contradictory.
If one follows this principle,
then [practices such as] distinct meditations, mutual empowerment, and the path of conduct [are likewise included].
Whether generally or specifically, as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
if it is a treatise on reasoning that can lead to subsequent stages, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*).
The preceding chapter explains liberation as well as the subsequent preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"In the stage where a bodhisattva of sharp faculties gradually abandons the hindrances..."

It is not necessary to separately give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), because [the abandonment and realization] can occur moment by moment. Thus, there are four [paths],
beginning with the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).
Moment by moment, as each preceding and succeeding instant is compared with the next, all [aspects] are capable of being fully present.
This is based on the Bodhisattva’s possession of sharp faculties;
thus, in every thought-moment, their modes of activity are able to be complete, differing from those of the three vehicles.
If it were not so, by what principle would the two vehicles be distinguished?
Based on this teaching,
all paths— whether contaminated or uncontaminated— of the two vehicles and other ordinary beings [are included].

In all cases, it is only the path of uninterrupted application (*ānantarya-mārga*) that directly abandons and suppresses the afflictions; within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it abandons and suppresses the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*).
It is not said that the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) or advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) possess this capacity.
For a bodhisattva with sharp faculties, all four paths— both with outflows and without outflows—
are capable of either suppressing or abandoning [the afflictions].
Suppressing them merely obstructs their manifest activity.
Cessation also extends to karma and its fruit;
alternatively, both may extend to them.
Cessation necessarily involves the realization of the Truth.
Subduing is not necessarily so;
when a bodhisattva subdues hindrances,
they also subdue them upon realizing the truth.
Those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings are not necessarily able to do so;
however, there is a distinction.
When the four contaminated paths first arise:
There is an interpretation that all three types of wisdom constitute preparatory cultivation (*prayoga-bhāvanā*), yet wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) is the most immediate.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma* states:
"The path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) also suppresses the afflictions."
The resolution that realizes characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedanādhimokṣa*) has not yet severed the afflictions; it is only through the stage of detachment (*viveka*) that they are severed.
According to one interpretation, the initial stages consist of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
When one subsequently enters into cultivation, it is precisely the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that can subdue the afflictions;

thus, the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* and other treatises state that the two types of attention— namely, "comprehending characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manaskāra*) and "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika-manaskāra*)— do not subdue the afflictions.
Because the first three grades have been abandoned but not yet fully exhausted,
it is described as "abandonment through distancing";
in reality, however, these are merely suppressed.
If one observes with true insight at the time of entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
the wisdom of the preceding six stages does not subdue [the afflictions],
because there is no sense of joy or aversion.
The preparatory application (prayoga) is able to subdue [the afflictions] because it is immediately followed by the untainted (anāsrava) state;
for within the tainted path (sāsravamārga), there is no such suppression.
It has not yet reached the state of the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*). At a later time, it also involves the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This refers to the initial arising of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
It must necessarily be attained at the beginning of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) by means of contaminated cultivated wisdom (*sāsrava bhāvanāmayī prajñā*),
because it is through the uncontaminated [wisdom] that afflictions are severed.
At a later time, one also attains the uncontaminated path of preparation.
However, preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*) itself consists of four paths,
and within these four paths it naturally encompasses three types of knowledge; therefore,
although preparatory knowledge is absent from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, [it is not entirely absent from the path].
There are four paths, as analyzed in the usual manner.
Fifth, the analysis based on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the analysis based on contemplation:
There are ten kinds of contemplation:
first, consciousness-only;
second, the emptiness of both [subject and object].
Three kinds of threefold wisdom;
four kinds of threefold knowledge;
five kinds of four foundations of mindfulness.
Sixth, the five patiences;
seventh, the six clear realizations;
eighth, the seven mental attentions.
Regarding the nine factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eighteenfold noble path (*āryamārga*),
the manner in which consciousness alone (*vijñaptimātra*) eliminates the hindrances has already been explained as before.
The second is the emptiness of both [person and phenomena]. This is the contemplation of the emptiness of persons,
which severs only the afflictive obscurations and their karmic results.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not severed because they are observed as coarse; however,
it is said that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) severs the heavy impediments (*dausthulya*).
Briefly, there are two interpretations:
first, that it refers to Bodhisattvas and not to the Two Vehicles;
second, that there are two types of *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness).
There are two types: coarse and subtle.
Now, while the subtle is not abandoned, the coarse can be eliminated.
Therefore, entering the second dhyāna is called the abandonment of the coarse heaviness of the faculty of suffering.
Because the two vehicles do not sever the subtle [afflictions], it is said that they do not sever them.
The contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) has three stages;
at both the initial and final stages, the contemplation of phenomena is able to sever both obstacles simultaneously.
Whether it be karma and its fruit,
all habitual tendencies,
or the realms of the miserable destinies, humans, and devas.
Accordingly, they are to be permanently abandoned.

Through the middle stage, the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one abandons only the active manifestations and seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), as well as all the latent dysfunctions (*dausthulya*) within both obstructions.
It is able to sever all categories of cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa), whether coarse or subtle.

That is to say, the subtle contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmaśūnyatā) during the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the ten stages necessarily entails the emptiness of persons (pudgalaśūnyatā); therefore, both are severed simultaneously.
Regarding the three types of wisdom that subdue [afflictions]: if one discusses their capacity for subduing and severing, all three are capable;
as for subduing through the power of their respective spheres of influence, this applies to both hearing and reflection.

It is not suppressed by correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). At the time of suppression by correct contemplation, it constitutes the four paths (*mārga*) and exists solely within the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
Nevertheless, even in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), by gathering and withdrawing the mind from its coarseness, one also suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one is able to abandon [afflictions] during the stages of hearing and reflection,

this is exclusively the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because the *Saṃgrahaṇī* explains it as the supramundane wisdom of calm abiding and insight (*lokottara-śamatha-vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are all able to endure, able to contemplate, and able to maintain [the Dharma].
Vasubandhu’s commentary explains:
This refers to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since they are explained in terms of the simultaneous practice of the ultimate and conventional truths,
what prevents hearing and reflection from also being able to sever and suppress [afflictions]?
Others are unable to do so;
this occurs in the higher realms,
not in the desire realm.
Regarding the four [types of] knowledge of the three [times]:
they subdue [afflictions] through the three knowledges;
their abandonment is not through preparatory effort.
The distinction between the gradual and the sudden has already been clarified as previously discussed.
The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that extinguishes present afflictions is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)."
The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that extinguishes future afflictions is called the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
These two types of wisdom are distinguished according to the great temporal stages of the initial and final moments of severing delusions regarding both principles (*tattva*) and phenomena (*vastu*).
In reality, both knowledges—exhaustion and non-arising—are [the truth].
Furthermore, as there is no scriptural authority for it, there is no need to reconcile [these views].
Regarding the five or four foundations of mindfulness:
Although the Mahāyāna does not practice the specific modes of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
its underlying principle is nonetheless subsumed under the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas;
it is a foundation of mindfulness that takes objects collectively, rather than one characterized by individual marks.
The contemplation that takes all phenomena as its object (*sarvālambana-dharmānupaśyanā*) is able to sever all afflictions,
as this is consistent across all texts; since the contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*) both take all phenomena as their objects, [they likewise possess this capacity].
Therefore, there is no contradiction;
otherwise, it would be merely suffering,
which would indeed constitute a contradiction.
Sixth is the patience of endurance (*kṣānti*). This refers to the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*) up to the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*).
The patience of subduing does not sever [afflictions] but is only able to suppress the obstructions.
The others are both abandoned and suppressed.
True outflow-free abandonment suppresses through the power of its functional influence.
Nevertheless, although there are also Buddhas within the state of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), [they do not manifest].
This is not included among the [afflictions] to be abandoned;
for since the stages of the path of the bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis are so extensive,
they involve both the abandonment and the suppression [of afflictions].
Regarding the seven and six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*):
the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) can only suppress [defilements] but cannot sever them,
because it pertains to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Faith, wisdom, the truths, and the precepts are included among the "limbs" (aṅga) that suppress and abandon [defilements].
The right abandonments and the auxiliary abandonments both receive the name "abandonment.
Faith also extends to the untainted (anāsrava).
Because it severs the afflictions associated with the extremes (*antagrāha*).
If one were to follow the *Abhidharmakośa*, the extreme [view] would consist only of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and thus could not sever them.
Now, the *Yogācārabhūmi* is taken as authoritative.
The ultimate contemplation is not [the object],
because it has already been abandoned previously.
This refers to the eight or seven modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
First, the characteristic of comprehension;
second, resolute conviction;
third, detachment.
Fourth, the stage of delighting in practice;
fifth, the stage of observation;
sixth, the stage of the culmination of application.
Seventh is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*).
If one follows the *Abhidharma* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they differ regarding the nine and seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The Eighteen Noble Paths. 6.
Analysis According to Practice. Regarding the analysis according to practice, there are three kinds of practice.
1. The practice of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
2. The six practices beginning with suffering and coarseness; 3.
The sixteen practices of the Four Noble Truths.
One who practices emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
If [these] are subdued, they all become penetrating.
The second fascicle of the *Fǎxiàn lùn* (*Abhidharmasamudaya-śāstra*) states:
If one speaks only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
they apply universally to both meditative concentration and the distracted state, as well as to both the tainted and the untainted.
The wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
or if one speaks of the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
these are exclusively concentrated and not distracted.
It is cultivated solely through meditation, not through hearing or reflection;
it encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
If one speaks of the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—[they are likewise so].
Since it is cultivated exclusively as untainted (*anāsrava*) and is subsumed solely within meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
we know that all three gates are capable of suppressing afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, the actual suppression of afflictions occurs only through the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By relying on the gate of the two emptinesses, one enters the stage of the Mahāyāna;
by contemplating the principle of the Four Noble Truths, one enters the stage of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, it encompasses all three practices.
This stage occurs within the four wholesome preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Regarding the correct abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*),
the various texts of the Mahāyāna present differing explanations.
Alternatively, it is said that among the sixteen aspects, two aspects constitute emptiness,
and ten aspects constitute wishlessness because they are conditioned.
The four practices are signless because they are unconditioned.
Some say they are empty as previously described.
The six courses of action are wishless because they are with outflows;
the eight courses of action are signless.
Because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Some say that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is as previously described,
while the six practices constitute the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
The four practices are signless (*animitta*).
The path consists of four [factors] and not three gates;
because it is not the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it is not empty (*śūnya*).
Because it is not with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is not "wishless" (*apraṇihita*);
because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not "signless" (*animitta*).
This is stated in the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
Two are emptiness;
six are wishlessness;
four are signlessness.
As before, the Path has four aspects and three functions;
for the Path is able to act as three gates.
They are subsumed under three gates.
Some say that the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) extends through all sixteen aspects;
the practices of wishlessness (*apranihita*) and signlessness (*animitta*) correspond accordingly to the same [categories] as before.
Some say that emptiness is not a truth to be cultivated through cultivation,
because it is the observation of what is grasped;
the other two [emptinesses] are, as appropriate, observations of the four truths.
Because the substance of the two natures is not fixed,
some say that all three gates penetrate all sixteen aspects;
regarding the meaning of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), they distinguish three gates within its contemplation.
The meanings are divided into sixteen.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, among its five categories of phenomena (*pañcadharma*), states:
"If one speaks in terms of the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*):"
It is subsumed by supramundane right knowledge.
Furthermore, the eighth fascicle of the *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"The three gates and the principle of the three natures are in reality all pervasive."
One immediately gives rise to the three gates regarding the ultimate truth.
Because there are these three gates, it is known that all [factors] penetrate the sixteen aspects.
Because the principles are differentiated within true contemplation,
if one practices separately,
one mostly employs only the gate of emptiness to sever delusions.
Because both types of self are empty,
this is the contemplation of emptiness as a universal object, not as a specific mode of emptiness.
This is because those who practice emptiness separately [realize] only the Truth of Suffering.
The meaning of the three gates is as explained in other places;
they should be subsumed accordingly within the two [wisdoms]: the fundamental and the subsequently attained.
There is no obstruction regarding the principle of abandonment and suppression.
As for the six modes of practice, such as the two types of suffering and so forth,
these six modes exist only within the stage of mundane expedient means (*sāsrava-upāya-bhūmi*).
Contemplating any one of the lower realm’s suffering, coarseness, or obstruction serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Contemplating any one of the upper realm’s tranquility, excellence, or detachment serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
These merely suppress the afflictions; they are not capable of severing them.
This applies to both ordinary beings and sages;
it pertains to those of the two vehicles and not to bodhisattvas.
A bodhisattva on the ten stages does not delight in the higher or feel aversion toward the lower.
Because it concerns taking birth,
the *Maulī Bhūmi* states that during the first eon,
the Bodhisattva’s initial stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) likewise employs the six practices.
However, since those who have practiced for a long time do not abandon their afflictions yet are born in the higher realms,
this [attainment] is not considered superior.
Nevertheless, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 69, states:
It is said that noble ones do not employ the six modes of conduct;
this is stated according to the majority case,
for in reality they do employ them as well.
The thirty-six modes of practice likewise only suppress [the afflictions] and do not eradicate them;
when entering true contemplation, they are no longer the sixteen modes of practice.

Because it is the path of seeing the marks (*lakṣaṇa-mārga*), and because one cultivates skillful means during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), it is not the correct, ultimate contemplation;
the Bodhisattva brings both forth concurrently.
The correct application of the Two Vehicles consists solely of that which is untainted (anāsrava), which is not attainable by ordinary beings.
Nevertheless, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:
For a śrāvaka of sharp faculties,
the first moment of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*),
characterized by the practice of non-self (*anātman*), universally severs the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) underlying the four noble truths within the three realms.
Śrāvakas of dull faculties possess sixteen modes of practice;
they sever the eighty-eight fetters beneath the four noble truths of the three realms individually,
distinguishing them further by dividing them into upper and lower, as well as sharp and dull.
This is not something to be realized or employed within the Mahāyāna;
there is no need to reconcile it with our system.
The Vātsīputrīya school asserts that there are thirteen types of mind.
The Truth of Suffering has three aspects:
first, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), which contemplates the suffering of the desire realm;
second, the vision regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-darśana*), which re-contemplates the suffering of the desire realm to examine thoroughly whether it has been exhausted or not.
Third is the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).

It is observed by synthesizing the two [truths] above, as there is no further suffering beyond them and thus no need for repeated observation. Thus, there are three [moments of knowledge] for each of the four truths.
Thus, twelve [moments] are established.
The first twelve moments of mind are called "practicing toward" (pratipannaka),
while the thirteenth moment of mind is called "abiding in the fruit" (phalastha).
This is not what our school maintains;
there is no need for further analysis.
7. The Seventh Chapter: Analysis According to the Bases (*Āśraya-vibhāga*). Regarding the analysis according to the bases:
An ancient master said:
"Some say that because the real manifests as the false, there is no falsity to be severed; thus they do not speak of 'categories' (pinda)."
Some say that throughout the three *kalpas*, one severs hindrances moment by moment and attains wisdom moment by moment;
thus said the Dharma Master Guji.
The noble path consists of nine grades, and its abandonment likewise consists of nine grades;
however, this is not the case here.
Within the seven consciousnesses, there exist both afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations.
Within the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), excluding the seventh consciousness,
the remaining six consciousnesses— each belonging to the three realms and nine stages—
are each divided into nine grades, totaling eighty-one.
The ten afflictions of the path of seeing are fixed in nine grades because of their differences in coarseness and subtlety; however,
the abandonment of the six innate afflictions is not uniform.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and their associated factors belong exclusively to the ninth category.
In terms of the nine stages (*bhūmi*), there are only nine categories.
Hatred (*pratigha*) belongs to only one stage and has nine categories.
The remaining eighty-one categories of independent greed, pride, ignorance, and so forth—
since there are nine grades for each level—
and the afflictive hindrances within the seventh consciousness across the nine levels, also have two different explanations.
There is an interpretation that the nine stages are identical only to the ninth category of the Non-ideation [heaven];
however, within those, there are nine distinct types of their own kind,
just as superior wrong views can sever the roots of goodness.
There are also nine grades;
those [attainments] are likewise,
differing only in that they share the same ninth grade as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
It is only when the vajra-like [samādhi] of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) arises that it is finally severed.
Because it possesses nine grades, its substance undergoes increase and decrease;
therefore, it becomes a perfuming agent (vāsanā).
According to one interpretation, there is one category for each of the nine stages;
when subdivided, these constitute eighty-one categories.

The power of the afflictions obstructed by these is identical to that of the lowest-of-the-low (adhamādhamā) category of afflictions in the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Therefore, the vajra-mind severs [the afflictions] all at once.
For this reason, it is said that once the categories of the afflictions have been severed,
one should speak by way of further differentiation.
Within the first six consciousnesses, nine grades [of afflictions] are distinguished;
however, for all three vehicles, the abandonment is definitively of only one grade,
namely, through the single-moment path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Some say that there are two types of abandonment: namely, the abandonment through the three minds of the path of seeing and so forth,
which consists solely of untainted right abandonment (*anāsrava-samyak-prahāṇa*) and not the abandonment by suppression (*vibhāvana-prahāṇa*).
Because the various mundane paths with outflows do not suppress the afflictions of views,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The mundane path is able only to suppress and eliminate innate afflictions."
Yet one is unable to subdue the afflictions of conceptual discrimination,
as well as the innate view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and its associated pride and arrogance;
this relies upon the six modes of practice.
It is not preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*), because that [knowledge] is capable of suppressing [the afflictions].
Even the conceptual activity (*vikalpa*) that manifests prior to the Bodhisattva stages is suppressed and does not arise.
It is not due to the six modes of practice;
rather, because the power of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and so forth does not operate,
the afflictions of discrimination within the six consciousnesses [arise].
Although the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are likewise of nine grades,
they are nonetheless abandoned definitively in either one or two grades.
Within the abandonment of two grades, which of the nine grades is abandoned first and which is abandoned later?
As stated in the ninth section of the *Xia shuyao* (Essential Points of the Lower Part) of the treatise:
among the six consciousnesses, the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*),
even when excluding their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), consist of nine grades.
The manner of abandonment differs.
Briefly stated, there are four categories of these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth:
first, abandonment according to the eighty-one distinct classes.
This is based on the gradual abandonment by those of the two vehicles and by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
However, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth are abandoned at the time of the ninth category;
the remaining [afflictions] are each abandoned through nine categories.
Second, according to the extent to which [the afflictions] have already been suppressed during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),

they are subsequently abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) upon entering the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*). It is not by means of what has not been suppressed or what is not abandoned that the categories [of practitioners] are differentiated.
After entering the stage of vision, they are then abandoned sequentially.
Third, the nine stages are combined into nine grades for abandonment,
just as the fruit of stream-entry bundles together all afflictions of the nine stages across the three realms.
In total, there are nine grades of abandonment for the attainment of the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*),
because it is attained through sudden transcendence.
Fourth, the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms are combined into a single grade of abandonment.
This refers to the stage of severance in the Mahāyāna’s adamantine mind (*vajracitta*).
Because afflictions are not severed during the causal phase of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
however, there remain the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the innate afflictions within the six consciousnesses.
Although there are nine grades,
each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) gradually eliminates these [afflictions],
because they obstruct the ten stages.
Because it is of the same category as the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa),
whether the seventh consciousness is said to have nine grades or one grade, it is abandoned in a single grade.
Because the diamond-like mind of the three vehicles must suddenly and instantaneously sever the obstacles to arhatship.
The same applies to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
However, regarding the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is not so;
for although the cognitive obscurations and their habitual tendencies, which are conceptualized within the six consciousnesses, consist of nine grades.
Some say that one category [of afflictions] is abandoned,
because the path of seeing occurs within a single moment of mind.
Others say that two categories are abandoned.
Because the three minds perceive the Path of Seeing,
they are not suppressed by the six classes of conduct in the same manner as the afflictions;
this applies to the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the six consciousnesses, along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
There are likewise nine stages with eighty-one categories.
If they function in conjunction with afflictions, they may also be said to be "suppressed," meaning they do not operate due to the power of another.
Regarding those that do not arise simultaneously:
although there are nine grades, none of them are suppressed by the six practices,
because they obstruct the realization of principle.
The preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*) is able to suppress them, effecting their abandonment in ten stages;
because they are abandoned across the ten grounds (*bhūmi*),
their abandonment is not described by distinguishing between coarse and subtle or by sequential order.
One does not abandon the subtle [afflictions] of the first stage while abandoning the coarse [afflictions] of the second;
rather, the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned at the first stage, and those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are abandoned at the second.
In short, whatever obstructs the wisdom of a particular stage is abandoned precisely at that stage.
Therefore, there is no sequence of before and after.
Although it is said that the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the seventh consciousness consist of nine grades, [they are actually simultaneous].
Alternatively, it is said that there are no categories;
nevertheless, they are abandoned in a single category,
because they are only permanently severed within the diamond-like mind.
This explains the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
it does not explain the abandonment of their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and so forth.

Although the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states that the second grasping consciousness (*dvitīya-grāhaka-vijñāna*)—which permeates the skin and flesh—is abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
However, that text contains errors and cannot be relied upon for practice.
The *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang jing) states:
"The first three stages eliminate the afflictions of form within the triple world."
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one abandons the afflictions of the mind pertaining to the three realms.
In the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, one abandons the afflictions of the habitual tendencies of form pertaining to the three realms.
In the tenth stage and the Buddha stage, one abandons the afflictions of the habitual tendencies of the mind pertaining to the three realms.
Form is coarse and mind is subtle; the arising of delusions is likewise so.
To distinguish the gradations of the five stages of patience, one speaks of the severing of afflictions;
it is not that there exists a separate category [of afflictions].
Nor is there any contradiction. 8.
The Eighth Chapter: Analysis Based on Obstructions. Regarding the analysis based on obstructions, there are nine [sections] therein.
There are two obstacles.
Those of the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*), exhausting both its manifest and latent seeds,
yet they have not exhausted the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
It is also able to permanently sever a small portion of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
yet there is a distinction:
in the gradual path, the first fruit (*phala*) severs only the conceptual afflictions (*vikalpakleśa*) of the three realms.
The gradual attainment of the fruit of once-returning also involves the six grades of the path of cultivation in the desire realm.
A gradual non-returner must necessarily abandon the nine grades of the path of cultivation in the desire realm.
As for the remaining [gradual attainments] up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) across the nine stages, they are not fixed.
Those who attain transcendence (skandhaka) are of indeterminate types.
Those who attain the first fruit through transcendence have either eliminated the afflictions of the desire realm along with five categories [of the path of cultivation],
or those who attain the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) through transcendence have eliminated up to eight categories of the desire realm.

The non-returner who attains transcendence (vyutkrāntaka) cultivates only nine [attainments], excluding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). There are also stream-enterers (srotāpanna) who attain transcendence and do not cultivate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is because both are able to abandon [the defilements] and attain two fruits.
Because even at the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one is still designated as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, however, are able to sever all [afflictions] of the three realms—namely, those of the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), as well as the meditative obstructions (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) and so forth.
Bodhisattvas are able to sever all [obstructions].
Those of the three vehicles are all able to subdue the active manifestation of the two obstructions,
because through such subduing they attain meditative concentration and so forth.
However, regarding the bodhisattva’s subduing [of afflictions], attainment of meditative concentration, and attainment of the fruits,
these are all explained as usual according to the stages of liberation (*vimokṣabhāga*).
Second, the analysis of the three obstacles.
There are three kinds of these three:
first, skin, flesh, and bone.
Second, there are the latent dispositions that accompany harm, the feeble latent dispositions, and the subtle latent dispositions.
These two preceding categories are explained as in the *Vijñaptimātra* chapter.
Third, there are afflictions, karma, and suffering.
All karma and suffering arising from the conceptualization of the two obstacles,
as well as those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), have already been explained above according to the Abhidharma texts.
[However,] all innate (*sahaja*) karma and suffering constitute both obstacles.
Regarding the statement that "afflictions, karma, and suffering never again arise once their permanent antidotes have reached the vajra-like mind": this refers to the stage where,
according to each respective level, the arising of fragmented existence ceases upon reaching the eighth bhūmi.
The non-arising of transformational rebirth exists at the stage of Buddhahood;
this is based on the general meaning.
If, however, specific karmas are severed...
There are four types of karma to be abandoned, such as "black-black" and so forth,
as explained in the commentary on the ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Among these are the dharmas of karma and its results within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The abandonments occur stage by stage throughout the ten stages.
The abandonment of the obscurations and the abandonment of karmic results occur in distinct paths,
because of the distinction between the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
It lies dormant in the eighth stage.
Regarding the three and four obstacles, there are two types of discrimination.
The first refers to those such as icchantikas who lack faith and so forth.
As explained in the "Chapter on Consciousness-Only," there are four types; furthermore,
there are only two obstacles, which are ignorance (*avidyā*).
First, the unshared;
second, the associated;
third, the enveloping.
Regarding the four latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
there are three that are not shared:
first, those that function independently and are not shared.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned solely by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
because in the fourth of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the "Stage of Noble Birth" (*janmakulīnāvasthā*), the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) have already been suppressed.
These two [types of abandonment] correspond to the common and the uncommon.
The ignorance associated with anger and the like comprises both the manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*)— both conceptual and innate— as well as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The stages for their suppression and abandonment are as explained above.
Third is the constant activity that is unique [to this consciousness],
namely that which is associated with the seventh consciousness;
it is severed only by the untainted [path] and not suppressed by the tainted [path].
When entering the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), it is also termed "subduing" (*vibhava*),
because the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) do not arise; thus, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are severed by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
The remaining three are explained according to the preceding discussion on the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The fourfold and fivefold classifications of hindrances refer to the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
First, seeing a single place;
second, craving for sensual desire;
third, craving for form.
Fourth, craving for the formless realms;
fifth, the ground of the abiding of ignorance.
Each of these has two aspects.
Together, these constitute the five active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*);
separately, they constitute the five latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
To perceive them as a single locus is the conceptualized afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The next three are the innate afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
and the final one is the obstruction to all that is knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These should be suppressed and abandoned according to their respective correspondences, following the previous method.

Question: If it is taught that when one enters the vision of a single locus (*ekadeśa-praveśa-darśana*), all differentiated afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned, why does the fifty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) state that greed (*rāga*) is abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*)?
In the second stage, hatred is abandoned;
in the third stage, delusion is abandoned;
and in the fourth stage, views are abandoned.
Regarding the statement that "the fifth stage eliminates doubt," the former masters' interpretation says:
this borrows the distinction between ordinary beings and sages as a metaphor for the ten stages.
From the third stage onward, one accords with the world;
therefore, the three poisons are severed.
In the fourth and fifth stages, one accords with the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Because the first fruit (srotāpanna) abandons views and doubt,
it is said that these are eliminated in the fourth and fifth stages; however,
in reality, they have already been abandoned in the first stage.
Now, "view" refers to the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
because it is abandoned through the four stages [of the path of seeing].
"Doubt" refers to doubt regarding phenomena (*vastu*).
It is neither affliction nor doubt.
Because it arises from the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its companion, it is abandoned in the five stages.
Furthermore, there are six types of distraction.
1. Distraction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*), which refers to the five sense-consciousnesses and so forth.
2. External distraction (*bahirdhā-vikṣepa*).
The five sensory desires cause outward distraction;
the three internal distractions consist of dullness and agitation, as well as attachment to the taste of meditative concentration during the cultivation of fixed samādhi.
Fourth is the distraction of feigning the practice of virtue;
fifth is the distraction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Due to the coarse and powerful force of self-grasping, pride, and so forth,
one clings to pleasure and other states as being "self" and so on;
consequently, the category of wholesome qualities remains forever unpurified.
Sixth is the distraction of mental application (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*).
This refers to the distraction arising when one abandons the previously practiced meditative concentration and enters the concentration of another vehicle;
for "mental application" consists of vitarka and vicāra (initial and sustained application of thought).
As stated in the Abhidharma-prathama,
there are furthermore six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
These six consist of the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
All are as previously explained.
There is a distinction in their opening and closing: namely, the affliction-obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arise solely through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*).
The remaining afflictions are also associated with innate [afflictions] and are abandoned accordingly through both methods.
Furthermore, there are seven outflows (*āsrava*).

These are the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*), the outflow of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-āsrava*), the outflow of craving (*tṛṣṇā-āsrava*), the outflow of mindfulness (*smṛti-āsrava*), the outflow of the faculties (*indriya-āsrava*), the outflow of evil (*pāpa-āsrava*), and the outflow of association (*saṃsevana-āsrava*).
The first two constitute the essence of the outflows,
while the latter five comprise their full extent.
They are abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
this should be understood according to the explanation.
Alternatively, they constitute a single entity.
The latter six constitute the "endowment" (*samanvāgama*),
as explained by their names.
Seventh, the eight types of discrimination give rise to three matters.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the thirty-sixth section of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are three types:
first, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which refers to the grasping of the essence of phenomena as real.

Second, the differentiation; third, the grasping at the meaning of all phenomena as a whole. The grasping at the meaning of all phenomena [is of two kinds]: first, the grasping at particulars; second, the grasping at the meaning of all phenomena as a whole.
One clings to the forest of the army of sentient beings and so forth as "I" and "mine"—
these are the four [types of] "I" and "mine."
Six are pleasant;
seven are unpleasant;
eight are neither.
The first three [mental factors] give rise to the objective referents that serve as the basis for discrimination;
the next two give rise to the objective referents for views and the conceit "I am";
and the final three give rise to the objective referents for greed, hatred, and delusion.
For the most part, these are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); however, according to principle, they may also be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Furthermore, there are eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
That is to say: torpor, drowsiness, restlessness, regret, envy, avarice, lack of shame, and lack of dread.
Because they frequently entangle and disturb the mind, they are abandoned only through cultivation; yet, according to principle, they also pertain to [abandonment by] vision.
Eighth are the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, according to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, there are nine underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Among the nine fetters, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) are abandoned only through the path of vision (*darśana-heya*).
The remaining six fetters are abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the nine underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
the first is the underlying tendency of sensual desire.
1. Latent tendency of hatred; 2.
Latent tendency of ignorance; 3.
The three poisons at the level of the highest degree of mental intensity; 4. The ground of the abode of ignorance.
Six are abandoned through the vision of the truths;
seven are abandoned through cultivation;
eight are the afflictions of the impure stages.
Regarding the afflictions of the nine pure stages (*śuddhabhūmi*):
those of the sixth stage are exclusively views (*darśana*), those of the seventh are exclusively cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
and the remainder pertain to both views and cultivation.
The limits of abandonment are explained according to what is appropriate:
ninth, the ten afflictions and the ten types of distraction.
Furthermore, regarding the first chapter on "Obstacles" in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, one should examine all [the points] according to the sequence of the stages at which they are to be abandoned. 9.
The Ninth Chapter: Analysis of the Basis (*Āśraya-vibhāga*). The Ninth Chapter: Analysis of the Basis.
Within this, there are two [types]:
first, based on the body;
second, based on the stage.
First, regarding the basis of the body:
if one suppresses the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), initially it pertains only to the desire realm,
and subsequently it extends throughout the eight stages of the three realms.
Because one who is born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) no longer suppresses [the afflictions],
the abandonment [of them] applies to all nine stages across the three realms.
This teaching refers to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), not to bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattvas sever their afflictions based solely on bodies in the desire and form realms, not by being born in the formless realm.
This is true for noble bodhisattvas;
it is not so for ordinary beings.
This concludes the general explanation.
To distinguish them specifically:
those of the three vehicles proceed directly toward their respective vehicles.

The abandonment of the two obstacles through analytical discernment occurs only among the six celestial realms and the three continents of the human realm within the desire realm, and not in other places,
because of the intensity of their wisdom and revulsion.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts state:
"Extreme sorrow does not pertain to the evil destinies;
extreme joy does not pertain to the two higher realms."
Only humans and devas of the desire realm [attain] the clear realization when a Buddha appears in the world;
noble ones of the form realm who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle abandon the cognitive obscurations.
It also extends to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Unlike the afflictions, which require a mind of superior revulsion,
this [state] therefore extends to that level.
If one severs the co-emergent afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa),
the bodies of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) pertain to all three realms and nine stages;
as for bodhisattvas, there are two meanings.
The first is common to both the desire and form realms,
because the body retained by one of indeterminate nature belongs to both realms;
the second belongs to the fourth dhyāna of the form realm.
Because those bodhisattvas who proceed directly are born in the abode of the wisdom of Maheśvara.
