Regarding those of indeterminate nature, although there are two explanations in the treatises,
they pertain to both realms.
This explanation is correct:
if one abandons the co-emergent cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
this applies to all five stages of both the desire and form realms, but not to the formless realm.
Because Bodhisattvas are not born in the formless realm.
Second, regarding the basis of the stages:
if one suppresses the afflictive obscurations.

The six stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the four stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) can all be suppressed by both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and fundamental (*maula*) [attainments],
because both the six types of cultivation and the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path] are capable of suppressing them.
The six modes of cultivation consist solely of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
The seven mental orientations (*manasikāra*) pertain to both the fundamental stage (*maula*) and the preparatory stage,
because the seventh mental orientation enters into the fundamental stage.
The untainted [path] subdues it.
The six stages of the form realm do not possess the three types of expedient means;
however, within the four stages of the formless realm, wherever there is an untainted state, one is able to subdue it.
Because it subdues their momentum so that they do not arise.
As for "correctly abandoning," the followers of the Two Vehicles abandon the afflictive obstacles of conceptual discrimination.
It relies solely on the five stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because the wisdom of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) therein is necessarily sharp and intense;
thus, although there may be untainted true paths in the intermediate stages, they do not enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The wisdom of the formless realm is inferior and is not a path for abandoning afflictions;
this is because the *Ṣaṣṭitantra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sixty-nine) states that the path of seeing exists only in five stages.
Furthermore, it arises based on three or five stages.
This is because it is not stated that there is a path of seeing (darśanamārga) in the intermediate state.
If the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are severed, they pertain to all nine stages:
six in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and three in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 100, states:
"The nine stages are able to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*);
namely, the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)."
This means that the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is not the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Furthermore, because it is said to arise based on three or five supports,
and because the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is obscured by darkness, it cannot eliminate the afflictions.
If a bodhisattva eliminates the two obstacles through discrimination,
it is because the merit of the fourth dhyāna alone is supreme; thus,
they enter the path of seeing by relying upon that superior basis.
If one abandons the co-emergent cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) along with the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
it occurs throughout the six form realms and the three formless realms;
if one abandons the co-emergent afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it occurs only in the fourth dhyāna.
Because one enters the abandonment of afflictions by means of the adamantine mind based on the fourth dhyāna,
as explained at length in the treatise;
fearing prolixity, I shall not describe it here.
10. The Tenth Section: Analysis through Question and Answer. Regarding the analysis through question and answer:
it is asked, among the three periods of time, at which point is this abandonment of afflictions said to occur?
The answer is that the explanations provided by the Sarvāstivādins and others differ.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58, states:
"It is not that the past, future, and present are annihilated."
However, it is said that the abandonment of the three time periods does not apply to the past,
because the mind accompanied by latent dispositions (anuśaya) ceases spontaneously;
since its nature has already ceased to exist, what is there to be abandoned?
The future nature has not yet arisen;
since its manifestation is non-existent, what is there to be abandoned?
As for the present, there is the mind accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
After this moment, the nature [of the mind] necessarily does not persist;
what else, then, remains to be abandoned?
Furthermore, there is no conjunction between the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the mind free from latent dispositions.
Therefore, it is also not something to be abandoned in the present.
Nevertheless, due to the two conditions of the sounds of another’s speech and internal correct mental attention (*manasikāra*),
a mind that serves as the antidote to the afflictions to be countered arises, conjoined with right view.
When the mind that is the object of abandonment— the mind accompanied by latent tendencies—
ceases, and this [antidotal] mind arises, they are perfectly equal in their arising and ceasing;
one should understand this principle of the arising of the antidote and the cessation [of the object].
The mind associated with right view is able to counteract [defilements];
it possesses no latent tendencies in the present life,
nor does it possess latent tendencies in the past life.
After this moment, the mind is free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
even in future lives, it will likewise be without latent tendencies.
From this point onward, the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parivṛtti*).
Having severed the latent dispositions (anuśaya) within the continuity of the personal existence,
one subsequently attains a mundane, wholesome, or indeterminate state of mind that—
whether in the past, future, or present— is entirely free from latent dispositions.
Therefore, it can be said that [afflictions] of the three periods of time are all abandoned.
Question: Regarding the afflictions that are abandoned, are there cases of falling back or not falling back?
Answer: According to the Sarvāstivāda school.
Having severed [the defilements] through the swift path of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one never regresses.

Regarding those who abide in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), those established in the immovable state do not regress; however, those of the regressive lineage (*parihāṇadharman*) may do so.

The one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman), the one of the nature of reflecting (cetayitṛdharman), the one of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇādharman), and the one of the nature of abiding (sthitākampya). The one of the nature of surpassing (prativedhanādharman) is by nature non-falling away.
One who was of the nature of falling away and has progressed [to a higher stage] will fall away.
The Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools maintain that one may fall away from the fruit of stream-entry, but not from arhatship;
for the paths of seeing and cultivation of an arhat are extremely firm and stable.
The path of seeing (darśanamārga) is not like this, and therefore there is falling back from it;

however, in the present Mahāyāna, the noble path (āryamārga) that eradicates the latent tendencies (anuśaya) necessarily does not involve falling back. As for those [latent tendencies] that are merely suppressed (vita), there is the possibility of falling back.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one abandons the afflictions by means of the mundane path,
they are said to be impermanent because they arise again."
The same applies to yoga:
the lineages such as "receding" (parihāṇadharman) are established based on obstacles to meditative concentration (samādhi-āvaraṇa),
not on the receding from the fruits [of the path].
However, because Bodhisattvas and others have suppressed [the afflictions] by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga),
they do not regress from their mastery.
For example, Śāriputra still regressed even upon reaching the sixth stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
This was because he had previously suppressed out-flowing contaminants (*sāsrava*) through the arousal of afflictions (*kleśa*), yet they remained latent.
Question: What is meant by "severance" (*prahāṇa*)?
If it refers to manifest activity, that has long since ceased of its own accord;
if it refers to the seeds, they cannot coexist with the Path.
How, then, can it be called "abandonment"?
The answer to the fifty-eighth [question] states:
"One merely abandons the latent dispositions (anuśaya),
because the active outbursts of affliction (paryavasthāna) have already been discarded."
It is called "abandonment" because of the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Why is this? Because even though the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) have already been abandoned...
If the underlying tendencies have not been abandoned,
the various afflictions and entanglements will repeatedly manifest; however, if the underlying tendencies are abandoned, [they do not arise].
When the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) never arise again,
this is also called the "abandonment of outbursts.
This explains that the Noble Path correctly abandons the latent tendencies.
If one suppresses and abandons them, one breaks the power of their seeds so that they do not manifest;
this is called "suppressing the active manifestation" (*samudācāra*). Although these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not coexist with the Path, [they are nonetheless suppressed].
However, as for the previous point raised: it is said that the dharma-contemplation of the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) which severs the three minds is subtle;
therefore, it must necessarily be accompanied by the arising of contemplation, which then severs the grasping at arising.
Why is it that the grasping at birth is severed by three moments of mind,
while the phenomena [of birth] pertain only to two?
It is because the three moments of mind are subtle, whereas the two moments of mind are coarse.
Answer: Although the contemplation of dharmas (dharmānupaśyanā) is subtle, it must necessarily be accompanied by the contemplation of arising (utpādānupaśyanā).
In the second moment, the grasping at arising is not yet severed, just as in the contemplation of dharmas that severs afflictions within the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi).
The latencies (*vāsanā*) can be severed, but the seeds (*bīja*) cannot be eliminated,
because they do not obstruct this path,
and because the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*) does not aspire toward their severance.
Both are abandoned through the two types [of cultivation].
Otherwise, it would contradict the treatise.
Question: Is it the attention that takes the aggregate as its object (*sāmānyālambana-manasikāra*) that is able to abandon the afflictions?
Regarding the claim that attention directed toward specific objects (*viśeṣālambana-manasikāra*) can sever the afflictions,
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* offers three brief explanations concerning their own and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). According to one interpretation:
The two types of valid cognition exist in the state of a distracted mind;
they are not said to exist in the state of meditative concentration. In the state of concentration, all objects of perception are subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Although this master states that the concentrated mind takes all things as its object,
he does not explain the general and specific characteristics of the concentration that abandons the afflictions;
nevertheless, one may know them by inferring from the meaning.
It is severed only by the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because a concentrated mind universally takes both the specific and the common as its objects.
The second master says:
The concentrated mind takes only specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object;
however, because it is induced by the skillful means of common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), it is said to take common characteristics as its object.
This principle that is revealed is stated from the perspective of such skillful means.
This is called knowing the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); that which is not thus is called knowing the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). By this principle...
Some say that suchness is called emptiness and selflessness, being the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Others say that suchness, as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, is not a common characteristic.
The intention of this master is as follows:

from the perspective of the preparatory means (*upāya*), it may be called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); from the perspective of what is realized within meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), it may be called the "specific characteristic" (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).

This clearly demonstrates that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, and not through common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The third master says:
"According to the true meaning..."
The presentation of specifically characterized (*svalakṣaṇa*) and generally characterized (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) phenomena in that *Hetuvidyā* treatise differs slightly from this.

It states that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena is termed "specifically characterized," because it is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) upon all phenomena.
Because each is attached to its own essence and is not shared with others;
if it were a conceptual mind,
one would establish a single category of signifier and signified that would apply universally across all phenomena.
For example, a thread threading through flowers is called a "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This is necessarily a conceptual construction (*prajñapti*) based on a distracted mind and is the object of inference (*anumāna*).
All states of meditative concentration (*samādhi-citta*) that are free from such conceptualization are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Although [characteristics] such as suffering and impermanence are conditioned by all phenomena,
they are each termed "specific characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa) because they exist individually within each phenomenon.
Although true thusness (tathatā) is manifested as a "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), [it is nonetheless the ultimate nature].
Because these dharmas possess their own actual nature and possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are not common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
One cannot designate them as common characteristics simply because they are neither identical to nor different from all other dharmas.
Because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is neither identical to nor different from all general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
the intended meaning of this point is that it is collectively manifested by the general characteristic of selflessness (*anātman*).
Each individual realization has as its essence the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);

thus it can generally serve as the object for both types of contemplation that are capable of severing [afflictions]. That which is capable of manifesting [the truth] is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
It is explained as being "consciousness-only," "selflessness," and so forth;
it is based on the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena,
for one is able to thoroughly understand the true principle of each and every phenomenon.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states:
"The noble wisdom of ultimate truth, regarding the non-established meaning within the sphere of ultimate wisdom,
is called 'simultaneous clear realization' (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*) because it takes the general characteristic as its object."
In a single moment, through the power of preparatory application,
one is able to universally know the cognition that takes the general characteristic as its object;
it is not that the sublime principle of *tathatā* (suchness) of each individual phenomenon is not known individually that it is called the "general characteristic."
Since they belong to the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), they are not contradictory.
Question: From what perspective are these afflictions said to be abandoned?
Answer: Afflictions can be abandoned by means of their associated factors (*samprayukta*) and their objects (*ālambana*).
Why is this? Because when the path of antidote arises,
the afflictions do not arise.
One attains the dharma of non-arising;
therefore, it is called the severance of those associated [afflictions].
This is because the seeds of affliction within the fundamental consciousness have all been completely severed.
When the mind arises, that which is not accompanied by afflictions is called "abandoned through dissociation" (*viprayoga-prahāṇa*).
Once abandoned through dissociation, it no longer takes objects as its cognitive support;
therefore, it is also said to be "abandoned" with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*).
Because there is no capacity to bind the mind to its object.
This passage is spoken in reference to the abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As for the Bodhisattva’s abandonment:
By practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā, one is able to sever the afflictions;
by practicing these two contemplations upon the signless,
one attains liberation from all bonds of signs.
Because they are liberated from the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*), they are also liberated from the bondage of all heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The bondage of signs binds sentient beings."
Furthermore, due to the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
one must cultivate both tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) together;
only then does one attain liberation in both respects.
Question: What is the sequential order for abandoning the various afflictions?
Answer: It is said that a householder should first abandon unwholesome actions and all evil views.
Next, one should abandon the obstacles to the joy of renunciation, namely the three types of discursive thought: sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty.
Subsequently, one should abandon the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for those whose minds are undisciplined.
This refers to the three types of discursive thought concerning one's retinue, country, and immortality.
Next, one abandons the obstacles to mental attention (*manasikāra*) consisting of the physical heaviness (*dausthulya*) associated with the category of delighting in seclusion.
Next, one abandons the afflictions of the path of seeing;
next, one abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
and next, one abandons the afflictions belonging to the categories of hindrances associated with suffering, sorrow, pleasure, joy, and equanimity within the various meditative absorptions.
Subsequently, there are further obstacles belonging to the category of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that must be abandoned.
According to the preceding sequence, both hindrances should be abandoned.
Question: Are the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) called the "path of correct abandonment"?
What is sudden and what is gradual?
The answer shall be extensively demonstrated in the Chapter on the Path of Vision (darśanamārga).
Regarding the meaning of the two truths: the meaning of the two truths is profound and subtle; it cannot be fully exhausted by brief words.
I shall briefly set forth this record of the essential framework,
analyzing it through three sections.
First, revealing the names and discerning the essence.
2. The Shallow and Deep of the Two and Three Vehicles;
3. Questions and Answers on the Subsumption by the Three Marks.
Section One: The Gate Revealing Names and Discerning Essence. This first gate has two parts.
First, the manifestation of the name;
second, the discernment of its essence.
Within the name, there are two parts.
First the enumeration,
then the explanation.
Within the enumeration, there are further two parts.
First is the general [classification], followed by the specific.
Regarding the listing of the general names:
in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, only one truth (*eka-satya*) is established.
Because ultimate reality is indestructible,
the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* explains the two truths in general;
this is because persons and phenomena each possess distinctions of superior and inferior.
Within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, each of the two truths has its own pair of ultimate and conventional truths,
as each possesses both middle and superior levels of wisdom.
In the *Prakaraṇāryavācā* and the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, there are three [truths] each for the conventional,
the dependent, and the perfected, due to their respective distinctions.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are four [truths] in each.
This shall be explained in detail below.
Within this general designation,
there is first the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It is also called the truth of concealment and manifestation (*saṃvṛti-paramārtha-satya*). Second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
formerly known as the truth of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is also called "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
To list its specific names:
here we clarify that the two truths differ in their ontological nature regarding existence and non-existence.
The facts and the principles differ;
the shallow and the profound are not the same;
the explanations and the underlying intent are each distinct.
Thus, each of the two truths has four aspects.
They are also termed the two truths of name and thing, the two truths of phenomenon and principle, the two truths of shallow and deep, and the two truths of expression and essence.
Regarding the four names for conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):
first is worldly conventional truth,
which is also called the truth of having a name but no reality.
Second is the conventional truth of reasoning,
also called the conventional truth of differentiation according to phenomena;
third is the conventional truth of realization.
It is also called the truth of provisional establishment through skillful means (*upāya-prajñapti-satya*).
The fourfold ultimate and conventional truth is also called the truth of non-establishment by way of nominal designation (*prajñapti-anupasthāpana-satya*).
The *Xianyang lun* states that all four types of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are established designations (*prajñapti*).
The first three are easily understood.
Why is the fourth also called "establishment"?
Because the nature of ultimate truth is personally realized within,
[this stage] is intended to accord with and induce the arising of that wisdom.
Based on the conventional, that which is established is called "conventional ultimate.
Of these, the first three types of characteristics may be considered as analogous;
the fourth is the conventional designation of the ultimate.
Regarding the four names for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):
first is the mundane ultimate truth,
which is also called the truth of the manifestation of essence and function.
Second is the ultimate truth of reasoning,
also called the ultimate truth of the differentiation of cause and effect.
Third is the ultimate truth of realization.
It is also called the "truth that reveals the ultimate reality by relying on the gateway [of conventional truth].
Fourth is the "ultimate ultimate truth," which is also called the "truth that discards the expression to discuss the intended meaning."
The first three types are called "established ultimate truth," while the fourth type is "non-established ultimate truth.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of their names:
First, the general name is explained;
second, the specific names are explained.
Regarding the explanation of the general name:
The Dharma-protector Śīlabhadra explains:
"In the world, it is said that 'concealment' (saṃvṛti) has the sense of being subject to destruction."
What is conventionally called "manifestation" follows worldly usage; according to the meaning of this principle of truth,
it should be named the "truth of concealment and manifestation."
The principle of emptiness is concealed while appearances manifest;
it is like tying a handkerchief into the shape of a rabbit or other objects—
the original handkerchief is hidden while the appearance of a rabbit manifests.
This is also like that.
Following ancient nomenclature, it is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In Sanskrit, it is called *saṃvṛtti*.
Therefore, the names are explained according to their meaning as the "hidden" and "manifest" truths (*satya*).
Furthermore, because its nature falls within arising and ceasing, it is termed the "worldly" (*loka*);
because its essential characteristics manifest, it is designated as the "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
"World" (*loka*) is the conventional name for the mundane;
this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Alternatively, it is also not contradictory to take "world" as the subject and "mundane" as its meaning.
"Truth" (satya) means the sense of reality:
that which exists as it truly exists, and that which does not exist as it truly does not exist.
Existence and non-existence that are not false are termed "truth" (*satya*).
"Conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
"Worldly truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
"Superior" (*viśeṣa*) means preeminent.
There are two kinds of meaning (*artha*):
first, that which is called "meaning" in the sense of an object;
second, that which is called "meaning" in the sense of a principle.
Regarding the fourth, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), most treatises explain that "ultimate" (*parama*) is itself the "truth" (*artha*);
thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Alternatively, all four types of ultimate truth are the "meaning" (*artha*) of being "supreme" (*parama*).
This is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
The treatise explains that the two natures— *paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*—
are, as appropriate, the objects of both fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) wisdom.
Therefore, most teachings primarily name [the dharmadhātu] by way of "appositional compound" (karmadhāraya),
emphasizing the excellence of the essence of True Suchness (tathatā); yet in reality, it also applies to the "possessive compound" (tatpuruṣa).
That untainted true wisdom, regardless of which truth it pertains to,
also takes "excellence" as its meaning,
because it has suchness as its object.
This is a comprehensive possessive compound (*vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*). As for the fourth, the term "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*) mostly relies on its etymological derivation;
it is not a [direct] object of experience, as it discards the conventional expression to discuss the intended essence.
The first three are the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"Object" (viṣaya) means the referent (artha),
and "truth" (satya) means reality (tattva).
Phenomena are as they truly are;
principles are as they truly are.
Because phenomena and principles are not erroneous, they are called truths (*satya*).
The ultimate is the truth that is the ultimate;
the two explanations are as before. Although there is no scriptural statement [to this effect], [it is so].
These two types may also be termed "Noble Truths," just like the Four Noble Truths;
for the Noble Ones are able to know that both the existence and non-existence of things and principles are entirely without error or falsehood.
This is designated as the truth.
Next, the specific names are explained.
Regarding "worldly conventionality":
They conceal the true reality;
following the sentiments of the age,
they fall into the midst of falsehood.
It is called "the world.
All ordinary people say it exists;
based on their perceptions, it is conventionally designated as "the conventional" (saṃvṛti).
Regarding the conventional by way of reasoning (*yukti-saṃvṛti*):
establishing phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*) in accordance with their respective meanings is called "reasoning."
The differentiation of the manifestation of phenomenal characteristics is easy to understand;
this is called the conventional (saṃvṛti).
To realize the conventional means—
To establish the distinctions between the causes and effects of affliction and purification,
thereby causing one to enter [the path],
is called "realization."
That which possesses characteristics and can be known is called the conventional (saṃvṛti).
As for the ultimate conventional (paramārtha-saṃvṛti):
That which excellently emerges from all phenomena and is known by the noble ones is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Provisionally established through conventional characteristics,
yet its essence is beyond verbal expression;
this is called the conventional (saṃvṛti).
In this context, "the world" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
and so on, up to "the ultimate" referring to the conventional truth.
All are *karmadhāraya* compounds.
Regarding "the worldly ultimate" (*loka-paramārtha*),
its phenomenal characteristics are coarse and manifest.
That which is subject to destruction is called the mundane;

Chapter on Primary Elements and Derived Matter:
The matter derived from the primary elements shall be analyzed by means of six topical sections.
First, the discernment of the essence;
second, the explanation of the names;
third, the clarification of the characteristics of formation through the five causes, such as arising and so forth.
Fourth, the analysis of the great elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (bhautika) by means of causes and conditions;
fifth, the analysis of their derivation through the mutual comparison of similarities and differences among the great elements;
sixth, the detailed differentiation through questions and answers.
1. Distinguishing the Essence. Regarding the distinction of essence:
the Lokāyatikas (Materialists) and the Tīrthikas (Non-Buddhists) do not separately establish the distinction between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative elements (*bhautika*).
Both are the four great elements;
however, their nature is eternal,
and there is nothing else besides them.
Vaiśeṣika: The four great elements are indeed real entities;
they possess resistance.
Ordinarily they are impermanent.
The eye faculty is fire;
the ear faculty is space.
The nose faculty is earth;
the tongue faculty is water;
the skin faculty is wind.
Visible form, taste, odor, tangible objects, and sound are comprised within the category of qualities (*guṇa-pada*);
however, they are unimpeded.
Among these, sound and odor are exclusively impermanent.
The remainder are generally impermanent.
The four kinds, such as form, are the four great elements (mahābhūta).
The four great elements are not the creators [of derived matter].
Form and so forth are not derived [from the primary elements].
Earth possesses color, taste, odor, and tangibility.
Water possesses color, taste, odor, and tangibility.
Fire possesses both visible form and tangibility;
wind possesses only tangibility;
and sound is a quality of space.
This is not the view of the four great virtuous ones.
The Sāṃkhya masters teach that the five kinds,
such as form and so forth, are called the five *tanmātras*.
These are the primary elements—earth, water, and so forth—that act as the creators;
earth, water, and the others then create the five sense organs, such as the eye.
Although both the primary elements and the derived matter are impermanent.
However, they are not subject to arising and ceasing;
rather, they are impermanent through transformation.

However, there are those that are produced separately,
and there are also those that are produced collectively.

The four subtle particles (tanmātra) act as the primary creators (bhūtakṛt) that create the four great elements (mahābhūta).
The four great elements constitute the five sense faculties (indriya),
which are exclusively derivative (bhautika).
The four objects (viṣaya) are exclusively productive;
the four great elements (mahābhūta) pertain to both [productive and produced]; and sound is also exclusively produced.
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda school maintain that the four great elements are the formative causes;
they are exclusively contaminated, possess resistance, and are subsumed under the sphere of the tangible.
The five faculties, the five objects, and the unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) within the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) are derived [matter].
The five faculties and the five objects are exclusively characterized by resistance and are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
The unmanifest (avijñapti) within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is said to include both the untainted (anāsrava) and is subsumed under the unimpeded (apratigha);
all of these are substantially existent (dravyasat).

The Sautrāntika masters say that although both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*) possess resistance (*sapratigha*), both categories encompass the conventional (*prajñapti*) and the substantial (*dravya*).
The atom is substantial;
coarse form is provisional.
Both are entirely with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The unmanifest is a conventional designation;
it is formless within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
It is not admitted that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) contains unmanifest form.
The Prajñaptivādins say:
whether the primary elements (bhūta) or the derived matter (bhautika) be coarse or subtle,
their substance is entirely real within the category of the aggregates (skandha).
Because it is an accumulation of meanings,
its substance is not an accumulation;
in terms of both the *dhātus* and *āyatanas*, it is entirely conventional.
Because both the basis and the conditions are all substantial aggregates,
they encompass both the contaminated and the uncontaminated;
this is the position of the Ekavyāvahārikas.
The primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived elements (*bhautika*) possess only a single name and lack any substantial reality.
The Lokottaravādins state that if the primary and derived elements are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are all merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
Because they arise from inversion,
all those that are untainted (anāsrava) are entirely real;
they do not arise from inversion.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna,

both the *spraṣṭavya-āyatana* (tangible base) and the *dharmāyatana* (mental-object base) possess great elements (*mahābhūta*), because there is a distinction between those arising from dispersion (*vikṣepa*) and those arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Derived matter exists throughout the eleven bases.
Both primary elements and derived matter are, as appropriate, subsumed under both the dependent and perfected natures.
Among the five dharmas, they are included within two dharmas: characteristics and correct cognition.
They encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) natures.
Contaminated derived matter (*bhautika*) necessarily belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Uncontaminated derived matter also encompasses both the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature.

The derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) of the outflowing realm (sāsrava) is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature; its conventional nature (prajñapti-svabhāva), however, pervades all three natures.
Thus, the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, fascicle 64, states:
Regarding visible form and sound, manifest form is conventionally categorized as either wholesome or unwholesome,
but in reality it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Since non-manifest form (*avijñapti*) is likewise conventional, [it shares this same status].

It is admitted that [the primary elements] may be associated with both the wholesome and the unwholesome; the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) great derivatives are exclusively wholesome. The great elements (*mahābhūta*) are exclusively substantial (*dravya*).
Derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) is both primary and secondary. 2.
Explanation of Terms: Regarding the explanation of terms, the third [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Because these primary elements (mahābhūta) are great by nature and because they serve as the seeds from which [all things] arise,
they are called "great elements" (mahābhūta).
The Great Element has four meanings.
First, because it serves as the basis;
it acts as the foundational locus for all derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
Second, because its essential nature is vast;
its essential nature is more expansive than derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
Third, because its form is great.
The great earth, the great water, the great fire, and the great wind;
because their characteristics are vast,
and because they give rise to four great functions.
Because the activity of the world's formation and destruction is vast,
"seed" (bīja) carries the meaning of cause or the meaning of category.
These four [great elements] can serve as the five causes, such as the cause of production, for the arising of various forms;
because they are distinct in their categories,
even though space is vast, it cannot serve as a cause.
Although internal seeds and the like can serve as causes, their essential nature and characteristics are not "great.
All other phenomena are neither great nor seeds.
Because earth and the other elements are both great and seeds, they are called the "great elements" (mahābhūta).
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
If one speaks of the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*),
the word "four" (*catur*) is a numerical term.
This is immediately followed by a numerical explanation.
Regarding the name "derived matter" (bhautika-rūpa),
the fifth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
This means that based upon the primary elements, other derived matter arises within the very locus of those primary elements;
for this reason, it is said that the four great elements produce the derived matter.
That which is derived is matter itself.
[The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] states in verse 54:
"To be gathered and maintained in the same location—that meaning is called 'derived' (*upādāya*)."
That which is derived is matter itself;
it is named after its function as "derived matter from the great elements. This refers to the derived matter of the great elements.
The term is designated based on its primary referent.
As for its specific name:
the meaning of "firmness" is the meaning of "earth."
The meaning of flowing and moistening is the meaning of water;
the meaning of warmth and heat is the meaning of fire;
the meaning of lightness and so forth, as well as motion, is the meaning of wind.
That ground is itself great;
even down to the wind, it is itself great.
In all cases, these are *karmadhāraya* (possessive) compounds.
The specific names of derived matter will be explained in the chapter on "Reaching" (*prāpti*).
Third, regarding the five causes such as arising (*jāti*) which clarify derived matter: by means of these five causes—arising and so forth—one distinguishes the producer.
As stated in the first [chapter] of the *Abhidharmapitaka*: [text follows].
"Derived" means that the four great elements serve as the causes for its arising, dependence, establishment, maintenance, and nourishment;
it is on the basis of these five causes that it is called "derived."
The "generative cause" (janakahetu) is precisely the "arising cause" (utpādakahetu),
because derived matter (upādāyarūpa) does not arise apart from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Although all derived matter arises from its own seeds, [it cannot do so independently].
If separated from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), [the derived matter] can certainly not arise.
The third question in the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"All phenomena arise from their own seeds."
"Would you rather say that the primary elements (mahābhūta) can produce all derived matter (rūpa),
up to and including its nourishment?
He answered himself:
All seeds of the primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa), whether internal or external,
are entirely dependent upon the internal, continuous mind;
the seeds of the primary elements have not yet produced the actual primary elements.
The seeds of derived matter can never produce [their effects]; rather,
it is necessary that the great elements (mahābhūta) first arise from their seeds,
and only then do the seeds of derived matter produce derived matter.
Because it acts as a precursor,
it is said to be able to produce [the effect]; therefore,
it is called the "productive cause" (janakahetu).
The sixty-sixth [treatise] explains this in the same way.
Now one should ask:
if that is so, then regarding the Prātimokṣa, the dhyāna, and the path-restraint (mārga-śīla), [how do they differ]?
Once separated from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), [the derived matter] should not arise;
however, whatever name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) it follows in its movement and what it protects,
that too is metaphorically designated as "derived from the great elements" (*mahābhautika*) in accordance with those two.
The meaning of "not being separated" has two aspects:
first, being in the same location;
second, necessarily depending upon one another.
The prātimokṣa vows and the like necessarily rely upon a great birth;
they do not necessarily occupy the same location,
yet they are also called "inseparable."
The same applies to sounds that are devoid of substance and to light.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 54, states:
"The matter that is the fruit of superior meditative concentration (samādhi) depends solely upon superior meditative concentration and does not depend upon the primary elements (mahābhūta)."
How does he resolve this?
He explains it himself, saying:
"However, it arises from a samādhi that has as its object an image of that same kind."
It is said that those [derived elements] are "created" by the primary elements; they are called "created" because they do not arise based upon them.
This shall be fully explained in the chapter on matter as the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
Alternatively, these five causes do not apply universally;
for instance, apart from wheels, light, and so forth, there would be no cause for support.
Regarding the causal basis,
the Abhidharma states that it is the transformative cause (*pariṇāma-hetu*).
This means that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), once abandoned,
lack the functional capacity to occupy a distinct location;
therefore, all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) can only arise by depending upon the primary elements.
Therefore, they do not abide in a location separate from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The third *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Because derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), having arisen, proceeds without departing from the location of the primary elements, it is called the 'causal basis' (*hetu-āśraya*)."
If that is so, how is it that [the sūtra] says there are fifty-four [qualities], such as the light of the wheel,
while the great elements, fragrances, and so forth are all unobtainable?
Now, based on the very substance itself, we shall distinguish the supporting cause (āśraya-hetu).
Since light and so forth, when separated from their substance, lack the sense of having a supporting cause, there is no contradiction.
Some say that those rays also possess the great primary elements (mahābhūta),
because wherever there is light, the great primary elements are present.
This explanation is incorrect.
Since sound and fragrance are separated from their substance,
by which of the great elements are they produced?
Therefore, what was previously stated is correct.
As for the establishment of the reason, it refers precisely to the concomitant cause (*anuvartaka-hetu*).
Due to great transformation,
the derived matter that serves as the support undergoes corresponding transformation; thus,
there is a relationship between the primary elements and the derived matter.
Safety and peril must be shared alike;
therefore, when a great transformation occurs, one creates [a state] that conforms to that change.
The third [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* says:
Because the primary elements (mahābhūta) cause benefit or harm to those [derived elements] that share their same state of stability or instability,
the prātimokṣa vows continue to arise in succession. How, then,
does the manifest action (vijñapti-karma), which undergoes transformation, continue in succession?
Some say that because the basis still exists at a later time,
it does not undergo transformation.
According to the true meaning, however:
This [protection] follows wherever one travels and prevents what is to be guarded against;
otherwise, since there is no basis for the restraint associated with the formless attainments or the Path, this cause would not exist.
If that were so, that which is prevented would have been long since severed and extinguished;
since there would be nothing capable of acting as its creator, there would be no basis for establishing it as a cause.
Furthermore, that which prevents another cannot be designated as "form."
One creates the unmanifest [karma] of oneself by means of the four great elements of another;
this is designated as "creating" in the sense that it is merely a distant counteragent (*prātipakṣika*) to that [other's action].
Because there has previously been a similar case;
the same applies to all non-informative [matter] from the two meditative absorptions upward.
The treatise states that it prevents others.
"It is composed of the four great elements.
This interpretation is incorrect,
because [the object] has not yet passed away and because it cannot be apprehended.
It should not be an antidote.
This meaning is that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is conventionally designated as "conditioning" (saṃskāra);
it is an antidote by way of remoteness.
Therefore, there is no fault.
To prevent one's own past transgressions of the precepts from afar,
one immediately creates present form based on what was previously constructed in the past.
Alternatively, there is no sense in establishing a cause for non-informative precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) and the like,

because they are established as possessing a cause based on substantial matter (*dravya-sat-rūpa*). If one were to take that which depends on the primary elements of the body (*kāya-mahābhūta*) as the "creation" (*nirmita*), [it would follow that such a cause does not exist].
If there were no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) for noble ones in the formless realm (*ārūpya*),
it would not be the Mahāyāna; furthermore,

this would contradict the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which establishes the nature of matter (*rūpatva*) based on the fact that the various vows (*saṃvara*) exist as matter even when they do not manifest.
Therefore, that which corresponds to the great elements (mahābhūta) being prevented is the sustaining cause;
this is precisely the abiding cause.
This means that because the various derived forms produced from the primary elements arise in a continuous succession and are maintained so as not to be interrupted,
the continued arising of the derived forms depends on the sustaining power of the primary elements.
Otherwise, derived matter would necessarily be discontinuous.
The third *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Because it does not perish according to the dimensions of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is called the sustaining cause (*dhṛtihetu*)."
Furthermore, since sound, light, and so forth differ in their magnitude,
how can it be said that they remain equal in size without being destroyed?
The Abhidharma provides a general explanation based on the totality of the parts, stating that they maintain their cause.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* makes this statement based on a partial perspective,
for it speaks of that basis (*āśraya*) as being the primary matter (*dravya*) from which derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) is produced.
Alternatively, the term "yoga" implies that the measure remains unaltered.
It is not that the two measures of the great elements are equal.
"Equal" (等) carries the sense of being similar before and after;
the former explanation is superior.
The cause of nourishment is the cause of growth; that is to say,
it is because the primary elements (mahābhūta) nourish those derivative forms (upādāyarūpa), causing them to increase.
By means of great nourishment, derived matter increases;
that which increases is either the cause itself or the cause of increase.
Therefore, it is called the "long-term cause.
The third [fascicle] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"By means of food, drink, sleep, and the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
Because the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) such as the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) increases and expands even further based upon them,
the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are said to be their nourishing cause (*puṣṭihetu*).
The nourishment of derived matter has causes and conditions:
the primary elements act as its cause of nourishment, and those [derived elements] act as its condition of nourishment.
Since each [position] relies on its own specific teaching, they do not contradict one another.
Furthermore, because those conditions first nourish the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
causing the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) to increase, there is no fault.
Alternatively, that [nutriment] is the cause of all phenomena, including the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), and the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).
However, this [nutriment] can only nourish derived matter as its specific cause;
because derived matter is dull by nature, it is not like the mind and so forth.
Therefore, they rely on the two kinds of sustenance; the mind and so forth do not. (54)
Question: Since all conditioned phenomena arise from their own seeds, why is it said that the primary elements (mahābhūta) produce the derived matter (upādāyarūpa)? Answer:
Because the latter undergoes transformation in accordance with the transformation of the former.
Because they are established and sustained by that [great element],
the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Five Aggregates) states:
"That which is based on the great elements and consists of other derived matter, being gathered together in one place, is called 'derived from the great elements' (*mahābhūta-nirmita*)."
This meaning demonstrates that [things] exist through mutual dependence;
this is the sense of "conditioning" (saṃskāra),
not the analysis of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Because they serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) when compared to their active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Fourth, regarding the analysis of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) by way of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):
first, the analysis of the causal derivation.
Next, the creation by conditions will be explained.
There are two types of creation by causes:
first, the ten causes.
Second, regarding the six causes and the ten causes that produce:
in terms of the relationship between primary matter (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), there are seven causes in total.
First, the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*);
second, the producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).
Within neutral causes (*avyākṛta-hetu*), there are those that have not yet been moistened and those that have already been moistened.
External grains, wheat, and so forth are [the cause] in relation to their sprouts and so forth;
third, the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*),
because it is that which appropriates the basis for human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Fourth is the cause of production;
fifth is the cause of specific determination.
This is because they induce the arising of similar types and [determine] their intrinsic nature.
Sixth is the cause of commonality;
seventh is the cause of non-contradiction.
These two encompass all the aforementioned causes.
Because contradictory causes are mutually capable of subverting one another,
there is no such thing as a contradictory cause;
because the Great [Reality] is beyond verbal expression, there is no cause of conventional designation.
Regarding the dependence cause (*apekṣā-hetu*), it is remote and lacks dependence;
according to one interpretation, there are eight [types], excluding only the cause of conventional expression (*vyavahāra-hetu*) and the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*).
This is because these two [categories] are also established through mutual dependence (*apekṣā*).
According to another interpretation, nine causes may be added by including the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*);
in this view, derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) can serve as eight causes in relation to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
First, the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*),
because sounds and speech function to express and differentiate the great [truth].
Second, the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Because they depend upon one another through mutual exclusion: third, the drawing-in cause;
fourth, the arising cause.
Within the causes of defilement and purity,
there are the vows of restraint and non-restraint,
as well as the morality associated with meditative concentration.
For the sake of these two— those not yet moistened and those already moistened—
there is the fifth, the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*), because it appropriates the basis for the functioning [of the seeds].
Sixth is the cause of distinct determination,
because it specifically brings about its own respective maturation.
Seventh is the cause of common activity.
The eighth is the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*).
This excludes the producing cause (*ākṣepaka*), because that which produces can serve as the cause for its own kind, for similar types, and for superior types.
It also excludes the contradictory cause (*virodhaka*), because these are not mutually compatible.
Alternatively, it may be said that there are nine causes by adding the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepahetu*);
the meaning is thus established,
because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) induce one another.
Alternatively, there are ten causes because of their mutual opposition.
Regarding the "six causes that produce," this refers to the six causes in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), chapter eighteen, states that all [causes] are predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The fourth chapter of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"It should be known that all causes are subsumed under the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)."
To clarify the meaning of their distinctions,
the other five causes are further established separately.
If one distinguishes the six causes based on the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises state that seeds, in relation to manifest phenomena,

function as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Furthermore, in relation to other seeds,
they also function as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
However, there is no ripening [result],
because it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
From the perspective of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is not any of the six causes.
Because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for manifestation act as ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*) in producing their respective effects.
Now, regarding the analysis of the six causes based on the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
the primary elements stand in relation to the manifested forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) as having only three causes.
First is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because it provides power by way of non-obstruction.
Second is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
In order to cause [the seeds] to increase,
the Abhidharma texts explain that they depend on the prior perfuming of seeds to bring about the arising of subsequent fruits;
they also explain this in terms of the mutual relationship between actual manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Regarding the non-seed in relation to the seed,
there are three types of co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*);
this is stated in the fourth [chapter] of the *Abhidharma*.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) are necessarily co-arising; therefore, they constitute a simultaneous cause (sahabhūhetu).
This is not because they share the sense of obtaining a single common fruit.
That which is neither mind nor mental factors lacks the associated cause;
that which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome karma lacks the ripening cause;
and because it is not of the nature of affliction, it lacks the pervasive cause.
Derived matter, when viewed in relation to the primary elements, also functions as three causes.
First is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because this cause is the most extensive.
Second, because both possess the cause of coexistence (*sahabhū-hetu*) and are not mutually dissociated;
third, because the causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*)—
namely, non-restraint, restraint, and the restraint associated with meditative concentration— are capable of producing great results.
Alternatively, there are four causes;
by adding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it functions as a productive cause (*ākṣepaka*).
There is nothing further to be known.
This explains that [the restraint] is created in the same world and not in another world;
because it exists based on its locus and does not belong to a different world, it consists solely of the matter of the vow (saṃvara-rūpa).
The nature of matter (*rūpa*) is established based on dharmas that do not manifest; furthermore,
because present matter is produced by past primary elements (*mahābhūta*) created in a different time period.
Tainted (sāsrava) form and sound are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
If they are in an untainted (anāsrava) state,
both the primary elements and their derived matter are wholesome (kuśala).
Therefore, one should simply follow what has been stated here;
it should be said that the past serves as the cause for the present.
The past and future are not causes;
the present acts as a cause for both the present and the future;
and the future is not a cause for the future.
Because the past and future do not exist,
the past is not stated here to be the cause of the future;
this is because both cause and effect would be non-existent.
Nor is the future limit the cause of the past limit,
for that would be a perversion of cause and effect. Having thus analyzed the construction of causes, [the text continues:]
Regarding the conditions for the formations (*saṃskāra*): among the great [elements] and the formations, they are mutually related as a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This is because, when considering their actual manifestation, they do not establish a distinct substantial entity.
It is not due to causes and conditions;
rather, it is because of the five causes such as arising and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
and not because of the mind and so forth.
There are no other two conditions.
This causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is explained in terms of its general characteristics;
it exists in relation to the outflow-free (anāsrava), the twelve bases (āyatana), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and the three realms (tridhātu).
They gaze at one another with mutual longing;
the great look upon the great,
or the created look upon the created.
The greater or lesser number of causes and conditions should all be reflected upon according to reason. 5.

Regarding the analysis of the similarities and differences among the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in relation to one another, and the analysis of the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) in relation to the primary elements: as for the analysis of the derived matter in relation to the primary elements—
First, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are examined in relation to one another based on their distinct categories;
subsequently, they are examined in relation to the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) based on whether they are identical with or separate from it.
This section clarifies the nature of the derived matter by examining the primary elements in relation to one another according to their distinct categories.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Three, states in verse fifty-four:
"There are three types of categories (*jāti*):
first, the category of maturation (*vipākajāti*)."
This is of two kinds.
The first is birth from karma;
this refers to that which arises at the very beginning.
Second, regarding the continuity:
the former is the general maturation,
while the latter is the specific maturation.
Alternatively, "the former is the first moment" and "the latter is at a later time" refers to the two types of nurtured [dharmas].
This also has two aspects. First,
it is extensive and pervasive,
being nourished by food, drink, sleep, celibacy, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
The two characteristics increase and flourish,
both because of nutriment and because it is their basis.
Because one cultivates sublime mental attention and because it has been matured over a long period,
it is said to be "nourished."
Regarding the three types of outflows,
there are four kinds: first,
the outflow of maturation (vipāka-niṣyanda).
Second, those that are nourished and are outflows (puṣṭa-niṣyanda), because both of the aforementioned two categories are outflows.
Third, those that are transformed and are outflows (vikāra-niṣyanda).
Fourth, those that are outflows of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-naiḥṣyandika*).
Since they are not subsumed under either the two types of maturation (*vipāka*) or accumulation (*aupacayika*), they belong to the latter two categories.
Regarding the five sense faculties (*indriya*), there are only maturation and accumulation.
Apart from these two, there is no other distinct outflow (niṣyanda).
This is stated based on the distinction of the three categories of substance;
all non-sensory forms (rūpa) possess these three categories.

Sixty-fifth: [They] exist simultaneously and are mutually inseparable,
