Regarding "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*):
the prefix *a-* has the sense of negation.
It is unrighteous;
it is not to be emulated as a model,
nor can it serve as a standard for ritual practice.
It is called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*),
just like "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth; furthermore, it is not formed by any of the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*).
It is not the same as "bad śīla" (duḥśīla) or "harming others' śīla" (para-śīla-dūṣaṇa),
where one takes śīla itself as the object of aversion; rather,
it is called "bad śīla" (duḥśīla) by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound (*saviśeṣaṇa*).
Śīla is a term from the Sanskrit language;
here it is called "cooling.
For those who commit evil deeds, their śīla is bad, and thus it is termed "bad śīla" (duḥśīla).
It is not that *śīla* means "evil reputation" or "bad morality.
An ancient commentator explained:
*śīla* has the meaning of "precept" (*śīla*).
"Bad śīla" refers to bad morality (*duḥśīla*).
For this reason, it is difficult to say that morality is defined by the prevention of what is non-virtuous.
There is morality that does not prevent wrongdoing;
there is action performed through the power of reflection;
and there is reflection that is not performed as action.
Now, this interpretation is incorrect.
This objection arises from a failure to properly understand the term;
*śīla* (ethical discipline) is not "torment" (*paridāha*).
How can a negative essence be ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
If that is so, the counter-objection follows:
a negative essence is not ethical discipline.
That which is evil regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called "evil ethical discipline" (*duḥśīla*);
likewise, it should be understood that its essence is evil and not [simply] a view (*dṛṣṭi*).
That which is evil regarding views is called "evil view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This objection is not uniform.
One seeks understanding by means of investigation;
both good and evil are investigated.
Purity is śīla; śīla is not of an evil nature.
For this reason, non-restraint (asaṃvara) cannot be a standard of conduct.
It is not a case of improper conduct.
Regarding that which is neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*):
it cannot be designated as "non-restraint" simply because its mode of conduct is not comparable to that of restraint.
If it were not the case that [it is] "not non-restraint," then it would be called "non-non-restraint" (an-asaṃvara), just as [the term] "non-restraint" (asaṃvara) is used.
Since there is this double negation, it cannot be explained by the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*).
It may also be explained as follows:
it is neither restraint nor non-restraint; this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
The term "restraint" (*saṃvara*) and so forth are themselves the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).
All are *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds.
[Thus,] it is the unmanifest of restraint.
All [of these] are *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds.
As for the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*), because they distinguish the specific from the general,
they may also be understood as *bahuvrīhi* (dependent) compounds.
2. Second, the Exposition of the Essential Nature. Regarding the exposition of the essential nature:
provisional bodily manifest karma has as its intrinsic nature the manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and other treatises state that informative vocal action (*vijñapti-vāg-karman*) has sound as its essence,
and that there are three types of volition (*cetanā*).
First is the volition of deliberation (*vitarkana-cetanā*),
so called because it first deliberates prior to initiating bodily or vocal action.
Second is the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*).
Because one gives rise to a resolute mind with the intention of acting,
a superior volition is activated;
this then initiates the actual activity of body and speech toward the task at hand.
The two types of manifest karma—of body and speech—are taken only as actual occurrences (*samudācāra*).
The third [type], which is the movement and initiation, has wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) as its intrinsic nature.
The mental manifest [karma] has the preceding two types of volition as its essence.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The volition that can move the body is called bodily karma;
the volition that can produce speech is called vocal karma."
Because it is associated with the two types of volition— deliberation and determination—
and because it moves the mind,
it is called mental action (manas-karma).
Non-restraint is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Regarding intermediate karma, one interpretation holds that it is also exclusively contaminated.
All the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the Buddhas and others are subsumed under restraint (*saṃvara*),
because all untainted wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are consistent with the Dharma.
According to another interpretation, the intermediate state (*madhyama*) also extends to the untainted.
Because other untainted [dharmas] and the Buddha’s other wholesome [dharmas] also pertain to them,
the former interpretation is correct.
Because all untainted wholesome dharmas can serve as the basis for such a rule,
this differs from the Hīnayāna view,
according to which only the karma of restraint is necessarily associated with the untainted.
The Master [Vasubandhu] and others maintain that there are also two types of untainted (anāsrava) informative action (vijñapti).
As for the prātimokṣa restraint and a portion of the intermediate non-informative action (avijñapti),
they exist upon the seeds of virtuous volition (kuśala-cetanā).
Its essence consists of the capacity to prevent misconduct of body and speech,
as well as the capacity to initiate virtuous conduct of body and speech;
this includes non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), as well as a portion of the intermediate non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Based upon the seeds of unwholesome volition,
there arises a capacity for unwholesome bodily and vocal actions;
its essence consists in obstructing the capacity for wholesome bodily and vocal discipline.
Although these aforementioned non-informative [forms] differ as virtuous or non-virtuous,
they are all established based on the distinct functional capacities of the seeds of volition (*cetanā*).
Because volition is delimited by aspiration or restraint, one takes up these distinct functional capacities.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"However, based on intention (*cetanā*) and aspiration (*praṇidhāna*),
as well as the limits of good and evil, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is conventionally established."
What contradiction is there with reason?
Furthermore, it is said:
"This [designation] is established based on the stage where the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions that initiate superior bodily and vocal actions increase."
The explanations regarding the accomplishment of karma through yoga are likewise the same.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas possess the precepts."
Although it is neither form nor color, it can be protected and maintained;
although it lacks tactile resistance, through the skillful cultivation of expedient means, it can be fully realized.
It is exactly like this.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirty-four, states:
"In the past, Prince Bodhi spoke these words:
'If there is a bhikṣu who guards and upholds the prohibitive precepts...'"
If one gives rise to an evil mind, you should know that at that moment the bhikṣu precepts are lost.
At that time, I spoke these words: "Prince Bodhi."
There are seven kinds of precepts.
From body and speech, there arises non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
It is by reason of this non-informative matter that [the precepts exist].
Although the mind may be within states of evil or the indeterminate, it is not called a loss of precepts;
it is still called maintaining the precepts.
For what reason is it termed "unmanifest form" (avijñapti-rūpa)?
It is not a cause for real form,
nor does it produce the fruit of real form. My disciples—
Having heard this explanation, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed,
"The Buddha taught that there is such a thing as unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa).
Based on this, the Sarvāstivādins assert that there exists a real, substantial unmanifest form.
In another sutra, I have spoken these words:
"Precepts are that which restrain and prohibit unwholesome dharmas;
to refrain from committing evil is called upholding the precepts."
When my disciples hear this teaching,
they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively taught that there is no such thing as unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas and others maintain that there is no such thing as unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Their intention in citing that sūtra is to show that it refers to the volition (*cetanā*) which initiates the forms of bodily and vocal action.
Because it is able to prevent the unwholesome forms of bodily and vocal misconduct,
it perfumes the seeds to constitute the form of non-informative (avijñapti) restraint.
This is because the function of these seeds of volition (*cetanā*) to prevent unwholesome forms continues in constant succession.
Although the mind may temporarily reside within the unwholesome or the neutral, it is not said that the precepts are lost.
This [precept] prevents the seeds of volition regarding evil bodily and verbal actions from being conventionally designated as "form.
Therefore, it does not act as a causal condition for the seeds of substantial form to arise as manifest form.
Nor is it the co-existent or homogeneous cause of the primary and derived matter that truly constitutes its creator;
for it does not arise from them,
nor do they arise from it.
Therefore, those who say that there is substantial matter (rūpa) but no formative action (karma) would not understand the intended meaning.
This manifest activity (pravṛtti), produced from the seeds of volition (cetanā), gives rise to body and speech; thus, it is metaphorically designated as "matter."
The restraint of unwholesome dharmas is what is called "precept" (śīla).
If one were to say that there is no such thing as non-informative precept (avijñapti-śīla) at all,
this too would demonstrate a failure to understand the intended meaning.
Therefore, one knows that there is no substantial reality;
that which possesses provisional form is called the "understanding mind."
This precisely accords with the present text.
Regarding the non-informative [matter] of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-avijñapti*), it exists within all seventeen levels of the two upper realms by the nature of things (*dharmatā*),
arising from the volition (*cetanā*) that manifests simultaneously with impure meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
Its essence consists of the functional capacity to prevent the unwholesome conduct of the desire realm.
This refers to the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) associated with the path, distinct from the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
Because coarse matter (*rūpa*) does not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
the discipline of material restraint (*rūpasamvara*) is omitted and not established there.
Although the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyānasamvara*) truly exists in the formless stages, it is not so designated.
It is not said that [the uncontaminated restraint] exists because it is not established in brief; rather,

the uncontaminated restraint consists in the volition (*cetanā*) that arises simultaneously with all uncontaminated paths belonging to the higher stages, by virtue of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
The essence of the ability to sever all transgressions of the precepts in the desire realm consists in non-functional [non-informative] matter (*avijñapti*).
It exists as appropriate throughout the two realms and ten stages.
This is because both types of precept-essence are active volition (*cetanā*) that operates in accordance with the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"Alternatively, it is established based on the volition (*cetanā*) that ceases the manifestation of bodily and vocal misconduct while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
All other types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) do not follow the mind."
Whether there is a mind or no mind, because the mind necessarily achieves accomplishment regardless of its nature,
it is established solely based on seeds;
for "volition" (cetanā) has the meaning of being able to perform an action.
Karma is that which is performed;
therefore, it refers exclusively to volition (*cetanā*) and does not depend on other factors.
Consequently, all forms of manifest and unmanifest discipline (*vijñapti-avijñapti-śīla*) are established based upon volition.
3. The Third Section: The Analysis of the Conventional and the Real. Regarding the analysis of the conventional and the real:
both manifest (vijñapti) and non-manifest (avijñapti) karma, as well as the three types of karma, are all conventionally established.
Nevertheless, there are distinctions between them.
The two types of action—bodily and vocal—are conventionally designated as having informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) as their essence;
in reality, however, they are informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) and do not possess the nature of action itself. This is stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other treatises.
Because the two types of manifest karma—of body and speech—are designated as wholesome or unwholesome based on their expression, they are conventionally termed wholesome or unwholesome;
in reality, however, they are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, they cannot bring about future ripened results (*vipāka-phala*).
Action is conventional;
therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Alternatively, bodily and vocal intimation arise from volition."
It is provisionally designated as "action.
As stated in the *Fifty-three [Treatises]*:
"All manifest actions (vijñapti-karma) are merely conventionally existent."
The volition that initiates and manifests bodily and vocal action is in fact of the nature of karma, because it draws forth maturation;
yet it is not itself the body or speech.
It is neither informative nor material;
it is conventionally designated as "informative matter of body and speech."
That which is produced is informative [matter],
because both that which is prevented and that which is produced are matter;
volition is designated as "matter" by way of metaphorical designation.
That which is called "unmanifest form" (avijñapti-rūpa) is in fact not unmanifest,
because it does not represent anything;
furthermore, its essence is not form.
Furthermore, that which is produced from [the mind] and that which is protected by it is conventionally designated as "form" (*rūpa*).
Thus, the *Xianyang lun* (Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra) states:
"The form of all vows (*saṃvara-rūpa*) is established as having the nature of form based on the dharma of non-manifestation (*apravṛtti-dharma*)."
This is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is that which is prevented [from arising];
it is so designated because of its determinateness.
The form of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-rūpa*) is established as having the nature of form based on the phenomena currently manifesting.
Because meditative concentration gives rise to bodily and vocal [actions].
However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This [non-informative matter] is established based on the stage when the seeds of superior wholesome or unwholesome volitions (cetanā) regarding body and speech have increased."
This has two meanings. One interpretation states that it refers specifically to the unmanifest [action] (avijñapti).
Since the initial stage of the perfuming thought (*vikalpa*) is also capable of initiating bodily and vocal actions,
the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang), relying on what is determinate,
states that the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*) is established based on dharmas that do not manifest (*apravṛtti*).
Second, it is said that because they manifest based on all forms of discipline (*saṃvara*),
their nature as form (*rūpa*) is established by virtue of their non-manifestation; however,
within the consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) system, there is also that which is produced based on the prātimokṣa.
Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"However, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is conventionally established based on the limits of wholesome or unwholesome volitions and aspirations."
Therefore, all are merely provisional existents.
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (18) states that among the seven categories of non-substantiality,
the sixth is the restraint (*saṃvara*).
The seventh is non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Therefore, both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
This is the same as in the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
4. The Number of Limbs. Regarding the number of limbs:
"limb" (aṅga) has two meanings.
First, it means a constituent part.
Second is the meaning of the categories of the branches.
As for the meaning of "branches," this refers to the gate of establishment and rejection.
The meaning of "limb" (*aṅga*) is the same as the meaning of "category" (*prakāra*).
Regarding the meaning of "constituent part" (*avayava*),
the fifty-third [fascicle] states:
The bhikṣu discipline is comprised of four branches: first,
the branch of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*),
which refers to the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the fourth proclamation (*karmavācanā*).
And by means of briefly embracing the training rules according to their grosser aspects,
one is called a "first bhikṣu" and possesses the bhikṣu precepts because of being endowed with these;
this is what is intended to be expressed.
At the initial reception of full ordination,
the formal motion (jñapti) is made, followed by the fourth proclamation (karmavācanā),
during which the four pārājika offenses and so forth are recited.
The formal declaration expresses the aspirant’s intention, which is universally vast;
that all actions of body and speech have both prohibitions and prescriptions is called the first limb.
In the case of the founding bhikṣus,
the ten precepts, the six rules,
and the explanation of the characteristics of taking refuge all constitute the first branch.
Second is the branch of training in accordance with the Dharma upon receiving [the precepts].
From the time one first receives them onward,
regarding the Vinaya and the Prātimokṣa:
He guards and practices all the precepts of a bhikṣu that accord with the discipline,
as well as the many rules of training derived therefrom, in their entirety.
By this, one is called "one who guards the prātimokṣa restraint.
This meaning is clearly indicated within the Vinaya,
the extensive discipline, and the Prātimokṣa-sūtra following the reception of the precepts.
To accord with the precepts one has received means to guard and practice the various natural and proscribed prohibitions—
such as those of restraint and maintenance— as well as the characteristics of the various active observances and prohibitions induced by them.
The training in the fundamentals, the precepts for male novices (*śrāmaṇera*), female novices (*śrāmaṇerī*),
and the three thousand rules of decorum (*trīṇi sahasrāṇi īryāpatha*) are all subsumed herein.
Third is the branch of protecting the minds of others.
By accomplishing the former two, one is fully endowed with the perfection of conduct;
this is what is meant by that statement.
Walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and so forth—
such dignified deportment in accordance with the Dharma is called being complete in ritual conduct (*ācāra*).
One does not enter the homes of laypeople by jumping.
This includes walking like a bull-king or taking the gait of an elephant-king and so forth.
Furthermore, one should not go to the houses of wine-sellers, royal households, caṇḍālas, or kaṭhina workers.
This is called being fully equipped with the objects of practice;
that is, being alone with a woman in a secluded place,
a concealed place, or a place suitable for sexual intercourse.
To sit and speak words that are contrary to the Dharma and so forth constitutes the fourth limb:
guarding according to the training rules as they have been learned.
This involves perceiving a profound sense of dread even regarding minor transgressions.
Regarding the points of training among all the various precepts, one is able to refrain from violating them; and should one violate them,
one quickly emerges [from the transgression],
by virtue of having a profound perception of dread and being possessed of wisdom.
The meaning intended here is that it is due to fear and due to wisdom.
Deeply fearing all transgressions, one dares not commit them; even if one should commit them, one is able to emerge from them.
Now, this [text] analyzes the characteristics of all precepts, both those prohibited by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and those prohibited by convention (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
They are designated as "limbs" (aṅga) by way of categorization according to their type. Therefore, by means of these four,
those who have gone forth [abide] regarding both natural precepts (prakṛti-śīla) and proscribed precepts (pratikṣepaṇa-śīla).
All are equally upheld, neither decreasing nor increasing;
this is what is called the Great Precepts.
Therefore, they are briefly summarized into four.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śrāvaka-bhūmi*, fascicle 22, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter 7,
state that there are seven branches,
as explained in the Vinaya.
If there are bhikṣus for whom the maturation of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the first abiding;
guarding the Prātimokṣa vows is the second;
and being fully endowed with proper conduct and deportment is the third and fourth.
To perceive even subtle transgressions with deep fear is the fifth;
to undertake and train in the precepts is the sixth; one who possesses these is called a possessor of ethical discipline (*śīlavant*).
That sixth is this first and second;
that third and fourth are this third;
and that first, second, and fifth are this fourth.
The increase or decrease in the number of names does not differ in their essential nature.
These characteristics of the six branches are explained in detail in the seventh chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts.
The lay practitioner's (upāsaka) discipline is comprised of three branches:
first, the branch of undertaking the abstention from the most significant matters that harm others,
namely, refraining from killing, destroying the property of others, and violating the spouses of others.
These three [actions] harm others;
the second [of the four] violates the branch of intensive practice that one has undertaken,
namely, abstaining from false speech.
If one speaks falsely regarding what has been received,
and being unwilling to undertake renewed practice,
one thus fails to transcend the third limb of what was undertaken.
That is, one should distance oneself from all intoxicants, which are sources of negligence;
for if one were to permit the drinking of alcohol,
one would frequently transgress and violate the precepts previously received.
The upavāsa restraint is comprised of five branches: first,
the branch of undertaking the abstention from harming others,
which consists of refraining from killing and destroying the property of others.
The second is the limb of avoiding harm to oneself and others,
which consists in abstaining from unchaste conduct;
for by abstaining from this, one avoids such harm.
One is not stained by one's own wife nor by the wives of others;
this is unlike the case of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), for whom one's own wife is permitted.
Third, there is the transgression of the branch of practice consisting of the weighty observances one has undertaken.
That is, one abstains from false speech.
Fourth, not transgressing the factors of the foundations of mindfulness as they have been undertaken;
these consist of three types.
First, singing, dancing, music, and the use of ointments, crowns, and fragrant garlands;
second, ascending high beds;
third, eating and drinking at improper times.
These three types [of conduct] are constantly practiced;
if one is separated from them, one should repeatedly recall to oneself: "I am now abiding in the definitive observance of the fast."
At all times, one should firmly maintain right mindfulness,
like a filial son; remaining free from all objects of pleasure,
one does not use a large bed and stays far removed from all forms of arrogance.
Without counting one's meals and purifying oneself while maintaining mindfulness, one is able to abide in the precepts;
thus, regarding what has been received, one does not transgress right mindfulness.
The fifth factor of unimpaired right mindfulness is that he abstains from all intoxicants and bases for negligence;
although he abides in this factor of right mindfulness, [he does not yet possess the other factors].
I now abide in the definitive observance of the fast and precepts;
yet if I were to become intoxicated by various liquors,
I would immediately fall into madness and lose my self-mastery.
Therefore, it should be prohibited.
Herein, the precepts of the five groups of renunciants are explained together as one.
Among the fifty-three [verses], after explaining the upper branches, it says:
Now, within this context,
whether it be a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā,
all are included within the category of those who have gone forth.
One should know that these are subsumed under the bhikṣu vows.
Furthermore, although the essential substance of the śikṣamāṇā and other precepts is narrower,
they are all equally maintained and protected in the same manner as those of a bhikṣu.
Therefore, the middle five groups are established and explained together.
As for the female lay devotee (upāsikā) discipline,
it is included within the category of householders.
Because it is manifested through a semblance of training,
it should be understood as being subsumed under the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) restraint;
the restraints of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the precepts beloved by the noble ones (ārya-kānta-śīla) are not mentioned.
It is not a non-restraint;
rather, it refers to the intermediate precepts, the ten wholesome precepts, and so forth, which possess varying numbers of constituent factors.
This is the intended meaning here.
Regarding the seven classes of precepts, the reason for their distinct classifications and differences lies in this;
it is not that other types of precepts possess such variations of increase or decrease.
To explain this underlying reason, the constituent factors (*aṅga*) are clarified.
If one speaks of the categories of the factors [of the path],
they must each be explained separately. Among the bhikṣuṇīs,
the śikṣamāṇā and śrāmaṇerī are divided into three parts.
The bhikṣu precepts are divided into two;
furthermore, the opening and closing [of categories] regarding the upavāsa, śrāmaṇera,
and other precepts shall be extensively analyzed in the questions and answers below.
The factors have been explained above.
What are the categories of factors?
They are the precepts of the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs.
There are only the three bodily and seven vocal branches of restraint;
for bhikṣus and others, through the mental aspiration of their resolve,
universally prohibit the nature of form that constitutes natural transgressions.
Although the characteristics of bodily and vocal actions are infinite,
when categorized according to their primary roots, they are all subsumed within seven;
for they do not exceed these seven.
The remainder are received solely for the purpose of protecting this [previously mentioned],
and there is no other distinct category;
thus, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
There are seven kinds of precepts.
From body and speech, they give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Nevertheless, they universally prevent the three stages: the preliminary (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*).
The meaning may also be stated as preventing all three time periods.
Since one establishes past and future in relation to present phenomena,
and because one already prevents present phenomena, the meaning thereby excludes the three [times].
This differs from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna),
for while the latter merely prevents [unwholesome states] in the present, this is not so;
through the two minds of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*), one accords with principle and is able to benefit sentient beings.
By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), because it destroys evil, it also possesses the seven [limbs].
Since there are no obstructing factors,
it can also be said that it universally prevents the non-virtuous actions of the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages throughout the three periods of time.
Since all three [types of unwholesome states] are extinguished at the moment they arise,
one may also say that the evils of the three periods of time are destroyed;
however, these two aforementioned categories actually prevent only the present.
Since the two periods of past and future lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),

There is also the sense of "derived from another," as when a person hears the Buddha preach the Dharma and enters the Path of Vision;
by becoming free from dust and leaving behind defilement, they enter samādhi and immediately obtain the precepts.
If that were so, one should also say that there is informative action (*vijñapti-karman*). This is not the case, however,
because this volition does not give rise to external body or speech.
Because this is untainted (*anāsrava*),
there is no manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*);
therefore, one can only say that there is unmanifest action (*avijñapti-karman*).
However, at the very moment one attains the non-informative [matter] of meditative concentration on the Path,
there is no mental engagement with external objects; how, then, can it be acquired?
It is said in the fifty-third [section] that they receive the name [of that discipline] by means of remote preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*).
If it refers to this very discipline (*saṃvara*) that is received:
Being able to remain free from transgressions,
one takes this as a basis for cultivating freedom from regret and so forth.
Up until they have fully entered the first dhyāna,
through the power of śamatha to suppress and subdue,
they suppress and subdue all seeds of transgressing the precepts.
This is called the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
This refers to those such as bhikṣus who,
having received the restraint, [abide in it].
One is able to remain free from transgressions and takes this as one's reliance;
because there is no transgression, there is no regret.
Because there is no regret, the mind is glad;
because the mind is glad, the mind is joyful;
because the mind is joyful, the mind is at peace.
Because the mind is at peace, one attains concentration;
if there is any transgression, one will ultimately not attain concentration.
As stated in the Mahāsāṃnipāta Sūtra:
The Buddha said:
"In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, I dwelt among ordinary beings;
my name was Cāṭadhara."
In the kingdom of Kālinga,
he acted as a merchant who traded in falsehoods and unreality,
committing various evil deeds that cannot be fully described.
At that time, it became known throughout the entire kingdom that this fool had murdered his father and committed incest with his mother;
he was no different from the six domestic animals.
The king wished to kill me;
fearing for my life, I fled to another land and became a śramaṇa, remaining so for thirty-seven years.
Because his mind was obstructed by the five heinous crimes, he could not attain meditative concentration.
Later, while begging for food,
he happened to find a single alms bowl.
Within this bowl is a dhāraṇī called the "Spell for Gathering the Dharma to Relinquish Suffering and Hardship.
He recited and maintained it without interruption for more than a year.
Only then did they attain meditative concentration.
As for those bhikṣus who had violated the heavy prohibitions,
their minds were filled with remorse and they were consumed by anxiety.
Because the mind is anxious, there is no joy;
because there is no joy, there is no peace;
because there is no peace, one cannot attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Therefore, through the observance of the precepts and so forth, one obtains the conditions for the meditative discipline (*dhyāna-saṃvara*). However,
if one has committed a grave transgression against the precepts within this body, [the discipline is lost].
One will certainly not attain meditative concentration,
because unwholesome thoughts extensively damage and deeply obstruct it;
[this is avoided] through the majestic power of the mantra.
If one first commits the five heinous crimes while in the state of a worldly person,
it can be attained in this very body.
As for what was stated above— that concentration is attained by means of the precepts— [it refers to those who have not committed such grave offenses].
There are also cases where the first dhyāna is attained not through ethical discipline,
such as the meditative concentration attained by the very first person at the time of a kalpa’s destruction;
this is because it is the natural beginning of the dharma.
Therefore, even the fixed rules of discipline have other conditions;
there are also those that do not depend on them.
Their path is shared with the precepts.
The Yoga [Śāstra] further states:
"If one is without deficiency or transgression regarding this very śīla-vinaya,
and furthermore relies upon the dhyāna-vinaya..."
Upon entering the clear realization of the truths and attaining the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*),
all seeds of unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*) are forever destroyed.
This occurs if one realizes the first fruit by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
At that time, all afflictions capable of leading to the miserable destinies are forever destroyed.
This describes the attainment of the transcendence of the third fruit,
as well as for those who follow the gradual path, relying on both the fundamental dhyānas and the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
It is taught that for all those who attain the precepts of the Path, one must first purify meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its prerequisite.
This is because the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and intermediate restraint (*madhyama-śīla*), [they are not so].
Whether born into that family or not born into that family,
one spontaneously gives rise to a vow of resolve.
Alternatively, they may obtain external conditions through mutual instruction and training between father and son or others;
or they may obtain them without depending on another.
Both [positions] are without fault;
they do not conform to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) tenets,
which hold that non-restraint is not acquired from another.
The preceding section explained the acquisition of the conditions.
Regarding the timing of acquisition:
first, it explains the time of acquiring the manifest action (*vijñapti*).
Regarding the later explanation of the time when one acquires non-informative matter (*avijñapti*):
for now, let us consider the case of a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī at the moment they acquire informative matter (*vijñapti*).
This means that it is obtained when one requests the precepts from the monastic community.
The [Mahāvyutpatti] 53 states:
"Furthermore, if one gives rise to the intention to go to the teacher's location..."
He earnestly exhorted [the teacher] and,
through skillful means, initiated acts such as prostration and reverence;
maintaining proper deportment, he stood before the teacher.

Furthermore, that which expresses one's intentions through speech and the performance of superior actions are called bodily and vocal informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman* and *vāk-vijñapti-karman*).
This is the same as in the *Karmasiddhi-prakaraṇa*.
I cannot cite further examples at length.
In essence, it is the volition that is currently active which serves as the immediate cause (*samanantara-samutthāna*),
while that which actually initiates bodily and vocal action serves as the causal agent (*pravartaka*).
This is the essence of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*). Therefore, it must be at this time;
if one were to speak of the mind at the prior stage when requesting from the Saṃgha, [it would not constitute such action].
The superior, middling, and inferior [levels] are distinguished by the karma;
when the third *karmavācanā* (formal motion) is reached, the prayer is fulfilled.
That which is expressed by the term "manifest" (vijñapti) pertains to the doctrine of the Hīnayāna;
it is not the system we follow here.
Because manifest karma (vijñapti-karma) is not subsumed under visible form (saṃsthāna),
and because it is subsumed solely under the volition that initiates bodily and vocal action;
at that time, there is no mind (acittaka).
It may be defiled or neutral, depending on the difference in its objective conditions.
By analogy with this, the same applies to the remaining three groups of renunciants, as well as those in the one-day vows (upavāsa) and the lay devotees (upāsaka).
All of them received the formal precepts (vijñapti-śīla) by performing prostrations and other rites before their teachers;
although they subsequently followed the teacher’s words,
it was not necessarily the case that they possessed a focused intention.
Yet it is not necessarily wholesome,
nor is it determinate; for it is a mind that follows along with the turning [of the object] rather than being the turning mind itself.
If one has made a vow in the presence of others to receive [the precepts] spontaneously,
and possesses the manifest actions of body, speech, and mind,
then they are obtained at the moment one requests prostration before the Buddha.
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, at the very moment they are requested and received,
one attains them at the time of the third cycle of the syllables because of the completion of compassion;
this is due to their definitive nature.
The paths of meditative concentration consist solely of non-informative action;
it is not said that they possess informative action at the time [of their attainment]. As for non-restraint...
When one is about to perform an action or when one issues an instruction,
it is only then that manifest karma (vijñapti-karma) arises.
The fifty-third [fascicle] says:
"If there is one born into a family of non-restraint who possesses discernment and spontaneously gives rise to a resolute vow,"
That is to say, one thinks, "I shall maintain my life by means of this livelihood," and further gives rise to a mind of desire, pleasure, and acceptance toward this livelihood;
at that time, one is called a person of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Because they are comprised within non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and because they are comprised within extremely heavy, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) that harms the mental factors,
they constitute merely vast roots of unwholesomeness (*akuśalamūla*).
However, the unwholesome karma produced by the act of killing and other unwholesome courses of action has not yet been fully accomplished,
so long as the intended object has not yet been carried out.
This means that whether one is born into such a family or not,
the arousal of the thought [of enlightenment] and its acceptance occurs precisely because of the establishment of those unwholesome roots.
It is named according to that which arises from it;
thus, one is called a "person of non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*).
That treatise further states:
Later, whether manifesting [in action], or to a small or great extent,
they further accomplish various unwholesome karmas as appropriate;
this is what is meant by that statement.
Later, whether one acts oneself or directs another to perform various deeds,
even if one's life has not yet been cut off, etc.
This constitutes the unwholesome manifest karma of body or speech regarding the taking of life;
subsequently, once that act has been performed by oneself or another,
the preceding life is severed, and because the objective is largely or entirely fulfilled according to one's intention, the original vow is completed.
Only then is the non-informative (avijñapti) fully established.
This differs from other schools, which hold that the matter is completed at the end;
here, both the informative (vijñapti) and the non-informative arise simultaneously.
The initial arousal of superior volition that gives rise to physical and vocal actions constitutes informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
As for its ultimate nature, it is either a concomitant (*anuvartaka*) or not a concomitant (*na-anuvartaka*).
Because one acquires non-informative action (avijñapti),
it is termed "non-restraint" (asamvara).
Informative action (vijñapti-karman) is as previously described.
The manifest karma of abstinence is acquired either at the time of making a formal vow,
or at the time of the distribution [of the precepts],
or through the performance [of the ritual].
The preceding discussion concerned the time at which the two types of manifest action—bodily and vocal—are acquired.
As for the manifest action of the mind, it is acquired as soon as the thought arises. Thus concludes the explanation of the acquisition of manifest action.
Regarding the attainment of non-informative action (*avijñapti*): there are three categories for the attainment of the non-informative action of the Prātimokṣa.
The first is the great precepts of renunciation (*pravrajyā-mahāśīla*).
When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, one obtains this matter by saying, "I shall uphold it. Likewise,
the Bodhisattva precepts are also obtained when,
at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, one replies, "I am able to uphold them."
Because the superior countenance sought through the previously generated aspirational resolve is now fulfilled,
and because the ritual activities of the Saṃgha are complete at this time,
although [the result] arises from the seeds perfumed by the mental expression of the preceding stage.
The ritual for the Dharma is now concluded.
Although one may have been without intention or possessed a mind directed toward other matters,
because of that prior commitment, the present vow has now been fulfilled.
From the moment after the first thought, the seeds of the prevention of evil thoughts increase twofold;
this is called "attaining the precept. Some say that the essence [of the precept] consists of these seeds of thought.

To claim that receiving the precepts occurs through a process of doubling and redoubling [the number of participants] is also incorrect; for it is at the conclusion of the ritual proceedings that one attains them.
If that [mind] is either without mind (*acittaka*) or has a different object-condition (*visaya-pratyaya*),
and since there is no perfuming by present volition (*cetanā*) or present manifest action (*vijñapti*),
how could the substance of the seeds suddenly attain new birth?
From this it is known that,
according to the conditions encountered, whether seeds are new or old,
and whether they are individual or collective, [they arise].
The seeds perfumed by volition (*cetanā*), which serve as the causal condition for present activity,
now reach the fulfillment of their conditions;
their functioning increases manifold, and this is termed the acquisition of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Since the morality that accords with the mind is not newly acquired in every single moment,
if its increase were merely an increase in its essence rather than an increase in its function,
how could it be that seeds are being perfumed in manifestation in every single moment?
Since the unmanifest (avijñapti) of meditative concentration and the path is itself present volition,
and since there cannot be multiple volitions within a single moment of mind,
it follows accordingly that the unmanifest of the prātimokṣa does not involve an increase in its substantial entity.
In the first moment, one set of seven factors is augmented;
in the second moment, there are two sets of seven branches, and so on,
increasing with each successive stage until they are relinquished.
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, fascicle 60, states:
"If an unwholesome course of action reaches its culmination,
it is also called a grave evil due to the fault of being defiled by attachment."
It constitutes a great unwholesome act that leads to superior, undesirable results. Why is this?
Because if one employs a defiled mind capable of inducing suffering that another finds undesirable and unpleasant, [the result is grave].
Because that person, through the power of their mental state associated with suffering, is able to provoke further suffering,
the thought of that *pudgala* results in the incurrence of vast demerit;
therefore, this is called the fault of defilement.
This means that whether one performs unwholesome courses of action oneself or causes others to perform them.
When an act such as causing another’s life to end reaches its completion, by the natural force of the situation (*dharmatā-vaśa*),
it can bring about the mental volition (*cetanā*) of both the one who acts and the one who orders the action.
One thereby incurs a vast offense.
Since one’s former intention has now been fulfilled and the suffering of others has also been fulfilled,
one personally incurs the name of an offense called "defilement."
That treatise further states:
"Even though they do not give rise to such a thought,
those who cause me suffering shall incur great transgression."
Nevertheless, it is the very nature of that [action] to encounter great transgression;

just as, for example, although a magnet does not intentionally think, "Let all iron come and attach to me," it is nevertheless the inherent nature of that [magnet] that whatever iron is near it [is attracted].
It does not approach the magnet by means of any effort;
one should know that the principle herein is likewise.
The analogies of the sun-gem and so forth should also be understood in this same way.
Furthermore, there is no separate entity apart from volition (cetanā) that arises through its power; rather,
it is that which comes to depend upon and adhere to [volition] which is termed "tainting" (vāsanā).
One should know that this is merely a transformation of this very volition, produced by its power;
this is what is meant.
One then reflects that the seeds [of karma] from previous moments of mind have now reached fulfillment,
whereby the suffering of others becomes complete;
as the functional activity increases, it is termed "transformation."
There is nothing else;
it is just as the Māra-king deluded and seduced the hearts of immeasurable Śāleyakās, brahmins, and householders,
causing them to transform the World-Honored One into something perverse and violent.
It is not that some distinct dharma is added to those minds and designated as "delusive enchantment" (māyā); rather,
it is solely through the application and majestic power of the Māra-king that those various minds are produced and caused to transform into something extremely violent and evil.
This case is likewise;
because these wholesome paths of action exist as the opposites of the unwholesome paths of action,
they constitute a "staining" [of the mind].
It is through doubling and further doubling [the factors] that the non-informative (avijñapti) is fully established.
Among the ten ways of acquiring the precepts,
those acquired by the Buddha spontaneously—
There are bodhisattvas who attain the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-janma-maraṇa*) at the very first stage (*bhūmi*),
or those who attain it at the eighth stage and thereafter no longer undergo rebirth. Furthermore,
regarding the prātimokṣa vows, there is even one type that, once obtained, is never relinquished.
They transform into the perfect, untainted dharmas.
It is likewise for śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage who, having attained the stage of no-more-learning, turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and undergo the birth of transformation.
This refers to the separate reception of the Prātimokṣa precepts,
not to the restraint-precepts within the bodhisattva precepts.
For what reason is it called "spontaneously acquired precepts"?
If considered from the perspective of the stage of attaining Buddhahood,
although it is not currently acquired through reception,
it is nonetheless termed "attained spontaneously."
Those who attain it spontaneously acquire the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) at the moment of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Even if there were manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), it would not give rise to the unmanifest,
because after attaining Buddhahood, there is no further habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
In the stage of the path of liberation for a pratyekabuddha’s mind,
one has not yet initiated bodily or vocal action; how,
then, could there be informative [action] (vijñapti)?
The attainment of the precepts upon entering the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is likewise.
For the five persons who realize the truths (satyadarśana), there is no manifest action (vijñaptikarma);
rather, upon first entering the realization of the truths, they immediately obtain the unmanifest action (avijñapti).
This exists at the initial moment but not at subsequent moments;
for while the Saṃgha exists later, it did not exist at the beginning.
Upon the words "Welcome, Yaśas," one immediately obtains the non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*).

All those among this great multitude who were simply addressed with "Welcome," whose hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and whose robes transformed into saffron-colored monastic garments, became śramaṇas;
they were all of this class.
Those who take the Buddha as their teacher have not yet seen the Buddha;
they believe upon hearing of him from afar.
It is obtained at the very moment of faith;
furthermore, there is no manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Some say that one obtains the non-manifest action only when, through seeing the Buddha, one attains faith and accepts [him] as teacher.
It was not the case that he had not seen it before.
Regarding those who attained [realization] through question and answer, Sūdhāya alone attained it the moment the words were spoken.
Nor is there manifest action (vijñapti-karman).
Furthermore, some say that [one] has not yet reached twenty years of age.
In response to her question, the Buddha instructed that she be ordained.
Regarding the eight rules of respect for those who revere them:
at that time, there were no *bhikṣuṇīs* present.
Upon hearing the teaching and respectfully observing the proper time, one immediately obtains the avijñapti.
Since there were no bhikṣuṇīs [at that time], it cannot be said that the avijñapti and the vijñapti occur simultaneously;
nor can it be said that they occur at different times.

In the case where one receives [the precept] by dispatching a messenger, the informative act (*vijñapti*) exists at the time of dispatch, while the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) is acquired subsequently; thus, it is only the latter that exists, not the former. As for the recipient who receives [the precept] through a messenger, the informative act exists at the time of dispatch, whereas the non-informative act is acquired [subsequently].
When the nun who was sent has completed her reception [of the precepts],
the group of five or the group of ten shall receive them from their teacher,
as previously explained.
The manifest [action] (vijñapti) is expressed at the time of the first taking of refuge when one first seeks to pay homage;
the non-manifest (avijñapti) is acquired at the conclusion of the three refuges.
These ten all exist while a Buddha is present in the world.
After the Buddha has passed away, only three remain:
first, the self-enlightened pratyekabuddhas.
In a community of twenty,
three who uphold the Vinaya serve as the fifth members;
for other [communities], it is not the case that they cannot obtain [the requisite] Buddhas.
The first category has been explained above.
Regarding the second category:
the three classes of renunciants and the lay follower obtain non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
One obtains it immediately upon completing the three refuges.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"By giving rise to a mind of earnest purity."
He utters words of truth, declaring:
"I am an upāsaka; may the Venerable One remember me with compassion and protect me with mindfulness."
At that time, one immediately generates the lay devotee (upāsaka) discipline.
Regarding the three groups of the ordained, the declaration of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) does not generate non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);
yet this non-informative matter is likewise obtained at the conclusion of the triple refuge.
Regarding the third category:
the upavāsa precepts have two meanings.
One says they are obtained upon the completion of the three refuges.
This is no different from the case of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Second, [the opponent] asks: "If that is so, why does the *Abhidharmakośa* not state that one obtains the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) immediately after completing the three refuges?
Why, then, is it said that their characteristics differ from those of a lay follower?"
The characteristics of the five precepts for lay followers (*upāsaka*) are explained individually;
the characteristics of the one-day fast (*upavāsa*) are explained through three consecutive cycles.
Furthermore, that verse states: "According to the instruction, the complete set of branches is taught."
It is not said that the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is also acquired through the three refuges;
therefore, one knows that the one-day and night fast (*upavāsa*) is not obtained by means of the three refuges alone.
Its mental resolve broadly excludes [unwholesome conduct] for one day and night.
Therefore, it is not acquired immediately at the outset.
From this, one knows that it follows the teacher’s subsequent instruction;
only upon the completion of the third cycle does the non-informative [action] (avijñapti) arise.
Regarding the non-informative [matter] of dhyāna:
when the first moment of the first stage— the single category of the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage— arises,
it is termed "first acquisition."
Subsequently, whichever level of the fundamental dhyāna or the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) arises, the mind of that level is said to be "accomplished.
The Abhidharma, in its eighth chapter, states:
"Karma subsumed under the dhyāna restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*)."
This refers to the renunciation possessed by one who has abandoned the desires of the desire realm, as well as the renunciation possessed by one who has abandoned the desires of the first,
second, and third dhyānas; [it is] that which can damage and eliminate the seeds of the afflictions that give rise to transgressions of ethical discipline.
He himself explains:
"One who is free from the desires of the desire realm" means by the power of the antidote through suppression.
Whether it be partial detachment from desire or complete detachment from desire, in the very beginning,
one has not yet reached the point of violating the precepts.
This is the antidote of abandonment.
All those mentioned above are the antidotes of distancing.
Furthermore, among the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the first six belong to the stage of the threshold (*anāgamya*).

The two types of attention— namely, that which discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) and that which involves resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*)— serve as the counteractive measures for suppression (*vihiṃsā-pratipakṣa*);
they have not yet severed the afflictions, for it is only through the attention of withdrawal (*prāvivekya-manasikāra*) that the afflictions are first severed.
There are two explanations for this.
First, it is said that "understanding the characteristics" still involves a mixture of hearing and reflection;
one initially contemplates the desire realm as coarse.
The higher stages are tranquil; however,
as they have not yet been able to abandon the hindrances,
one repeatedly contemplates them through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
From this point onward, one exclusively cultivates the mental application of characteristics (*nimitta-manasikāra*).
Because these two types of mental application are involved, they are termed "overcoming through revulsion" (*vidūṣaṇa*).
It is only upon reaching the third mental application, that of "separation" (*viveka*), that the upper three grades [of afflictions] are finally abandoned.
Since the counteractive measures of suppression and subjugation already constitute cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
both the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-prativedha*) and resolute belief (*adhimokṣa*) have already attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Regarding the first point: for the abandonment of afflictions in the three superior grades, one must reach the third stage of attention (*manasikāra*);

therefore, it is said that only through "separation" (*viveka*) can one abandon the afflictions. Regarding the second point: the "comprehension of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) abandons the highest of the high grades.
Through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one abandons the upper and middle grades; through distancing (*dūrībhāva*), one abandons the lower and upper grades of afflictions.
When the upper grades are entirely exhausted, it receives the designation of "abandonment."
Since one does not suppress the afflictions within the stage of "perceiving characteristics," the precept co-arising with meditative concentration is attained at the very first moment; thus,
there is no contradiction or difficulty.
It should be stated in verse:
"The discipline of meditative concentration consists solely of non-informative matter;
the initial preparatory stage is called 'abandonment'."
The remainder possesses the nature of being remote;
this is called the restraint of the dhyāna code.
As for the untainted (anāsrava) non-manifestation (avijñapti):
The very moment one first attains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is simultaneously called "attainment.
Upon entering the path of seeing, the five stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) all constitute the antidote that abandons [the afflictions].
The remaining [factors] of the form and formless realms all constitute the remote category;
this is the meaning of the extended explanation.
If one relies on the six stages of the form realm and the first three lower types of the formless realm:
The stream-enterer who leaps over to realize the fourth fruit is like one cutting bamboo:
he severs the afflictions crosswise.
Within the desire realm, there is a counteractive agent for abandoning the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
the others are termed "distancing."
Although there are sūtras stating that one attains this first fruit by relying on the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) and does not further cultivate the higher untainted (anāsrava) stages,
it is certainly not the case that this is exclusively so.
It may be as previously stated. Otherwise,
since the formless realm lacks the antidote that severs [defilements],
this concentration and the morality of the path would have to follow the mind.
Merely attaining that mind is what is meant by "attainment";
it does not depend upon outward manifestation.
By the very nature of things, the meditative states and the supramundane paths are inherently opposed to evil.
Therefore, both of these must necessarily possess non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Regarding the acquisition of non-discipline (*asaṃvara-avijñapti*),
that non-discipline is based on the ninth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
There are twelve kinds:
first, sheep-slaughterers;
second, poultry-sellers.
Third, selling pigs;
fourth, catching birds;
fifth, snaring rabbits.
Sixth, the thieves;
seventh, the executioners;
eighth, the jailers.
9. Slandering with False Accusations;
10. Adjudicating Legal Cases;

If that were not the case, then Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward who have attained sudden enlightenment, as well as Buddhas—
who reside solely in the fourth dhyāna—
would lack wholesome karma of body and speech.
Just as for the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses, those that are with-outflows (sāsrava) do not exist in the higher stages,

so it should be for bodily and vocal karma.

may be considered the antidote of maintenance (*dhṛti-pratipakṣa*).
All of the above constitute the counteractive measures for the distant portion (*vipakṣa-pratipakṣa*).

Alternatively, it is comprised within the restraint of abandonment that is the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and attainment (*samāpatti*).

The fruit of abandonment is precisely this twofold restraint; it is not the abandonment of transgressions, because it is the fruit born of meditative concentration.

Why must one rely on a physical basis? Therefore,
through both the fundamental [attainment] and the preparatory stages,

It is the nature of things that all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are capable of subduing the non-virtuous;

For this reason, it differs from the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school.
The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) extends throughout the ten stages:
six in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and four in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because there exists the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). If it were a counteractive agent (*pratipakṣa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), then—
since the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) among the five stages of the form realm lacks the path of seeing— it would not exist there.
The rest are all held as distant divisions.

If one admits that the first fruit leads to the attainment of the fourth fruit,
why discard reliance upon it?
Although we know that the treatises cite the analogy of the fingertip for analytical discernment.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. As for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), it possesses only the sense of being "distant" and not the sense of being "abandoned."
The bodies born within the three realms can all give rise to it;
however, the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of non-restraint is bound only to the level of the body-ground of the desire realm.
Because they are exclusively unwholesome,

Because one sustains life with a lack of malicious intention;

that which abides in the intermediate state (madhyastha) extends throughout the three realms,
depending on the physical body and giving rise to the matter of bodily and vocal actions.
They exist in two stages, the desire realm and the form realm.
Those consisting of mental expression and so forth, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*), pertain to the bodies based upon all three realms;
they exist in all higher stages.
Because, apart from the wholesome states of restraint (*saṃvara*), all others are intermediate (*madhya*).
Regarding the seventh point, what among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is it derived from?
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it says:
The nature of matter in the case of restraint (*saṃvara*) is established based on dharmas that do not manifest;
the nature of matter in the case of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is established based on dharmas that manifest.
This is the general meaning.
The vows of manifest and unmanifest discipline both rely upon the body and speech that they restrain as nominal form;
this specifically reveals the distinct forms of the three realms, including the prātimokṣa, dhyāna, and untainted (anāsrava) precepts.
All of these are produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the body and speech that constitute the evil actions prevented by the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Even if the Buddha’s body possesses untainted (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), it is co-existent with the formless meditative concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
It is also produced by the four great elements of the past desire realm;
since it is metaphorically designated by the remote term "name-and-form," it is also metaphorically designated by the remote term "produced by name."
Therefore, one does not name it according to what has been produced,
nor does one construct it through names,
because it is indeterminate.
It is not necessarily the case that there is something which originates body and speech;
thus, the meaning of the two types of manifest action— bodily and vocal— is also understood to include the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that originates them,
namely, the form derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This [karma] is established based on the stage in which the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions that have given rise to superior bodily or vocal actions increase."
Although it is known that even when there is no manifestation during the state of scattering, bodily and vocal actions are still initiated,
