It is exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
it is exclusively of the nature of outflows (*sāsrava*).
As for the dharmas that are fruits, they encompass both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
It is exclusively untainted and exclusively of a wholesome nature.
Regarding the term "non-contradictory cause":
it refers to a non-contradictory cause that is pure.
The cause is broad while the fruit is narrow;
if it were a pure phenomenon, there would be no contradiction,
as the cause would be narrow while the fruit is broad.
This follows the previous explanation.
Regarding the second [section], the ten causes of affliction (*saṃkleśa*):
according to their actual meaning...
It is merely the cause for the conventional designation of defiled phenomena. Why is this?
Because within the Mahāyāna, sound is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous by nature.
If it is derived from the manifest [action], it is conventionally designated as having both virtuous and non-virtuous natures;
by this principle, there are also two interpretations.
If it is the descriptive cause (*anuvāda-hetu*) of defiled phenomena.
The substance of the cause (hetu) pervades the three natures (trividha-svabhāva) and is both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava),
being exclusively conditioned (saṃskṛta).
The resultant phenomena (phala-dharma) pervade the three natures.
It is exclusively conditioned and exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If that which is defiled is what is designated as the cause,
then the essence of the cause permeates all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
Only those that are with outflows (sāsrava) and conditioned (saṃskṛta).
As for the resultant dharmas, they are obtained throughout all [categories].
This is according to the sense of successive transmission.
Furthermore, it is because [the mind] can take True Suchness (tathatā) as its object. As for the condition of dependence (apekṣā-hetu):
if it is the condition of dependence for defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma),...

The nature of the cause (hetu) pervades the three natures (trividha-svabhāva), as well as the contaminated (sāsrava), the uncontaminated (anāsrava), the conditioned (saṃskṛta), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The nature of the fruit (phala), however, pervades the three natures but is exclusively contaminated and exclusively conditioned.
If defilement is the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), its essential nature (*svabhāva*) permeates all three moral natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*);
it is exclusively outflowing (*sāsrava*) and exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The essence of the fruit is universally attainable by all;
this is the general statement.
To speak of it specifically:
This consists of four propositions:
if there is a capacity to perceive dependent upon that which is perceived,
then the essence of the cause pervades all things.

The resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and, when with outflows (*sāsrava*), they pertain to all three moral natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*). If one considers that which experiences and that which is experienced,
the nature of the cause (*hetu*) pertains to all three moral natures, yet it is exclusively with outflows and conditioned.
The resultant phenomena (phala-dharma) are universally applicable to all and are thus attained.
If one considers the capacity to receive [the result] in relation to the recipient,
the nature of cause and effect is identical.
Among these, there are distinctions that should be reflected upon according to reason:
since in the Mahāyāna there is no unwholesome form and so forth,
there is consequently no object of experience nor anything dependent upon such experience.
If one bases this on manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*),
it begins from the bone of the foot waiting for the bone of the ankle, and so forth;
thus, the nature of cause and effect is pervasive.
What logical flaw is there in this?
Both the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the productive cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*) are *karmadhāraya* compounds.
Because their causal nature is identical:
if one relies on karma to draw forth the arising of the five fruits such as consciousness,
there is little that constitutes a projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*) among the defiled phenomena.
The essence of the cause (hetu-tattva) pertains to both natures.

Only conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) and outflowing phenomena (sāsrava) are [causes]; the fruit (phala), however, is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), exclusively outflowing, and exclusively conditioned.
As for what is called the "appropriating cause" (parigraha-hetu):
If it is the grasping cause (*parigraha-hetu*) of afflicted phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*),

its causal substance (*hetu-bhāva*) pervades the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) and includes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the outflowing (*sāsrava*), and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
The nature of the resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) is the same as before.
If defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are what is grasped,
then their causal substance (*hetu-bhāva*) pervades all three natures;
they are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The nature of the fruit pervades all things.
As for "inducing," it refers to the inducing cause of afflicted phenomena.
The substance of the cause permeates all three natures;
it is exclusively contaminated and exclusively conditioned, not unconditioned.
The nature of the fruit is the same as before;
alternatively, this explanation may be omitted.
If defiled phenomena were themselves the producing cause (*ākṣepahetu*), [then...]
The essence of causes pervades all three natures.
Only conditioned, outflowing (*sāsrava*), and resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) pervade all three natures.
Outflowing and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) phenomena are exclusively conditioned.
If, based on the cause, one takes the wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas that have been abandoned as the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*),
what prevents the resultant dharma from also including the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
As for the statement that it must necessarily differ from its cause:
If one must distinguish the specific causes for the various defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*),
then with respect to those that take the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) as their fruit,
the resultant phenomena are exclusively indeterminate, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and outflowing (*sāsrava*).
The substance of the cause (hetu-tattva) pervades both the wholesome and unwholesome natures;
it is exclusively conditioned (saṃskṛta) and with outflows (sāsrava).
If the three natures constitute the fruit (phala), [the following applies].
Defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma) are precisely the causes of distinctness (pratiniyama-hetu).
Both cause and effect encompass all three natures (tri-svabhāva),
yet they exist only as conditioned (saṃskṛta) and outflowing (sāsrava).
Regarding the cause of commonality (*samānārthatā-hetu*):
if it is the cause of commonality for afflicted phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*), the essential nature of that cause permeates all three moral qualities (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*).
Conditioned and unconditioned, with outflows and without outflows:
resultant phenomena (phala-dharma) pertain to all three natures;
however, [the nature of] being conditioned and having outflows applies only to them.
If defilement (*saṃkleśa*) were identical to the cause of common purpose (*samānārtha-hetu*),
the nature of the cause would be narrow while the nature of the fruit would be broad.
As for what is called the "contradictory cause" (*viruddha-hetu*):
It possesses only that which is contradictory to the signs of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Its substantial nature (*hetu-tattva*) encompasses both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
and it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).
The resulting meaning would then be narrow.
To say there is no contradiction: if it is analyzed as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
The essence of the cause is narrow, while the essence of the fruit pervades all.
If analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound,
the fruit is narrow and the cause is broad.
Regarding the ten causes for the third category, the indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas:
if one takes external phenomena as indeterminate dharmas,
there is only the indeterminate cause of designation (anuvyavahāra-hetu).
The nature of the cause can be understood as pertaining to all three moral natures,
because it is manifested within the causal state;
thus, it is established that the actual indeterminate nature resides in the fruit.
The cause includes both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava),
and is exclusively conditioned (saṃskṛta).
The essence of the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Only those that are with-outflows (sāsrava) and conditioned (saṃskṛta).
Regarding the statement that "the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is itself the cause":
if one refers to internal sound, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is indeterminate.
Regarding the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*):
it consists of those indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena that serve as the cause of designation.
Its essential nature is exclusively indeterminate, exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), and exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The result applies to all things.
If sounds such as those of the wind are capable of signifying meaning,
what prevents external phenomena from being the very cause [of that signification]?
Regarding the term "contingent upon" (*apekṣā*),
there are four propositions therein:
that which is contingent upon what is experienced, and that which is experienced.
That which is depended upon serves as the cause,
and that which depends [upon it] serves as the effect;
such is the nature of effect and cause.
Because shape and so forth depend on water and other factors for their manifestation through causes;
since shape and the like function as both cause and effect,
if there is that which is experienced and that which depends upon it, there must also be an experiencer.
This is because their nature is likewise identical, such as in the case of cause and effect;
they both function as the "condition of dependence" (apekṣā-hetu) by being mutually enumerated.
If one follows this meaning,
there is no such phrase regarding external phenomena. If, however,
one relies on the existence of an object of experience, there must be an experiencer.
That which is received is the cause.
It is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma;
that is, its causal substance is exclusively indeterminate, exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The nature of the fruit (phala-bhāva) pervades all three moral natures;
it is exclusively conditioned (saṃskṛta) and not unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
It pervades both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava), and consists solely of mind, mental factors, contact (sparśa), and feeling (vedanā).
If one waits for that which is capable of receiving [the fruit] and that which is received,
the nature of the cause is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), permeated by outflows (*sāsrava*), and includes all three moral natures (*trividha*).
The nature of the fruit, however, is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), exclusively with outflows, conditioned, and consists solely of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*).
If the neutral (avyākṛta) dependence-condition (apekṣā-hetu) has a broad causal essence but a narrow nature as a result,
then that which is neutral is itself the dependence.
The nature of the cause is narrow while its fruit is broad.
Regarding the two causes— the projecting cause and the producing cause—
they function as causes only for dharmas that are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
This is because the seeds of external barley and so forth are merely conventional designations.
As for what is called the "appropriating cause" (parigraha-hetu):
it refers to the appropriating cause of indeterminate phenomena (avyākṛta-dharma).
There are only two types of dependence:
namely, functional dependence (*kāritra-puruṣakāra*) and causal dependence (*hetu*). These causes pertain to all three moral natures.
Only conditioned and out-flowing phenomena [serve as causes];
the fruit is exclusively indeterminate, and only conditioned and out-flowing phenomena [are the fruit].
If indeterminate phenomena were to include the appropriated cause, [it would lead to error].
The nature of cause and effect is the same.
As for the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*), it consists solely of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas; that is, only indeterminate dharmas constitute the projecting cause.
The nature of cause and effect is identical.
As for what is called a "distinct cause," it can only be that indeterminate dharmas are themselves distinct.
Regarding the identity of fruit and cause,
as for what is called the "common-functioning cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*):
it refers to the common-functioning cause of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.
The cause is broad while the fruit is narrow;
this can be understood by analogy with what preceded.
If it is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma, it is the cause of "common function" (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The cause is narrow while the fruit is broad.
Regarding what is called a "contradictory cause," there exists only a contradiction with respect to the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The nature of cause and effect is the same.
If snow and the like are external indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
what prevents there also being indeterminate dharmas that serve as contradictory causes?
The essence of cause and effect is identical.
Regarding what is called a non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*):
if it is a neutral (*avyākṛta*) non-contradictory cause...
The substance of the cause pervades all things,
whereas the fruit is extremely narrow;
if it were indeterminate, it would contradict the nature of a cause.
Regarding the nature of cause and effect, etc., the fourth section clarifies the establishment and rejection [of categories].
Question: For what reason are there ten causes?
Answer: Briefly, there are six distinctions.
(5–10 missing) Regarding the meaning of the five fruits, they are analyzed briefly by way of ten gates. First, the definition of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, the explanation of the names;
third, the establishment and abolition [of categories]; fourth, attainment through four causes and two causes.
54. Attainment through conditions. 65. Attainment through bases.
7. How many causes and fruits of the Three Vehicles are possessed?
Eight, the classification of the conditioned and unconditioned, the outflowing and non-outflowing, and so forth;
nine, the classification of what is abandoned by vision and so forth;
ten, the classification of questions and answers.
Regarding the three types of "establishment" (pratiṣṭhāpana):
"fruition" (phala) has the meaning of accomplishment;
there must be a phenomenon (dharma) that exists as such.
It is not that they are non-existent;
rather, there are two kinds of fruits realized through causes:
first, unconditioned fruits (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
There are two types of conditioned fruits.
The unconditioned fruit is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*);
the conditioned fruit is called the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Because the unconditioned has no manifold distinctions,
it is not further analyzed;
whereas the conditioned possesses distinctions.
Furthermore, it should be established that there are cases where something is obtained through causes and through unobstructed power;
such instances merely receive the designation of "predominance" (adhipati).
There are those obtained through causes involving superior grasping and giving;
among these, there are those obtained through causes involving the collective designation of a person,
and those obtained through causes involving individual dharmas.
The name "result of human effort" (*puruṣakāraphala*) is generally applied to that which is obtained by a person as a whole.
As for other distinct dharmas that are also obtained as results of human effort,
they are designated by this name because they resemble the general category through their connection to it.
Within this, based on the establishment of the general,
there are further two categories of results obtained through specific dharmas.
The first is sameness of nature;
the second is difference of nature.
That which is of a different nature is called the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
That which is of the same nature is called the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) is superior, being obtained through the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is distinct.

As for the other fruits not resulting from analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-phala*), such as those obtained through the six paths of action, they are merely fruits of dominance (*adhipati-phala*).
If it is not that which brings about excellence, it is merely termed "predominant";
that which does bring about excellence is termed "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) and so forth.
Therefore, the five fruits are neither increased nor decreased.
Furthermore, it is revealed that the categories of causes are numerous and can be divided into ten types,
while the results, though difficult to establish due to their multiplicity, are collectively posited as five;
this is based on the authoritative scriptures.
This explanation is provided because it is taught that the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) both extend to include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
What is obtained through this is nothing more than existent phenomena (*dharma*).
These are categorized as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As for the unconditioned, there are not many distinctions.
Since there is only a single nature,
it is established as a single fruit called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), however, possess many distinctions and differ in their three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
That which is obtained from a cause of the same nature is called the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*);
that which is obtained from a cause of a different nature is called the result of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
Within the acquisition of results from causes of the same nature, however, those results drawn forth by a predominant power are specifically termed results of outflow.
Therefore, both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the superior class (*viśiṣṭapakṣa*) serve as causes;
they do not function as inferior causes.
Within the category of dissimilar classes (*vipakṣa*), the nature of the cause is distinguished by its superiority.
The manifestation of the fruit-characteristic is called maturation (*vipāka*).
Therefore, with respect to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, [the neutral nature] exists within those wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Viewed from one another, none of these are its fruit;
the substance of the cause is not superior,
and the fruit is not manifest.
It is not established as a result because there is no distinct characteristic by which it could be known;
rather, it is subsumed within the general category of results.
However, in the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*...
It is said that there are two kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*):
first, those of similar outflow (*niṣyanda*),
and second, those of maturation (*vipāka*).
Because it comprehensively subsumes all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*),
it is established that there is no distinction between the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and thus one and two fruits are established.
However, what has been described above constitutes the distinction between the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) fruits.
Each of these two possesses proximate power, distant power, superior power, inferior power, direct power, indirect power, supportive power, and non-obstructive power.
Among the unconditioned phenomena,
those that are obtained through being proximate, superior, intimate, or supportive causes are established as the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If it is obtained through the power of that which is distant, inferior, remote, or non-obstructive,
it is called the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
These two are the common fruits of both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
All [these fruits] receive the designation "human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) based on distinct dharmas.
This fruit has as its essence all four types of dharmas:
those that arise simultaneously, those that follow immediately, those that are separated by an interval, and those that do not arise at all.
Regarding "simultaneously arising results" (*sahaja-phala*): because they are dharmas that arise at the same time.
As stated in the second fascicle of the *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra):
Seeds produce the manifest, just as the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) attains the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
Alternatively, the seventh [chapter] states:
"All dharmas possess the fruit of human effort."
Regarding the "immediately succeeding fruit" (ānantarya-phala), it refers to the dharmas that arise immediately thereafter.
Thus, the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
The "all-aspect" (sarvākāra) [attainment] yields the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*),
because within the category of the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), it is designated as the fruit of human effort.
As the eighth fascicle states:
The causes such as the productive cause (āvāhaka-hetu) obtain the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala). As for the "separated fruit" (vyavahita-phala),
it is because one plants in the spring and reaps the fruit in the autumn.
All treatises agree that this is the "virile effect" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Alternatively, the "ripened effect" (*vipāka-phala*) may also be separated [from its cause].
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsaptati* states:
Because the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) is established with respect to the *vipāka-phala* (fruition result).
Furthermore, the eighth [chapter] states:
"The projecting [cause] and the producing [cause] obtain the *puruṣakāra-phala*."
Regarding "that which does not produce a fruit":
this refers to the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) obtained based on the locus of true vision.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
The cause of appropriation (parigraha-hetu) obtains the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
Although the two bases for the activity of human effort are included within this cause,
since it brings about that which is to be obtained as human effort, [it is so designated].
How could this preclude the true vision from obtaining its *puruṣakāra* (human effort/result)?
Therefore, we know that distinct dharmas also possess *puruṣakāra*.
Furthermore, the fruit of *puruṣakāra* also encompasses all four types [of fruits].
By virtue of this, these five fruits neither increase nor decrease.
The explanation of the meaning of the five fruits in fascicle sixty-five is somewhat superior;
it differs from other versions, so one should examine it.
The Forest of Meanings regarding the Form of the Dharma-base (dharmāyatana-rūpa) is analyzed in general through five sections:
first, the opening and closing, as well as the setting aside and establishing;
second, the discernment of its essential nature.
Third, the explanation of names;
fourth, the differentiation between the provisional and the real;
fifth, the existence or non-existence of the reflection and its substance.
1. Opening and Closing, Abolishing and Establishing. Regarding "opening and closing, abolishing and establishing," there is one [category] in total within the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, namely:
matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa*).
The *Pañcaskandhaka* states that there are two types of matter in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*):
first, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), and second, the result of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*).
The third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains it in the same manner.
The first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that there are three types:
first, restraint (*saṃvara*).
Second, non-restraint;
third, mastery over meditative concentration.
The first three mentioned in the fifty-fourth [chapter] are the same as these.
Furthermore, in that same fascicle,
it is explained at length that atoms are merely disintegrated by the power of analytical wisdom (*buddhi*).
If they are not included within the category of "dharmas," under what category would they be subsumed?
Based on this, four types are established within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana);
the Abhidharma treatises speak of five,
as listed in the text itself.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), chapter eighteen, states:
"The matter included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) has twelve characteristics.
The first is the reflected image (*pratibimba*)."
Second, maturation through activity;
third, non-visibility;
fourth, non-obstructiveness.
Five are the non-substantial great elements;
six are the characteristics associated with the mind;
seven are worldly.
Eight: the inconceivable;
nine: the fruits of mundane concentration;
ten: the fruits of supramundane concentration.
Eleventh, the objects of one's own and others' stages;
twelfth, the sovereign transformations of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the "one" among the hundred dharmas, it is because they are explained according to their locus and category.
The *Pañcaskandhaka* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* each state that there are two types [of atoms]:

the "extremely concise" (*parama-saṃkṣipta*) and the "extremely remote" (*parama-viprakṛṣṭa*). These two are essentially identical to the atom (*paramāṇu*), which is produced by breaking down gross, substantial matter (*rūpa*) into its constituent parts.
Because the provisional follows the real and the subtle follows the coarse,
no further separate explanation is given regarding the various bases of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
This refers to the non-lucid consciousness that arises from pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa).
It arises from the conceptual construction of the faculty and its object acting in conjunction;
with the perfumed seeds as its cause, it subsequently produces the faculty and object.
Thus, the cause is designated by the fruit, and the reflection is designated by the substance.
Nor is it mentioned separately within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Because all non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) has a hidden nature and belongs to the same category,
they are collectively established as a single "non-informative" entity.
Although the fruits of mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi-vaśitā-phala) pertain to both the conventional and the ultimate,
they are all produced by concentration and are established collectively as a whole.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth, some sources state there are two, not many;
while the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* each state that there are three.
Although all types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) are similar in their general characteristics,
they are divided into two kinds because their natures as wholesome or unwholesome differ.
That which is wholesome is called restraint (*saṃvara*);
that which is unwholesome is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Regarding those situated in between, there is either no unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) established, or it is not established at all.
Alternatively, for those of that class, no further distinction is made and the remainder is not mentioned; it should be understood according to the preceding principle.

Therefore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts state that there are only three [natures], whereas those who speak of four maintain that the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature) may possess an objective basis (*vastu*).
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is not established separately according to its substance or its fruit;
rather, it is established separately because atoms (*paramāṇu*) lack substantial form.
As for the spheres of distant space and clear light, they are not differentiated because their categories are identical.
Regarding this statement that there are five [types],
the objects of consciousness occurring independently (svatantra-manas) differ from those based on a physical basis (sapratigha-rūpa) in terms of their substance and function,
because they are contrasted with the sense faculties (indriya).
All that has an essential nature (svabhāva) subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is called an image (pratibimba);
it is termed "arisen from conceptual construction" (parikalpita).
The wise analyze this into two categories: first,
mutual [destruction], and second, the destruction of one [by another].
It is solely that which is observed.

Because it is extremely concise, extremely remote, and an object of uncontaminated mental factors—whether conceptual (prajñapti) or substantial (dravya)—it is collectively termed "born of meditative concentration" (samādhija).
Therefore, it is divided into five types.
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), in its eighteenth chapter,

explains that the twelve [characteristics] refer exclusively to the various characteristics— whether provisional or real— which are the fruits of meditative concentration; these are distinct from other categories,
and nothing else is further discussed.
The twelve types of characteristics are all distinctions within the fruits of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
they do not exhaustively represent the principles.
In reality, only three types are established for the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
First are images: all atoms,
as well as those constructed by the solitary and dispersed mind— such as sense organs, objects, mirror-images, and the moon reflected in water—
all such categories are equally devoid of reality.
Because they are reflections of the mind,
both are established under a single heading.
Second is the unmanifest (avijñapti).
Whether in a state of concentration or distraction, whether wholesome or unwholesome,
none of these can represent another; since their characteristics and functions are thus equivalent.
They are established as a single category based on three factors: first, by their basis; second, by their nature;

and third, by their fruit of meditative concentration. Whether they are contaminated or uncontaminated, and whether they are provisional or substantial, all arise from meditative concentration and are thus established as a single category.
Therefore, regarding the five aggregates and so forth, the latter two types [of form] are taught.
If one considers the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*), one proceeds from the provisional to the real, and from the subtle to the coarse.
If one considers the form of conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), one proceeds from the cause to the effect, and from the reflection to the substance.
Furthermore, if one does not separately establish the form of a reflected image,
then the non-informative (avijñapti) should likewise follow the real from the conventional;
it would not be a form derived from form, and thus would not be mentioned separately, but only as the fruit of meditative concentration.
Since that is not the case, how could this be so?
Therefore, it should be stated that the three are neither to be increased nor decreased.
As for why the present treatise states that there are five: [it is because...]
Furthermore, when a single defiled mind arises as a distracted thought,
it takes as its collective object the sense faculties, their respective domains, the moon reflected in water,
and images in a mirror; all of these are coarse.
When the sense faculties are analyzed down to the level of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), they are no longer coarse but only subtle.
Although they are equally like reflections, their degrees of coarseness and subtlety differ entirely;
likewise, the mental states of cognition, conceptualization, and mind that take them as objects are also distinct.
Therefore, having set aside the imagined nature, atoms are established separately.
Within the category of obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), there are briefly two types:
first, that which is merely obstructed by others but cannot obstruct them.
This refers to the distinct colors such as light and so forth within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
As stated below in the third section, because they are not obstructive, [the following applies]:
that which can obstruct others is also itself obstructed.
Apart from the color of distant space and so forth,
all other resistant forms are mentioned below in the third [section] because they are mutually obstructive;
it is by virtue of this that these two types of coarse form differ.
When analyzed down to the ultimate subtle particles, there is still differentiation.
That which was previously obstructive is broken down to the ultimate subtle particle and is called "extremely distant matter" (*paramāṇu-pratibhāga-rūpa*).
That which was subsequently obstructive together with it is broken down to the ultimate subtle particle and is called "extremely concise matter" (*paramāṇu-saṃkṣepa-rūpa*).
Based on these categories, two types are distinguished.
The objects and consciousnesses manifested through the two gates differ;
accordingly, their coarse or subtle nature, as well as their opening and closing, are also distinct.
Coarse forms are easy to understand and are thus collectively termed "images" (*pratibimba*);
subtle forms are difficult to comprehend and are therefore analyzed through two distinct gates.
Thus, the treatise states that these five [categories] cannot be reduced or increased.
It penetrates deeply into all texts and precisely accords with the profound principle. 2.
Distinguishing the Essential Nature (Tattva). Regarding the second point, distinguishing the essential nature:
First is the most concise form (*paramāṇurūpa*).
This treatise itself states that its substance is the atom (*paramāṇu*),
which consists of the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*).

Excluding the color of distant space and so forth, the remaining five types of sensory objects, the four great elements, and the real matter of the *dharmāyatana* have atoms (*paramāṇu*) as their nature.
This is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the fifty-fourth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The establishment of atoms consists of fifteen types:
namely, the five atoms of the sense faculties such as the eye,
and the five atoms of the objects such as visible form.
The four great elements consist of four atoms;
the real matter of the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) consists of one atom.
Therefore, these fifteen constitute the nature of "extremely condensed" matter (paramāṇusaṃghātarūpa).
Second is the color of extreme distance.
The treatise itself states:
"This is precisely that color which is free from other obstructive contacts."
It has as its substance the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the matter of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*).
The treatises state that "distant color" (*prāntavarṇa*) consists of light and darkness;
one should know that the colors of light and shadow are subsumed under distant color.
The heat of the sun is called "light" (āloka);
other forms of heat are called "luminosity" (obhāsa).
Shadow and darkness are the opposites of these.
Is it only light and darkness that constitute distinct forms?
We have merely explained light and darkness by citing a limited portion.
However, as for the form of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), there are distinctions in its perception from above and below.
It is divided into distinct color (*prāthakavarṇa*) and that which is manifested as space (*ākāśaikaprakhyāna*).
Therefore, the matter of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) comprises six kinds of matter.
When reduced down to its ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is collectively termed "ultimate distinctness" (*paramaprāthaka*).
The reason for establishing this should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding "matter induced by the three feelings," the treatise itself states:
This refers to non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
According to one interpretation, there are only two types,
having the non-informative matter of restraint (saṃvara) and non-restraint (asaṃvara) as their essence.
Since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) exists only in these two locations— namely, wherever there is the teaching of the Dharma—
and because non-informative matter arises only from seeds of intense volition (*cetanā*),
some maintain that it also has as its nature non-informative matter that is neither discipline (*saṃvara*) nor non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
In this eighth [chapter], it is taught that there are three types of karma:
first, restraint;
second, non-restraint.
Third is that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
As for that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
it refers to all wholesome and unwholesome karma belonging to those [states].
Whether it be acts such as giving or acts such as striking,
these are karmas not subsumed under either discipline (*saṃvara*) or non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
All these are included herein.
Regarding the fifty-four explanations,
as for the differentiation of the functions of form (*rūpa*):
This refers to the activity subsumed under the categories of manifest and unmanifest restraint, non-restraint, and that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint;
for it is said that giving and so forth constitute this karma.
It is certain that this karma also possesses the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Since the three categories— manifest (*vijñapti*), unmanifest (*avijñapti*), and restraint (*saṃvara*)— are explained as being the functions of matter (*rūpa*),
for what reason do only two possess both manifest and unmanifest aspects?
In this context, does neutral karma consist solely of informative action (*vijñapti*)?
No; since the threefold classification is not explicitly stated, it is subsumed within the two types—wholesome and unwholesome.
Therefore, that which is induced by undertaking (*samādāna*) necessarily pertains to all three types.
There are three types of discipline non-manifestation (saṃvara-avijñapti) in total.
The first is the non-manifestation of individual liberation (prātimokṣa), which consists of the precepts of the seven classes of practitioners.
The two meditative absorptions both possess non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
All contaminated precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*) associated with the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are also termed the "meditative restraint" (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
It is named after the deportment of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
There are three types of untainted non-informative matter (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-avijñapti*):
the various untainted precepts that coexist with the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
If there are the non-manifestations of the Prātimokṣa, the non-manifestations of non-restraint, and the non-manifestations of the intermediate state—
these three are all established based on the stage where the seeds of motivating volition, having prevented the arousal of bodily and vocal actions, increase their capacity for good or evil.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that this [karma] is established based on the stage of the increase of the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) that give rise to superior bodily and vocal actions.
This is as explained in the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
When one initiates an excellent volition capable of producing either restraint or non-restraint,
it perfumes the continuum to form two types of superior seeds; as long as these remain undestroyed,
they are conventionally designated as the virtuous or non-virtuous unmanifest (avijñapti) of restraint.

The two kinds of uncontaminated non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) coexisting with meditative concentration are established based on the functional capacity of the present volition that restrains evil within those two states; thus,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
Alternatively, it is established based on the volition that ceases the manifestation of bodily and vocal misconduct within meditative concentration.
These various types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) have as their essence that which is induced by undertaking [a vow].
Fourth, there is matter arising from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).
The treatise states its own explanation:
"That is to say, the form of images arises independently;
the dispersed mental consciousness transforms the faculties and objects through the three natures, functioning as if they possessed faculties and so forth where none exist."
The moon in water and reflected images—
these are not one and the same;
they are produced by the conceptualization of the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and the forms of meditative states.
The useless image is the substance of form produced by this pervasive conceptualization;
as for the forms produced by the five masteries:
The treatise itself states:
"It has as its essence the form that is the object of the meditative absorption of liberation.
This is stated in [Treatise on the] Fifty-three.
By virtue of the power of supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains mastery over all forms;
thus, its essence consists precisely of the objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch transformed by that concentration.
3. Explaining the Names. Regarding the threefold explanation of the names:
first, "extremely abbreviated matter" (*paramasaṃkṣiptarūpa*).
"Extremely" (*parama*) means "to the limit."
"Ultimate" (qióng) means "limit" (biān).
Briefly stated, it has two senses.
First is the general meaning:
by collectively reducing all forms (*rūpa*) down to their ultimate limit, they are called "extremely reduced form" (*paramāṇurūpa*).
Second is the limited meaning.
When the various faculties and their objects are broken down to their ultimate minimal point, it is called "extremely reduced matter" (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta-rūpa*).
Therefore, it is termed "extremely reduced" (*paramāṇu*) and not "atom" (*paramāṇu*);
for "reduced" (*aṇu*) means that which is aggregated, and this refers to the ultimate limit of such aggregated matter.
"Extremely subtle" (*paramāṇu*) refers to that which is the most subtle among the subtle, or the ultimate limit of form;
it should be understood according to the two grammatical interpretations: *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional).
Regarding this term "form" (*rūpa*), although both interpretations are established as general designations for the five types [of sense objects],
the *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) interpretation is superior.
Regarding "extremely remote color":
remote color is itself the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Remote color becomes manifest only when it is free from obstruction.
It is established by the name "distance" (*dūratā*).
This ultimate distance is itself matter;
it is the limit of distant matter.
Regarding the phrase "the ultimate color of the remote," the two explanations apply according to the context.
Since "color" (rūpa) is a general term, [it encompasses both].
The understanding of the beginning and the end is superior.
Although light and darkness and so forth are also subject to refutation,
light and the like are specific instances [of that].
The "distant color" (prāgbhāra-rūpa) is the general [characteristic];
it is a vast location and can also serve as a basis.
It is not termed "extremely luminous" and so forth, but is simply called "extremely remote color" (prānta-varṇa).
However, this remote color and space appear as one;
they differ only in their respective categories of upper and lower.
Both belong to the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*) and are forms (*rūpa*);
yet they are not called "ultimate space" (*atyantākāśa*) or "ultimate distance" (*atyantadūra*).
This is because one fears that [the term] might be confused with empty space (*ākāśa*), which is also of the nature of form.
Furthermore, while the pervasive nature of remote color extends through space,
remote color alone does not constitute "ultimate space" (ākāśa); it is merely termed "ultimate remote."
Regarding "matter derived from what is acquired" (*upātta-rūpa*):
"acquisition" (*upādāna*) means to take up;
it refers to taking up an object due to instruction or due to a teacher.
"Projection" (ākṣepa) means "initiation.
That which is projected by feeling is called "projected by feeling.
Matter that is projected by feeling is called "matter projected by feeling."
The two names, "separation" and "union," constitute two distinct interpretations.
Although the attainment of the precepts of the path of concentration does not depend on the teacher's instruction,
at the time of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), it likewise depends on the teacher's instruction.
Non-restraint is either undertaken by making a personal commitment or received from another;
for these reasons, it is collectively termed "induced by undertaking."
Furthermore, the non-informative [matter] of the Prātimokṣa and of unwholesome discipline necessarily arises from formal undertaking;
it does not follow the mind.
The meditative concentrations and the paths follow one another;
they are also termed "induced by undertaking.
Furthermore, although one may attain them, they do not necessarily derive from others.
All types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) are called "induced by undertaking" (*samādāna-ākṣepa*).
There are also those induced by attainment (*prāpti*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the Path (*mārga*);
for this reason, they are collectively termed "matter induced by undertaking."
Regarding form arising from pervasive conceptualization:
the mental consciousness, through its three natures, is capable of pervasive conceptualization;
from this, the objective realm arises.
The name is that which arises from what has arisen;
that is, form is called "arisen form," which is the form arisen through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
That which is called "form arising from pervasive conceptualization" also admits of two interpretations;
as for "form produced by mastery," it refers to...
Mastery is defined as meditative concentration and supernormal powers being free from obstruction.
That which arises from that [mastery] is called "produced by it.
This produced [state] is form; thus, it is called "form produced [by mastery]."
Form produced by the sovereign is called "form produced by the sovereign.
The two explanations are as before.
Regarding the fourth point, the discrimination between the provisional and the real:
the sixth [fascicle] below states that atoms have no substantial entity.
Regarding the analysis by means of wisdom, the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings), fascicle 5, states:
"Wisdom analyzes coarse matter down to its most subtle limit."
The establishment of the atom is not due to its having substantial existence; therefore,
it is said that the atom is without arising and without cessation.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:
"Within an aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), there has never been an atom (*paramāṇu*).
When arising from seeds, it arises solely as a collection."
Nor is it that coarse matter is formed by the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"The atom is a conventional designation established upon the limit of matter."
The fifty-four [dharmas] and others are all explained in the same manner.
Therefore, both of the first two types of form are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
This refers to the designation of "non-informative action" (avijñapti) based on the limits of wholesome or unwholesome volition and aspiration;
it is also stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* that it is established based on the state in which the two seeds have not yet been destroyed.
The designation of the non-informative matter (avijñapti) of virtuous and non-virtuous discipline is established through many such proofs; therefore,
matter derived from undertaking (samādāna) is also conventionally existent (prajñaptisat).
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter eighteen, states that seven things lack substantial reality:
the three images and the four echoes.
Therefore, even the form (*rūpa*) of the parikalpita (imagined nature) is merely conventionally existent.

Fifty-fourth discourse: Regarding the matter of form included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), there are both those that are substantially real and those that are nominally designated.
If it is an object traversed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) possessing majestic power (*prabhāva*), [it is substantially real].
It is like a magical transformation;
it is that fruit, that object,
and the objective form of the consciousnesses associated with them.
These exist as real entities;
this is established by the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
which states that the ālayavijñāna transforms into the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the manifest forms included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Therefore, the substance of matter produced by meditative concentration (samādhija-rūpa) is substantially existent.
Regarding this, there is an interpretation that among the five kinds of matter, the first four are conventionally existent (prajñaptisat).
Only the fifth is real.
In the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, among the seven types of provisional phenomena (*prajñapti*),
it mentions only the provisional nature of restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
It is not said that the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) is also conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*); rather,
the *Yogācārabhūmi* states only that among the forms of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*),
the forms of majestic power resulting from meditative concentration (*vaśitā-samādhi-rūpa*) are substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
Furthermore, it is not said that these necessarily pertain to matter within the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*), for they also pertain to that which is conventionally existent.
According to one interpretation, the fifth [category] also pertains to that which is conventionally existent.
For Bodhisattvas, followers of the Two Vehicles, and others,
regarding the liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
and spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), all conventional characteristics and forms are entirely devoid of substantial reality.
If it were not subsumed under this [category], under which color would it be subsumed?
Because it is the object of meditative concentration,
it is not subsumed under the five sensory objects.
Its nature is not that of atoms,
nor is it non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);
those [factors such as] liberation and so forth are certainly not conceptual constructions (*parikalpita*).
For this reason, it is not any of the first four types of form;
nor, if it were not the fifth, would it have no category to which it belongs.
Thus, these five types of form would fail to encompass all phenomena exhaustively.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that [the object] is subsumed under "imagined form" (parikalpita-rūpa) by virtue of being a reflected image (*pratibimba*).
For would it then follow that all meditative minds (*samāhita-citta*) constitute conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
while uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) and the like lack any semblance of appearance (*nimitta*)?
Because the Buddha’s wisdom is fully capable of manifesting all reflected images,
this treatise also states:
"The forms that are the objects of the sphere of meditative concentration and liberation."
It is called "matter produced by meditative concentration" (*samādhi-ja-rūpa*).
However, because all that is transformed by noble ones (*ārya*) is capable of becoming truly real and is extremely sublime,
the *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks of it specifically as being produced by meditative concentration.
Because those conceptualized [objects] are not sublime, they are omitted and not explained.
The transformations produced by ordinary beings can only be seen by others; they are incapable of being utilized.
Is this not a provisional designation?
The first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"The matter induced by meditative concentration."
From the three grades of mind, there arise the nature of the materiality that is the reflected image of that object, as well as the nature of the materiality produced by its maturation.
The former is conventional materiality;
the latter is substantial materiality.
Furthermore, the eighteenth chapter of the *Xiányáng shèngjiào lǎojí lùn* states that among the seven types of conventional matter (*rūpa-prajñapti*), reflected images are conventionally existent.
Moreover, it is stated that the matter of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) possesses twelve characteristics.
Regarding the first image:
if a provisional image were not the fruit of meditative concentration,
that treatise would not state that it exists outside of the fruits of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) produced by concentration.
Furthermore, there is the form of the "sphere of phenomena" (dharmāyatana-rūpa). Under which category of form is that reflected image-form subsumed?
Therefore, one knows that the fruits of meditative concentration exist both as provisional and as substantial.
The latter interpretation is superior,
as it accords with both principle and scripture.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of the five shadows and their substantial bases:
The seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"There are two kinds of objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*): first, the direct; second, the indirect."
Second, the remote [object]:
if it is not separate from the substance of the perceiving faculty,
it is that which is internally relied upon as the object of consideration by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth.
It should be understood that this is the directly perceived object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Although it is physically separated from the nature of the cognizing subject,
it serves as the objective basis (*ālambana*) upon which the internal cognition relies, acting as its substantial support.
One should know that these are remote objective conditions (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*).
Although these five kinds of form are for the most part conventional (*prajñaptisat*),
the proximate objective characteristics (*sākṣādālambananimitta*) of the cognizing mind are invariably present in all cases.
Therefore, he further states:
"The immediate object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) exists for all cognizing subjects;
apart from that which is internally relied upon as the object of consideration, [cognition] can never arise."
The nature [of these] is dependent, arising from causes;
all non-substantial forms are produced from seeds such as the cognitive faculties (*ālambana*),
because they lack the function of form.
Alternatively, because there is no distinct seed that constitutes its substantial nature,
it arises from the same seed;
however, it lacks practical efficacy.
If it were substantially existent,
it would arise from a distinct seed because it possesses the function of being a form;
it does not arise from the same seed as its corresponding cognitive object.
As stated in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-śrī-mūla-ṭīkā*:
"Either it transforms to resemble matter,
or it possesses the functional activity of matter."
Based on these two principles, because they are the direct objects of cognition (*ālambana*),
all five [aggregates] are called "form" (*rūpa*);
this is according to the *Saṃtānāntarasiddhi*.
The distant object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is definitely present in all arising states of mind;
this is taught in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other texts.
When non-conceptual wisdom takes suchness as its object, it likewise transforms an image;
therefore, every arising of mind necessarily possesses an objective basis (bimba). It is precisely based on this principle that [the following is stated].
Among these five, four types of matter necessarily possess a substantial basis (*dravya*).
The first is extremely concise matter (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta-rūpa*);
the others are the ten bases of material form within the desire and form realms.
The substantial form that is the fruit of the meditative attainments of the form and formless realms takes [the subtle matter of] the desire realm as its essential nature;
this is because the treatises state that there are fifteen types of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Next, the "color of extreme clarity" takes the sense-base of visible form within the desire and form realms as its essential nature.
Because there are no distinct locations in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
all that is described herein takes as its substance that which is produced by the disintegration of coarse matter (rūpa).
There is no such category that can be said to have matter derived from sensation as its substantial essence;
since such matter is not a transformation of the mind.
Because it is not a reflection,
the objective basis (svabhāva) is not mentioned; it is that which arises from pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita).
This is because the ten material bases of the desire and form realms, as well as the matter produced through meditative concentration in the two higher realms,
can all serve as the objective basis (bhāva),
upon which [the mind] relies to transform into an image.
The matter produced by meditative concentration takes as its essential nature the matter of the sense faculties and their objects belonging to the desire and form realms;
this is stated in fifty-four [treatises].
It is the matter that is the fruit of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*). However, it arises from a samādhi that takes as its object an image (*pratibimba*) of that same category;
it is so described because it is said to be "greatly derived" (*mahābhūta-nirmita*).
Taking the various forms of the two realms as its substance:
whether there is a substantial form or no original object,
it always takes the verbal designation as its fundamental substance.
Since it is admitted that the activity of consciousness extends to both the visible object and its reflection,
we know that the objective referent (*ālambana*) must necessarily possess both a reflection and a substantial basis (*bimba*).
By this, all four types of matter (*rūpa*) are established as having a substantial basis.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The remote object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) may exist for a cognizing subject,
because [cognition] can arise even apart from an external basis upon which it relies."
Regarding the objective entities (ālambana-vastu) relied upon by these various mental states— the eighth and the sixth—
such entities may either exist or not exist;
thus, the presence or absence of a remote object-condition (parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya) is indeterminate.
If one relies on this meaning,
then regarding the colors produced by extreme condensation, extreme distance, and universal conceptualization,
the causes for perceiving these various colors— namely the names, teachings, and essential natures— are as previously described.

Based on one's own conceptualization, one imagines various selves and phenomena— such as flowers in the sky, the horns of a rabbit, the past, the future, the end of an eon, permanence, and the infinitesimal— which,
not being derived from the instruction of another, all lack any essential nature.
Furthermore, the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (dhyāna-phala-rūpa) undergoes transformation and manifestation;
it arises in dependence upon others and is produced through the power of meditative concentration.
If the transformation that takes another as its object necessarily possesses an intrinsic essence,
then the power of the transformative concentration and the state of mastery do not depend on something else for its production.
Therefore, the existence or non-existence of this intrinsic nature is indeterminate.
Although it is said that the characteristic of formations (saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa) is common to both the primary vision and its reflection,
who would grant that it pervades all states of mind?
Because correct wisdom takes suchness as its object and functions as a single condition,
if the wisdom that takes suchness as its object also possesses an image,
who could illuminate it and know that suchness exists?
In that case, there would likewise be no distinction between fundamental wisdom and subsequent wisdom.

the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* has not yet been circulated.
Furthermore, according to the present teaching:

the others represent only partial aspects of the demonstration of the path and the life of the path.
The noble lineage is subsumed within the Sangha Jewel;
ordinary beings who demonstrate the path and live by the path are śramaṇas who,
though possessing ethical discipline and right view, are able to bring benefit to sentient beings.
This is a true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
It is not included within the Jewel of the Saṃgha because it lacks the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
This is because the meaning of "field of merit" is broad, whereas the meaning of "Jewel" is restricted.
The Three Jewels of identical substance (*sābhinnatva-triratna*), which set aside conventional designations to reveal the ultimate reality, are not subsumed under the Four Noble Truths;
rather, by relying on these designations to manifest the intended meaning, they are categorized under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

As for the Three Jewels of distinct substance (*prthaktva-triratna*), as well as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) in their true nature, all are common to both the Truths of Cessation and the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Accordingly, the abiding nature is also subsumed under suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
"Abiding nature" refers to the Buddha-jewel,
which has only the four bases as its intrinsic nature.
Because the relics and images have color, odor, flavor, and tangibility as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
the Dharma Jewel generally has the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as its nature. "Teaching" refers to sound, which is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The syllable *ya* refers to the four bases (*āyatana*), and "conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the three types of action (*karman*),
or alternatively, the nature of the five aggregates (*skandha*). Therefore, this Jewel of the Dharma has the five aggregates and seven bases as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*),
the images of the presiding elders (*sthavira*) and others within the Saṃgha have the four sense bases (*catvāry āyatanāni*) as their nature.
Among the two types of śramaṇas— the "guides" and the "path-makers"—
there are those who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those fourth-type śramaṇas who defile the path;
they have violated their precepts, hold wrong views, and do not sever their roots of goodness.

The "repentance of the category of offenses" refers to the provisional person consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which takes the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its intrinsic nature. 3.
Explanation of Names, Part Three: Regarding the explanation of names—
First, the general name is explained.
"Three" is a number,
referring to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
These three types, when referred to as "jewels," possess six meanings.
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, it is asked: "In what sense are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha called 'jewels'?
The verse says:
A true jewel is rare in this world;
through its brilliance, purity, and power,
it is able to adorn the world.
Regarding "supreme, unchanging," and so forth:
based on those six kinds of similarities and correspondences,
the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are designated as "jewels."
It is difficult to encounter in this world,
for sentient beings lacking in virtue cannot obtain it even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
this true jewel is rare in the world.
Second, they are stainless,
because they are extremely luminous and pure, being free from all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*).
Third, they possess majesty, being endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
Possessing majestic power, sovereignty, and influence, or alternatively,
they are the four adornments of the world,
because they are able to adorn the supramundane dharmas.
This, too, can adorn the world; it is fivefold, supremely wondrous,
because it is the most excellent among supramundane dharmas.
Sixth, it is unalterable;
because one has attained the untainted state, the eight worldly dharmas cannot shake or move it,
for it is constant and immutable.
Just as the seven worldly treasures possess these six characteristics,
so too do the three substances;
therefore, they are all called "jewels."
This is an explanatory gloss with numerical indicators. The meaning of "analogy" (*upamā*) refers to similar correspondence;
in Sanskrit it is called *upamā*, which is corruptedly abbreviated as *phu-t'o*. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Buddha" means "awakened."
Having already awakened to realization oneself, one is further able to awaken others.
It is like a person who, having perceived the presence of a thief, finds that the thief can do no harm;
so too, the Bodhisattva is able to perceive immeasurable afflictions [for what they are].
Having already awakened to this, one renders all afflictions powerless;
for this reason, one is called a Buddha.
This is stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Because one attains equal awakening regarding the dharmas of the three aggregates,
one is called a Buddha.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Possessing two kinds of wisdom, one is able to awaken both oneself and others;
that which possesses awakening consists of both general and specific wisdom,
and is named after its governing factor (*tatpuruṣa*).
Dharma is translated as "dharma" (fa).
The *Fen Guang Jing* states:
"That which serves as a standard or rule is called dharma."
The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "Dharma" means that which provides a standard and maintains its own nature;
for it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and serves as a standard that gives rise to understanding.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Dharma" means non-awakening;
"Saṃgha" means the assembly.
Because there is no conflict regarding either principle or phenomena,
this consists of three types.
The first is the harmony of the Saṃgha regarding principles.
Although one must have three or more individuals to be designated as a "saṃgha," the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas and other noble ones are also included,
because even if they appear alone, they belong to that same category.
They may also be called "monks.
In two matters, they constitute a harmonious Saṃgha;
from three persons upward, all possess the essential nature of the Saṃgha.
According to the majority of treatises,
the custom of that country is to call one "one" (eka) and two "body" (kāya).
From three upwards, they are all termed "many.
For instance, when performing a formal legal act (*dharmakarma*), four persons are required for it to be valid.
One person makes the announcement, saying: "Venerable Sangha, please listen."
Since the three individuals who constitute the harmony are designated as the "Saṃgha," if there were four,
how could those who are themselves members of the Saṃgha perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for themselves?
To demonstrate that a harmonious assembly arises from many individuals,
those consisting of three or more are all designated as *saṃgha*.
Third is the *saṃgha* that performs formal acts (*karmas*).
This refers to groups of four, five, ten, or twenty persons;

because they are fully endowed with both the formal motion (*jñapti*) and its announcement (*anujñā*), and because they perform the legal affairs (*dharmakaraṇīya*) in complete harmony, they constitute a legitimate assembly (*saṃgha*). It is not otherwise.
These names for the Dharma and the Saṃgha are not all formed by the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaṭ-vibhāṣā*).
This is because they consist of single words that lack any distinction [of qualifier and qualified]. If the word "jewel" (*ratna*) were added, [the analysis would differ].
All three are *dharmadhātu* (bases of phenomena) by way of their activity (*karmadhāraya*). 4. Regarding the fourfold analysis of abandonment and establishment:
there are briefly four meanings.
The *Ekasāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"It is for the purpose of overturning the heterodox Three Jewels of the non-Buddhists.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states:
Having taken refuge in the Buddha, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever take refuge in Maheśvara or other such deities.
Having taken refuge in the Dharma, one will never take refuge in the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths.
Once one has taken refuge in the Saṃgha, one will never again take refuge in the heterodox assemblies of external paths.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* state this as well.
The second volume of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, in the "Chapter on the Three Jewels," says:
Based on three meanings:
first, the Teacher who is the trainer;
second, the Dharma of that Teacher.
Third, regarding those teachers and disciples:
because the immeasurable categories of what they have realized are identical, they are established as a single dharma;
however, because the two categories of the cause and fruit that realize them are distinct, [they are further differentiated].
It is divided into the sections on the Teacher and the Disciples.
Thirdly, that treatise further states:
for the sake of those with superior faculties who seek the Bodhi of a Buddha.
He spoke of the Buddha Jewel for those of middle capacity who seek self-arisen wisdom and penetrate the principle of dependent origination;
he spoke of the Dharma Jewel for them.
For those of inferior faculties who receive the principles of the Dharma from a teacher, there is no contradiction in practice;
thus, the Sangha Jewel is taught.
Therefore, that treatise states:
The Three Jewels are taught in reliance upon six types of persons:
first, the great; second, the middling; and third, three types of those of the Hīnayāna.
These are called the "six types" because they correspondingly believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
In four places, it is stated everywhere that the Buddha is like a skilled physician and the Dharma is like a wondrous medicine.
Because the Saṃgha views it as such, these Three Jewels neither decrease nor increase. 5.
Revealing the Distinctions, Part Five: Revealing the Distinctions.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Sixty-fourth Section) states that the Three Jewels are distinguished by six characteristics. First,
by way of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, the characteristic of self-awakening is the Buddha Jewel;
the characteristic of the fruit of awakening is the Dharma Jewel;
and the characteristic of practicing correctly according to the instructions of others is the Sangha Jewel.
Second, by way of activity:
the activity of turning the true teaching is the Buddha Jewel;
the activity of relinquishing the objects of affliction and suffering is the Dharma Jewel.
The Saṅgha Jewel consists of those who increase their courageous activity through three kinds of resolute belief (*adhimukti*): namely,
they should cultivate resolute belief toward the Buddha Jewel by approaching, attending upon, and serving him.
Regarding the Jewel of the Dharma, one should establish the conviction of aspiring to realize it;
regarding the Jewel of the Saṅgha, one should establish the conviction of dwelling in harmony with a single commonality of dharma-nature.
Fourth, because of practice.
This refers to the correct practice of making offerings and serving the Jewel of the Buddha;
and the correct practice of the skillful means of yoga with respect to the Jewel of the Dharma.
Regarding the Jewel of the Saṅgha, one should cultivate the correct practice of sharing material goods and the Dharma;
for this reason, one should recollect the Jewel of the Buddha by means of other characteristics through the five recollections.
One should recollect the Jewel of the Dharma with other characteristics;
one should recollect the Jewel of the Saṅgha with other characteristics, namely:
"This is the Blessed One."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding the "merit produced by the six":
this refers to the production of the most supreme merit toward the Jewel of the Buddha based upon a single sentient being.

Regarding the Jewel of the Dharma, the most excellent merit arises based on this very Dharma; regarding the Jewel of the Sangha, the most excellent merit arises based on many sentient beings. 6.
