The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Sixty-ninth Chapter) speaks of ten knowledges:

conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) encompasses all three types of wisdom, both with and without outflows (anāsrava).
The eight intermediate knowledges are exclusively without outflows and are exclusively wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā).
The final knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) encompasses both [with and without outflows].
It is also exclusively the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, there is the knowledge of the ten powers (*daśabala-jñāna*), namely:
the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), up to the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
It exists only within the continuum of a Tathāgata;
it is exclusively untainted (anāsrava) and exclusively the wisdom resulting from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
In the Abhidharma, thirteen knowledges are taught:

the knowledge of conviction, the knowledge of reasoning, the knowledge of non-distraction, the knowledge of internal realization, the knowledge of other-natures, inferior knowledge, superior knowledge, the knowledge of revulsion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of non-origination, the knowledge of arising, ultimate knowledge, and the knowledge of great purpose.
That treatise itself explains:
the first three are the three types of wisdom;
the fourth is ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
Fifth, the knowledge of others' minds;
sixth, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna);
seventh, the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
The subsequent four types of knowledge regarding the ultimate realization of the Four Noble Truths are the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The nine types preceding these consist exclusively of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The wisdom of the great meaning is the wisdom of the Mahāyāna;
it encompasses all three types of wisdom and is ultimately comprised solely of cultivation.
Furthermore, the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), Chapter 16,
and other texts state that one contemplates the Four Noble Truths to give rise to the sixteen modes of knowledge (*ṣoḍaśākārajñāna*).
Each preceding mode serves as the basis for each subsequent one.
That is to say, for the purpose of eliminating the four inversions,
there are four aspects of the Truth of Suffering.
First, in order to eliminate the inversion of permanence, one cultivates the aspect of impermanence.
Second, in order to eliminate the inversion of pleasure and purity, one undertakes the practice of asceticism (*duḥkha-caryā*).
Third, in order to eliminate the inversion of self, one undertakes the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*).
Fourth, precisely for the sake of eliminating this [inversion], one undertakes the practice of non-self (*anātma-caryā*).
The contemplation of emptiness [is established] because the nature of self in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is empty;
this contemplation [is established] because the self external to these phenomena is empty;
and the contemplation of emptiness [is established] because there is no self within all conditioned phenomena.
This is because the essence of this contemplative practice (bhāvanā) is not of the nature of a self;
this is the distinction between the two.
Next, regarding the four—permanence, bliss, purity, and self—which constitute the origin of craving within the truth of the origin of suffering (samudaya-satya):
The four aspects of origin, accumulation, arising, and condition; and subsequently,
regarding this truth of cessation,
the four aspects of cessation, stillness, excellence, and renunciation.
Next, regarding this path that realizes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*),
there arise four modes of practice— path, suchness, practice, and emergence—
all of which consist exclusively of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
It encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). In the stage of completion (*niṣpannāvasthā*), it consists exclusively of the cultivation of the uncontaminated.
This is stated in the seventeenth fascicle of the *Xiányáng shèngjiào lùn* (*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*).
There are eighteen kinds of clear realization (abhisamaya):
first, that through hearing;
second, that through reflection.
Third, the wisdom produced through cultivation;
fourth, the wisdom of the levels conducive to penetration;
fifth, the path of seeing.
Sixth, the path of cultivation;
seventh, the path of final realization;
eighth, impure mundane knowledge.
Ninth, the mundane wisdom that is virtuous and pure;
tenth, the wisdom of ultimate meaning;
eleventh, the wisdom involving conceptualization regarding unvirtuous and impure conduct.
12. Wisdom with conceptual differentiation regarding thoroughly purified conduct;
13. Non-conceptual wisdom regarding thoroughly purified conduct;
14. Wisdom that precedes the fulfillment of what is to be done.
15. The wisdom of accomplished action;
16. The subsequent wisdom following accomplished action;
17. The wisdom of the śrāvakas and others.
The eighteen types of bodhisattva’s equalizing wisdom (samatājñāna),
when based on actual realization, have as their essence only the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā);
they are subsumed within the five types of present realization (abhisamaya) that include hearing and other factors as aids to cultivation.
Within this, there are five categories.
Based on the five stages, there are seven types of path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*). There are also the three types of wisdom consisting of hearing and so forth (*śrutamayī-prajñā* etc.).
Because it is established within the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*),
there are three types of wisdom based on the contemplation of the two truths: the wisdom that contemplates conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Because there are two distinct types of objects—wholesome and unwholesome—there are three [types] based on the mode of the perceiving consciousness.
Within the category of conceptualization, there are two further classes: contaminated and uncontaminated.
Based on the two types of emptiness and the two types of true wisdom, there are three [stages],
distinguished as the preparatory, the fundamental, and the subsequently attained.
Based on the vehicle, there are two.
Because there is a difference between the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas regarding the Great and Small [vehicles],
the tenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains forty-four types of knowledge (*jñāna*). That is to say,
the contemplation of the members of dependent origination, beginning with old age and death, constitutes four [types of knowledge].
First, the suffering of old age and death;
second, the origin of old age and death;
third, the cessation of old age and death.
Fourth, one contemplates old age and death as tending toward cessation;
one applies this contemplation to all factors up to the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) has no cause.
Because they lack the seeds of wisdom,
it is not said that they contemplate them.
When the Bodhisattva was formerly beneath the Bodhi tree, [he contemplated them].
Regarding the contemplation of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in their defiled sequence and reverse order, this contemplation is performed within the reverse order.
Because it relies on the initial skillful means, the treatises state that one retreats as far as consciousness (*vijñāna*).
All are exclusively the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because at the time of attainment, one observes through the wisdom of cultivation; however,
the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the initial observation also includes the wisdoms of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*).
The appearance [of these] as distinct from ordinary beings is comprised solely of the tainted (sāsrava);
in reality, they are untainted (anāsrava).
That treatise further speaks of seventy-seven knowledges (jñāna).
This refers to two types of knowledge conditioned by present old age and death:
first, that old age and death exist because there is present birth;
second, that it is not the case that old age and death do not exist because there is present birth.
Because one currently acts for oneself,
there are two types of knowledge regarding past old age and death:
first, that old age and death exist conditioned by past birth.
Second, it is not the case that old age and death arise without having birth as their condition;
for when one contemplates the past limit, there is no beginningless cycle of old age and death that does not have birth as its condition.
Regarding old age and death conditioned by the future, there are two types of knowledge:
first, that old age and death exist because of birth in the future;
second, that it is not the case that old age and death do not exist because of birth in the future.
Although they have not yet arisen in the future,
because it is possible for them to possess the meaning of the cessation of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*),
one now contemplates these afflictions, whereby two types of knowledge are established.
Within these three temporal limits,
the first wisdom contemplates that the fruit has a cause, thereby revealing its origin;
the subsequent wisdom contemplates that the fruit has a cause, which is not indeterminate.
This refutes the false calculations of outsiders who claim that things arise from an unequal cause or without a cause.
These preceding six knowledges are called "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*);
the seventh is the "knowledge of the abiding of phenomena" (*dharmasthitijñāna*).
Regarding those phenomena not subsumed under the [twelve] limbs:
because all contaminated wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) has the nature of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
it is known that the teachings on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) pertaining to the three times are termed "not subsumed under the limbs."
From this it may be known that the bodies of noble ones also possess the knowledge of the persistence of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna),
and that within the bodies of ordinary beings there is also true knowledge (tattva-jñāna);
for by contemplating the teachings and the factors of enlightenment, the seven knowledges are produced.
Even in the case of the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), these seven [aspects] are likewise present; however,
because the seeds of wisdom (*jñāna*) are lacking,
the final contemplation is accomplished by excluding the link of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is comprised solely of the wisdom resulting from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). At the initial stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), it also includes the wisdoms resulting from hearing (*śrutamayi*) and reflection (*cintāmayi*).

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it includes the wisdoms of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the wisdom of the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the wisdom of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the wisdom of non-contention (*araṇā*), the wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the [ten] powers (*bala*), the [four] fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the [three] foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the [all-aspect] knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the wisdom of the unshared Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
The first five supernormal powers (abhijñā) are both mundane and supramundane (anāsrava),
because it is taught that they arise in the bodies of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) as well as in noble ones (ārya).
The last one is exclusively supramundane.
Because they are subsumed under two types of wisdom, all six are wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The wisdom of the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is subsumed under the cultivation of wisdom because it is a door of liberation.
Emptiness is subsumed under eight knowledges.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) is subsumed under six knowledges;
the signless (*animitta*) is subsumed under five knowledges;
and so on from the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) up to the knowledge of the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma-jñāna*).
This is exclusively wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). As appropriate, it may be either untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*),
because it exists within the bodies of Arhats and so forth, as well as within the Tathāgata.
7. The Seventh Chapter: The Differentiation of the Practice of Dharma (*Dharmacaryā-vibhāga*). Regarding the differentiation of the practice of dharma, there are ten types of such practice.
As stated in the third fascicle of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*:
That is to say: writing it down, making offerings to it, giving it away, listening to it from others, reading it aloud,
receiving and upholding it, and correctly expounding it.
By reciting, contemplating,
and practicing these ten dharmas, one obtains an immeasurable mass of merit;
for it is supreme and inexhaustible.
Because of unceasingly gathering others in;
as stated in the forty-second fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, some say this.
If, regarding the Three Pitakas and the twelvefold teaching,
one upholds, recites, and masters them so that they are widely disseminated and renowned, this constitutes the wisdom born of hearing;
based upon this, the wisdom born of reflection is produced.
Based on this, the wisdom born of cultivation arises; by means of this,
one abandons the afflictions and realizes nirvana,
just as gold is produced from gold ore.
Based on gold, diamond is produced;
this is capable of destroying such things as mountains and stones.
The critique states that one should explain it in this way.
If one receives, maintains, recites, and fully disseminates the Three Pitakas and the twelve divisions of the teaching,
this is the wisdom acquired at birth.
Based on this, the wisdom arising from hearing is produced;
based on this, the wisdom arising from reflection is produced;
and based on this, the wisdom arising from cultivation is produced.
This abandonment of afflictions and realization of nirvana is like a sprout arising dependent on a seed,
or a stalk arising dependent on a sprout.
Just as branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits grow and develop depending on a stem,
so it is according to the thirteenth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
What is the stage consisting of what is heard (*śrutamayi bhūmi*)?
Briefly stated, it refers to the immeasurable distinctions among the sets of names, phrases, and syllables within the five fields of knowledge,
which are preceded by awakened wisdom.
Hearing, receiving, reciting, and recollecting;
furthermore, correctly understanding the meaning thereof—
this is called the stage consisting of what is heard (*śrutamaya-bhūmi*).
The meaning intended here is as follows:
regarding the immeasurable varieties of the collections of names, phrases, and syllables within the five fields of knowledge,
that which is preceded by awakened wisdom—
This is the wisdom acquired at birth;
it consists of hearing, receiving, reciting, and remembering,
as well as the unerring understanding of their meaning.
This is called the wisdom of hearing;
it reveals the general characteristics within the teachings of the five sciences.
Any wholesome mind characterized by inferior, obscure, and dull discernment is called innate wisdom (*upapattipratilambhikā prajñā*).
Any clear wholesome mind that arises from subsequent attention (*manasikāra*) following hearing is called wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*).
Prior to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka,
both hearing and receiving [the Dharma] arise from innate wisdom (*upapattipratilambhikā prajñā*);
thus, regarding the Tripiṭaka, one does not need to exert effort.
The dull and inferior wisdom and virtuous mind that are produced [by birth] are called innate wisdom (*upapattilābhikī prajñā*);
they do not accord with the supramundane.
That which does not arise through effort,
whose nature is not clear,
and which arises spontaneously when reading or interpreting the meaning of texts, is called "wisdom acquired at birth."
Therefore, although one may uphold the teachings of the Tripitaka and so forth,
there is also that which is acquired by birth; furthermore,
if one possesses a virtuous mind characterized by superior, clear, and awakened wisdom produced through the application of effort toward the essential points of the Tripitaka.
It is called "wholesome through application" (*prayoga-kuśala*); it is conducive to the supramundane, arises through effort,
and its nature is extremely lucid.
The application of reading and interpreting the meaning of texts is termed "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the wisdom derived from hearing also exists in the retention and upholding of the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and so forth.
Otherwise, how could the wisdom that precedes the awakening to the teachings of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā-sthāna*) be called "innate wisdom" (*upapattilābhikī-prajñā*)?
Hearing and receiving [the teachings] is called the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states that the wisdom born of hearing, through contemplating the Mahāyāna, enables the element of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla-dhātu*) to increase.
The wisdom arisen from reflection contemplates the Mahāyāna and is able to correctly awaken to and enter into the sought-after true meaning;
the wisdom arisen from cultivation contemplates the Mahāyāna and is able to bring the sought-after undertakings to fulfillment.
This means that because one is able to enter and cultivate the stages [of the path],
these three types of sublime wisdom take the ten dharma-practices as their companions and are sustained by those ten dharma-practices.
The first eight modes of practice (*dharmacaryā*) are termed wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The ninth mode of practice is termed wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
The tenth mode of practice is subsumed under wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
By means of these three types of wisdom, one practices all dharmas within this Mahāyāna and attains the greatest fruit,
because it is the most supreme.
Second, because it is inexhaustible;
since it is able to encompass and benefit all other sentient beings,
the Mahāyāna is said to be supreme.
Because, although one has realized nirvana without remainder,
the activity of benefiting others never ceases;
for this reason, the Mahayana describes it as inexhaustible.
The Lotus Sūtra states:
"If one receives and upholds this sūtra— whether by reading it, reciting it, explaining it, or copying it—
that person shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye, up to twelve hundred merits of the mind."
If one merely attains the wisdom born of acquisition (*upapattilābhajñāna*) through receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Tripiṭaka,
how could one possibly perform the ten dharma-practices (*dharmaparyāya*) and obtain such a vast accumulation of merit?
It is through these five kinds of Dharma-preachers that the six thousand virtues are accomplished.
Wholesome dharmas of application arise only through exertion,
because one must clearly understand what the mind ought to attain; therefore,
this should be understood as it is explained in the Mahāyāna.
8. The Eighth [Section]: On the Similarities and Differences between Dhāraṇī and Prajñāpāramitā. Regarding the similarities and differences between dhāraṇī and prajñāpāramitā:
there are two types of dhāraṇī.
The first is that which is able to retain.
Various sūtras and other texts speak of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining (*śrutadhāraṇī*).
Regarding the two types of that which is retained,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that there are four kinds of dhāraṇī.
First, the phenomenon;
second, the meaning;
third, the ability to attain bodhisattva patience.
Regarding the fourth, the explanation of mantras:
*dhāraṇī* is here translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). According to various treatises, its essential nature consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
In this context, "hearing and retaining" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
That which is retained therein is the object of the wisdom of hearing.
To clearly remember and not forget the meaning of the Dharma and so forth that one has heard is called "hearing and retaining."
Regarding this point, there should be further analysis:
why is it that only the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is called "retention" (*dhāraṇī*),
while the wisdoms born of reflection (*cintāmayī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) are not also said to be included within retention?
It is said that from hearing, internal superior wisdom arises;
because it is the initial wisdom that takes external objects as its dispersed domain,
this excludes those who have not yet accomplished hearing and do not maintain it.
It is uniquely called "dhāraṇī" because the two types of wisdom— contemplative and cultivated— arise from internal differentiation;
since it involves certainty regarding the meaning, it is not merely the initial [hearing] wisdom.
In principle, it could be maintained; however,
because the meaning of "distinguishing" (viveka) is subtle,
the designation "maintaining" (dhāraṇa) is not established.
Therefore, regarding the third stage, it is said that two delusions are abandoned:
first, the delusion of desire-attachment,
which obstructs the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā).
The second is the delusion regarding the perfection of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention.
This can obstruct the wisdom of hearing and reflection associated with total retention (*dhāraṇī*),
because desire and greed are not said to be obstacles to total retention.
One interpretation holds that "retention through hearing" (*śrutadhāraṇī*) is itself the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, the dharmas and meanings held by the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are the objects sustained by the wisdoms of reflection (*cintāmayī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).
Through the wisdom of hearing, one hears the dharmas, meanings, and so forth in their entirety, clearly memorizing them so as not to forget.
It is called "hearing and retaining" (śrutadhara).
It arises through the internal causal power of the two types of wisdom— reflection and cultivation—
and is able to reflect upon and cultivate the fourfold clarity regarding phenomena, their meanings, and so forth, such that one remembers them without forgetting.
These four types of retention (*dhāraṇī*) are established for him;
otherwise, having already attained *śrutadhāraṇī* in the third stage,
he would already be able to maintain those four.
Having already explained the abandonment of the obscurations regarding the ignorance of hearing and reflection through the *dhāraṇī*,

it is further stated that on the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*), one abandons the subsequent ignorance regarding the mastery of wisdom and eloquence (*pratisaṃvid-dhāraṇī-vaśitā*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Chapter 9).
The mastery of dhāraṇīs regarding the immeasurable teachings expounded refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*);
it is the mastery of retention (*dhāraṇī*) with respect to that which is expressed.
To manifest all meanings within a single meaning is the mastery over immeasurable dhāraṇīs of names, phrases, and syllables;
this refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
One immediately attains mastery over the dhāraṇī of expressive designations,
because within a single name, phrase, or syllable,
all names, phrases, and syllables are manifested.
What does that sustain?
Because the three stages have already been attained, it is sustained by the two types of wisdom—
contemplative and meditative— which possess the power to produce subtle internal factors that are otherwise hidden.
The meaning of this distinction is subtle:
when explaining the characteristics of the supported, it is said that the wisdom of hearing necessarily arises through the power of external conditions.
The meaning of "distinguishing" (*viniścaya*) is superior; it emphasizes the capacity to maintain the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
rather than stating that which is maintained.

Therefore, the statement regarding the "two perfections of the *vijñaptimātra* [teaching] for those who hear and retain the *dhāraṇī*" refers precisely to that which can obstruct the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) within this context;
for the wisdom of reflection is also termed a *dhāraṇī*.

Therefore, it is known that the ninth stage speaks of the severance of the delusion regarding the mastery of dhāraṇīs and the attainment of the unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena and meaning;
this is because these are sustained by the dhāraṇīs of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

9. The Differences in Realization in the Ninth Ground. Regarding the differences in realization in the ninth ground, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one who upholds this sūtra..."
Whether reading, reciting, explaining, or transcribing it,
one will obtain twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty.
By means of this purified mental faculty, [one attains such qualities].
Even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase,
they penetrate immeasurable and boundless meanings;
having understood these meanings, they are able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse.
Whether for one month, four months,
or even up to one year,
all the teachings he expounds accord with their underlying meaning and do not contradict the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna),
their faculty of mind (manas-indriya) is pure;
such is the case for this person regarding whatever they contemplate, deliberate upon, or express in speech.
All these are the Buddha-dharma and none is not true.
This passage reveals that one has not yet entered the ten stages (bhūmis) to realize the superior wisdoms of hearing and reflection.
Furthermore, it is stated in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging":
The Bodhisattva Asaṃkīrṇacaryā, practicing the conduct of not disparaging others,
was on the verge of passing away when [the Buddhas] appeared in the sky before him.
Having heard the Lotus Sutra as originally preached by the Buddha King of Majestic Sound— consisting of twenty quadrillion verses—
he was able to receive and uphold them all in their entirety,
and immediately attained the aforementioned purification of the six sense faculties.
Furthermore, their lifespan will increase by two hundred trillion nayutas of years.
After the end of that life,
they will encounter two thousand billion Buddhas.
They were all named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Later, they encountered two thousand billion Buddhas,
all of whom were named Meghasvararāja.
Within these teachings of the Buddhas,
they shall receive, uphold, read,
and recite them, and expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.
Therefore, he attains this constant purity of the eye, and purity of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
He teaches the Dharma to the fourfold assembly with a mind free from fear.
The intent of that sutra is to say that when the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging was about to pass away,
he heard the Lotus Sutra, whereby his six sense faculties became pure and his lifespan was extended.
This refers to the four stages of the roots of goodness prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is because [the Buddha] did not speak of attaining the constant purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*),
nor did he speak of the fearlessness in preaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanāvaiśāradya*).
Therefore, this is certainly not spoken of in reference to the stage of a sage on the ten bhūmis.
Upon the end of this life, one will encounter many Buddhas and attain the constant purity of the six sense faculties.
He expounds the Dharma with a mind free from fear and enters the first stage (bhūmi). From this,
it is known with certainty.
This is not the stage of liberation for those with the forty minds;
because at that stage, one has not yet attained the constant, pure faculties and a mind free from fear,
even when looking back upon the preceding text from a distance.
Although one has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*),
the fact that the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is thus purified indicates the stage of the four roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
This explains the superior attainment prior to the stages of hearing and reflection;
regarding that which is produced through cultivation,
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises state:
Why is the third stage called "The Luminous" (Prabhākari)?
Because it is the basis for non-retrogressive meditative concentrations and attainments,
and because it is the basis for the great light of the Dharma.
Wu-xing’s commentary states:
"This means that within this stage, one realizes a rare samādhi,
which is able to give rise to the light of wisdom that illuminates and clearly perceives all phenomena."
Therefore, it is called "The Radiant.
All meditative absorptions of the form realm (dhyāna-samādhi) are termed "concentrations" (samāpatti),
while all formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) are termed "attainments" (samāpatti).
Alternatively, "samādhi" refers to one-pointedness of mind,
while "samāpatti" refers to the actualization of meditative attainment.
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
The practice of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation in the first, second, and third stages is similar to that of worldly beings;
however, as stated previously, one attains superior cultivated wisdom in the third stage.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*, and other treatises all explain ten obstacles;
the third is dullness of faculty,
which causes one to forget what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.
By means of abandoning those [obstructions],
one attains the three types of superior wisdom— those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This explains that the three types of superior wisdom are attained in the third stage.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and other texts that the ten pāramitās neither increase nor decrease:
this means that within the ten stages (bhūmis), they serve as the remedies for the ten obstacles.
One realizes the ten true suchnesses because they are without increase or decrease;
this reveals that the fifth stage attains superior meditative concentration (samādhi).
One practices the perfection of meditative concentration through right application,
while also cultivating the remaining perfections according to one's power and capacity.
As stated in Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*:
Regarding the meaning of being the basis for mastery over karma and so forth:
it means that this dharmadhātu is the basis for mastery over the karma of the body and so forth,
as well as the basis for mastery over the gateways of dhāraṇīs and samādhis.
If one knows in this way,
one attains entry into the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
This explains that it is only upon reaching the ten stages that one attains supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This concludes the preceding section.
Regarding those who attain the three types of mundane wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) in their superior form, this occurs during the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).
As for severing conceptual grasping and attaining uncontaminated cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*), this takes place in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
Having severed the hindrance of dullness, one attains the three types of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that illuminate the Mahāyāna teachings.
This occurs in the third stage (*bhūmi*),
where one correctly cultivates various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), attaining mastery over entering and emerging from them, thereby benefiting both oneself and others.
It eliminates the obstacle of distraction and occurs in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*),
wherein one is able to endure, contemplate, and maintain all phenomena (*dharma*).
Regarding the division of the single function of wisdom into three types of wisdom,
this occurs in the eighth stage,
as has already been explained in detail previously in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
Having attained unimpeded eloquence and dhāraṇīs, with superior reliance on wisdom cultivated through meditation, one dwells in the ninth stage;
there, manifesting great supernormal powers throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one extensively practices for the benefit and happiness of others.
In the tenth stage, because these teachings explain that the realizations of the stages differ,
when one infers this through reasoning, there is no contradiction between them.
10. The Tenth Section: Analysis by Way of Various Gates. Regarding the analysis by way of various gates, there are ten gates in total. First:
An inquiry as to how many of these three types of wisdom take specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects.
Question: How many types of common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) as conditions are there? Answer: There are many kinds;
briefly stated, there are three.
The specific characteristic of a single locus:
phenomena such as form and sound are called specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);
the impermanence of the aggregate of form and so forth are all common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the two types of characteristics:
dharmas such as blue, yellow, and so forth are called specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa);
the sense bases such as form and sound are called common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Third, regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): that which is inexpressible by nature is called a specific characteristic;
all other things, such as those that are expressible, are called common characteristics.
One should understand this according to the meaning, as extensively supported by reason and scripture:

that self-characteristics are attained only through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), whereas other characteristics— both self-characteristics and common characteristics— are attained through the wisdoms of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains the distinctions between specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). By extension of this principle, the same applies here.
Second, how many are causes and how many are effects?
Answer: There are two kinds. First, the arising of superior and inferior characteristics.
Second, the cultivation of the characteristics of superiority and inferiority.
Regarding the first meaning:
hearing serves as the cause for the three types of wisdom.
Reflection is the cause for two types of wisdom;
cultivation is the cause for one type of wisdom;
and cultivation is the fruit of three types of wisdom.
Reflection is the fruit of two types of wisdom;
hearing is the fruit of one type of wisdom.
This is because that which is inferior serves as the cause for that which is superior, while that which is superior serves as the fruit of that which is inferior.
If one were to argue that this is not the case because the meanings of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) differ, it would still not be so;
for volition (*cetanā*) is not a cause of cultivation (*bhāvanā-hetu*).
Cultivation is not the fruit of volition,
because they belong to different realms.
According to the latter sense:
If it causes the power of the sphere of influence (*pradeśa*) to increase through the function of perfuming,
the meaning of "cause" is as previously explained. If,
by virtue of this, the power of the essence of that [perfumed] entity increases through cultivation, [it is a cause].
Regarding that which subsequently manifests as extremely clear and pure:
the wisdom derived from hearing is solely the cause for the wisdom of hearing,
while the wisdom derived from reflection serves as the cause for the wisdom of reflection.
The wisdom produced by cultivation serves as the cause for the three types of wisdom.
As for the two types of wisdom—those produced by hearing and reflection—they do not arise based on meditative concentration;
when they manifest, their power is inferior.
It cannot cause others to develop superior power or produce subsequent clarity and purity;
cultivated wisdom is not like this,
and therefore it serves as a cause for others.
Alternatively, a subsequent superior dharma may serve as the cause for a preceding inferior one,
because cultivation causes it to become superior;
however, a previously arisen inferior dharma is not the cause for a subsequent superior one.
Because its power is weak, it cannot cause subsequent states to become clear and pure.
Third, [the question]: with how many faculties (*indriya*) is it associated?
Answer: The wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) is associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya),
because it exists within the five sensory consciousnesses.
Regarding the superior dharmas above, there is sorrowful desire to realize them,
which is associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Alternatively, it may be associated with all five faculties;
since it is admitted that the category of wisdom derived from hearing exists within the five sensory consciousnesses,
it is also associated with the faculty of suffering.
According to the true meaning,
it excludes [feeling] accompanied by suffering, grief, pleasure, joy, or equanimity;
rather, it is associated with the wisdom of reflection that seeks to realize the end of sorrow.
Its nature is not the wisdom derived from hearing;
because it is not oppressive, it is not associated with the faculty of grief.
It is the wisdom derived from reflection.
They are associated with joy, sorrow, and equanimity;
they do not exist in the stages of the form realm,
because [those stages] lack the five sensory consciousnesses.
The wisdom born of cultivation is accompanied by pleasure, joy, and equanimity;
it is not a dharma of the distracted stage,
because the five [hindrances] are absent there.
Question 4: How many are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and meditative equipoise (*samāhita*)?
Answer: All are associated with meditative concentration, because they are specifically determined numbers.

One interpretation holds that wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) are not associated with meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) or meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); this may be the case for wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
but the two types of wisdom— those from hearing and reflection— are scattered wholesome dharmas (*vyagracitta-kuśala-dharma*).

Because they are not states of meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*). According to one interpretation, hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) are also states of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) and attainment (*samāpatti*),
since it is universally accepted that hearing and reflection exist in the eight stages (*bhūmi*) and beyond.
Question: How many wholesome factors are associated with the eleven [mental factors]?
Answer: According to one interpretation, the two types of wisdom—conceptual (cintā-mayī) and meditative (bhāvanā-mayī)—are associated with all eleven wholesome factors.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* maintains that because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm possesses pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is dispersed and remote.
There are only the remaining ten,
because there is no *praśrabdhi* (serenity) in those states arising in the distracted position. In terms of the actual meaning,
these are the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Eleven are associated with the wholesome.
This is because it is accepted that untainted (anāsrava) consciousness possesses both hearing and reflection.
Question six: How many are indeterminate, and how many are associated with the four?
Answer: All three types of wisdom are associated with vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), because they can all arise within both concentrated and non-concentrated states.
Remorse and drowsiness are not associated with the wisdom of cultivation.
Because of the difference between concentration and distraction,
there is the view that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are not associated with hearing (*śruta*) or reflection (*cintā*),
as their mental aspects (*ākāra*) are coarse and vulgar.
Furthermore, because [the former] is obscure and concise,
while hearing and reflection are subtle and superior;
and because [the latter] is clear and extensive.
The factors of true meaning (bhūta-artha) are associated with hearing, reflection, and also regret and sleep.
Hearing and reflection are associated with regret;
this is because even in the state of sleep, one listens to the teachings and contemplates their meaning.
As stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are seven questions regarding how many [factors] are bound to the three realms (*traidhātuka*), and so forth.
The answer provides one interpretation: they are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Contemplation (*cintā*) is bound only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) extends to the upper two realms and is also unbound (*anivṛta*).
In terms of ultimate reality, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) extends to the desire and form realms and is also unbound.

The wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) is associated with the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) as well as unassociated (apratisaṃyukta). The wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) is as previously stated.
Both the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) and the wisdom of reflection may be unassociated.
It relies solely on the level of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because there is a category [of beings] there who hear [the teachings], and because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of reflection (*cintā*) is extensive.
All three types take both the bound and the unbound as their objects.
Regarding the eight questions concerning how many are "in training" (śaikṣa) and so forth:
the answer is that the wisdom consisting of cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā) pertains to all three types.
Regarding the two types of wisdom— those arising from hearing and reflection—
there is one interpretation that they are exclusively neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee;
however, the true meaning is that they are exclusively both trainee and neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Because it is said that the Buddha is "non-existent" [in that sense].
If the body of one beyond training possesses wholesome states that accord with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*),
they are also called "one beyond training."

The two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—also extend to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). They universally take the three kinds [of objects] as their cognitive domain.
Regarding the nine questions concerning how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and so forth:
Answer: Regarding the severance of bonds,
there is the interpretation that [the factors] of hearing and reflection are severed only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because they are not defiled and thus are not severed by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Because they are not untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the eleven categories, beginning with the wholesome (*kuśala*), are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the five faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because they are not [to be] abandoned [by insight].

Wisdom produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) is abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as being non-abandonable (*aheya*), because it is both with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Wisdom based on non-arising (*anutpāda-adhiṣṭhāna*) is also abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*),
because it is stated that the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth are abandoned only by seeing.
As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are two meanings of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

[The following] ten questions concern how many are acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*), how many are acquired through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-labdha*), and how many are acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
Answer: These three types of wisdom are all not acquired at birth, because they are not obscure;
rather, they are all obtained through application, as they are wholesome states resulting from application.

Because they have all attained freedom from defilement, having abandoned the obstacles of the three stages, they attain the three superior types of wisdom; and because they have abandoned the defilements of the eight stages,
they attain the three untainted (anāsrava) types of wisdom.
Furthermore, because one has abandoned the defilements of the nine stages and attained superior cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
although these three were practiced in previous lives,
they [attain them] within this present life.
Since these three cannot possibly be obtained spontaneously,
they are not innate; rather,
they necessarily depend upon a small amount of effort.
It is precisely because one is able to attain it that what is accomplished by the Buddha is necessarily attained through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-lābha*).
Because there is no preparatory effort (prayoga),
the stages of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva are attained through both types [of acquisition].
From the eighth stage onward, there is no application of effortful cultivation because there is spontaneous application. Regarding the three wheels:
[the three wheels are] the forest of meanings of the three wheels; the meaning of the three wheels.
It is analyzed by means of seven gates:
first, the determination of its essential nature;
second, the clarification of its names.
Third, the establishment and abolition;
fourth, the manifestation of characteristics;
fifth, the capacity of the three vehicles to arise.
Sixth, the activities of the three bodies;
seventh, the distinctions among the transformations of sentient beings.
First, regarding the establishment of the essential nature: as for the establishment of the essential nature—
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Chapter Sixty-nine:
It is stated that the first five supernormal powers, when they arise in ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) or those in training (śaikṣa),
are all with outflows (sāsrava).
Those that arise for one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are all untainted (anāsrava),
because the power of the path of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and those in training (śaikṣa) is inferior.
Because the power of the path generated by those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is exceedingly strong,
that which is generated by a Buddha is exclusively untainted (anāsrava), namely the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna-abhijñā).
That treatise states that its nature consists of the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*),
because it takes the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) as its object; it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and arises within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted.
The supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā) of Arhats and others has ten knowledges as its nature. Regarding this,
there is one interpretation.
The body in which outflows (āsrava) have been exhausted is termed "outflow-free" (anāsrava);
this does not mean that the outflows have been severed.
This clearly indicates that the three wheels (trimaṇḍala) also pertain to the outflowing realm (sāsrava).
There is an interpretation that the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) are accomplished within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa);
because they are all free from outflows (āsrava),
they are collectively termed "outflow-free" (anāsrava).
This demonstrates that the three wheels accomplished by those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not pertain to the contaminated (sāsrava).
All three are mundane because they instruct others through the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna).
These three depend exclusively upon the levels of the dhyānas.
It is of the nature of the outflow-tainted and outflow-free subsequently attained wisdom associated with the mental consciousness;
it is specifically the wisdom among the five object-determining mental factors, which functions with deliberation for the sake of transforming others.
It is not preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*),
though it may also be common to that;
as stated in [Treatise] 69.
Because all supernormal powers and so forth take all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as their basis and are capable of inducing them;
although the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) also exists in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), [it does not depend on the meditative absorptions].
The various bodhisattvas, in accordance with that mind, comprehend all phenomena;
they are also able to transform objects and so forth based upon it,
such as the fragrance [emanating] from those standing beside the Buddha and from the palaces.
Because its function is narrow,
it is not called "universal" (sarvatraga);
the mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu) is broad.
Excluding the stage of the threshold (anāgamya),
the various supernormal powers (abhijñā) can exist there,
because concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā) are in equilibrium.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (in thirty-seven fascicles) states that the three wheels are themselves the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
therefore, they are identical to the supernormal powers and do not exist in other stages.
2. Second, the Analysis of Names. Regarding the analysis of names:
Yogācārabhūmi, Fascicle 79.
Question: As it is said that the three times and the three wheels are pure, how should this be understood?
Answer: By virtue of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva),
when one correctly observes with wisdom according to reality that phenomena of the past, future, and present are perfectly equal and uniform, [one realizes this].
To be without longing, expectation, or attachment toward phenomena of the past, future,
and present is called the purity of the three wheels across the three times.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun), chapter seventeen,
states: "All" refers to the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
First, the object of knowledge;
second, the wisdom that knows;
third, the knower.
He states that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess these three [natures];
this is for the purpose of eliminating the grasping at dharmas by contemplating the emptiness of these three essences,
thereby destroying that grasping.
All that precedes is not the meaning clarified here.
Now, the three kinds of crushing will be explained,
so as to cause pure faith to arise in those who have not yet attained it.
It is called the "three wheels" because it causes those who have already gained faith to practice, and it causes those who have already practiced to attain the fruit.
The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, chapter six, states:
"In this way, all the supernormal powers, prophecies, and instructions of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas..."
The functions of the three kinds of supreme wheels are unimpeded.
"Three" refers to their number;
this is what that sutra states.
It is like the wheel of the vehicle ridden by a universal monarch (cakravartin),
or the wheel that leads at the front;
this is what was intended by the initial statement.
That which functions by relying [on others] is called a "wheel" (cakra).
It is that upon which the noble ones of the three vehicles rely;
it moves itself and moves others.
Because it revolves and proceeds there, it is designated by the term "wheel.
This refers to what was intended by the subsequent statement:
"Just like the wheel-treasure possessed by a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
The king proceeded at the head of his procession for the sake of pleasure;
he was able to subdue those who were unsubmissive, having already pacified those who had been brought under control.
The three wheels are likewise so:
for those who have not yet developed faith and so forth, they cause them to give rise to faith and so forth;
for those who already possess faith and so forth, they cause them to become firm and so forth.
This is an explanation by way of enumeration.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twenty-five,
it is also titled "Instruction and Admonition on the Three Supernatural Manifestations."
The three types of miraculous transformations (ṛddhiprātihārya) are: first, the miraculous transformation of supernormal power (ṛddhi-prātihārya);
second, the miraculous transformation of mind-reading through speech (ādeśanā-prātihārya).
Third is the miraculous transformation of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*).
In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, twenty-seven [types] are also called the three types of instructions on miraculous transformations.
First is the miraculous transformation of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Second is the miraculous power of mind-reading;
third is the miraculous power of instruction.
These are the fruits of cultivation, consisting of wisdom endowed with majestic power.
Its functioning being difficult to fathom is called "spirit" (shen);
its shifting and changing without constancy is termed "transformation" (bian).
That which transforms is the object.
The Spirit is wisdom. The transformation of the Spirit is its capacity to transform;
the transformations of the Spirit are that which is transformed.
These are all *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds.
"Spirit" (*śen*) is itself the transformation; the "transformation" (*bian*) belongs to that which undergoes transformation (*neng bian*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Here, only the first and last of the two explanations are taken:
the instruction exhorting one to give birth to the wholesome.
"Instruction and admonition" refer to the subduing and extinguishing of evil.
"Instruction" (jiao) and "admonition" (jie) are distinct. "Instruction" refers to teaching; "admonition" refers to warning. Thus, instruction and admonition differ.
Both interpretations are acceptable;
however, the single category of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is particularly distinguished by its functional efficacy.
The ability to transform and emanate is precisely what is termed "supernatural transformation" (*vikurvaṇā*).
Therefore, among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), only this one is termed "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*).

The functions and characteristics of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) are not as preeminent as those of the power of transformation (*ṛddhiviṣaya*). Thus, they do not equal the power of transformation.
Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), it is not designated as "divine power" (*ṛddhi*);
yet, within the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), it is also given the name "divine.
It is capable of transforming the minds of others.
It is capable of bringing about the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) because it excels others;
the other three are inferior by comparison.
Nor is it called a "wheel.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twenty-five,
states that all three types are designated as "instruction" (*avavāda*) and "admonition" (*anuśāsana*).
All three cause the arising of the wholesome and the cessation of the unwholesome;
because two of them differ [in their mode of operation],
twenty-seven [treatises] state that all three are called "miraculous transformations" (ṛddhi-prātihārya) in their instruction.
It merely causes the arising of the wholesome and does not speak of the cessation of the unwholesome;
or rather, the causing of the arising of the wholesome is itself the cessation of the unwholesome.
Therefore, the three types of supernormal transformations (ṛddhiprātihārya) are also explained by the *karmadhāraya* compound.
That which subdues, overcomes, and restrains for the dual benefit of self and others is called a "wheel" (cakra).
That its wondrous essence is without fixed direction while manifesting the virtue of its function is called "divine transformation" (ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa).
The designation "supernatural transformation" (ṛddhi-prātihārya) is common to all three vehicles;
however, the title "wheel" (cakra) is attained exclusively by Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas,
because they excel in relying upon it to subdue and set [the wheel] in motion.
The *Daśacakra* further states:
"A wheel" refers to being without any obstruction regarding all phenomena,
just as the light of the sun universally illumines everything.
To those of the three vehicles' faculties, according to what is appropriate for each,
he proclaims the True Dharma without attachment;
this teaching is perfectly complete, universally illuminating, and unimpeded, like the orb of the sun.
Therefore, that which is produced by those of the two vehicles is not a wheel.
Furthermore, the supernormal transformations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are superior to those of the two vehicles.
Including the power of majesty (*prabhāva*),
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 37) states:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess, in brief, three kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prabhāva*)."
However, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-seven, states:
"They are called the three demonstrations (*nidarśana*).
Because they are able to demonstrate and lead, they receive the name 'demonstration'."
