however, because their true qualities are identical in meaning,
his wisdom and principle are in profound union.
Self-benefit is not distinct [from this].
The Svabhāvakāya and Sambhogakāya, when combined, are termed the Dharmakāya; it is only through the provisional distinction of their qualities and marks that they appear different.
Manifesting diverse forms at will,
appearing or remaining hidden for the benefit of others, they are divided into the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and the Transformation-body (upapattikāya).
Thus, the three Buddhas are established as neither decreasing nor increasing.
Furthermore, the categories of hindrances are briefly of two types:
first, the category of afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Second, regarding the category of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): in order to suppress and extinguish the active manifestations of both categories of hindrances,
the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is manifested.
The response body (nirmāṇakāya) is manifested in order to sever the seeds of the two categories of hindrances;
[the enjoyment body] is manifested in order to eternally extinguish the latencies (vāsanā) of the two categories of hindrances.
Thus, while the Dharmakāya is revealed,
those three [aspects] do not themselves constitute the three bodies.
It is for the sake of severing these three that the Buddha manifests the three bodies.
Fourth, furthermore, according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*,
those who enter the stage of the Tathāgata attain supreme purity for the sake of three kinds of purification:
first, the purification of afflictions (*kleśa-viśuddhi*).
First, it is able to manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), because it transforms according to the various types of beings without engaging in strife.
Second, it is the purification of suffering.
It is able to give rise to the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*),
because it manifests perfect enlightenment by being free from all suffering.
Third is the purity of marks (*lakṣaṇaviśuddhi*).
It is able to manifest the dharmakāya because it is free from the grasping at subject and object, having realized the wisdom of fundamental cognition.
The two aforementioned afflictions are obstacles.
The latter is the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the three bodies (*trikāya*), the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other texts provide four brief explanations.
First, because sentient beings of the past perceived illusory objects,
their minds were constantly deluded and obscured;
they gave rise to karma and experienced suffering.
In contrast to those [two], the first two bodies are taught:
first, by overturning the false to reveal the true;
second, by reversing ignorance to achieve wisdom.
The true realm free from entanglements is called the Dharma-body;
actual wisdom free from darkness is called the Enjoyment-body.
The wisdom of principle is difficult to fathom and cannot be known through brief means.
That which manifests coarse wisdom and principle for sentient beings is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body),
because it causes them to first know the coarse and subsequently realize the subtle.
Second, the category of afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is able to obstruct *nirvāṇa*.
This very nirvāṇa is also called the dharmakāya.
Thus, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:
"The One Vehicle is the Mahāyāna."
The Mahāyāna is itself the Buddha-nature;
the Buddha-nature is itself the Dharma-body;
the Dharma-body is itself the realm of Nirvāṇa.
The nature of afflictions is bondage;
the nature of nirvāṇa is liberation.
This is because their natures are mutually contradictory.
One attains the Dharmakāya by severing [the afflictive obscurations] and the Saṃbhogakāya by severing the class of cognitive obscurations;
it is only when ignorance is eliminated that [wisdom] becomes actual wisdom.
The foolish and the wise are opposites; by severing the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one attains the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This Enjoyment Body is also called *bodhi*, because the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that both the awakening (*bodhi*) and the severance of [obscurations] (*bodhiccheda*) are termed *bodhi*.
To enable those of the three vehicles to attain these two kinds [of bodies], the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is made manifest.
Third, the Buddha possesses three virtues—namely, wisdom (jñāna), abandonment (prahāṇa), and grace (anugraha).
To manifest these three, he teaches the three bodies: the dharma-body (dharmakāya), the enjoyment-body (sambhogakāya), and the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Fourth, there are briefly two kinds of results achieved through cultivation:
first, the dharma-joy experienced;
second, the capacity to experience dharma-joy.
Having personally attained it,
and for the sake of providing the means for others to attain it as well,
he speaks of the three bodies (trikāya).
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Śāstra* by Asaṅga states that there are three kinds of bodies:
first, the Dharma-body of teaching.
This is precisely the teaching of Prajñā.
When the two wisdoms mutually reach their fulfillment, one attains the Dharmakāya;
this is precisely Bodhi-wisdom.
The three types of meritorious action culminate in the attainment of the Dharma-body;
this excludes the fruits of giving and so forth that are distinct from wisdom,
as well as other forms of meditative concentration and other wholesome qualities.
The intended meaning of that treatise is that because one hears the verbal teachings from the nirmāṇakāya,
it serves as the cause for the dharmakāya.
Upon attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, one is able to give rise to the two types of *dharmakāya*: the *jñāna-dharmakāya* (wisdom body) and the *puṇya-dharmakāya* (merit body).
These three abodes are precisely the *dharmakāya* of suchness (*tathatā*), which is the principle of signlessness (*animitta*).
The preceding causes and effects, as well as the bodies, can only be realized by relying upon this very body.
Although that [text] also speaks of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) as the locus of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*),
the Sūtra states that one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of marks.
The physical body (rūpakāya) is refuted as not being the true essence of the Buddha;
therefore, it is not mentioned here. Since the Dharma-body and Reward-body (dharmakāya and saṃbhogakāya) are not refuted, it is said that there are three bodies.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the "wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata" and so forth refers to the nirmāṇakāya (transformation Buddha);
the "inexhaustible form of the Tathāgata" and so forth refers to the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment Buddha);
and the "permanent abiding of all dharmas" refers to the dharmakāya (dharma Buddha).
This is identical in meaning to the three [treatises] on the Buddha by Maitreyanātha Bodhisattva, such as the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa*;
therefore, they are not discussed here.
Regarding the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, that treatise explains it as follows:
Leaving the palace of the Śākyas is the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
That since attaining Buddhahood it has been immeasurable kalpas is the saṃbhogakāya (reward body).
To know and see the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are is the dharmakāya (dharma body).
It is also the same as that [previous case],
and therefore it is not explained separately.
Alternatively, four bodies are taught.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states:
first, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha;
second, the Guṇakāya Buddha.
Third is the Wisdom Buddha;
fourth is the Suchness Buddha.
The first is the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya).
The next two are the enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*);
they are divided into two kinds because of the distinction between merit and wisdom.
The last is the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also states that there are four [bodies]:
there is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that is not a response body (*sambhogakāya*).
This exists because, although the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, he does so through the power of mastery over his vows.
Such a body is precisely the *nirmāṇakāya*.
This explains that although the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,
through the mastery of his vows, he manifests for the sake of sentient beings in the forms of nāgas, ghosts, and so forth.
Because it is subsumed within the [ordinary] realms of rebirth, it does not manifest as the body of a Buddha;
it is called a *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and not a *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). There are cases where there is a *saṃbhogakāya* that is not a *nirmāṇakāya*.
The body prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is precisely the same as the body of the response-emanation (*nirmāṇakāya*).
It is merely that the Buddha-body manifested for the sake of bodhisattvas prior to the stages arises based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it manifests in the form of a Buddha, it is not subsumed within the five destinies;
thus, it should be called "responding" rather than "transformative.
It refers to the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body) Buddhas seen within the great trichiliocosm during the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).
The third is both the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body) and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body).
It refers to the Tathāgata’s body abiding in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*,
which appears as a Buddha-body for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) during the stage of the forty mental states (*cittotpāda*).
The manifestation of signs arises from meditative concentration (samādhi) cultivated through practice;
because it manifests the physical form of a Buddha, it is called "Nirmāṇakāya" (the Manifested).
It manifests as being of the same class as ordinary beings, possessing various sufferings and so forth.
It is also called "transformation.
The fourth is neither the response-body nor the transformation-body;
it is the Buddha's Dharma-body.
Observing this scriptural passage,
the first three are the transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya),
while the latter is the dharma body (dharmakāya) and the self-enjoyment body (svasaṃbhogakāya).
It is not taught that this is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas of the ten stages;
by principle, it must certainly be a response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and not a transformation body,
because it is what is perceived during the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) in the stage prior to the [ten] stages.
The Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm is a response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
he is not a being of the [six] destinies.
This is a response, not a transformation.
The Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) is also subsumed under this phrase;
it is not discussed here because, by mentioning the first, the subsequent ones are implied, and thus they are omitted for brevity.
Otherwise, under which phrase would that body be subsumed?
In the section on "Transformation within the Non-Corresponding," it is stated only that the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa and manifests through the power of his vows;
it does not mention the transformation bodies manifested while the Buddha is still present.
This is because when the master is present and initiates a transformation, it is easily understood.
Because the Master [Nāgārjuna] spoke without raising the objection regarding transformational arising,
that very sūtra states:
"This first body manifests in dependence upon the enjoyment body."
This second body manifests based upon the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The dharma-body, being ultimate reality, has no locus of dependence. Since it has been stated that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests based upon the response body (*saṃbhogakāya*), [it follows that the response body likewise depends on the dharma-body].
It is said to be difficult because there is no need for it to arise through transformation.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* also speaks of four kinds:
first, enjoyment that is not transformational.
That is to say, the portion pertaining to self-benefit is the actual *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body);
the second is the non-enjoyment,
namely the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
In order to transform various classes of beings prior to the stages,
[the teachings] are sometimes coarse and sometimes subtle,
or intended to bring them joy.
Or it may cause fear,
leading to instability and change;
such is merely called "transformation" (nirmāṇa) and not "enjoyment" (saṃbhoga).
It is not for the purpose of causing them to experience happiness in the present life.
The third [body] is both an enjoyment body and a transformation body;
that is to say, it refers to the various transformation bodies manifested for the sake of bodhisattvas on the stages.
Because it causes all bodhisattvas to experience the joy of the Dharma;
because it changes according to the occasion and is not fixed;
and fourth, because it is neither experienced nor transformed.
This refers to the svabhāvakāya (self-nature body).
Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra speaks of ten buddhas,
the first of which is the Buddha Unattached (Asaṅga-buddha).
Because he dwells peacefully in the world and attains perfect enlightenment,
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* also speaks of ten types of Buddhas;
that [type] is named the Abhisambodhi-buddha (the Buddha of Manifest Perfect Enlightenment).
Second is the Buddha of Vows;
because he brings them forth,
he is named the Buddha of Great Resolute Vows.
The Buddha of the Retribution of the Three Karmas:
because faith is perfected,
all practices first arise through faith as their cause.
Therefore, they are specifically designated as the Buddha of the Maturation of Karma,
and the Buddha of the Four Supports.
Because he conforms to the world without interruption,
he is called the Buddha of Sustenance and the Buddha of the Fivefold Nirvāṇa.
Because he manifests nirvana,
he is called a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha).
Sixth is the Dharma-realm Buddha (dharmadhātu-buddha).
Because he manifests everywhere without exception,
he is the seventh: the Buddha of Mind,
because he dwells securely in goodness.
The second is named the same as that:
the Buddha of the Eight Samādhis,
because he has accomplished immeasurable merit and is free from all attachments.
That is called the Buddha of Certainty;
it is the Buddha of the Nine Natures,
because of its excellent determination.
That is named the Buddha of Essential Nature (Prakṛti-buddha).
He is the Buddha of Ten Sovereign Powers (Daśa-vaśitā), because he universally covers all.
Regarding those, the former five are conventional Buddhas,
while the latter five are ultimate Buddhas.
They are subsumed within the three bodies as appropriate.
Among the five conventional [bodies], they are subsumed within the nirmāṇakāya;
among the five ultimate [bodies]—
The fundamental nature of the dharma-realm is subsumed within the dharma-body;
the remaining three bodies constitute the enjoyment body.
Within the realm of emanations, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment and displays the entry into parinirvāṇa;
he establishes the first and the fifth [stages],
demonstrating the practice of correct conduct.
Furthermore, because one attains superior fruits by making auxiliary vows,
the second and third [categories] are established;
and because images and relics continue to abide and be maintained after his parinirvāṇa, the fourth is established.
These five are established because the transformation buddhas increase accordingly;
within the dharma body,
they consist of the fundamental qualities of merit and the intrinsic nature of the three bodies.
It is divided into the dharma-dhātu and the Buddha of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-buddha),
which is the self-enjoyment body (svasaṃbhoga-kāya) distinct from worldly consciousness.
Furthermore, through the arising of merit,
they are divided into the Mind-Buddha and the Meditative Buddha.
The Body of Enjoyment for Others is called the Buddha of Accordance with Delight.
Therefore, although the three bodies are divided into ten types,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 568, further explains ten bodies: first,
the body of equality (*samatā-kāya*).
Second, the pure body;
third, the inexhaustible body;
fourth, the well-cultivated body.
Fifth, the body of the nature of the five dharmas;
sixth, the body free from vitarka and vicāra;
seventh, the inconceivable body.
8. the body of tranquility;
9. the body of space;
10. the body of wondrous wisdom.
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
"In the first stage,
one attains the body of equality and penetrates the nature of phenomena."
Because they are free from all crooked views and attain equanimity,
in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*) they obtain a purified body,
being free from the transgression of precepts and the loss of purity.
In the third stage, one attains an inexhaustible body because,
having abandoned desire, greed, and hatred, one has attained superior meditative concentration.
In the fourth stage, one attains a well-cultivated body.
Because they constantly and diligently cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
in the fifth stage they attain the dharma-nature body (dharmatākāya),
for they contemplate the principles of the truths and realize the dharma-nature.
In the sixth stage, one attains the body free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
because one contemplates the principle of dependent origination and is thus free from applied and sustained thought.
In the seventh stage, one attains the inconceivable body.
Because the practice of the wisdom of skillful means is perfected,
one attains the body of tranquility in the eighth stage,
being free from all afflictions and the proliferation of conceptual constructs.
In the ninth stage, one attains the body of space,
because its physical characteristics are inexhaustible and pervade all things.
In the tenth stage, one attains the body of sublime wisdom.
Because the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) has been perfected, Śvetaketu asked:
"Is there no distinction between the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?"
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
"There is no difference in their bodies,
yet there are distinctions in their merits."
Because all phenomena share the same single dharma-nature, there is no distinction in their bodies.
As for the difference in merit:
the Buddha is fully endowed with merit, whereas the bodhisattva is not.
It is like a precious gem:
whether it is adorned with ornaments or not,
the gem itself remains no different.
The extensive explanation of parables states that while the dharmakāya which is realized has no differentiation,
there are distinctions in the jñānakāya of the qualities that realize it.
The Buddha is not like this;
even the body that realizes [enlightenment] has no differentiation.
Now, these ten bodies are all subsumed within the Dharma-body.
According to the differences in the qualities realized at each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*),
ten types are taught.
Although there is no textual passage stating that the *vipākakāya* (retribution body) of a bodhisattva also has ten types, [it follows logically].
The principle of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) that accords with sentient beings likewise has ten aspects.
Since its virtuous functions differ, its names should also be distinct;
this is based on the ten dharma-bodies (dharmakāya) corresponding to the principles realized.
The designation "Ten Grounds" (daśabhūmi) is itself the name for the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya).
The various stages of the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmyajñāna) and so forth are called "grounds.
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states:
This is the body of the first Buddha.
Because it accords with the various inclinations of sentient beings, it manifests in various forms;
therefore, it is said to be manifold.
Because it manifests in many forms such as monkeys and so forth, it is the second Buddha-body.
Because the disciples are of a single mind, it manifests a single appearance; therefore, it is called "one."
Because disciples delight in seeing the manifestation of the Buddha’s form,
this is the third Buddha-body,
which transcends all characteristics of every kind.
It is not an object characterized by grasping at signs;
therefore, it is called "neither one nor two.
This is because numbers such as "one" and "two" are all based on grasping at signs.
Furthermore, just as suchness is non-dual while the wisdom of suchness is not unitary, the Dharma-body is therefore neither dual nor unitary. 4.
The Fourth [Section]: The Characteristics of the Result Arising from Causes. Regarding the characteristics of the result arising from causes:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises explain a single cause.
The sixth fascicle of that treatise states:
"How should one view the entry into the characteristics of the knowable?"
"The basis for the cultivation of extensive learning (*bahuśruta-vāsanā*) is not subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna*, and so forth.
Furthermore, it asks:
"By what means can one enter [this state]?"
Because it is sustained by the power of the roots of goodness,
and so forth, as explained at length;
for the cultivation of hearing is the nature of the seed of supramundane mind.
This explains the initial cultivation of the four superior practices:
first, approaching virtuous persons as the supreme condition;
second, hearing the true Dharma.
Third is reflection in accordance with reality;
fourth is practice in accordance with what has been taught.
The latter three constitute internal practice.
Regarding internal practice, one must first cultivate through extensive hearing (*bahuśruta*);
for those who have heard little cannot possibly achieve it.
This seed of extensive hearing—
Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and related texts, there are briefly three interpretations.
The first holds that it is solely through new perfuming (*navavāsanā*);
that is, only impure seeds serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) to directly produce the pure [seeds].
Although this has already been extensively refuted in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
according to the fifty-second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
it asks: "If all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) comprise all seeds (*bīja*)," [how is it that they do not arise simultaneously?]
Furthermore, regarding what is called the "pervasive heaviness" (sarvatraga-dausthulya):
from what kind of seed do all supramundane dharmas arise?
If one were to say that they arise with the seeds of the nature of heaviness as their cause, [it would be untenable].
This is not logical. Therefore, it is known that contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are not the direct causes and conditions for the arising of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena;
both exist only as original [inherent] states.
The various untainted seeds prior to the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment are termed the "nature-lineage" (prakṛti-gotra);
from the time the resolve has been aroused onward, they are termed the "cultivated lineage" (samudānīta-gotra),
because the cultivation of their functional activity causes them to gradually increase.
Prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) cultivation through hearing can produce actual manifestations (*samudācāra*),
while the untainted (*anāsrava*) has not yet arisen;
taking both of these together, they are termed the "wholesome states conducive to liberation and penetration" (*mokṣabhāgīya* and *nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Although the wholesome [states] of the *viniścaya-bhāga* are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*),
they are nevertheless established as being of an untainted nature (*anāsrava*) and subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*)."
After the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) then arise as actualized manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Prior to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), these two types arise in a mixed manner.
After attaining Buddhahood, all tainted virtues (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and those [virtues] that have the untainted as their cause [arise].
All these are simultaneously transformed and extinguished;
the various fruits of outflow-free perfection arise.
Therefore, it is said regarding nirvāṇa:
One abandons impermanent form and attains permanent form;
the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Now, observing that meaning, it is seen that only the original seeds give rise to the manifest.
There is no manifestation whatsoever that newly perfumes seeds;
this has already been extensively refuted in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Third, seeds are all of two kinds.
Regarding the "original existence" (mūla-astitva) and "newly perfumed" (nava-vāsanā) seeds:
prior to the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), they are explained according to the second [position].
After the path of seeing, the various untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja) of original existence manifest as actualities (pravṛtti).
The new manifestations of mental activity, in turn, permeate to form new seeds.
Briefly stated, there are two meanings:
first, transformation and cessation.
Second is the transformation of the limit (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Regarding the meaning of "transformation-cessation":
it is like the seeds of superior preparatory wholesome states and untainted wholesome states that have existed since beginningless time within the stage of the Mahāyāna.
Because they have not yet encountered the necessary conditions, they are all exclusively of an inferior grade.
Prior to the Path of Seeing, the outflowing perfumations of hearing serve as the predominant condition,
thereby supporting the inferior untainted seeds and gradually causing them to increase and become superior.
Upon reaching the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), [the afflictions] arise in their lower manifestations;
these manifest activities further perfume the seeds of the lower categories.
This occurs because the cultivation of the Path of Seeing serves as the condition.
Upon reaching the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seeds sown during the preceding moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are extinguished;
within the path of cultivation, seeds arise, and within those [seeds], active manifestations (*samudācāra*) arise.
The manifest activities further perfume the seeds within the storehouse consciousness;
through the cultivation of the path as a condition,
this continues until the ultimate stage is reached.
In the preceding moment,
the middling-grade uncontaminated seeds cease;
in the subsequent moment, [they arise].
The seeds of the superior grade of the untainted arise because there is nothing further upon which to rely and because the Path has already been perfected.
No further perfuming occurs;
originally there was only one category.
Because the inferior is extinguished and the superior arises, it is called "transformation-extinction" (parāvṛtti).
Because they are cultivated later,
the preceding similar types cannot act as similar causes to draw forth subsequent similar results. In this way,
there are various untainted seeds of the lower, middle, and upper grades within each respective stage.

It should be understood accordingly that all the various types of contaminated seeds— whether superior, medium, or inferior, and whether belonging to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) within the various levels—
persist until the stage of Buddhahood.
Only those that are untainted (anāsrava), superior, and perfect;
as well as those that are untainted but middling or inferior;
and all those that are tainted (sāsrava).
Both are abandoned and extinguished;
therefore, the Sūtra speaks of abandoning impermanent form and so forth.
Second, they are equal in their transformation.
By the nature of things (*dharmatā*), seeds are all of three grades.
Because one first cultivates the inferior grade, when reaching the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*),
the inferior-grade untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) arise as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
The manifest activity further perfumes the seeds of the lower categories;
if there were no cultivation, they would arise spontaneously in the lower states.
However, through cultivation, one reaches the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The seeds of the medium grade give rise to medium-level active manifestations;
these active manifestations, in turn, perfuse the seeds of the medium grade.
Furthermore, the previously existing seeds of the inferior grade are also transformed into the medium grade.
If it were not perfumed, it would arise spontaneously; however,
through the power of cultivation, upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood,
the seeds of the superior lineage give rise to the superior manifest activities.
Because the Path has already been fulfilled and there is nothing further to be perfumed,
it is no longer subject to perfuming.
The seeds of the middle grade all transform into the superior;
the preceding seeds of the middle and lower grades no longer continue.
Because they become equal to the subsequent excellence, it is called "transformation to equality" (*parāvṛtti*).
Therefore, the Sūtra states that one "abandons impermanent form" and so forth;

These seeds of the cultivation of hearing,

Therefore, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:

"One who has no doubt regarding the tathāgatagarbha enveloped by immeasurable stores of afflictions will likewise have no doubt regarding the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, which is free from those immeasurable stores of afflictions."

The others refer to the Buddha adorned with the marks and signs resulting from the maturation of karma, and the Buddha of transformation (nirmāṇakāya) adorned with the marks and signs;

Second, regarding the aids:

All contaminated cognitions (*sāsrava-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) serve as auxiliary causes for manifestation (*vyañjaka-hetu*), but they are not seeds (*bīja*).
This is because they lack the condition of hearing [the Dharma].
This explains how a single cause can produce two types of results.
In relation to its own kind, it acts as a generative cause;

As for the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is likewise produced by a generative cause.
Within this context, regarding the dharma-body:

Although those of the two vehicles attain the true suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*), [they do not realize the dharma-body].

This is due to the causes of compassion and wisdom, which are cultivated through repeated hearing, reflection, and meditative practice.
From the first bhūmi upward, the two obstructions are gradually severed;
as the locus of these virtues, it is called the Dharmakāya,
as stated in the previously cited Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
In the first stage (bhūmi), one attains the body of equality;
up to the tenth stage, one attains the body of sublime wisdom.
For the World-Honored One himself has declared that this is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Through the tenfold distinctions of the wisdom that realizes that principle,
the dharmakāya which is realized is likewise shown to be tenfold;
this continues until, upon attaining Buddhahood, both obscurations are entirely exhausted.
Because the two wisdoms are perfected and merit is fulfilled,
the realized body of principle (*dharmakāya*) manifests with brilliant purity and without further differentiation;
it is collectively termed the *dharmakāya* and also the *svabhāvakāya*.
Just as when the sky is cleared of cataracts, it becomes bright, pure, and expansive— not newly possessing emptiness—
so too is the Dharma-body.
This is called the Dharma-body attaining Buddhahood through the cause of realization.
That is, prior to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga),
by repeatedly hearing, reflecting upon, and cultivating the causes of great wisdom,
the power of the untainted seeds (anāsravabīja) is made to increase.
From the first bhūmi upward, one is able to give rise to the manifest activity of all untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-jñāna*);
thus, the distinctions in the stages of these various wisdoms are termed the "ten bhūmis.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The stages of the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena are called *bhūmis*.
Following this, there are briefly two types of bodhisattvas:
those who, fearing the afflictions (*kleśa*), analytically suppress them so that they no longer function.
From the first bhūmi onward, one receives a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Based on this, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* divides the bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis into three types of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*).
There are those who receive the transformation body only when the seventh bhūmi is about to be completed.

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states based on this that those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and bodhisattvas who have attained mastery constitute the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
This is because those prior to the seventh stage do not yet fear the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As explained in the *Two Kinds of Birth and Death* (Erzhong shengsi yi lin),
the realized truth is called the tenfold Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
and the meritorious qualities that realize it are likewise called the tenfold Enjoyment-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This is for the sake of experiencing the bliss of the Dharma.
However, in the past, as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they performed the karma of the ten kings;
from the first bhūmi onward, they experience the fruit of those ten kings.
Eighth, the physical form transformed by the five consciousnesses:
it is a contaminated maturation,
including the marks and signs of excellence and supernormal powers.
All these gradually become complete;
subsequently, based upon this, they further transform into a superior form characterized by the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana),
which is comprised within the untainted (anāsrava).
They are born in various pure lands and adorn the sites of enlightenment.
Within a single body, they manifest as two types of transformations;
their appearances are so similar that those who behold them perceive them as one.
These are collectively termed "enjoyment.
Those who fear the afflictions are born in the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) after the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Those who take the causes for manifesting their bodies as the basis for transformation and do not fear the afflictions are born in the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven only upon reaching the final mind of the seventh stage.
The material basis manifests as bodily karma and transforms into the *pariṇāmika* (transformational) body.
This meaning is explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the enjoyment [body] of the ten stages, there should be ten names corresponding to what is realized therein.
The principle that they share the same name as the Dharma-body is likewise unerring;
for the Dharma-body is manifested by virtue of the qualities of realization.
Alternatively, the names of the ten stages themselves are the names of the Enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya) of those ten stages.
Because those names are established based on those bodhisattvas,
these ten stages (bhūmis) become progressively more sublime until one reaches the tenth stage,
at which point they are about to attain buddhahood.
In the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, there appeared a great jewel lotus,
as numerous as the atoms in ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of trichiliocosms.

At the stage of the Vajra-mind (*vajra-citta*), there still remains a body that is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and inferior uncontaminated (*hīnānāsrava*).

The material bodies transformed by the eight consciousnesses when they are untainted are also entirely untainted.

The continuity remains serene, extending to the limits of the future,

Although this *parabhogika* [body] has parents and also manifests birth,

Amitābha Buddha’s father was named Candrottara,

This mark is manifested because he transforms the *paricchinna-śarīra* (segmented body);

both Māra and his followers will all protect the Buddha-dharma.

The *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states:
"The lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is immeasurable;
even after hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, it shall reach its ultimate end."
After his parinirvāṇa,
when the light of dawn appears, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will appear.
Beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment,
becoming the Buddha named Universal Radiance Mountain King of Merit.
His land was named Adorned by the Universal Gathering of All Jewels.
The land of the Victorious Amitābha Buddha cannot be compared to even a hundred thousand million billionth part of this [land].
After this Buddha has passed into extinction, Mahāsthāmaprāpta will attain Buddhahood,
named the Buddha King of the Jewel of Well-Abiding Merit.
Since the capacities and conditions of those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have already matured,

He attains Buddhahood in this very body while seated;

Therefore, from the first bhūmi onward, the wisdom of equality can manifest in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings;
because it has been permeated and refined by great compassion prior to the path of vision,
from the first bhūmi onward it can function in accordance with the three vehicles.
Manifesting various bodies according to what is appropriate for those to be taught,

He subsequently entered nirvana;

This is as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures.
Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous voice is entirely through his supernatural power;
for those who should be delivered by means of the three vehicles,
he manifests in their respective forms and preaches the Dharma for them.
Therefore, throughout all ten stages, one is able to manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The transformations based on the five [sensory] consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Within the same location, similar perceptions appear as one;

Because those who hold base ascetic practices in contempt and value wealth and status were to be converted,

This is stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The Buddha’s transformation body can manifest the eight phases:

Seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma;

first manifesting his renunciation, he subsequently underwent ascetic practices.

this transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), perfumed and refined by great compassion,

The teachings state that there are three types of bodhisattvas.
The first are those bound by a single birth,
such as Maitreya and others.

Looking toward his future status as a Buddha, there should be four births:

Regarding the body of self-enjoyment, that which exists prior to the seventh bhūmi is called "bound to one birth," while that which exists from the eighth bhūmi onward is called the "final body," as there is no further rebirth.
Abiding upon a lotus seat is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).
The Body of Enjoyment for Others is like the previous body of Avalokiteśvara;

The body of Avalokiteśvara is called the "final body," and his dwelling upon the seven-jeweled throne is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).
Since the Dharma-body is unborn, these [conventional] meanings do not apply.
However, these three bodies are neither definitively identical nor distinct.
The body of self-enjoyment constitutes the characteristic of its own nature;
the dharma-body is the rational essence of this very body.
The profound and subtle principle of wisdom is not known by others;

while that perceived subtly by those of the Ten Stages is named the *saṃbhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others).
Because their modes of perception differ and their characteristics and natures are distinct,
the accumulation of qualities and meanings is divided into three bodies (*trikāya*).
This is not like establishing three types based on the individual, separate entities of sentient beings.
Because there is no fixed difference, yet it is not the case that they are not different;
they are neither fixedly one nor different,
just like the Buddha, the Able One of Tranquility.
That which is perceived by those on the ten stages is called the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*);
that which is perceived by the followers of the two vehicles is called the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
and when non-conceptual wisdom contemplates ultimate truth, it is called the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).
True wisdom is profound and subtle; having long cultivated its causes until they are fulfilled, one personally experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
This is not known by others, and is thus called the "body for self-experience."
Knowledge and vision differ; they are not definitively one nor different.
This is the characteristic of the causal arising of a result from the cause of production.
Nevertheless, there is a single result.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

As with the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*),

Because it is that which is currently arising,

for it projects the remaining fruit.
Now it is explained that [the dharmakāya] enjoys one fruit from two causes;
if viewed in relation to the dharmakāya, there is one fruit and one cause;
if viewed in relation to the nirmāṇakāya, there is one cause and two fruits.
Furthermore, the two fruits of the Buddha are obtained through two causes,
namely the causes of principle and wisdom;
as stated in the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra.
There are two kinds of the Tathāgatagarbha’s wisdom of emptiness:
that which is separated from, liberated from, severed from, or distinct from all the store of afflictions;
and that which is not separated from, not liberated from, not severed from, and not distinct from the inconceivable Tathāgatagarbha.
This explains that the essence of the afflictions is called "store" (ālaya) because it can conceal [the true nature];
it is called "empty" (śūnya) because it is false and unreal, and ultimately subject to destruction.
Vimalakīrti said:
"The category of afflictions is the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Before attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all dharmas— whether wholesome,
unwholesome, or indeterminate— are called the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, the Sūtra states that there are two kinds of the Tathāgata-garbha’s wisdom of emptiness.
This is because afflictions are also termed the Tathāgata-garbha,
and because the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is manifested by means of emptiness and is itself the nature of emptiness.
It is termed "emptiness.
When the cause of the dharmakāya is shrouded by afflictions, it is termed the tathāgatagarbha;

realizing the self-nature liberation of the Dharmakāya.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
He appears in the world in order to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

he causes them to abandon the two illusory cities and reach the place of the true treasure.

First question: "Is it the case that all who are born must perish?

The second question asks: "Does that which has been extinguished arise again?
The answer states: "This is a conceptual distinction.

"In what direction do you reside?
"I reside according to whatever direction [you point to].

Although it is not permanent, it is nevertheless said to be permanent;
thus, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:
"The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible."
Wisdom is likewise so;
because the emanations of the Buddha appear repeatedly and are never permanently severed,
it is like the worldly expression "one who constantly gives food."
Although it is not continuous, giving repeatedly with a mind that does not cease is called "constant giving of food.
It is the same for the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya).
Because they manifest repeatedly and do not cease forever,
the two bodies are said to be "permanent"; this is permanence in the sense of intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-vacana*).
Second is the gateway of the dual benefit of self and others.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"Good son, all Buddhas bring about the ultimate benefit of both themselves and others."
Self-benefit is the suchness of phenomena (dharmatā-tathatā);
benefit for others is the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna).
Regarding the matter of benefiting oneself and others:
All attain mastery because they accomplish various and boundless functions; therefore,
one distinguishes the Buddha-dharma.
There are immeasurable, boundless, and various distinctions.
The *Saṃyukta-ābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is supreme in terms of self-benefit.
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is supreme in benefiting others;
the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) is supreme in benefiting both self and others;
and although the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) is included within benefiting others, [it is also supreme].
Because the noble wealth of the Dharma received through one's own enjoyment is most preeminent,
it is described as solely for one's own benefit; this is according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* on the stage of Buddhahood.
All [teachings] speak of the dharmakāya as tranquil and blissful;
because it is devoid of activity,
it correctly comprises self-benefit.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* explains that what constitutes one's own benefit is the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*).
Because it does not state that there exists a capacity to act as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for benefiting sentient beings, it also encompasses the benefit of others.
Furthermore, it serves as the basis for the twofold benefit of both [self and others] and is subsumed by that twofold benefit.
There are two types of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*).
The self-enjoyment body fulfills its own vows and practices;
it is able to personally enjoy the sublime bliss of the Dharma and is comprised within the correct benefit for oneself.
The other-enjoyment body fulfills the vows and practices of others.
It causes all bodhisattvas to experience the great joy of the Dharma, which is subsumed under the benefit of others; because of these two,
it is sometimes said that such enjoyment is subsumed solely under self-benefit.
Whether one speaks of the benefit of others or the benefit of both,
there is no contradiction between them.
Conversely, it is revealed that the scriptural statement regarding the ability to benefit others refers to suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*);
it simply states that suchness-wisdom alone is capable of benefiting others through the enjoyment and transformation bodies (*saṃbhoga- and nirmāṇa-kāya*).
This wisdom is not obstructed and constitutes self-benefit;
the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), however, exists solely for the benefit of others,
as the manifestation of various transformed forms is subsumed under the benefit of others.
There are three gates concerning difference and non-difference.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Because there is no distinction in the basis, intention, and activity of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas."
One should say they are not different,
because the manifest perfect enlightenment occurs based on immeasurable bodies.
One should also say they are different.
Wu-xing (Asvabhāva) explains, saying:
"True Suchness is without difference;
its basis is without distinction."
Their intention to bring benefit and happiness is identical;
their mental disposition is without distinction.
Their perfect awakening, nirvana, and various activities are the same.
There is no distinction between the karma;
this is said because the support and the supported are identical, and thus there is no difference.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The true nature of the Dharmakāya is common to all Buddhas;
therefore, there is no distinction."
Because there is a distinction in the causes for their realization,
they are conventionally described as being distinct;
however, with respect to their basis alone, they are said to be without distinction.
Because their essence is non-dual;
yet, if one speaks in terms of the dependent attributes,
there is a distinction because their essences are different.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
"As it is with the Dharma-body, so it is with its enjoyment;
for there is no distinction in their intention or activity."
It should be said that they are not different,
not because there is no distinction in their basis,
but because immeasurable distinctions in their bases arise.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is likewise.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the remaining two bodies [are also thus].
Each distinct cause brings about its own distinct self-nature;
there is indeed a real differentiation.
This is precisely what the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Because the body of infinite reliance manifests perfect enlightenment,
one should say that there is a distinction;
yet, there is no separate grasping.
The equality of the intention for benefit and happiness and of their activities is taught as being without distinction;
thus, there is no contradiction.
Section Four: The Gate of the Dimensions of the Three Bodies.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the Dharma-body is boundless.
It is just like space, which pervades all places;
its form and magnitude cannot be described as large or small.
In terms of its characteristics, it is like space, being without boundaries.
The body of self-enjoyment possesses both form and non-form;
that which is non-form is shapeless,
and its dimensions— whether large or small— cannot be described.
The body and its objects may also be said to pervade all places.
As for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*),
through cultivation over great eons (*mahākalpa*), one attains superior faculties and their corresponding objects.
Each of the primary and secondary marks pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
unlike those born of the karma of birth-and-death,
which have limitations such that the resulting physical forms may be small or large.
The Buddha’s untainted body, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
has encountered boundless Buddhas and severed boundless obstacles.
Because it arises from the cultivation of immeasurable goodness for the sake of benefiting boundless sentient beings,
its fruit is likewise boundless.
Because the bodies manifested by the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom are limitless,
those manifested by all Buddhas, though occupying the same place at the same time,
are similar in appearance and do not obstruct one another.
They enjoy the dharma-joy without interruption until the very end;
this is known only by the Buddha,
and is not within the scope of other faculties or objects.
Therefore, the holy teachings state that the mark of the invisible crown of the head and the boundless sound of the Dharma each possess infinite qualities and functions.
The Enjoyment Body (*sambhogakāya*) manifests various bodies for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
its speech, sounds, marks, signs, form, and dimensions are not fixed.
As stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:
I, now Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus throne;
even down to a single Śākyamuni in a single land, and so forth.
Huayan and others state that a bodhisattva on the first stage sees one hundred buddha-lands;
each such land is equivalent to one great trichiliocosm.
In one realm there is one emanation of Śākyamuni;
in each of the four continents of a world-system there is one emanation;
and within that entire realm there is one Great Śākyamuni.
That which is seen by those in the four roots of goodness;
that which is seen by the remaining three vehicles within the ten billion minor Śākyas;
and that which the first-stage bodhisattva sees for themselves as one hundred thousand million-world systems, [all presided over by] one Vairocana.
The magnitude of Amitābha Buddha is as it is seen here;
likewise, on the second stage one sees a thousand,
and on the third stage ten thousand, and so forth.
The accumulation of numbers should be understood as follows:
when a Bodhisattva of the Vajra-mind on the tenth stage is about to attain Buddhahood,
the sign of a great precious lotus flower appears in the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha).
Its circumference is equal to the number of atoms in ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems.
Each single atom therein is a great thousandfold world system;
upon it, the Bodhisattva sits and attains perfect enlightenment.
The dimensions of the Buddha’s body as perceived by him are difficult to know;
he does not perceive the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts describe the dimensions of the buddha-field of Ānanda when he attains buddhahood.
According to this principle, it should be understood that the Buddha-body is subsumed under the "body for others' enjoyment" (parasaṃbhogakāya); the same logic applies to all [other cases].
As for the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), it transforms beings prior to the [first] bhūmi.
The distinctions between the two stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*) are as follows:
their physical dimensions are not fixed, being adjusted according to what is appropriate for sentient beings;
for example, Śākyamuni is sixteen feet tall, while the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) are twice that height.
Maitreya is a thousand feet tall; it is appropriate for him to appear as he is seen.
The other bodies he receives are all transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya), which are of the nature of the four or five subtle particles (paramāṇu).
Although non-material qualities lack physical form,
they nevertheless manifest through transformation;
this is stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The spiritual power of the Unsurpassed Awakened One is inconceivable;
thus, he is able to manifest formless phenomena,
such as desire and hatred, so that others may come to know them.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that transformations cannot perform four things:
first, the mind.
Second, mental factors;
third, faculties;
fourth, the fruits of karma.
Although they lack actual utility,
the mind and mental factors that appear as if they exist are precisely the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of the mind.
The transformations resemble the substance of the five sense organs and the nature of the four sense objects;
although they appear as the nature of karmic fruit, their essence is untainted (anāsrava).
This includes the six years of ascetic practice, the horse-barley, and the golden spear.
Although they all appear to be suffering,
they are in fact untainted (*anāsrava*);
this is the fifth [point], the gate of common and uncommon [characteristics] regarding the sentient beings to be converted.
In the nature of self-nature and self-enjoyment, these conceptual distinctions do not exist;
however, they do exist in the case of other-enjoyment and transformation bodies.
Regarding this point, there are briefly three explanations in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
First, they are all equal because each and every Buddha is able to manifest through transformation,
and their merit and wisdom are equal.
Having practiced for a long time together in the common pursuit of bodhi, it is as stated:
the sentient beings transformed by one Buddha are those of all Buddhas.
Therefore, know that they are shared in common.
Second is the non-common [transformation body],
because that which is emanated by the Buddha is fundamentally connected to his own characteristics. Therefore, Śākyamuni—
During the time of Buddha Tiṣya,
he once served as an attendant to that Buddha alongside Maitreya;
the Buddha then observed those to be converted.
Śākyamuni will attain maturity first,
and Maitreya will attain maturity later;
however, observing those capable of transformation, Maitreya will achieve success first.
He attained enlightenment after Śākyamuni;
he entered the fire-light samādhi to allow Śākyamuni to see him,
and for seven days and seven nights, he stood on one foot in praise.
He caused Maitreya to transcend him and attain Buddhahood first.
Furthermore, Śākyamuni said:
"Those whom I was to deliver have all already been delivered."
Furthermore, a sutra states that at the time of his parinirvāṇa,
the Buddha observed a single being to be converted who was currently residing in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
He should be born in this realm to receive the Buddha’s transformation;
leaving behind a single emanation body to dwell secretly in this world while manifesting his own entry into nirvana,
he passes away from that state and is reborn here.
The transformation body remains until the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) is attained; only after becoming one who has nothing more to learn does the transformation body cease.
Furthermore, this is stated in various places.
The relationship between the transformer and the transformed is determinate;
therefore, it is unique. According to the true meaning, however, there are both common and unique aspects.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* also states this:
those who are to be converted together [experience] the same place at the same time.
Each of the Buddhas transforms themselves into bodies and lands;
their forms are similar to one another, yet they do not obstruct each other.
Interacting and blending with one another as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
they cause the consciousnesses of those to be converted to manifest their own perceptions, such that in a single land there appears the body of a single Buddha,
who manifests supernatural powers and preaches the Dharma for their benefit.
Regarding that which is unique:
it is solely the Buddha who transforms all classes of sentient beings,
having done so since beginningless time.
The nature of the spiritual lineage (gotra) is such that they are mutually interconnected;
either many belong to one, or one belongs to many.
Therefore, those beings who are transformed have both common and uncommon [destinies].
Otherwise, it would be truly useless for many Buddhas to remain in the world for a long time,
each undergoing such arduous toil.
1. Because a single Buddha can benefit all sentient beings; this point is explained extensively in such works as the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.

2. The section on the characteristics of the three bodies (*trikāya*). 3. The section on through how many masteries one attains mastery. 4. The section on how many locations the three bodies rely upon. 5. The section on by how many qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) they are sustained. 6. The section on the association with meritorious qualities (*guṇa*).

All that above is as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. The twelfth section, on the transformation of the twelve types of consciousness—both with and without outflows—is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

As explained in the *Paryāyārthavana*, there is the section on the distinctions in the preaching of the Dharma by the four bodies and the three bodies,
such as in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
Since the distinctions among these three bodies are boundless, fearing that excessive detail might weary the reader, I shall provide here only a brief indication.

Such as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the two *Prajñāpāramitā-upadeśa-śāstras*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.

Chapter Six: The Meaning of Buddha-lands (*buddhakṣetra*). Chapter on Buddha-lands.
It is analyzed by way of eight gates:
first, the manifestation of its distinctions;
second, the determination of its essential nature.
First, the causal practice of the three knowledges;
second, the manifestation of the characteristics of the fruit;
third, the explanation of their dimensions.
Sixth, the locus of liberation;
seventh, the shared and unshared;
eighth, the analysis by way of various gates.
1. First, the Manifestation of Distinctions. Regarding the manifestation of distinctions, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states:
"The Buddha-body is twofold."
First, the body of birth;
second, the dharma-body.
Whether it be the essential nature body (svābhāvika-kāya) or the actual enjoyment body (sambhoga-kāya), both are termed the dharma-body.
Because it is accumulated from all dharmas of merit,
both the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the body of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) are called "bodies of birth" (*janmakāya*),
as they manifest repeatedly according to what is appropriate for sentient beings.
All Buddha-fields must necessarily have a physical abode.
Since there are two kinds of bodies, the fields are likewise so.
The lands where these bodies are born are common to both the pure and the defiled.
The realm of the Dharma-body is exclusively pure.
Alternatively, there are two types of bodies:
first, the real [body].
The two are provisional;
the real is the Dharma-body,
and the provisional is the essence of birth.
The lands are likewise twofold,
pure and impure, as previously described.
This is stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.
The Buddha-body is threefold.
The verse says: "The essential nature, the enjoyment, and the transformation."
Regarding "differential transformation," that treatise states:
"The dharma of intrinsic nature is precisely the Tathāgata’s initial body of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvakāya*)."
Because its essence is eternally unchanging, it is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*);
because it is the locus upon which all meritorious qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) rely,
it is also called the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*).
The "enjoyer" is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*),
because it enables both oneself and others to enjoy the various great joys of the Dharma.
The "transformative" is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
In order to bring benefit, welfare, and happiness to sentient beings,
various manifestations and transformations are displayed; thus,
although the essential nature of the pure dharma-realm is without differentiation, [these manifestations appear].
However, there are three bodies with various differing characteristics;
because their transformations are not the same, they are called "distinctions.
Since the bodies are threefold, the lands that correspond to them are likewise so.
First, the dharma-nature realm;
second, the enjoyment realm.
These two are exclusively pure.
Third, the transformation lands (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*),
which encompass both the pure and the defiled.
This is stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra).
The Buddha-body has four [aspects], and the Buddha-lands are likewise.
First is the self-nature body (svābhāvika-kāya),
which is based upon the land of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-bhūmi).
The *Mahāyānaguṇaparikīrtana-sūtra* states:
"The Bhagavat, dwelling within the treasury of the dharmadhātu, preached that sūtra."
It dwells in the realm of the dharma-nature.
Second is the self-enjoyment body,
which relies on the self-enjoyment realm.
Third is the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*),
which relies upon the Land of Enjoyment for Others.
As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
Abiding in the most supreme radiance is the eighteenth perfection.
Fourth is the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body),
which relies upon the nirmāṇa-bhūmi (emanation realm).
This sūtra refers to residing in the city of Vaiśālī.
In the first three [buddha-fields], the bodies and lands are exclusively pure and not defiled;
in the subsequent transformation land, both the pure and the defiled are included.
For Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, he manifests bodies and lands that are not defiled but exclusively pure.
For Bodhisattvas prior to the stages and for the assembly of those of the two vehicles,
he manifests both the pure and the defiled.
If it is for those who have not yet exhausted the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
and have not yet realized the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness, the manifested bodies and lands appear as either pure or impure.
The bodies and lands manifested for those who have exhausted the obstacles of dualistic discrimination and have already realized the two kinds of emptiness must necessarily be pure;
thus the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The three bodies have four permutations.
First, the enjoyment body that is not the transformation body;
this refers to the self-enjoyment body.
Second, it is transformational but not enjoymental;
this refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Third, it is both enjoymental and transformational.
That is to say, the Body of Enjoyment for Others;
fourth, that which is neither Enjoyment nor Transformation,
namely, the Essential Body (svābhāvikakāya).

This is also consistent with the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) doctrine. The third fascicle of the fifth hundred and sixty-eighth assembly, the *Jin-tian-wang-hui* (Assembly of the Victorious Heavenly King), of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
states that the Buddha possesses ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
First, the body of equality;
second, the pure body;
third, the inexhaustible body.
Fourth is the body of well-cultivated virtue;
fifth is the body of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
sixth is the body free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Seventh, the inconceivable body;
eighth, the tranquil body;
ninth, the space-like body.
The ten wondrous bodies of wisdom.
The Heavenly King addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"In what stage can one attain the ten bodies of the Tathāgata?"
The Buddha said:
"In the first stage, one attains the body of equality and penetrates the nature of phenomena."
Because they are free from all crooked views and attain equanimity,
in the second bhūmi they obtain a pure body,
being free from the transgressions of the precepts and the loss of purity.
In the third bhūmi, one attains an inexhaustible body,
because one has abandoned desire, greed, and hatred and attained superior meditative concentration.
In the fourth bhūmi, one attains a well-cultivated body.
Because they constantly and diligently cultivate the factors of enlightenment;
because in the fifth stage they attain the body of the dharma-nature by contemplating the principles of the truths and realizing the dharma-nature;
and because in the sixth stage they attain the body free from applied and sustained thought.
Because one observes the principle of dependent origination free from applied and sustained thought,
one attains the inconceivable body in the seventh stage through the fulfillment of the practice of skillful means and wisdom.
In the eighth stage, one attains the body of tranquility,
because one is free from all afflictions and the proliferation of conceptual elaborations.
In the ninth stage, one attains the body of space.
Because the physical marks are inexhaustible as they pervade all things,
in the tenth stage one attains the body of wondrous wisdom,
through the perfection of the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes.
The Heavenly King spoke again:
"Is there not a distinction between the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
The Buddha said:
"O Heavenly King,
there is no distinction in their bodies, yet there are differences in their merits.
Because all dharmas share the same single dharma-nature, their bodies are without differentiation."
The bodies of all Tathāgatas are endowed with all virtues, whereas Bodhisattvas are not so; thus their virtues differ.
This is extensively demonstrated through immeasurable analogies.
Therefore, one should know that all ten bodies are exclusively the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since the Dharma-body possesses ten names according to its various meanings,
True Suchness (*tathatā*) accordingly accords with these preeminent qualities.
It also accomplishes ten lands: first, the land of universal practice;
second, the most excellent land;
third, the land of superior flow.
Fourth, the realm without appropriation;
fifth, the realm without distinctions among categories;
sixth, the realm without defilement or purity.
Seventh is the realm where phenomena have no distinction;
eighth is the realm that neither increases nor decreases;
ninth is the realm of mastery over wisdom.
The ten lands of mastery over karma are also divided into ten distinct lands according to their respective capacities for realization,
as they differ in meaning.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Furthermore, other sūtras speak of ten kinds of Buddhas,
namely those mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
First, the Buddha of manifest perfect enlightenment;
second, the Buddha of great aspirational vows;
third, the Buddha of karmic maturation.
Fourth, the Buddha who abides and maintains;
fifth, the transformation Buddha;
sixth, the Dharma-realm Buddha.
Seventh, the Buddha of Mind;
eighth, the Buddha of Concentration;
ninth, the Buddha of Original Nature.
The ten Buddhas of Accordance with Inclination:
the first five are conventional,
and the latter five are ultimate.
They are subsumed within the three bodies according to what is appropriate.
To briefly assign them to the three bodies based on their coarse characteristics:
the first five are the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
The next two are the dharma-body,
and the final three are the enjoyment-body;
since these are precisely the three bodies.
The lands are likewise three;
there is no other meaning.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle four, states:
Furthermore, there is the abode of Maheśvara, which transcends the Pure Abodes.
Therein dwell Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage who have attained birth there through the thorough cultivation of the tenth stage.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"There is a wondrous pure land that transcends the triple world;
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage shall be born therein."
This is also what is meant by the "Ten Stages":
because one receives the rank of Buddha as a benefit in the present life;
and because one is born in the abode of the wisdom of Maheśvara as a benefit in a future life.
In Sanskrit he is called Maheśvara,
which is what is referred to as Maheśvara in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
he is a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage.

When a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is about to attain Buddhahood, they proceed to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and sit upon a great precious lotus flower to achieve perfect enlightenment; it is for this reason that they bring forth this land.
Once they have attained Buddhahood, the land becomes boundless, and there is no other separate location.
The *Abhidharmapāda* (Dharma-skandha), chapter six,
states: "Furthermore, there are pure worlds that are not subsumed under the Truth of Suffering."
Because it is not produced by the power of karma or afflictions,
nor is it arisen through the predominance of karma or afflictions; rather,
it is induced by the predominance of pure roots of goodness resulting from great vows.
The place where this is produced is inconceivable;
it is realized only by a Buddha,
and is not even within the meditative range of those who have attained dhyāna.
How much more so for those who merely investigate:
this land of self-enjoyment is known only by the Buddha;
it is not even within the realm of those on the ten stages or of the followers of the two vehicles.
How much less could those outside the ranks of the noble ones who possess discursive thought know it?
Although there are various differing teachings as mentioned above,
the distinctions between bodies and lands do not exceed three or four types.
No further explanation is provided;
it should be understood in its entirety according to the principle.
2. Establishing the Essential Nature. Regarding the second [section], establishing the essential nature:
The self-nature body and its land are the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).
Although there is no distinction in the essence of this body and its land,
they belong to the Buddha-dharma.
Because their characteristics and natures differ:
the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is taken as the body (kāya),
and the essential nature (svabhāva) is taken as the land (kṣetra).
Taking the characteristic of awakening as the body and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the land,
its essence is endowed with the merits of true principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This Buddha-body and its land are neither subsumed under form (rūpa),
