Therefore, those beings who are transformed have both common and uncommon [results].
Otherwise, if many Buddhas were to remain in the world for a long time,
each undergoing such arduous effort, it would truly be of no benefit.
Because a single Buddha can benefit all sentient beings, for this reason, these transformation lands of others' enjoyment (paranirmita-vaśavartin) are both common and uncommon. 8.
The eighth section, "Distinguishing by Various Gates. Regarding the various gates:
Among these, there are ten:
first, the sovereign of the land;
second, the supporting ministers.
Third, the retinue;
fourth, the support;
fifth, the activity.
Sixth, gathering and benefiting;
seventh, fearlessness;
eighth, the path of travel.
Ninth, the vehicle;
tenth, the entrance.
First, the lord of the land.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"That which is the capital of the Tathāgata refers to the buddha-fields where all Buddhas are the sovereigns."
Because it is so preeminent, it is not the seat of others;
it belongs exclusively to the World-Honored One,
or is sustained and upheld solely by the World-Honored One.
It is not something that others are capable of;
that is, each of the three Buddha-bodies is the sovereign within its own land and no other.
Specifically, in the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), the single essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the sovereign.
Although the land of self-enjoyment pervades the entire dharma-realm,
each manifests it individually for itself, acting as its own sovereign without mutual obstruction;
this also applies to the land of other-enjoyment and the land of transformation.
Although all Buddhas undergo transformation,
they nevertheless possess a unified totality and a body of a single characteristic.
Each, according to its respective capacity, takes another as its presiding lord without mutual obstruction.
As for the two auxiliary wings:
they are the Dharma-nature realm (*dharmatā-kāya*) and the self-enjoyment realm (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*).
Only the Buddha dwells therein without any auxiliary support.
Although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages can partially realize it,
they are not capable of assisting or supporting the Dharmakāya.
Because the Dharma-body is signless, it is not described [in that way].
Regarding the Land of Other-Enjoyment,
the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
It is a place where a multitude of great bodhisattvas has gathered like clouds;
that is to say, this pure land is constantly attended by an immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas who always come to provide support and protection.
Therefore, no enemies can cause harm or opposition.
The Buddhas, out of their great compassion, manifest lands— both coarse and sublime—

within their own consciousnesses according to what is appropriate for each bodhisattva; these bodhisattvas, in turn, perceive them in accordance with the power of their own roots of goodness and aspirational prayers.
Within their own consciousnesses, there appear manifestations resembling the pure lands produced by the Buddha;
although these are individually manifested by each person's own mind,
they appear in the same location with similar forms.
This means that they gather together within a single land.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The pure lands thus transformed by these ten stages..."
Is this with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)?
Briefly stated, there are three meanings.
According to one interpretation,
it is untainted (*anāsrava*); because it is sustained by the power of vows and its own untainted seeds, it transforms and manifests a pure land,
wherein one enjoys the Dharma-bliss of the Mahāyāna.
Because it can realize *tathatā* (suchness) and attain true, untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom while constantly beholding all Buddhas,
it is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). According to another interpretation, it is tainted (*sāsrava*).

This means that through the power of aspiration, the seeds of the pure land— which are the outflows-tainted (*sāsrava*) seeds of preparatory application within one's own mind— transform and give rise to a pure land,
wherein one experiences the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Prior to the seventh bhūmi, afflictions manifest.
Throughout the path of cultivation up to the tenth bhūmi, the seeds of the afflictive obstructions and the cognitive obstructions remain,
because the substance of the eighth consciousness is able to sustain them and is directly perfumed by them.
It is still with outflows (sāsrava) and is subsumed under the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature; therefore,
it is not without outflows (anāsrava).
Furthermore, sentient beings do not possess two actual bodies.
Since the body is with outflows (sāsrava),
how could its supporting pure land be without outflows (anāsrava)?
Therefore, it is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*) and is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
According to the true meaning:
There are two types of pure lands manifested by the minds of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Those manifested on the eighth stage are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
because they are subsumed under the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the contaminated eighth consciousness.
Because it serves as the basis for the outflow-tainted body,
although its characteristics are pure and sublime due to being permeated by the power of untainted goodness,
it remains outflow-tainted.
It appears in accordance with the preparatory practices and so forth in that same manner.
If it subsequently transforms into the image of a pure land by means of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
it is subsumed under the characteristics of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).
Because it arises from untainted (anāsrava) wholesome seeds, its essence is untainted and is subsumed within the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
Its transformation land (nirmāṇakṣetra) is where the assemblies of the three vehicles gather.
Because it is the gathering place for the noble ones of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and ordinary beings;
that which is transformed by the Buddha is exclusively untainted (anāsrava),
whereas that which is transformed by others is otherwise.
One interpretation holds that it is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
because the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) cannot transform [the environment] into the appearance of a pure land.
Another interpretation holds that it is also uncontaminated.
The post-attainment wisdom of the untainted [state] also transforms the characteristics of things through the power of the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) as manifested by the Buddha;
since this is not logically inconsistent,
the previous explanation is correct.
Third, regarding the retinue:
the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that he is constantly attended and followed by immeasurable devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others.
In both the Dharma-nature land and the self-enjoyment land, there are no accompanying retinues;
they are signless as previously described.
In the other-enjoyment land, there are only devas and humans as its retinue.
There is no other category [of being],
for although they transcend the heavens and so forth of the triple world, they are still subsumed within the triple world.
Such is the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
It is not contradictory because [the Buddha] manifests such transformations as an act of embracing [beings] to adorn and purify the buddha-fields; or else,
it is for the purpose of bringing the sentient beings to be converted to spiritual maturity.
He manifested such varieties of transformations;
for instance, in order to subdue King Kapphiṇa,
he manifested as an immeasurable multitude of universal monarchs (cakravartin) surrounded by their retinues.
Either the Buddha himself manifests these,
or various bodhisattvas manifest such forms,
to sustain the adornments and offerings of the pure land.
They lead the retinues of Tathāgatas from other directions.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* also states that the kalaviṅka birds and others are all emanations created by Amitābha Buddha.
Transforming into the Two Vehicles,
the adornment of the Pure Land is likewise so.
Within the land of transformation, it is also supported by the eight classes of beings who are truly real.
In the land of enjoyment for others, the bodhisattvas are the true ones;
the followers of the two vehicles and the eight classes of beings are all provisional manifestations,
for they do not truly attain birth therein.
In the transformation lands (*nirmāṇakṣetra*), the two vehicles and the eight classes of beings are all real,
while the bodhisattvas of the ten stages are all provisional manifestations.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages should not be born in transformation lands.
Because the provisional manifestation of the transformation body arises therein.
Fourth, regarding "sustaining":
in the Dharma-nature land, the Buddha does not rely on sustaining.
The self-enjoyment realm maintains the dharma-pleasure for oneself;
regarding the other-enjoyment realm,
the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
It is sustained by the joy and bliss of the vast flavor of the Dharma;
it is sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
"Food" has the meaning of that which enables one to abide [in this state], which is the sense of "sustenance."
That which has already transcended the nature of the three realms is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it can sever the tainted, it should not be called "nutriment" (*āhāra*);
yet, because it is a cause for sustaining [the body], it is also called nutriment.
Just as contaminated phenomena, although they obstruct the uncontaminated,
are called "nutriments" because they sustain the contaminated,
so too it is with the uncontaminated.
Although they have severed the outflows (*āsrava*), how is it that they still maintain the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
It is because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through their subsequent sublime wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-prajñā*),
are able to expound and receive the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma, thereby giving rise to great joy and bliss.
Alternatively, the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) experiences the flavor of suchness and gives rise to great joy and bliss;
it is able to sustain the body so that its continuity is not severed and nourishes wholesome dharmas, and for this reason it is called "food."
Prior to the seventh stage, there is still birth in segmented form;
it is not that the four [nutriments] of physical food, contact, and so forth are not utilized.
From the eighth stage upward, as well as for all Buddhas, physical food is no longer utilized.
It may be said that it is supported by other [nutriments].
This is because various treatises state that it is included within the demonstration of the supports for dwelling and sustenance.
If the transformation land (*nirmāṇakṣetra*) were truly sustained by the four nutriments, [it would be so].
It can also be said that the flavor of the Dharma serves as sustenance,
for by hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one may abide for sixty kalpas.
However, in this sutra, the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa-paṭala*) states:
Having partaken of the dharma of immortality,
one returns to drink the flavor of liberation;
for those who take the deathlessness of nirvāṇa as their food.
Since the sublime object realized gives rise to joy and bliss,
it may be called "nutriment"; thus,
there is no contradiction in applying the term "nutriment" to that which sustains the untainted state.
However, regarding the substance of this food, the various teachings differ;
this is explained in detail in the separate chapter and the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
Fifth, as for the activity:
That Buddha-dharmakāya is either solely for self-benefit,
serving as the basis for the two [form] bodies;
or it pertains to both self-benefit and benefit for others.
The body of self-enjoyment possesses only self-benefit;
whereas the body of other-enjoyment and the transformation body belong exclusively to the benefit of others, as they are manifested for their sake.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"While performing all that is beneficial for the sake of all sentient beings,
the Buddha remains in tranquil meditative absorption."
By the power of the aspirational prayers cultivated through prior application,
one is able to spontaneously accomplish every benefit for all sentient beings;
in the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* realm, the sublime Dharma is extensively taught.
They perform few supernatural feats for the benefit of tenth-stage bodhisattvas;
rather, they primarily employ supernatural feats within the transformed lands to bring about the various benefits of the Three Vehicles through the rare preaching of the sublime Dharma.
Sixth, regarding "benefiting others":
the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) and its realm, as well as the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*),
are not said to benefit others because they have already severed [defilements] and are perfected.
Regarding the meaning of "benefiting others through other enjoyments," the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"It extinguishes all afflictions, calamities, entanglements, and stains."
Thus, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*) and "impurities" (*mala*).
In this way, they are called the causes of all calamities and misfortunes.
Since afflictions, entanglements, and impurities are absent herein, [it is free from them].
Furthermore, there are no calamities or misfortunes here;
as for afflictions, there are ten, which,
when combined with those abandoned through seeing and cultivation across the three realms, total one hundred and twenty-eight types.
There are eight kinds of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):

namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), drowsiness (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).
There are six kinds of stains (*mala*).
Namely: malice, resentment, vexation, guile, deceit, and arrogance.
Calamities and misfortunes are the karma produced by these and the fruits thereof.
Within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the seeds are termed afflictions (*kleśa*).
Manifestation is termed the "impurity of entanglement" (*paryavasthāna-mala*).
To be free from these two is called "beneficial inclusion.
This is like a worldly lord who, though not formally taking possession [of his subjects], [still benefits them].
However, they do not cause calamity;
when sealing the doors, they also say, "The Master protects and benefits me.
This case is also like this.
Furthermore, because they have directly realized liberation from afflictions, calamities, entanglements, and stains,
and possess superior merit and wisdom, they are called "beneficial.
The same applies accordingly to the noble beings of the two vehicles within the lands of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Although ordinary beings and bodhisattvas have not yet permanently severed [the afflictions],
their suppression of active manifestations is also termed "beneficial gathering.
For those prior to the [first] bhūmi, this is called "diminishing power and augmenting capacity."
Because they are able to transform the path,
these various stages gradually subdue the two obstacles through the forty mental states of analytical discernment.
Within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) of the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), one can suddenly suppress and exhaust [the afflictions].
That which is called "comprehensive benefit" refers to the sudden severance [of these] in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
As for the two innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*), they are gradually suppressed within the path of preparation.
The ten stages can gradually eliminate these afflictions as appropriate;
from the first stage upward, they can suppress them all at once.
Therefore, it is called "gathering and benefiting."
The seventh fearlessness is that which possesses internal benefit and is free from external fear.
Regarding the Dharma-nature body and its lands, the bodies of self-enjoyment and others' enjoyment, as well as the transformation body,
he has long been fearless.
As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
One remains far removed from all māras.
A māra refers to the four māras,
which are the causes of fear.
Because these [factors] give rise to various fears,
and because the Buddha is entirely devoid of them, he is without fear.
This refers to the Land of Enjoyment for Others.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are free from the four coarse māras and lack the five fears:
those of afflictions, the aggregates, and death.
The stages of gradual severance should be explained according to their respective applications;
their meaning is thus understandable.
Within the transformation lands (nirmāṇakāya-bhūmi):
The noble beings of the three vehicles are likewise able to abandon [afflictions].
Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (daśabhūmi) achieve the path through the eight phases (aṣṭamārga) and are able to subdue the celestial Māras;
even within the stage of the preparatory path (prayogamārga), they are able to suppress afflictions of conceptual discrimination (vikalpakleśa).
One is free from the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*),
because within the fourth stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmakulīnabhūmi*),
one abandons birth and death and emerges from the triple world (*tridhātu*).
One separates from the Māra of death;
upon entering the first bhūmi, one separates from the death of segmented existence,
which is also called separating from the Māra of the five aggregates.
Therefore, there is fearlessness.
Regarding the eighth path of practice,
the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
Great mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct serve as the path for his wandering.
Regarding this, the commentary explains:
"The great mindfulness of the Tathāgatas is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)."
Because one abides in the principle of suchness through mindfulness,
non-conceptual wisdom serves as the path traversed by the *dharmatā*-realm;
"great wisdom" (*mahāmatis*) refers precisely to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Because they differentiate the ultimate and conventional characteristics of all phenomena,
they serve as the paths for the two types of enjoyment and transformation bodies.
Since both possess the sovereign karmic function of constructing pure lands, they are both termed "conduct" (*caryā*).
Because they both lead to birth in the Pure Land, they are equally called "paths.
Alternatively, the practice of great mindfulness is a practice for one's own benefit,
because it is internally comprised within [the category of] recollection.
This is the land of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-kṣetra*) and the path of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*).
O Mahāmati, this is the practice for the benefit of others,
because it is free from external conceptualization.
This refers to the paths of the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
Having already explained the Buddhas above,
[we now discuss] the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Great mindfulness is the wisdom arising from hearing;
great wisdom is the wisdom arising from reflection;
and great practice is the wisdom arising from cultivation.
These three types of wisdom, according to their respective suitability, mutually support one another through the relationship of being either proximate or remote,
serving as the paths for both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) stages;
for all three types of wisdom penetrate both the outflowing and non-outflowing realms.
In the case of the transformation lands,
even those of the three vehicles prior to the [first] bhūmi take the three types of wisdom as their path of travel; furthermore,
the wisdom of cultivation of the two vehicles also includes the untainted (anāsrava).
For ordinary beings and bodhisattvas, only that which is with outflows serves as their path of travel.
As for "that which is mounted upon in the ninth [stage]," it refers to riding that vehicle to traverse this path.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"Great tranquility (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*) serve as the vehicle.
Here, "tranquility" refers to *samādhi*, which is meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*).
"Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because calm abiding (*śamatha*) and contemplation proceed in equilibrium, it is called "that which is mounted.
"Path" (*mārga*) is the general designation for the stages.
Within the state of cessation, one contemplates the distinct names of that which is mounted.
The three bodies of the Buddha constantly mount these and enter the three Buddha-fields;
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages mount these and enter the land of other-enjoyment.
Those of the two vehicles prior to the stages likewise mount this vehicle of śamatha and vipaśyanā according to their capacity to enter the pure lands.
If they transform impure lands,
they universally employ both distraction and meditative concentration, as well as wisdom, as their vehicle.
Otherwise, there would be no basis for being born in a Buddha-field.
Regarding the tenth entrance-gate:
it is so called because one proceeds from that entrance-gate to enter this one.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"The gates of entry are the liberations of great emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Liberation is nirvāṇa."
Because of this sublime wisdom, it is called a "gate.
Alternatively, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is also called "liberation" (*vimukti*),
because it is free from bondage.
Therefore, one enters the Pure Land by means of these three gates.
To state one meaning: by means of the gate of signlessness (*animitta*), one enters the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
By contemplating that phenomena are signless, one realizes suchness;
by means of the gate of wishlessness, one enters the self-enjoyment realm,
for within the triple world there is no longer any wishing or seeking.
By means of the gate of great emptiness, one enters the *parabhogika* (enjoyment for others) and *nirmāṇa* (transformation) lands;
this is because one realizes the non-existence of the two selves and thus has no entry into the two lands.
Alternatively, it is said that all three gates enter the three types of Buddha-lands.
The treatise explains that one contemplates the three natures either through each gate individually,
or because all [three gates] are capable of contemplating the three natures.
This explains the Buddha-gate.
If bodhisattvas enter the Land of Enjoyment for Others by means of these three types of untainted gates,
and if the two vehicles prior to the stages likewise do so by means of the three untainted [gates].
Alternatively, there are those with outflows who enter the transformation land;
ordinary beings and bodhisattvas enter the transformation land solely by means of these three types of samādhi with outflows.
It is not called a gate of liberation because it is not subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*). In reality, however, this is the case.
The enjoyment lands (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation lands (*nirmāṇakāya*),
which include the gateways of the path for traveling by means of the vehicle of phenomena (*dharmayāna*),
are taught in terms of practice in order to inspire sentient beings toward genuine virtues.
The nature-realm body (*dharmatā-kāya*) and the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*) are both immeasurable in extent;
it is not said that they possess distinct features such as gates or other characteristics, whereas the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*) does indeed have limitations.
All are established upon lotus flowers.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"It is established upon a great jewel lotus."
The *Contemplation Sūtra* also speaks of forming the visualization of a suspended drum,
upon which there is a lotus seat; thus,
the transformed land is not fixed.
"Whether it exists or not":

based on this, since there are no lotus flowers in this Buddha-field [of Akṣobhya], the *Dharmaparyāya-vana-artha-kāṇḍa* (Chapter on the Forest of Meanings in the Garden of the Mahāyāna), Fascicle Seven, was completed with the addition of punctuation on the sixth day of the fifth month of the tenth year of Tenmon, the *kōshin* year; the work was finished at the hour of Wei.
Following the completion of the decree issued from the residence of the Chief Abbot (Sōjō) Kanji,

this one scroll concerning the matter of the granting and withholding of the rank of Gokō by the five masters, including Kakushō, regarding all other extant copies, has been submitted and returned after the full circumstances of its attainment were reported.
Recorded on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the twelfth year of Tenpō (1742), the year Kiei (癸卯), by the former Great Archbishop (Daisōjō) Kaneki.
On the day of the tenth month of the twelfth year of Kōbun (1672), the year Jinushi (壬子), the repairs were completed.

On a day in the first month of the seventh year of the Enpō era (the *Ren’in* year), I, Seikan Hōin, have respectfully finished reading the *Kun-gyō kai* (Explanatory Precepts) in its entirety, sixteen volumes. Recorded on the fourteenth day.
